<meta>This page follows the table of contents and begins the formal dedication of the volume. It is the start of the biographical preface written by Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (the nephew of the philosopher) to Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan.</meta>

Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to Ludovico Maria Sforza, Visconti-Anglus, <note>The term "Anglus" refers to a claim of the Sforza and Visconti families to be descended from a legendary Trojan companion of Aeneas named Anglus, a common piece of Renaissance genealogical myth-making.</note> Duke of the Milanese. Greetings.

Those who have handed down the lives of illustrious men, most illustrious Prince, recorded in writing for the readings of posterity, have done so with different aims. Some acted so that the names of those to whom they were bound—whether by the ties of blood or by a debt of shared discipline—would not fade away through the voracity of antiquity, but would instead be utterly vindicated from the injury of oblivion. This was the kind of devotion <note>original: "pietatis". In Latin, "pietas" refers to the duty and respect owed to family, teachers, and gods.</note> that Pliny the Younger showed to his uncle Pliny, and Porphyry showed to his teacher Plotinus. <note>Pliny the Younger (61–113 AD) documented his uncle’s scholarly life; Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was the student and biographer of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus.</note>

Others, however, have performed this very task with an even more favorable purpose: namely, that they might look not so much to the eternal memory of the deceased as to the shaping of the lives of those surviving. Therefore, we find that Jerome recorded the tireless studies, most exact morals, and most distinguished works of Hilarion; Athanasius did the same for Anthony; Sulpicius Severus for Martin; and Paulinus for Ambrose. <note>This list refers to famous biographies of saints: St. Hilarion by St. Jerome; St. Anthony the Great by Athanasius of Alexandria; St. Martin of Tours by Sulpicius Severus; and St. Ambrose of Milan by Paulinus the Deacon.</note> From these accounts, the glory of God has spread throughout the world, and even now men are spurred toward living a good and blessed life by both their teachings and their conduct. Enticed by these examples, I thought I would be performing a worthwhile task if—

<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication to the opening of the biography itself. Giovanni Francesco Pico begins by asserting his objectivity as a biographer despite being the nephew of the subject, before detailing the family lineage and the miraculous circumstances of Giovanni Pico's birth in 1463.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN MOST CONSUMMATE IN EVERY BRANCH OF KNOWLEDGE, PUBLISHED BY GIOVANNI FRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE GALEOTTO PICO.

<note>Rectangular stamp: Royal Library of Munich</note> As I begin to write the life of Giovanni Pico, my paternal uncle, I consider it essential to first declare to my readers—lest they suspect I might speak out of favor, in the manner of flatterers, because I was either his brother's son or his pupil—that nothing here has been granted to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing has been repaid in fictitious praise for the benefits which were indeed very great toward me. My narrative is as far removed from adulation as the necessity for flattering was absent. I have taken great care that those reading should not think me either lying or excessive in my praise. Indeed, if I had committed to writing everything I had begun to learn about him, there might perhaps have been a risk that his own lofty virtues, or those who defend them, could accuse me of being too sparse in my account. This may be seen from this very evidence: many of the most learned men of our age, and indeed the foremost among them, have provided most abundant testimony in their scholarly writings, not only to the things we are about to say, but also—both while he enjoyed this light of life and after he exchanged it for a better one—have excelled me in their public praises of his character and learning. I have ordered some of these praises to be added at the end of this book, after his own commentaries, so that a firmer faith might be placed in witnesses who are not of his own kin.

<margin>Paternal lineage</margin> <margin><note>original: "picus pnepos cōstantinj"</note> Pico, great-grandson of Constantine</margin> Leaving aside the paternal lineage (although it is recorded in memory to have drawn its origins from the Emperor Constantine through his great-grandson Pico, from whom the surname of the entire family is derived), we shall take our beginning from the time of his birth itself. This is because he perhaps conferred no less honor upon the family than he received from it, and because I have judged it right to reveal his personal gifts of mind and the remaining sequence of his whole life and death, which I have either drawn from my own ears or eyes, or received from most reliable witnesses.

Setting aside the family tree and the famous deeds of his ancestors, his birth is to be recorded in the <term>year of the Virgin's childbed</term> <note>A traditional way of dating from the birth of Christ.</note> 1463, while the holy Pius II presided over the Church as Supreme Pontiff and Frederick III held the reins of the Roman Empire. <margin>Mother Julia</margin> <margin>Giovanni Francesco the father</margin> <margin>Galeotto and Antonio Maria, brothers</margin> <margin>Sisters</margin> <margin>Alberto Pio</margin> His mother Julia, from the noble Boiardo family, bore him to his father Giovanni Francesco as her final child. She had already given birth to Galeotto (the eldest, from whom I was born), Antonio Maria, and two sisters. One of these, having married Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio, one of the princes of Carpi, and is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other married Pino Ordelaffi, prince of Forlì; after his death some time ago, she was granted a second marriage to the Count of Monteagano.

<margin>The Omen</margin> A no small omen appeared before his birth. For a circular flame was seen to stand over the chamber of the mother in labor and soon vanished; perhaps it was suggesting to us that he would be most similar to a circular figure in the perfection of his intellect—he who was brought forth among mortals at that same hour...

<margin>Ambrose</margin>

<margin>Paulinus</margin>

<margin>Appearance and physical build.</margin>

<margin>Progress in humanities at a tender age</margin>

<margin>A swift mind</margin>

<margin>Very quick minds are rarely strong in memory <note>Handwritten in red ink.</note></margin>

<margin>As a boy, he mastered canon law.</margin>

...and throughout the entire globe of the earth, the excellence of his name was to be celebrated everywhere. His mind, like a fire, would always seek celestial things, and his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his flaming mind, would one day celebrate with all its might our God—who is a consuming fire. But we read that he vanished from the sight of men just as suddenly. Indeed, we are taught by the most learned men that the births of even the holiest of men have sometimes been preceded or followed by unusual signs, as if the divine will were setting their infancy apart from the company of others, indicating they were born for the greatest deeds. Thus, to omit the others, a swarm of bees grazed upon the mouth of the great Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note>; they entered it and then, exiting and flying very high, they hid themselves among the clouds, eluding the gaze of his father and the others present. Paulinus <note>Paulinus of Milan, who wrote the Life of St. Ambrose.</note>, the writer of his life, made much of this omen, explaining that the honeycombs signified the celestial gifts he would proclaim, which would lift the minds of men from the earth to heaven.

As for his appearance, he was of remarkable and noble form: a tall and lofty stature, of soft flesh, and a generally charming face. His complexion was white, interspersed with a becoming redness; his eyes were greyish and watchful, his hair blond and natural. His teeth were also white and even. Sent to masters and disciplines under his mother’s authority, he cultivated the studies of the humanities with such an ardent spirit that he was soon—and not without merit—to be ranked among the chief poets and orators of that time. He was indeed very swift in learning, endowed with such a ready intellect that he could recite poems heard once from a reader in both direct and backward order to the great wonder of all. He retained them with a most tenacious memory, which is often the opposite for others; for it is often natural for those with a quick wit not to be strong in memory, while those who perceive with labor turn out to be more tenacious in what they have grasped.

When he was fourteen years old, at the command of his mother—who strongly desired him to be initiated into sacred orders—he moved to Bologna for the study of canon law <note>original: "ius pontificium"</note>. After tasting it for two years and seeing that it relied on mere traditions, he turned elsewhere—though not without producing good fruit. For even as a boy, and a tender one at that, he compiled a certain epitome or breviary from the letters of the High Pontiffs (which they call Decretals), in which he summarized all the judgments of those decrees as concisely as possible. This was no small task even for seasoned professors. 

But as a curious explorer of the secret natures of things, leaving these well-trodden paths, he dedicated himself entirely to the speculation of the intellect and to philosophy, both human and divine. To acquire this knowledge, he traversed the literary schools <note>original: "gymnasia"</note> not only of Italy but also of France, most scrupulously seeking out the famous doctors of that age in the manner of Plato and Apollonius. He devoted such tireless effort to those studies that he was, and was considered to be, both a consummate theologian and a philosopher while still beardless. He had already spent seven years among them when—eager for human praise and glory, for he had not yet been warmed by divine love, as will become clear—he moved to Rome, and there he showed...

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>Continuing the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page discussed his physical beauty and his transition from the study of law to deep philosophical inquiry. This page details his arrival in Rome, the publication of his 900 theses, and the beginning of the theological opposition against him.</meta>

...wishing to show how much envy would later await him from his inferiors, he proposed nine hundred questions <margin>Nine hundred questions</margin> on logic, mathematics, and natural and divine matters. These were drawn not only from Latin stores, but also excerpted from Greek archives, unearthed from the mysteries of the Hebrews, and tracked down from the secrets of the Chaldeans <margin>Conclusions to be debated, proposed at Rome</margin> and the Arabs. 

Likewise, he included many things from the ancient and obscure philosophy of Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the "Hermetic" corpus of philosophy and magic was attributed.</note>, and Orpheus. He also included much concerning the **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: A school of thought in Jewish mysticism; Pico was one of the first to attempt to harmonize it with Christian theology.</term>, which is the secret reception of Hebrew doctrines. Origen <margin>Origen</margin> and Hilary <margin>Hilary</margin> <note>Origen (c. 184–253) and Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367) were prominent early Church Fathers.</note> among our own writers particularly recalled this. He wove into those questions much concerning **natural magic**, which he taught should be separated by a significant gap from that which is impious and wicked. 

This he proved most elegantly by the testimony of many. Nor were there lacking seventy-two new physical and metaphysical doctrines—his own inventions and meditations—adapted to elucidate any philosophical questions. To these, he annexed a new system of philosophizing through numbers. He posted all of these at once in public places so they might be more easily publicized, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who traveled to Rome from distant lands for the sake of debating them. 

But due to the animosity of detractors (which, like fire, always seeks high places), he could never arrange for a day for the debate to be set. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year. During this time, those fault-finders did not dare to attack him openly or in a free examination. Instead, corrupted by pestilential envy, they attempted to revile him with tricks and snares, and to undermine him with hidden weapons. 

(For this was the opinion of most.) It was estimated that they were driven to this spite for this reason: many who had long applied themselves to literary business—perhaps out of ambition or greed—thought it would be a mark against them <margin>Envy <unclear>with</unclear></margin> if that young man, abounding in the wealth of his ancestors and great learning—like a lush, fertile field—did not fear to test his learning and genius in the foremost city of the world regarding natural and divine things, and many matters inaccessible to our people for several centuries. 

And when they realized they could achieve nothing against his doctrine by true means, they brought forward the torments of calumny, shouting that thirteen of the nine hundred questions were suspected of being contrary to the true faith. To these detractors, some joined themselves who attacked those questions—since they were unfamiliar to their ears—perhaps as much out of a lack of learning as out of piety, using the zeal for faith and the pretext of religion as an excuse. 

Yet many celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved these same questions as pious and pure, and had signed their names to them. Among their number was counted Bonfrancesco, Bishop of Reggio <margin>Bonfrancesco</margin> <margin>Bishop of Reggio</margin> <margin>Bishop</margin>, a man distinguished by every kind of learning, the sharpest judgment, and gravity of character. At that time, he was serving in Rome as the legate to the Pope on behalf of the Duke of Ferrara. Nevertheless, those babblers attempted nothing against him, since perhaps they felt his reputation could not be undermined by them.

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>Continuing the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page described Pico’s arrival in Rome and his proposal of 900 theses for public debate, covering diverse fields from logic to Kabbalah and natural magic.</meta>

...they should have shown reverence, since whatever he treated he had submitted to the correction of mother church and the Pope. But he, not enduring this loss of his reputation, published an **Apology** <margin>Apology</margin>; a work of great variety and elegance, filled with knowledge of many things worth knowing, and composed by the burning of the midnight oil over only twenty nights <note>Pico’s claim that he wrote the *Apologia* in just twenty days was intended to demonstrate his intellectual fluency and the divine favor he felt he possessed.</note>. By this publication, it was granted to be seen clearer than light: it was not so much that his conclusions could not bear Catholic interpretations, as that those who had previously barked <note>original: *adlatrauerant*. The author uses the imagery of barking dogs to characterize Pico’s theological critics as irrational or instinctively hostile.</note> against them were to be convicted of insolence and ignorance. 

He submitted the book itself, and whatever he might write in the future, to the judgment of mother church and her most holy leader, in the manner of a most Christian man. For he was most firmly persuaded that this ought to be done either explicitly or implicitly, as if he were quoting that saying of Augustine: "I may err, but I cannot be a heretic" <note>original: *Errare possum hereticus esse non possum*. This famous distinction suggests that intellectual mistakes are part of human nature, whereas heresy requires a "perverse and obstinate will" to persist in error against the Church.</note>, since the one is a human trait, the other belongs to a perverse and obstinate <margin>Pope Innocent VIII</margin> will.

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>Continuing the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, following the discussion of his Apology and his submission to the authority of the Church. This page marks the turning point in Pico’s life, where his intellectual focus shifts from secular philosophy and youthful poetry to a total devotion to sacred studies and Christian piety.</meta>

...the first beam of divine light had shone upon him, it showed how much he had changed from the man he had been before.

For it seems that all the remaining works which he wrote afterward—though they are various and diverse—nevertheless flow from this single source and spring, as it were.

He committed five books of elegiac verse, in which as a younger man he had sung of the levity of his youthful loves, to the flames for the sake of religion. In the same way, he had composed many playful pieces in Tuscan rhymes <note>original: *Rhythmis hetruſcis*. This refers to Italian vernacular poetry, such as sonnets or lyrics, which were common among Renaissance courtiers but which Pico later viewed as frivolous compared to divine study.</note>, which a similar fire consumed for that same cause. Then, with a most ardent zeal, he turned to Sacred Scripture, <margin>Sacred Letters</margin> and he devoted himself to it so entirely that he seemed to be consumed by it. He also began to distribute his wealth to the poor, and of his great family inheritance, he kept back scarcely a quarter <note>original: *quadrans*. A term for a small Roman coin, used here metaphorically to indicate that he retained only a tiny fraction of his former estate.</note>.

Which thing he did, however, not out of a desire for human praise or to appear holy, but so that he might more easily follow the footsteps of Christ, his leader, and that he might not be hindered by the weight of earthly things in his journey toward the heavenly home.

As soon as he was freed from these worldly cares and burdens, he began to live a life that was more like that of a monk than a nobleman. He spent his days in prayer and his nights in the study of the most profound mysteries of the faith, seeking to use his vast knowledge of languages and philosophy solely for the explanation of the divine word.

[Marginal notes:]
<margin>The eloquence of the ancient law</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Septimius <note>Tertullian</note></margin>
<margin>Eusebius</margin>
<margin>Cassiodorus</margin>

<margin>The booklet *On Being and the One*</margin>

<margin>Note</margin>

<margin>Antonio of Faenza</margin>

<margin>Some Platonic matters</margin>

[Main text:]
...said that eloquence excelled in the writings of everyone, specifically citing the late-night labors of Cicero himself and Demosthenes, whom he called (as they say) the primary masters of the art of speaking. This was not because their works were, so to speak, scorched with curling irons <note>original: *calamiſtris inuſtæ*. A metaphor for an overly ornate or artificial rhetorical style, comparing it to hair that has been artificially curled with hot irons.</note> or smeared everywhere with coral pigments and crowded with ringlets, but so that they might smell and taste of a true and solid eloquence, supported by true sentiments and true art. They were, to put it briefly, not filled by accident with the wealth of the Egyptians. <note>original: *egyptiorum opibus*. This refers to the "Spoiling of the Egyptians" (Exodus 12:35-36), a common theological metaphor used by Augustine and others for taking the "gold" of pagan philosophy and using it for Christian truth.</note> | Furthermore, he proclaimed that all the utterances of the ancient law <note>The Old Testament.</note> were full of the most consummate knowledge and wisdom. Even if others—especially Augustine in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, as well as Septimius Tertullian, Eusebius Pamphili, and Cassiodorus—clearly showed and affirmed that the grammarians, rhetoricians, orators, and all the ancient philosophers had drunk the streams of their eloquence and learning from the fountains of the Divine Scriptures, he himself pursued this with innumerable other reasons. It is worth the effort to see a part of these in the introductions to the most celebrated *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s work providing a sevenfold interpretation of the six days of Genesis, attempting to reconcile the creation story with Greek philosophy.</note> and in the preface of the second exposition itself. Amidst so many ongoing examinations of the divine law, in the second year after the publication of the *Heptaplus*, he completed a small work titled *On Being and the One*, divided into ten chapters. It is brief in body but great in strength, filled everywhere with the deepest doctrines of the philosophers and with theological insights. In this work, he shows that "being" is not superior to "the one," but that they correspond to each other and are equal in scope. He reviewed the controversy held on this subject by the followers of Plato and Aristotle, asserting that those Academics who contended for the opposite had not grasped the true doctrine of Plato. He was prepared to demonstrate that there was no lack of a total commonality of meaning between Aristotle and Plato regarding "the one" and "being"—just as with other matters—even if their words seemed to disagree. | In the final chapter of the work, he turned the entire disputation toward the instruction of life and the improvement of morals, with no less ingenuity than piety. Against this work, Antonio of Faenza, <note>Antonio Trombetta (1436–1517), a Franciscan theologian and professor at Padua who famously disputed Pico’s attempt to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note> otherwise an excellent philosopher, brought forth some objections in four letters. Giovanni himself responded to three of them, but as for the fourth—either because it was not accurately delivered, or because he thought it could be answered based on what he had already written, or for some other reason which must be believed to be just—he made no mention of it as far as I know. After he departed this life, we <note>Likely Gianfrancesco Pico, the author of this biography and Giovanni's nephew.</note> ourselves took up the duty of responding, so that no opportunity would be given to the malevolent for false barking, nor to the unrefined for believing something sinister. We took the greatest care to show that he had, for the most part, already responded through his preceding opinions. | We also saw some Platonic matters composed by him in the vernacular tongue, <note>Italian (Tuscan), as opposed to the scholarly Latin.</note> in which many things serving to untie the knots of ancient theology are found, along with many things hidden in enigmas and riddles that recall the insights of the wise. Perhaps, having obtained greater leisure, we will attempt to translate these into Latin, lest the surpassing learning of such a man regarding these matters—which is very accessible to everyone—be carried before the eyes of the common people. <note>The author worries that Pico’s deep philosophical insights, if left in the common Italian tongue, might be misunderstood or cheapened by the general public who lacked the proper training to interpret them.</note>

[Marginal note 1:]
<margin>The Old Testament interpreted</margin>

[Marginal note 2:]
<margin>A booklet on the truth of Jerome’s translation</margin>

[Marginal note 3:]
<margin>A booklet on the true calculation of time</margin>

[Handwritten note in red ink:]
<margin>The seven enemies of the Christian faith</margin>

[Main Text]:

Thus far we have spoken of the completed late-night labors <note>original: *lucubrationibus*. This refers to scholarly works produced by the light of a lamp during the night, symbolizing intense intellectual dedication.</note> which he had published before his death, like messengers and precursors to the magnificent works he had conceived and was even then forging. For he had already illuminated the Old Testament with the torches of interpretation, and was girding himself to perform the same service for the New. Nor had he brought forth only those meanings which the literal sequence of the text could carry; rather, in those places where it was appropriate, he built upon them the three other senses belonging to the divine word. <note>In medieval theology, the "fourfold sense of Scripture" included the literal, allegorical (symbolic), tropological (moral), and anagogical (heavenly) meanings.</note> He also compared the differing passages in our own manuscripts with the Greek and Hebrew originals. But this sat most prominently in his mind—this was more deeply rooted than all the other projects he had conceived in the genre of commentary—that he would not merely cite the dogmas of others (since these were already available, read, and known), but would instead set forth his own discoveries and meditations. In this way, he hoped to satisfy hungry souls seeking the truth to the best of his ability through his own resources, rather than those of others.

After this, being proficient in the Hebrew tongue, he published a small book on the truth of Jerome’s translation <note>The Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible translated by St. Jerome in the 4th century.</note> against the slanders of the Jews. He also wrote a defense for the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> regarding the Psalms against those same critics. Likewise, he composed a booklet on the true calculation of time. <note>A work of chronology, attempting to align historical events with Biblical timelines.</note>

Finally, he had turned his mind to defeating the seven enemies of the Church. For whoever does not obey Christ or His Church is consequently His enemy: either as an impious person who accepts no creed to be believed; or as one who serves false idols and worships demons under the guise of these statues; or as one who observes the Mosaic Law after the ritual of the most abandoned Jews; or as one who follows the unspeakable Muhammad, enslaved to his detestable decrees; or as one who lives a Christian life in name and hearing only, but not in deeds and a sincere mind, thereby perverting the gospel teachings; or as one who, not consenting to the Catholic Church, kicks back with an obstinate heart <note>A reference to the "heretic."</note>; or, while receiving the Gospels, does so with a faith that is not pure, but rather adulterated and profaned by various superstitions; or, though he may have received the faith as solid, bright, and constant, he opposes it by his actions.

Therefore, he had summoned these seven—who are like captains under whom the rest are contained like common soldiers—to a confrontation, intending to fight them with their own weapons. Against the impious philosophers—who, weighed down by no yoke of religion and devoted to no deity, worship only natural reason—he fought with those same reasons. Against the Jews, he battled most powerfully using the declarations of the Old Testament and the specific authorities of the Jewish school. With the Muslims, he joined battle relying on the Quran. He had also prostrated the worshippers of idols with many wounds and no small force, as they were ensnared in vain superstitions. This was especially true for those who follow divinatory astrology; he had sharply rebuked them with both true philosophy and the specific logic of the astrologers themselves. He had already pursued their delusions in twelve books—quite polished ones—out of the thirteen destined for this purpose. Finally, he attacked hydromancy, geomancy, pyromancy, haruspicy, <note>Forms of divination using water, earth, fire, and the inspection of animal entrails, respectively.</note> and other vanities of that kind.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically detailing his systematic intellectual assault on the enemies of the Christian faith. It transitions from his general scriptural studies to his specific polemics against astrologers, heretics, and hypocritical believers, concluding with his grand project to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

<margin>Mad Orestes</margin> <note>original: *insanus horestes*. A classical reference to the Orestes of Greek tragedy, used proverbially to describe someone utterly devoid of reason; here, Pico applies it to those who follow the "insanity" of superstitious astrology.</note>

...explodes everything, point by point. But he had directed his battle-line <note>original: *cuneum*—a wedge-shaped military formation used to break enemy ranks</note> specifically against the prophesying astrologers, and had readied his battering ram with all his might. For when the other superstitions seek out supports for their errors in the futile and weightless dogmas of these men—either weighing the moments of a birth-chart <note>original: *geneseos*—referring to the calculation of a nativity or horoscope at the moment of birth</note> or in choosing hours, or arranging those aspects they call "benign," such as the hexagonal or the trigonal <note>In astrology, these are "sextile" (60°) and "trine" (120°) aspects, believed to bring good fortune.</note> and other things of this sort—not even a "Mad Orestes" would agree with them. | Nor was he content to have utterly overturned all of astrology; he wished to show the astrologers of our time (who are mostly ignorant of the Greek language) that astrology—the most vain of all professions—has been rendered even vainer, if such a thing can be said, by perverse translations. <margin>Ptolemy’s Centiloquium turned from Greek into Latin</margin> While writing against these men, as if performing a secondary task, he translated the *Fruits of Ptolemy*—commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>original: *Centiloquium*—a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms falsely attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy, widely used in the Middle Ages.</note>—from the Greek into the Latin tongue. He graced it with a most elegant explanation, in which book he demonstrates that more errors (if I may put it so) than words are contained in that common translation. Nevertheless, his ignorant followers always guarded that version among their secrets like a precious treasure. | Moreover, regarding those who hold false opinions about the Christian faith and do not obey the authority of Mother Church—whom we call by the customary name of "heretics"—he had attacked them with a new instrument <note>likely referring to his "900 Theses"</note> and with reasons in a distinguished rebuke. Nearly ninety heresies are commonly known; but he, having searched through everything, discovered two hundred. He intended not only to eliminate and drive these out one by one, but likewise to teach from which part of philosophy, when not rightly understood, they had drawn or "forked" their errors. | Finally, he had veered vehemently against those Christians whose faith is seen to be without works. He had diligently investigated how it could be that men believe there is a fire established in the very center of the earth, in which the bodies of the damned are to suffer perpetual punishment, along with other unimagined tortures of both soul and body—as well as the immense joys of the divine life with which souls joined to bodies are blessed—and yet they are not obedient to the dictates of the Church which compel them to believe. <margin>Note</margin> Instead, they run riot everywhere, sinking into vices and the accumulation of wealth; they fear nothing less than punishment, and desire nothing less than the kingdom of God. He also attempted to apply suitable aid according to the quality of the diseases: namely, to cauterize foul and naturally impure diseases with sharp and stinging medicines, but to soothe with gentle and placable treatments those wounds which were infected with less malice and depravity and which desired to be covered by a scar. For those who had regained their health but feared a relapse, he prepared most wholesome potions and celebrated antidotes. | He had begun many other works <margin>The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle</margin> by which it could be hoped that the study of philosophy would flourish everywhere, once errors were eliminated and barbarism exploded. | Among these, the most important was considered the **Harmony of Plato and Aristotle**, which he had already begun...

<meta>This page continues the description of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s intellectual mission. Having moved past his critique of astrology, the text now describes his ultimate goal: the "Concordia," or the reconciliation of all philosophical schools into a single, unified system of truth.</meta>

...which he would have brought to perfection, if life had remained his companion for just a few more years. For he had nourished philosophy from its very cradle <note>original: *incunabulis*—literally "swaddling clothes," referring to the very beginnings of human thought.</note> with suckling, and had led it forth as a fully grown adult even to our own times. He did this so that a philosopher of our current age would find nothing more to be desired: neither in the Greek, nor the Latin, nor even in the "barbarian" <note>original: *barbaris*. In Pico’s context, this refers to non-Classical sources, particularly the Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic texts he studied to find the "Prisca Theologia" or ancient theology.</note> manuscripts. Through his effort and grace, he would have summoned the "watery" Thales <note>Thales of Miletus, who believed water was the primary substance of the universe.</note>, the "fiery" Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus, who identified fire as the fundamental principle.</note>, and Democritus surrounded by his atoms; Orpheus likewise, and Pythagoras, and other ancients would have convened together in the Academy <note>A reference to the Platonic Academy, representing the harmonious gathering of all schools of wisdom.</note>.

|Finally, the princes of philosophy—namely, Plato, who is enveloped in the veils of myths and mathematical coverings, and Aristotle, fortified by his theories of motion—would have clasped right hands and sworn an oath of future friendship.| <note>This refers to Pico’s famous project to prove that Plato and Aristotle were in fundamental agreement despite their different terminologies.</note> He would have also secured a truce in many matters—if not a universal peace—between Averroes and Avicenna <note>The two most influential Islamic philosophers in the Latin West.</note>, and between Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, representing the Dominican school of thought.</note> and Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, representing the Franciscan school of thought.</note>, who had long been in conflict. For in many of their controversies, if someone were to examine the words of disagreement more attentively, weigh them more precisely, and more scrupulously...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s literary remains and a detailed analysis of his rhetorical style. ...interpretation of the Lord’s Prayer alone. And about fifty rules for living well, which were certainly too brief and unexplained; if he had lived, he would have expanded them into many chapters. He had also composed two prayers to God, one in Italian rhymes <note>original: *rhithmis hetruſcis*—referring to the Tuscan dialect, which became the basis for standard Italian.</note> and the other in elegiac meter, so that he might soothe his mind, exhausted by weightier studies, by singing to the lyre. <margin>Cultivated music</margin> For in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised, and the harmonies noted with proper chords, were held in high renown. We have also seen many things in his desks, though they are unorganized, from which I believe something useful could be compiled, especially a commentary on the Psalms. <margin>Multiform letters</margin> Moreover, about fifty letters published at different times emerged: some personal, some scholarly, and some exhortatory, together with the oration <note>This refers to the *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, intended as an introduction to his 900 theses.</note> he would have delivered in Rome if the debate had taken place. This oration reflects not only the most perceptive genius and abundant learning of a young man not yet twenty-four (as all his writings do), but it also offers us the wealthiest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. <margin>A proven style of speaking</margin> He always used a style that was highly commendable—not borrowed, but natural, and multiform according to the variety of subjects. Although it might be said he consumed the entire "perfume box" <note>original: *myrothecion*—a Greek rhetorical term for a collection of polished ornaments.</note> of Isocrates, he nevertheless preserved the purity and the ornaments of majestic decorum. <margin>Styles of speaking</margin> For those celebrated styles of speaking—of which Aulus Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered without effort from his commentaries. <margin>Copious and brief</margin> There is the "copious" style in which Cicero is said to dominate, and the "brief" style ascribed to Sallust. <margin>Dry, flowery, and rich</margin> There is the "dry" style given to Fronto, and the "rich and flowery" style in which Pliny and Symmachus were said to have indulged. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this "copiousness" weak <note>original: *elumbem*—literally "lacking loins," meaning feeble or spineless.</note>, nor would Sallust have called it immoderate. A righteous judge would easily perceive that Fronto’s "dryness" was moistened, Sallust’s "brevity" extended, and Pliny’s "flowers and richness" carried into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy, perhaps without that provincial "Paduanism" <note>original: *patauinitate*—a famous criticism by Asinius Pollio regarding Livy's local dialect.</note>, with many little flowers of Apuleius added. Truly, he did not exercise himself here in philosophy borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>A reference to the *Noctes Atticae* of Aulus Gellius.</note>, nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>A reference to the work of Macrobius.</note> manufactured almost entirely to praise Virgil’s *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in mere natural history empty of the highest and most difficult contemplations. But rather, he labored over that admirable "fabric of the world," in attacking the enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, and he grew weary in eliminating the astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions, in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato, and devoted himself to explaining the sacred oracles. He spent his effort in advising and encouraging friends. But he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak, that he rather condemned those who, too scrupulously seeking "painted allurements," devoted all their mental powers to investigating the origins of words. All these...

<meta>This page continues the biography and intellectual profile of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his literary style to his voracious reading habits and his balanced respect for both Classical and Scholastic (medieval) authors.</meta>

...it turned many more toward admiration of him the more he had spent a long and very eager time among the writings of those who did not profess Latin letters filled with the flowers of eloquence. Let those who are too much in love with antiquity endure this with an even mind; for even if these things are written more concisely and briefly, they are perhaps more true, as men more learned than I—Ermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have related. He read through and excerpted extensive libraries of both Latin and Greek works with <margin>Speed of reading</margin> incredible speed; and he never passed over any commentaries (if the opportunity was given) without reading them. He had acquired such great knowledge of the ancient doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even in one who had spent his entire life solely in turning over their pages. Regarding the modern <note>original: *neotericis*—referring to the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages, who were "modern" compared to the Church Fathers.</note> theologians indeed, who used that style which is commonly called the "Parisian style" <note>The Scholastic method of rigorous logic and dialectic associated with the University of Paris, often criticized by Humanists for lacking classical beauty.</note>, such great judgment resided in him that if someone had unexpectedly asked for the unraveling of an abstruse and poorly explained question by any one of them, he would open it up with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that you would say he had all the sayings of that doctor before his eyes and ready for use. He had become familiar with all their works in the same way; he had examined every sheet, yet do not believe him to have been so addicted to any one of them (as is the custom among our people) that he despised the others. For he had been so instructed from a tender age, and so minded, that he sought the truth in them, and he would venerate the truth when found with equal honor as soon as it shone forth, stripped of any private affection. Nevertheless, what he thought of each of those who are considered more famous in general can be seen in the preface to his *Apology*, when he reported the properties and peculiar praises of the Barbarian, Greek, and Latin philosophers. He used to praise Thomas <margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin> Aquinas above all others whenever mention was made during conversation about these philosophers or theologians who wrote by debating in the French <note>original: *gallico*—another reference to the Scholastic style of Paris.</note> manner, as one leaning upon a more solid base for the battles of truth. He also calls him "the splendor of our theology" in his *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's 1489 work offering a sevenfold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis.</note>. When asked about this very frequently, even by me, he gave the same answer. Nor should certain things to be disputed, contained in his *Apology*, persuade anyone to the opposite—otherwise openly contradicting the opinions of Thomas—since he was then quite a young man, and eager for glory, seeking fame in that most celebrated city [Rome] in the manner of <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> Gorgias of Leontini <note>A Greek Sophist (c. 483–375 BCE) famous for his ability to argue any side of a debate and his claim to be able to answer any question.</note>, by defending any side. Add to this that out of ten thousand propositions, that he did not agree with only three or four, but rather opposed them, does not prove [a lack of respect]. Furthermore, he was most skilled in disputing, and he spent frequent and very intense effort on literary contests while his mind was fervent. In objecting, one could easily have detected the <margin>Scotus's sharpness</margin> sharpness and vigilance of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a premier Scholastic philosopher known as the "Subtle Doctor" for his complex logic.</note>, the stinging force of Francis <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes (c. 1288–1328), a follower of Scotus known for his rigorous debating style.</note>, and the abundance and <margin>Aureolus</margin> multitude of Aureolus <note>Peter Aureol (c. 1280–1322), a Scholastic theologian noted for his prolific and detailed writings.</note>; nor were those knots missing, complicated by many twists, nor supported by such tickling subtleties as by gravity in responding...

<margin>Ercole
d'Este</margin>

<margin>An Adage</margin>

<margin>The traps
of the sophists
and Swinesheadian
trifles</margin>

In him, one could see the strength and vigor of Thomas <note>original: *Thome*—referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the premier Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> and the immense breadth of Albert <note>original: *Alberti*—referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), known for his expansive knowledge of the natural sciences.</note>. Yet, he had long ago sent word that he was withdrawing from these public conflicts <note>Referring to the formal academic debates common in the Renaissance.</note>; and day by day he was more and more reluctant to take up that duty. He refused so consistently that even when Ercole d'Este, the Duke of Ferrara, asked most earnestly—both through messengers and in person—that he might not be loath to engage in a dispute while the General Synod of the Friar Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> was being held in Ferrara, he still resisted for a long time. Finally, however, yielding to many requests, he obliged that prince, for whom he felt a no small affection. From this event, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. Indeed, from the mouth of the debater, such cheerfulness of mind was always evident that he seemed to be discussing a pleasant and gentle matter rather than one that was sharp and difficult. For this reason, those listeners who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him. 

But he held a frequent adage: that such a display was the duty of a <term>dialectician</term> <note>One who focuses on the formal rules of logic and debate.</note>, not a philosopher. He likewise said that those disputes were beneficial which were carried out with a calm mind to track down and investigate the truth in private places, away from witnesses. But he believed those held in public were extremely harmful, as they were done to show off learning or to catch the breeze of the common people's favor and the applause of the unlearned. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which drives those "forehead-wandering" <note>original: *frontivagi*—likely referring to those who seek public attention or display their cleverness openly.</note> debaters—not to be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the opponent's disgrace and confusion; he saw this as a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to Christian charity. 

Absolutely nothing was hidden from him regarding the <term>traps</term> <note>original: *captiunculas*—logical fallacies or "gotcha" questions used in formal debates.</note> and cavils of the sophists, nor those "Swinesheadian trifles" <note>original: *suiseticas quilquilias*—a disparaging reference to Richard Swineshead, an Oxford "Calculator" whose complex logical-mathematical works were famously difficult and criticized by Humanists as uselessly subtle.</note> which are called "calculations." These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural speculations with thoughts that are perhaps more "morose" than they are subtle. Truly, even if he were learned in them and had read such writings—which perhaps Italy did not then know in full (for no path of literature could be found so trackless or inaccessible that he had not thoroughly explored it by his own tracks)—he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he noticed that their common use served only to bring infamy upon one's companions and to trip up the memory during a rebuttal; he believed they contributed nothing, or very little, to finding the truth, to which he thought one should devote tireless effort. 

But, lest I go on too long and detain the reader, I will summarize briefly. One man may shine in eloquence but be disgraced by an ignorance of the secrets of nature. Another may know foreign languages but lack mastery of the universal decrees of the philosophers. One man reads the discoveries of the ancients but composes no new doctrines. Another seeks knowledge only for the sake of men and human glory, rather than for the benefit of the Christian republic or for things divine and human. He, however, had embraced all these things with such equal zeal that they seemed to have flowed into him in crowds and heaps. He was not like many who, excelling in no single thing, merely participate in all...

It also details his disdain for overly technical "calculations" and logical puzzles, emphasizing his preference for the private pursuit of truth over public glory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, moving from his intellectual reputation in public debates to an analysis of his genius and his eventual renunciation of worldly power and wealth.</meta>

But he had progressed so far in all branches of knowledge that whichever of them you considered in him, you would have judged that he had chosen that one as his own and peculiar specialty. These things were all the more wonderful because he had attained them by the force of his own intellect and a love of truth, almost without a teacher, so that we might say of him what Epicurus used to say of himself: "That he was his own master." <note>original: *Se sibi ipm. s. fuisse magistrū* — This highlights Pico’s status as an "autodidact" or self-taught scholar, a point of great pride in Renaissance humanism.</note>

<margin>To which wonderful effects</margin>
<margin>Five causes</margin>
<margin>for such wonderful</margin>
I find that five causes combined to produce such wonderful effects in so short a span of time: an incredible genius, a most tenacious memory, ample means—by which he was aided in purchasing books in our own [Latin], Greek, and foreign <note>original: *barbaræ* — referring here to "barbarous" or non-classical languages like Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean, which Pico studied extensively.</note> languages (for I recall from memory that he spent seven thousand gold coins <note>original: *Septē aureorum nūmū milia* — a massive sum, equivalent to millions of dollars today, illustrating the immense cost of building a private library before the full impact of the printing press.</note> up to that day in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature for himself)—constant and indefatigable study, and finally, a contempt for earthly things. 

<margin>effects</margin>
<margin>Seven thousand gold coins spent in acquiring books</margin>

If, therefore, that ancient age of the Spartans <note>original: *laconū tempore* — referring to the Laconic Greeks, known for their austerity and wisdom.</note> had produced this man, he would have been called "divine" if we are to believe Aristotle. But the virtues of the intellect must now, I think, be set aside, and the noble parts of his soul which concern his actions must be followed. His most exacting character must be brought into public view, so that his soul, inflamed with love for God, may become known; so that his wealth, bestowed upon the needy, may be praised; and so that those who are finally devoted to the divine law may be provided with an abundant occasion to give thanks to the Author of all good things. 

Three years before he died, so that he might set aside the cares of ruling and live in deep peace, indifferent to where the scepter <note>The symbol of sovereign power over his ancestral lands.</note> might fall, he handed over all the patrimonies he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia—that is, a third part of them—to me, whether by gift or sale I know not. This act was later confirmed with imperial generosity by the August Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, who is our king and immediate lord (for we have recognized no other over so many centuries since Mirandola and Concordia were built, except for whoever sits successively upon the royal or imperial Roman throne). 

<margin>Distribution to the poor</margin>
Whatever money he received from this transaction he distributed partly to the poor and partly spent on purchasing lands from which he and his household might be sustained. Specifically, he had acquired for himself estates <note>original: *corbulas* — likely referring to the territory of Corbola in the region of Ferrara.</note> in the Ferrarese territory for many thousands of gold coins. He likewise distributed many silver vessels and pieces of precious furniture for the use of the poor. 

<margin>A modest table</margin>
He was content with a modest table, yet retaining a certain level of former elegance regarding the courses and silver vessels. Each day at the appointed hours he poured out prayers to God. He always gave money to any poor people he encountered; and not content with that, he entrusted Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico, who became a follower of the reformer Savonarola.</note>, a learned citizen of Florence whom he loved dearly for his great charity and integrity of character, to always assist the needy with his own money. He also provided dowries for young women to be married <note>original: *Nuptū quoque uirgines tradderet* — a common form of Renaissance charity to prevent impoverished women from falling into vice or being unable to marry due to lack of a dowry.</note>, and ordered that Benivieni should report to him immediately so that he could restore the spent coins as soon as possible. Indeed, he had delegated this duty to him so that he might more easily...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his intellectual pursuits to his private acts of charity and ascetic devotion. The author is likely his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, providing an eyewitness account of his uncle's character.</meta>

...as if to a faithful messenger, he was able to relieve the calamities and miseries of poor citizens which would have remained hidden from him. Perhaps considering that regarding the goods of the Church—the greatest part of which is owed to the poor by hereditary right—it was not fitting to maintain a magnificent display. Likewise, he kept before his eyes the examples of the holiest men—namely <margin>Ambrose</margin> Ambrose, <margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine, <margin>Martin</margin> Martin, and others—who fled from the dignity of the episcopate <note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note> when it was offered to them, and for a long time refused that office before they undertook it. 

Furthermore, he had read that the most holy <margin>Celestine</margin> Celestine had abdicated not only from the cardinalate itself, but even from the supreme power of the high papacy, and had shaken from his shoulders the burden of the entire Christian commonwealth. <note>Referring to Pope Celestine V, who famously resigned the papacy in 1294 to return to a hermit's life.</note> A burden, truly, for which the greatest reward is prepared for those who undergo it—namely for those who, being unwilling, embrace it only for the sake of obeying and helping. 

He was thoroughly convinced that for a philosopher, it was no matter of praise to have accumulated riches or to have sought honors, but rather to have refused them; and that by refusing shadow-like glory, one attains true glory, which always accompanies virtues like an inseparable companion and attendant. He <margin>Contemner of human glory</margin> held human glory as next to nothing, and said quite often that <margin>of human glory</margin> fame would benefit the living somewhat, but the dead not at all. We recognize that he valued his own learning only so much as it might contribute to the utility of the Church and to the elimination and rejection of opposing errors. 

Indeed, we perceived that he had reached such a goal of perfection that <margin>Note</margin> he cared little if his commentaries were published without his own name, provided that the very thing he would have done under the name of Pico brought benefit to men. He was least affected by other books, except for the Old and New Testaments, and he had decided to consume the remainder of his life in constantly turning their pages, unless public utility spurred him on. This was especially true when he saw that so many and such great things as he had conceived and labored over were not only being demanded by everyone everywhere, but were even being required before they were mature. 

He <margin>The institution of a truly Christian mind</margin> valued the smallest possible affection toward God from a devout person—whether a <margin>of a truly Christian mind</margin> little old man or a little old woman—more than all his own knowledge of human and divine things. He very frequently warned his close friends during conversation to notice how much mortal things struggle and falter, how fleeting and fluid is this life we live, and how firm and stable is that which we shall be in the future. Whether we are cast down to the depths or raised up to the heavens, he exhorted them to turn and incite their minds toward loving God, <margin>What to say about loving and knowing God in this life</margin> a work which would outweigh any <margin>judgment of love</margin> knowledge we could have in this life.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his refusal of titles to his personal virtues, specifically his preference for divine love over mere intellectual knowledge, his extreme indifference to wealth, and his moral influence on his companions.</meta>

In the body, we are capable of more than we can either express or know; by loving, we benefit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him more. Yet we always prefer to never find through knowledge what we seek, rather than to possess through loving that which, without love, would be found in vain. <margin>A saying that was frequently on his lips</margin> **That saying of Saint Francis—"A man knows as much as he works"—was also frequently on his lips.** <note>original: "Tantum scit homo quantum operatur." I remember when I was with him in Ferrara, a steward <note>original: "obsonatorem" — a person in charge of purchasing provisions, particularly food.</note> presented a small sheet and asked for his approval of the expenses. Furthermore, when his chief steward interrupted him to ask that he order an audit <note>original: "dispunctionem" — a formal checking or balancing of accounts.</note> of the money he had handled for many years, so that he might put his own mind at rest, and had brought the account books before him, we heard that he replied with these words: "I know that I could have been, and can be, cheated by you very often. Therefore, there is no need for a release of these expenses. If I owe you, I shall pay the coins as soon as possible; if you owe me, pay it now if you can, or in the future if you lack the means, settle the debts then."

<margin>Benevolence toward friends</margin> **He always treated his friends with great indulgence, using encouraging words to lead them toward living well.** I knew a man who, while speaking with him relying on his teaching and fame, and as the conversation turned to morals, was so moved by only two of his words that he abandoned the path of vice and reformed his character. <margin>Two most wholesome remedies against vice</margin> The words were of this sort: **"If we held before our eyes the death of Christ, suffered out of love for us, and reflected upon our own death from time to time, we would guard ourselves against vices."** <note>Though the text says "two words," it refers to these two central themes of meditation: Christ’s Passion and *Memento Mori* (remembering one's own death).</note> He showed admirable modesty and courtesy toward those whom he felt bound to himself, not because they were proven by strength or fortune, but by their loves and learning. <meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his life and intellectual habits to the specific circumstances of his early death and his pious conduct during his final illness.</meta>

<margin>In what year of his life he died</margin>
...in the year 1494 of our redemption. While he was completing the thirty-second year of his age and staying in Florence, he was seized by a most insidious fever. This fever spread so violently through his humors and internal organs that it resisted every kind of medicine applied to it, and within thirteen days, it compelled him to satisfy the debt of nature <note>original: "naturae satisfacere." A classical euphemism for dying, suggesting that death is a debt every living thing owes to the natural order.</note>. 

<margin>How he conducted himself during his illness</margin>
But as to how he conducted himself during his illness, although I was far away from him at that time, I shall nonetheless not hesitate to relate what I have received from the most reliable witnesses who were present. 

<margin>The praiseworthy end of a Christian man is recounted</margin>
What a moment it was when, after receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist, the image of the crucified Christ was offered to him! He was encouraged to take full drafts of love from it, in memory of that ineffable Passion endured for the sake of our salvation, before he breathed out his soul. This was intended as a most powerful defense against any adversity and a most strong bulwark against wicked demons. 

<margin>The image of God</margin>
An elder soon asked him whether he firmly believed that to be the true image of the true God and true man—who, as He is God, was begotten by God the Father before all time and eternity, equal to Him in all things; and who, with the Holy Spirit (who is also God, proceeding co-eternally from Him and the Father, which three are one), was conceived in time in the womb of Mary, ever virgin; who suffered hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and vigils; and who finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of Adam and to unlock the great gate of heaven through the immense charity with which He embraced the human race, poured out His most precious blood willingly and most freely on the altar of the cross. When asked if he believed these and other such things usually recounted, he replied that he not only believed them, but was **certain** of them.

<margin>Alberto Pio</margin>
<margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius, Averroes</margin>
And likewise, there is the account of what happened with **Alberto Pio**, his sister's son—whom we mentioned at the beginning of this life as a young man distinguished in intellect, the study of the liberal arts, and character. Alberto attempted to make the approach of death more peaceful for him, using the same reasoning by which **Alexander of Aphrodisias** and **Themistius** (in the prefaces to their commentaries on the *Physics* <note>original: "auscultatoriorum librorum." This refers to Aristotle's *Physica*, often called the "Lectures on Nature." These commentators argued that studying the laws of nature could provide the soul with the fortitude to face death without fear.</note>) declared that fortitude against the fear of death is drawn from physical contemplations—an opinion which **Averroes** soon adopted. Pico replied to Alberto in this manner: his mind was not calmed by that reasoning alone, nor were the torments of death set aside by it. Rather, he was at peace because an end was now being put to his offenses against his God; for he believed that a longer life would only result in more frequent offenses against the Divine. 

<margin>That the Queen of Heaven came to the sick man at night</margin>
Furthermore, he revealed to several most approved witnesses from the college of preachers, and to Alberto himself, that the **Queen of Heaven** <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> had come to him at night, fragrant with a wonderful scent. He claimed she refreshed all his limbs, which had been bruised and broken by that fever, and promised that he would not yield to [eternal] death at all. It was discovered that he had lain in his bed while ill with a cheerful and peaceful countenance. And even amid the stings of death which he sustained, he was accustomed to speak as if he saw the heavens opened to him. He greeted everyone, and when they offered their services (as is the custom), he responded with the gentlest...

<meta>This page continues the account following Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's death. It addresses the skepticism surrounding his purgatorial state and defends the possibility of divine revelations through the theology of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</meta>

I heard that someone who had been present at the sermon approached the preacher and, in order to give more strength to the things he had made public, reported that the deceased had appeared to him surrounded by fire, and was still suffering the punishment for his ingratitude. 

**Moreover, a certain nun, famous for many** prophecies, who had predicted many future events to him while he was alive—all of which came true exactly—offered this specific prophecy among others two years before he departed this life: that in the "time of the lilies," through the effort and encouragement of Friar Girolamo (of whom we have made mention), he would dedicate himself to the college of the Friars Preachers <note>The Dominicans, or Order of Preachers.</note>. And at that same time, a certain Florentine family (called the Pazzi <note>original: "pactiam." The Pazzi family were rivals of the Medici who had been exiled after the failed Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478.</note>), then living in exile, would return to their homeland. Many to whom this report had come were marvelling at this naming of the "lilies," thinking she was speaking of the springtime when lilies bloom. But it was discovered that this "Lily" was actually the King of the French <note>Charles VIII, whose royal emblem was the fleur-de-lis.</note>, who entered Florence with a great retinue while traveling through Tuscany to seize the Kingdom of Naples by force of arms. He arrived just the day before Pico would have made his religious profession—for so he had vowed before he died—and four days after that exiled family returned to their home city.

**But before** I reach the end, I think it useful to say a few more small things at the conclusion of this work. Indeed, I seem to see hounds <note>original: "molossos." A Molossian was a famous ancient breed of large guard dog.</note> barking at these revelations as if at the shadow of the moon. I must throw them a few more bones (since the previous ones perhaps did not satisfy them), lest they beat the air with their barking in vain. I also see laughter breaking out among the foolish; I see a mockery being made by those who consider themselves "know-it-alls" <term>know-it-alls: a translation of "sciolo," referring to those with superficial or pretentious knowledge.</term>. They will perhaps argue that souls ought not to be tortured by fire for an unfulfilled religious vow, or that in our time no men can be found who are inspired by the divine spirit or who enjoy conversations with Christ.

Yet if they considered that sins worthy of pardon—rather than death—must be punished by the fire of Purgatory, they would not marvel that even the just must pay a penalty. Likewise, if they were not ignorant of the fact that a servant who knows his master’s will but does not fulfill it "will be beaten with many stripes" (as Truth itself bears witness <note>A reference to Luke 12:47: "That servant who knows his master’s will and does not get ready or does not do what his master wants will be beaten with many blows."</note>), then they would realize that this man, who knew God’s will and delayed in fulfilling it, would have to suffer punishments even if he were free from all other faults. It would not be reported that he entered directly into ecstasy. 

On the other hand, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the crude and tasteless cunning of those who, while they believe that Christ died for mankind, do not believe that He can easily speak to those same men. They argue even more vehemently that mortal men cannot become sharers in the speech of the Virgin Mother, the angels, or the spirits of the blessed. They surely ought to observe that all lower things are governed by the higher, as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on the celestial hierarchy were highly influential in medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> testifies in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. There, we learn that minds of a lower grade and nature, to whom the care of men is entrusted, are illuminated by higher minds, which in turn draw divine mysteries from the highest spirits or from God Himself. Thus, men inspired by the divine spirit receive these revelations to be made known to the multitude of people when it is expedient. This is the sacred law of divinity, which we are taught by the same Dionysius in his book on the *Celestial Hierarchy*: that through the first things, the things that follow are raised up toward the most august light. Such critics are, without a doubt, ignorant of the divine scriptures...

<meta>This page concludes the biographical account of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, following the defense of his character and the prophecies concerning his death and spiritual state. It transitions from defending the validity of prophecies to a final commendation of his soul to God.</meta>

...of a persistent and stubborn mind. For in such instances it is granted to us to behold divine mysteries of the future, which are sometimes made known not only through good men, but even through wicked men and false prophets. What, then, prevents us from placing faith in this woman, who is empowered by both learning and so many virtues, and who predicted many future events that have now come to pass? Add that the philosophy of Aristotle <note>The author argues that even secular "Peripatetic" logic does not contradict these spiritual claims.</note> does not cry out against these things, and Platonic philosophy supports them—though I would not accept anything as grave testimony unless it were from the authority of Divine Scripture. Nevertheless, it is not absurd to cite these external sources occasionally, so that the arrows of the malevolent might return upon their authors with even greater force than that with which they were sent.

But we must now return to ourselves. We should not mourn so much that we have lost such a man, but rather we must give thanks to the King <note>Referring to God as the King of Heaven.</note>, to whom all things live, for what we have had and still possess. Indeed, having performed the duty of mortal life, and having long conversed with those dwelling in Kedar <note>original: "cedar." A biblical reference to Psalm 120:5, used here as a metaphor for the dark or sorrowful dwellings of the earthly world.</note>—whom he had drenched with no small light—he is now even now entering the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly homeland. There, he shall enjoy without end the ineffable divinity, and he shall continue to bring aid to us daily.

# THE SEVENFOLD EXPOSITION OF THE SEVENFOLD NARRATION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, ADDRESSED TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

### PROLOGUE

**M**Y RIVALRY WITH YOUR OWN STUDIES, Lorenzo de' Medici, moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses. Last winter, in what leisure was granted to you from the affairs of the Republic <note>original: "re.p." (res publica). Lorenzo was the effective ruler of Florence, and Pico notes that even in his busy political life, Lorenzo prioritized the study of scripture.</note>, I observed that you applied yourself to no labor more willingly than to that reading. Then, a private reason also invited me to this task: for some time now, another of my works has been growing under your auspices and in your name, in which I have attempted not only to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms of David.</note> translated by the Seventy <note>original: "LXX." Referring to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>—which resound continually in the Church—from every suspicion and calumny, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation. For that work, no treatment is found more useful, none more fruitful, and none more necessary than a study of those books of Moses. 

It happened, moreover, during these days, that I was diligent in studying the fabric of the world and those celebrated works of the six days. Great reasons offer themselves to make us believe that the secrets of all nature <margin>In the Genesis of Moses are the mysteries of all nature.</margin> are contained within them. For even if I set aside the fact that our prophet <note>Moses.</note>, being full of God and acting under the dictation of the heavenly spirit—the master of all truth—received all these things, do not the testimonies of our own people, his own people, and finally the gentiles, present him to us as most learned <margin>Moses was most learned by the testimony of all.</margin> in human wisdom and all doctrines and letters? 

There exists among the Hebrews a book by that Solomon, surnamed the Wisest, titled *Wisdom* <margin>The legitimate book of Solomon which is called Wisdom.</margin>—not the one now in common use, which is the work of Philo, but another composed in Jerusalem in what they call the more secret language <note>Referring to a Hebrew or Aramaic version, possibly a Kabbalistic text.</note>. In that book, the author, who is considered an interpreter of the nature of things, confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner chambers of the Mosaic law. 

There are also, as far as our people are concerned, both Luke and Philo, most weighty authors, who testify that Moses was most learned in the universal doctrine of the Egyptians. Moreover, all those Greeks who were held to be more divine—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—used the Egyptians as their teachers. That saying of Numenius the philosopher is well known: that Plato is nothing other than an "Attic Moses" <note>original: "atticum Moſem." Numenius of Apamea suggested that Plato’s philosophy was simply the wisdom of Moses expressed in the Greek (Attic) dialect.</note>. Furthermore, Hermippus the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. 

If, meanwhile, Moses appears in his books to be unpolished and popular <margin>Why Moses appears unpolished and popular.</margin> rather than a philosopher, a theologian, or a craftsman of some great wisdom, let us recall that it was a celebrated custom of the ancient sages <margin>The custom of the ancients in writing divine things.</margin> to write of divine things either not at all or in a concealed manner. Hence they are called "mysteries" <margin>Mysteries.</margin>, for they are not mysteries if they are not hidden. This was observed by the Indians, and by the Ethiopians who are named for their nakedness <margin>Gymnosophists.</margin> <note>The "Gymnosophists" or "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian or African ascetics.</note>, and by the Egyptians <margin>Egyptians.</margin>. This is also what those Sphinxes before the temples suggested <note>In the Renaissance, the Sphinx was viewed as a symbol of the silence and secrecy required for sacred knowledge.</note>. Instructed by them, Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras.</margin> became a master of silence; he himself committed nothing to writing except for a very few things which he commended to his daughter Damo as he was dying. For the *Golden Verses* <margin>Golden Verses.</margin> of Pythagoras that circulate are not his, as is commonly believed even by the more learned, but were written by Philolaus <margin>Philolaus.</margin>... <margin>Pythagoreans.</margin> <margin>Lysis.</margin> <margin>Hipparchus.</margin>

<margin>The second difficulty</margin>
For he <note>Referring to Moses as the author of Genesis.</note> neither should have, nor could he have, nor did he want to help the learned any less than the unlearned. The second difficulty is that the same thread of interpretation must be consistent with itself, fitting in its own right; the entire sequence should be led as if by a single path, so that it returns to that same meaning from which it first set out, as if mindful of its original purpose. <margin>How difficult it is to do what he undertakes</margin>
Such is the perplexity, such the ambiguity, and such the variety of the entire reading.
