<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s introduction to his Heptaplus. Having established the difficulty of interpreting Moses, he now moves into the core of his cosmological framework: the division of the universe into three distinct but interconnected "worlds," a concept central to Renaissance Neoplatonism.</meta>

->### ANOTHER PROLOGUE TO THE WHOLE WORK<-

Antiquity represents three worlds: the highest of all is the **ultramundane** <note>Literally "beyond-the-world," referring to the realm of pure spirits and divine ideas.</note>, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers call the intellectual; Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sung its praises worthily enough. Next to this is the **celestial** world, and the last of all is this **sublunary** <note>The region "under the moon," consisting of the Earth and the four elements, subject to change and decay.</note> world which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness, while that is the world of light; the heavens are tempered from both light and darkness. This world is marked by water as a flowing and unstable substance; that world by fire, through the brightness of light and the sublimity of its location. The heaven, being of a middle nature, is therefore called by the Hebrews *shamayim* <note>original: "sciamaim." Pico is using a traditional Hebrew etymology where the word for "heavens" (shamayim) is seen as a compound of "fire" (esh) and "water" (mayim).</note>, as if composed from *esh* and *mayim*—that is, from the fire and water we mentioned. Here, there is the alternation of life and death; there, perpetual life and stable operation; in the heavens, there is stability of life but an alternation of operations and locations <note>Referring to the constant, circular motion of the planets.</note>. This world is made from the perishable substance of bodies; that world from the nature of the divine mind; the heaven is constituted of body, but an incorruptible one, and of mind, but one bound to a body. The third world is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many other differences between them which I do not intend to recount here, where we are merely passing through rather than dwelling.

I should not overlook the fact that these three worlds were most clearly symbolized by Moses in the construction of that admirable Tabernacle of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, each of which could not more expressly represent the individual worlds we have mentioned. Indeed, the first part, protected by no roof or shade, was open to rain, snow, sun, heat, and cold; it is the most evident image of our sublunary world. It was inhabited not only by men—the pure and the impure, the sacred and the profane—but also by animals of every kind. Within it, there was a perpetual alternation of life and death due to the sacrifices and constant offerings. The remaining two parts were both covered and free from any outside injury on all sides, just as both the celestial and super-celestial worlds are incapable of injury or insult. Both were also honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the one which was more secret was called the **Holy of Holies**, while the other was decorated only with the title of **Holy**. In the same way, although both the celestial and angelic worlds are holy—since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, there is not and cannot be any stain or sin—the angelic world is nevertheless considered far holier and more divine than the celestial.

But why do we pursue these more distant comparisons? For if the last part of the Tabernacle was common to both men and beasts, the second part—which shone entirely with the splendor of gold—was illuminated by a candelabrum distinguished by seven lamps. As all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, these signify the seven planets. In the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged cherubim. Do these not set the three worlds before our eyes? This world which both beasts and men inhabit, the celestial world in which the planets flash, and the super-celestial dwelling place of the angels. We are reminded from this also of a higher evangelical mystery. For since for us to the super-celestial world...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s explanation of the three worlds. <margin>Every world is in every other world</margin>
...who flies upon the cherubim, the entrance having been closed from the beginning because of the sin of our first parent by the laws of justice. This is enough regarding the three worlds, in which this must first be greatly observed (from which almost our entire intention depends): that these three worlds are one world. This is not only because they are all referred to one principle and the same end,

<margin>Three reasons why the world is one</margin>
nor only because they are bound together by tempered numbers and a certain harmonious kinship of nature and an orderly series of degrees, but because whatever is in all the worlds together is also contained in each one individually. There is not one among them

<margin>Anaxagoras, the Pythagoreans, and the Platonists</margin>
in which all things are not found that exist in the others. I believe this was the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who famously taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we think he was understood correctly, which was later explained by the Pythagoreans and Platonists. Truly, those things which are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but in a better form; those

<margin>How the worlds are within one another</margin>
which are in the higher worlds are also seen in the lowest ones, but in a degenerate condition and with an adulterated nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elemental quality; in the celestial bodies, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me say something

<margin>An example of the proposed truth</margin>
more clearly. Among us, there is fire, which is an element. The Sun is fire in heaven. In the region beyond the world, fire is the Seraphic <note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels, traditionally associated with the "fire" of divine love.</note> intellect. But see how they differ: the elemental fire burns; the celestial fire gives life; the super-celestial fire loves. There is water among us; there is water in the heavens—the Moon, which is the mover and mistress of this gateway to the heavens; there are also waters above the heaven:

<margin>The ten spheres of the intellectual world</margin>
the Cherubic <note>The Cherubim are the second order of angels, associated with the "waters" of divine wisdom and understanding.</note> minds. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: the elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; the celestial moisture nourishes it; the super-celestial moisture understands it. In the first world, God—the primary Unity—presides over nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being himself unmoved, he moves all things toward himself.

<margin>The ten spheres of the celestial world</margin>
In the middle world—that is, the celestial—the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most refined part of the physical heavens, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note> similarly presides over the nine celestial spheres like a leader over an army; and while each of these revolves with unceasing motion, the Empyrean remains still, representing God. There are

<margin>The ten spheres of the elemental world</margin>
also in the elemental world, after prime matter which is its foundation, nine spheres of corruptible forms. First, three of bodies lacking life, which are the elements

<margin>Body, Nature, Soul</margin>
and the mixtures between them—those which are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions that occur in the heights <note>Referring to "metereological" phenomena like rain, snow, or lightning, thought to be imperfect mixtures of elements.</note>. Then, three of a vegetable nature, which is first divided into three kinds:

<margin>Each of these is divided into three parts</margin>
herbs, shrubs, and trees. Finally, three of the sensory soul: that which is either imperfect, such as in "zoophytes" <note>original: "Zoophitis." Organisms like sponges or corals that appear to be between plants and animals.</note>, or perfect but within the limits of irrational imagination, or that which is the highest among the brutes and even capable of human instruction—which is a sort of middle ground between man and brute, just as the zoophyte is a middle ground between brute and plant. But of these things, I have said more than is necessary. Let us only add this:

<margin>Testimony from the Sacred Scriptures</margin>
that the mutual containment of the worlds is also indicated in the Sacred Scriptures. For it is written in the Psalms, "He who creates the heavens in understanding," <note>original: "qui creat celos in intellectu." A reference to Psalm 136:5.</note> and we read that the angels of God are "spirits" and his ministers are "a flame of burning fire." <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4.</note> Hence, celestial names are often given to divine things, and often even

<margin>Only the most learned men can correctly write or interpret allegories</margin>
terrestrial ones: while they are symbolized now by stars, now by wheels and animals, and now by elements. Hence also, celestial names are often given to terrestrial things. Since all these worlds are bound together by the chains of concord, they grant each other names as well as natures with mutual generosity. From this principle (if someone perhaps has not yet noticed it) has flowed the entire discipline of allegorical interpretation. Nor could the ancient fathers have fittingly represented one thing by the figures of another...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument that the various realms of existence—the intellectual, celestial, and sublunary—are interconnected through a system of cosmic sympathies. ...to represent them unless they had been taught the hidden friendships and affinities, so to speak, of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they would have represented this thing by this image rather than another, or vice versa. But being experts in all things and moved by that Spirit which not only knows all these things but made them, they very aptly figured the natures of one world through those things which they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is needed—unless that same Spirit is also present—by those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings.

<margin>The fourth world / man is the lesser</margin>
Moreover, besides the three we have described, there is a fourth world in which all those things found in the others are also discovered. This is man himself, who, for this reason—as the Catholic doctors say—is designated in the Gospel by the name of "every creature."

<margin>every man</margin>
Although the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to brutes or angels, Christ nevertheless commands that it be preached to "every creature" <note>This refers to Mark 16:15: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Pico uses this to argue that man contains all other creatures within himself.</note>.

<margin>How man is the lesser world</margin>
It is a well-worn saying in the schools that man is a "lesser world" <term>microcosm: the philosophical concept that human beings contain the entire universe (the macrocosm) in miniature</term>, in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of brutes, reason, the angelic mind, and the likeness of God.

<margin>Of all these worlds</margin>
If, therefore, we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, intending to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of these.

<margin>Moses treated [the worlds]</margin>
And since a writer portrays nature—if he is as well-versed in nature as we believe our Moses to be—it is credible that he arranged his teaching about them in no other way than Almighty God the Architect arranged them within themselves. Thus, this scripture of Moses is truly an expressed image of the world, just as we read that it was commanded of him on the mountain where he learned these things: that he should make all things according to the pattern <note>original: "secundum exemplar." Pico references Exodus 25:40, where God instructs Moses to build the Tabernacle according to the heavenly model shown to him on Mount Sinai.</note> he had seen on the mountain.

<margin>This scripture is an image of nature</margin>
First, therefore—and this is the greatest point of all—since we have shown that those things which are in all worlds are contained in each one, Moses, as an emulator of nature, ought to have dealt with no single one of those worlds without dealing with all of them together at the same time, under the same words and in the same context.

<margin>No part of the work in which he does not treat all worlds simultaneously</margin>
From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: first, we should explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. Second, everything likewise concerning the celestial world. Then concerning this sublunary and corruptible world. Fourth, concerning the nature of man.

<margin>Root of the fourfold exposition</margin>
For if, for instance, the intelligible world is treated anywhere, since it contains all lower natures within itself, the scripture should also remind us of the remaining worlds; we certainly can—and indeed must—interpret every small part in terms of all of them.

<margin>Root of the fifth exposition</margin>
Conversely, just as the natures, although promiscuously contained within one another, have nevertheless been allotted distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws, so too, if the fourfold nature is discussed in the same series of letters in each part of the present work, it must be believed that the first nature is dealt with more specifically in the first part, and so on in order for the rest. From this, the necessity of a fifth exposition arises.

<margin>Root of the sixth exposition</margin>
Additionally, by the same reasoning that these things are distinct—since there is no multitude that is not one—they are bound together by a certain "discordant concord" <term>discordia concors: a classical and Renaissance concept where harmony is achieved through the balancing of opposing forces</term> and are tied by multiform chains of connections, as it were. Since it is likely that Moses does this throughout the entire work, it calls us, even if unwillingly, to a sixth interpretation.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Pico concludes his introductory remarks on man as the "microcosm" and begins the "Heptaplus" proper—his seven-fold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis. He establishes his methodology here, explaining why he will avoid long-winded academic debates in favor of revealing the hidden "mysteries" of the text.</meta>

It is fitting that we—after the orders of the realms distributed by God have been set forth, and their union, difference, covenants, and relations explained—should now, in a seventh and (as I might call it) **Sabbath-like** narration, touch upon the happiness of creatures and their return to God. This return, achieved through the Mosaic and Christian law, was granted to man after he had been distanced from God by the sin of our first parent. We shall report what Moses most clearly concealed regarding these matters in the present scripture <note>Pico is referring to the opening chapters of Genesis.</note> [red circle around **Moses**] so that it may become clear that a most explicit prophecy of Christ’s coming, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the Gentiles is read here. *That this book truly is,* if any other be such, a book sealed with seven seals, full of all doctrine and all mysteries.

We will not, however, imitate those who, having undertaken to explain this creation of the world, have heaped together here whatever has been disputed among philosophers and theologians regarding God, angels, matter, <margin>Isaac the Persian / Samuel Ophinides</margin> heaven, and all of nature. In this, among the Hebrews, Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides <note>Isaac b. Kanpanton and Samuel ibn Tibbon (or similar commentators) were known for their philosophical/astronomical approaches to scripture.</note> especially erred. Instead, we shall strive to declare, according to our strength, only what the Mosaic letter intends: what the context of the words either indicates or signifies. 

Nor, if we show that by the "firmament" is meant, for instance, the eighth sphere, will we immediately begin a dispute about how it carries the other spheres along, how many signs it is distinguished by, with what images, or whether it is rotated by a simple motion, or rather by two, or more truly by three diverse ones. Or if we say that some word indicates the human soul, we will not digress to unravel all that is written about the soul, but we will briefly and cursorily annotate only those things about each matter of which the author seems to make express mention. *I have said briefly and cursorily,* because the purpose of this work is not that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time; rather, it is that they may recognize what they already know to be true in the words of the prophet. By understanding how the prophet, in a few words, both included and concealed what they have read digested in the immense volumes of theologians and philosophers, they may hear the lawgiver speaking with an "unveiled face" <note>original: "revelata facie" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:12-18, suggesting that the "veil" of Moses's literal text is removed to reveal spiritual truth.</note>. 

But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of <margin>Paul</margin> "holy simplicity" <note>original: "sanctæ rusticitatis" — a phrase often used to describe a pious but unlearned faith.</note>, does not approve of these mysteries sought from on high, but rather desires a simpler and more accommodating explanation of the sacred context, I will first bid him remember Paul commanding that neither he who eats should despise him who does not eat, nor he who does not eat should judge him who eats <note>Romans 14:3</note>. Then I will address <margin>Augustine</margin> him not with my own words, but with those of Augustine in his own exposition on Genesis, in this manner: "If you can grasp these things, do so; if you cannot yet, leave them to those who are more capable. But as for you, make progress while Scripture does not desert your weakness and walks more slowly with you in a motherly gait." <margin>The virtue of scripture</margin> For she speaks in such a way as to mock the proud with her height, terrify the attentive with her depth, feed the great with truth, and nourish the small with kindness. *But let us return to ourselves* and, beginning from this very corruptible world in which we dwell, let us provide as much as we can of what we have promised. Otherwise, in great things it is enough to have willed them: and <margin>Pomerius</margin> as Pomerius <note>Likely Julianus Pomerius, a 5th-century priest and author of "The Contemplative Life."</note> says, a great effort in great things is itself a form of progress.

<margin>Why darkness was over the face of the abyss.</margin>
...as something accidental: and over it <note>Referring to "the earth," which Pico identifies as prime matter.</note>, extended into the three dimensions of the abyss, sat the **darkness of privation**. <note>original: *privationis tenebras* — In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form or quality that a subject should naturally possess. It is one of the three principles of nature alongside matter and form.</note> This darkness was not indeed in the innermost parts of matter (for privation is not the essence of matter, as **Aristotle** proves), but rather occupied its outermost face. We likewise saw that "over the waters"—that is, the fluctuating dispositions of matter—present as if to the earth, the **spirit of the Lord** was moved. By this is meant the power of the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being; here, Pico distinguishes between God as the primary cause and the "Spirit" as the active instrument.</note>, acting not as the principal cause, but as the spirit of the Lord—that is, the instrument of divine art, just as our own **vital spirit** <note>In Renaissance medicine and philosophy, the "vital spirit" was a subtle substance that acted as a bridge, allowing the non-physical soul to move and animate the physical body.</note> is the instrument of the soul. And immediately, as the spirit worked upon those waters and pervaded the underlying subject at the command of **God the Craftsman**, **light** arose—that is, the beauty and splendor of **form**. <note>original: *formae decus & splendor* — Pico interprets the biblical creation of light as the philosophical moment when matter receives "form," giving it identity, beauty, and structure.</note>

...birds of the air are introduced by him <note>Referring to Moses, whom Pico treats as the "divine philosopher."</note> as flying from there: that is the region in which those sublime **impressions** <note>original: *sublimes illae impressiones* — In Aristotelian meteorology, "impressions" or "meteors" refer to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and comets.</note> appear: rain, snow, lightning, thunder, comets, and others of that kind. Above it, the elements are pure; below it, they depart from elemental simplicity through a perfect mixture. There, mixtures are formed, but they are imperfect and intermediate, so that one might most truly say it lies between the nature of mixed bodies and pure elements.

->### Chapter Four<-

But let us see what further Moses philosophizes: <margin>The waters are gathered into one place and the earth appears.</margin> "Let the waters which are under the heaven," he says, "be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear." The **dry land** <term>Arida: Pico identifies "the dry" with prime matter, which is "dry" because it lacks the "moisture" of form.</term> is matter, as we have already established. Matter does not appear or become visible unless it is clothed in the appearance of forms; but neither does it appear clothed only in the appearance of a **simple element**. For, as we have said and as the philosophers prove, a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor can it fall under any sense at all. 

Therefore, if the earth which was once invisible is to come into view, it is necessary that the "waters" which are under the heaven—that is, under the middle region of the air—be gathered into one place. This means they flow together into a common mass of mixture <note>original: *colluuiem* — a collection of fluids or dregs.</note>, yet are prescribed by certain laws as if by shores, to coalesce into a single form of mixture. This happens to the lower waters, as we have shown, but not to the higher ones, where there is either no mixture at all or only an imperfect one. 

<margin>The earth germinates plants.</margin> Since the **vegetative soul** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, the "vegetative soul" is the most basic level of life, responsible for nutrition and growth in plants.</note> immediately follows upon the form of mixture, what else should we expect from our philosopher than that, after that gathering of the waters, he would immediately introduce the earth as fruitful with herbs, shrubs, and trees?

->### Chapter Five<-

Although from here it seemed that, in the following order, one should transition to animals, whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetative soul; nevertheless, because one proceeds from animals to man (in whom every treatise on the corruptible world concludes), Moses therefore interjected some things about those things which occur in the firmament, and with which it is adorned—just as the earth is adorned by the metals, plants, and living creatures produced within it. 

These are those **impressions** which occur on high, that is, in the middle region of the air. Above, he called this both "heaven" and "firmament"; but here he calls it the **"firmament of heaven,"** so that we may know it is not that which is truly heaven, but that which lies beneath heaven. For this reason, <margin>Ennius</margin> **Ennius** <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), a Roman poet. Pico references his play *Achilles* to show that even ancient poets understood this region as "sub-adjacent" to the true heavens.</note> in his *Achilles* called this part the "sub-adjacent," because it is placed nearest under the heaven. 

It is too well known to need further proof that these secondary "impressions" are called **stars**, **constellations**, and **heavenly bodies** by the philosophers; nor should it seem at all harsh to anyone that we explain here what is said about the stars in relation to them. Since all the diversity of these things is referred to two primary causes—heat and cold—we shall appropriately refer those which are hot by cause to the **Sun**, and those which are cold to the **Moon**. These things claim the names of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars for themselves not only because they are to the lower heaven what those stars are to their own (albeit more divine) heaven, or because they show themselves to men with a similar appearance—equally shining and glittering—but because some of them follow one star in heaven and some another, as if following a prince and leader. 

Hence they are also **signs** of those things which the stars, by which they were stirred up, are accustomed to portend for lower things. An argument for this matter is that they follow the motion of the stars; for it is by the stars' power and influence that they consist of material gathered from the earth—that is, from a **vaporous exhalation**. <note>original: *uaporoso halatu* — In ancient physics, "exhalations" rising from the earth were thought to be the material that formed clouds, rain, and even comets.</note>

->### Chapter One.<-

Wherefore, by an analogy of reason, since the light of the heavens which we see emanates from and is preserved by those supreme spheres (for he who gives light also preserves it), those supreme spheres are rightly compared to olive trees, while these lower ones are compared to the lamps and the bowl. Truly, if two primary sources of the same water cannot be established, it is necessary that out of those two supreme spheres, one must be the principle of all light. The "waters which are under the heaven" <margin>Waters under the heaven</margin> are the seven planets <note>original: *septem sydera* — in the traditional geocentric model, the "seven stars" included the Sun and Moon along with Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> which are under the firmament that he called "heaven"; the first of which is Saturn. <margin>gathered together into one place</margin> These "waters" are gathered into one place for this reason: because the entire power of the planets is collected in the one Sun. All philosophers and all mathematicians confirm this with one voice. And if this gathering of waters is called the "sea," then it is not absurd to say that this is that "Ocean" <margin>Ocean</margin> which is called the father of gods and men by those who deigned to name the planets after the names of gods. 

Furthermore, what else shall we say the "earth" <margin>The Earth appears</margin> is, if not the Moon? For it was so named by Aristotle and the Pythagoreans. When it is completely overwhelmed by the waves of the aforementioned "sea" <note>The author uses "sea" as a metaphor for the Sun's overwhelming light during a solar conjunction.</note>, it is neither useful to us nor visible; but it becomes suitable for the needs of animals and ourselves when, moving away from that sea, it comes more and more into view. 

Then it is fertile, then it is fruitful, especially of those things which are of a vegetative nature, whose gifts are growth, nutrition, and generation. For in these things lies the chief power of the Moon, <margin>The chief power of the Moon</margin> as the Chaldeans <margin>Chaldeans</margin> <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers famous for their planetary observations.</note> said. This is also most aptly demonstrated here by Moses: when the Moon appears, he makes her the parent of grasses, shrubs, and trees. See how he has indicated to us the nature of the Moon and the Sun in very few and figurative words. 

But why is he silent about the rest, when we promised in the prefaces that he would treat all things sufficiently and learnedly? <margin>Why no mention of the four planets</margin> Why, I ask, when he has mentioned the tenth, ninth, and eighth spheres, and likewise Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, has he not said a single word about the four remaining—Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and Mars? 

You might say perhaps <margin>First solution</margin> that this was done because an unrefined people <note>Refers to the ancient Hebrews whom the author suggests required a simplified version of cosmology.</note> knew only the Sun and the Moon. But I have blocked this escape for myself, <margin>Refutation</margin> nor can I turn there without blushing, for I have already testified above that nothing was omitted by Moses that would lead to a perfect understanding of all the worlds. 

Another might say <margin>Second solution</margin> that by dealing with the Sun and Moon, he dealt with the rest; for these hold the kingdom of the sky, and while the power of the others is particular, these two stars prevail with universal influence. But this does not satisfy us either; <margin>Refutation</margin> for by the same reasoning, he should have omitted Saturn, yet we have shown that he made mention of it. 

I believe a deeper mystery <margin>Third solution</margin> lies hidden in the ancient discipline of the Hebrews. Among their dogmas concerning the heavens, this is the chief: <margin>Dogma of the ancient Hebrews regarding the stars</margin> that Jupiter and Mars are included in the Sun, while Venus and Mercury are included in the Moon. Nor is the reason for this opinion obscure if we examine the natures of these stars, even though the Hebrews themselves offer no reason for their dogma. 

Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the Sun is hot; but the heat of Mars is sharp and violent, while that of Jupiter is beneficial. In the Sun, we see that sharp and violent quality of Mars and the beneficial property of Jupiter— <margin>Affinity of the Sun with Jupiter and Mars</margin> that is, a nature mixed from these, tempered and, so to speak, intermediate. Jupiter is auspicious, Mars is unfortunate; the Sun is partly good and partly bad: good in radiation, but bad in conjunction <note>In traditional astrology, a planet is "combust" or weakened when too close to the Sun, though the Sun's light itself is the source of life.</note>. Aries is the house of Mars, Cancer the exaltation <note>original: *dignitas* — a position in the zodiac where a planet's influence is most powerful.</note> of Jupiter; the Sun, having achieved its height in Cancer and its dignity in Aries, shows a manifest kinship with both stars. 

Let us come to the Moon, which clearly participates in the "waters" of Mercury, <margin>Affinity of the Moon with Venus and Mercury</margin> and indicates how great an affinity it has with Venus, especially from the fact that it is so exalted in Taurus (the home of Venus) that it is judged nowhere more happy or more beneficial. 

Thus, concerning the Empyrean heaven, the ninth sphere called the firmament, the star of Saturn, and the Sun and Moon (which embrace the remaining planets, reminding us of this inclusion by their very silence), enough has been said so far. <margin>Epilogue</margin>

It remained that after they had spoken of the nature of the stars, they should discuss their works and their office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were delegated by God. Know, moreover, that the discussion is still about the heaven as a luminous body; nothing has yet been said by the prophet <note>original: *a propheta* — referring to Moses as the author of Genesis.</note> about its intellect or its moving force. This is the same order that Timaeus <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, used here to represent Platonic cosmology.</note> follows: first fashioning the body, then, once the body is complete, adding the soul. Two operations of the celestial bodies are universally manifest: **motion** and **illumination**.

Motion is established as twofold: one of the whole world, by which the heaven and the ether are revolved through the entire space of the universe in a perfect circuit within twenty-four hours; the other is the specific motion of the stars, which is manifold and various, among which the principal is the motion of the sun, which circles all the signs of the Zodiac in the space of twelve months. The former creates the day, whence it is called "diurnal"; the latter, however, creates the year. The remaining motions of the stars are completed through various intervals of time. Rightly and briefly, therefore, did Moses remind us of all these things when he said the stars were placed in the firmament *for days, years, and times*. He added *for signs*, which I pass over because it is sufficiently explained by other interpreters.

He furthermore expressly indicated the other operation of the stars, which is illumination, when he said they were appointed *to shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth*. Although there are diverse opinions among the ancients regarding what celestial things <term>influence</term> <note>original: *influant* — the "in-flowing" of celestial power or astrological effects onto the earthly realm.</note> lower things, the words of Moses fit any of them quite aptly. For if they influence nothing other than light—which Aristotle seems to have intended, if we interpret his words religiously and not according to our own whim—nothing could be thought more consistent with the Mosaic sayings. If, besides light, they also influence heat, and nothing else besides—as Averroes the Arab <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> and Abraham the Jew <note>Likely Abraham Ibn Ezra, a medieval polymath known for his biblical commentaries and astrology.</note> hold—it was enough to have spoken of light, from which these same authors admit heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold virtues are sent down from the heavens, as was the view of Avicenna and the Babylonians, the mention of light alone was not made rashly; for as Avicenna himself writes, it is light alone that carries all other virtues from heaven to us. The bodies of the moon, the sun, and the stars are distributed into these ministries.

### Chapter Five

It remained that he should mention the signs which are visible in the Zodiac, and those which, although invisible to us in the crystalline and ninth spheres, are nonetheless far more effective in the heaven. For nothing has been said of these so far. This, therefore, is the meaning of the "living creatures" <note>original: *animalia*</note> which the waters bring forth and the earth brings forth: namely, those waters which are above the heavens and the earth which is the firmament itself, as was proven above. For the signs seen in those two spheres take the form of animals, such as those noted among us by the Egyptians and Indians <note>Ancient astronomers from these regions were traditionally credited with the first mapping of the constellations.</note>; they were able to perceive these more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the flatness of the ground and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the perishable production of animals that are here on earth pertains no more to these two elements, earth and water, than to the others, namely fire and air. And since he gave the name "waters" to the crystalline sphere, he consistently called the animals there "fish"; conversely, in the firmament which he calls "earth," he called them "cattle and beasts."

### Chapter Six

Thus far concerning the corporeal nature of the heavens. Now, intending to declare them as endowed with a rational soul, he mentions "Man" allegorically—not indeed that man who is perishable and earthly and whom we see, but the one by whom, as Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> says, the visible man is ruled. That is the rational soul itself; since Timaeus <note>Referring to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the Creator mixing the World Soul and human souls in the same vessel or "bowl."</note> constitutes it from the same elements and in the same bowl from which he also made the soul of the heaven...

What is appropriately said concerning the soul of man is also transferred to the soul of heaven. [Marginal note: Sacred Scripture] **Sacred Scripture** agrees with our exposition; in its pages, the entire angelic and rational nature is often designated by the term "man." This is most frequent in the prophets when speaking of the good angels, and even of the evil demon—who differs from them in nothing regarding his nature—it is written in the **Gospel**: *An enemy man has done this.* <note>original: *inimicus homo hæc fecit* — quoting Matthew 13:28. The author argues that "man" is used as a category for rational spirits, whether human, angelic, or demonic.</note> Therefore, God added a living and rational substance to the **celestial machine**, <note>term: *celestial machine* — a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely-ordered mechanism.</note> a participant in intellect, and thus created in His own image and likeness. He willed for this substance to preside over those living things of which we spoke shortly before: namely, the [Marginal note: Celestial bodies obey their motors] **stars**, all the **signs of the Zodiac**, and the **planets**. These turn at His nod and obey His word so perfectly that there is no delay and no rebellion. This is unlike what happens with the brute bodies of the four elements. You will find that the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> labor over nothing more than proving that the celestial body does not resist its "motor" (its moving spirit) in the way our earthly bodies resist our wills. For this reason, the celestial bodies feel no weariness, difficulty, or fatigue from their perpetual motion.

This is the "dominion" over the animals that **Moses** touched upon regarding the "celestial man." Nor is it without mystery that he created that man **male and female**. [Marginal note: How the celestial man is male and female] This is the prerogative of celestial souls: that they perform both duties at once—both **contemplating** and **ruling** the bodies—without one role interfering with or obstructing the other. This was a concept used extensively by the ancients; we observe in the **Orphic hymns** that these two powers in the same substance—one which contemplates and the other which presides over the body—are designated by the names "male" and "female." [Marginal note: Epilogue] These things concerning the celestial world, the divine body, the number of the spheres, their nature, properties, and office—and finally, concerning its moving force, its rational substance, and its character—are handed down to us by the prophet.

### Chapter Seven
[Marginal note: To what extent we should honor heaven]

This is a noble creature, worthy of our respect and celebration. But even if we follow the [Marginal note: Plato] **Platonic sentiment** (to say nothing for a moment of the theologians) which we recently mentioned—that our own souls were tempered by God the Maker in the same mixing bowl and from the same elements as the celestial souls—let us see to it that we do not choose to be the slaves of those whom nature intended to be our brothers. <note>original: *in eodem cratere* — referring to the "mixing bowl" in Plato's *Timaeus* where the Creator mixed the substance of the soul of the world and human souls.</note> We should not measure our condition by this weak, physical body. For man is not, as written in the *Alcibiades*, <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato emphasizing that the soul, not the body, is the true person.</note> this fragile and earthy thing we see, but is instead the **soul**; he is the **intellect**, which exceeds the entire circuit of heaven and the whole course of time. 

We must therefore be careful not to do what many do: giving more to the heavens and attributing more to them than is necessary, thereby resisting both the will of the Maker and the order of the universe. In doing so, we might even displease the heaven itself—which holds God's counsel and the world's order most dear—while we are trying to please it. [Marginal note: Chaldeans] The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and astrologers.</note> warn of this, saying: *Do not increase fate.* [Marginal note: Jeremiah] This is what **Jeremiah** proclaims: *Do not fear the signs of heaven which the nations fear.* [Marginal note: Moses] This is what our prophet **Moses** commands elsewhere, warning that a man must be careful when looking up at the sun, moon, and stars, lest he be led astray to worship those things which God created to serve all nations. 

If someone does not accept the sense that those celestial bodies "serve" us like ignoble or dead bodies, let us at least understand that the author or master of our nature cannot be a substance whose secondary part is found to be even more "lowly" than the noble part within us. For in any work, nothing can or should be more perfect than the qualities found in the maker. Let us, therefore, fear Him from whom all [Marginal note: Christ alone is to be worshipped] things come; let us love and venerate Him. In Him, as **Paul** says, all things were created, whether visible or invisible...

->### THIRD EXPOSITION ON THE ANGELIC AND INVISIBLE WORLD.<-
->### PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK.<-

Thus far we have disputed, according to the strength of our wit, concerning the celestial world, revealing the mysteries of **Moses**. Now, however, "who will give me wings like a dove, wings silvered and gleaming with the paleness of gold?" <note>A poetic blending of Psalm 55:6 and Psalm 68:13, expressing a spiritual longing to ascend beyond the physical world.</note> I shall fly above the celestial region where there is true rest, true peace, true tranquility—peace, certainly, which this visible and corporeal world cannot give. Unveil my eyes, O spirits beyond the world, and I shall contemplate the miracles of your city, which God has stored up for those who fear Him; "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor heart conceived." <note>1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> Since many things are handed down concerning this **angelic and invisible nature** by the ancient Hebrews, and many also by [margin] **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose "Celestial Hierarchy" was the standard medieval authority on angels.</note>, it was my plan to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both families. But since what is said by the Hebrews—being [margin] **Ancient dogmas of the Hebrews** unusual among the Latins—could not be easily understood by our men unless we began "from both eggs" (as they say) <note>original: "a gemino qd' aiūt ouo" — a classical idiom meaning "from the very beginning," referring to the myth of Helen of Troy born from an egg.</note> and narrated many and almost all the dogmas of the ancient discipline of the Hebrew people, I thought it best to defer this until we have written more extensively elsewhere on these matters and made their opinions known to our own people. There, we shall examine how much they harmonize with **Egyptian** monuments, how much with **Platonic** philosophy, and how much with **Catholic** truth. Wherever they agree with us, we shall command the Hebrews to stand by the ancient traditions of their fathers; wherever they disagree, being instructed by Catholic legions, we shall make an assault upon them. Finally, whatever we [margin] **Dionysius, Paul, Hierotheus** find alien to the evangelical truth, we shall refute as manfully as we can; whatever is right and true, we shall transfer from the synagogue—as from an unjust possessor—to us, the legitimate Israelites. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of **Dionysius**, or rather of **Paul** and **Hierotheus** <note>According to tradition, Hierotheus was the teacher of Dionysius, who was himself a convert of St. Paul.</note> whom he followed, we shall strive to bring light into the darkness of the Law—which the Spirit of God, the author of the Law, placed as his hiding place—for the sake of our own weakness.

->### Chapter One.<-

[margin] **Unity** Whatever exists after Unity is **Number**, and is perfected and completed by Unity. ...we can understand nothing of what He is, except that He is the very Being that He is. Other things are not that—that is, Being itself—but they exist by it. Therefore, an angel is not unity itself; otherwise he would be God, or there would be many gods, which is an inconceivable notion. <margin>Angel</margin> For what will be one if unity itself is not one? It remains that an angel is a **number**. But if he is a number, in one part of himself he is a multitude, and in another he is a single multitude. Now every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel we should attribute to the angelic multitude, which he has from being a number (that is, a creature); and whatever is perfect, we attribute to the approaching unity, which he has from being joined to God. We find a twofold imperfection in an angel: First, because he is not **Being itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse" — In Scholastic philosophy, God is defined as the only being whose essence is his existence (Being itself); all other beings merely "have" existence.</note> but only an essence to which **participated being** <term>Participated being: The concept that creatures do not possess existence inherently, but "share" or "borrow" it from God.</term> happens so that he may exist; second, because he is not understanding itself, but it comes to him that he understands, though by his nature he is an intellect capable of intelligence. The second depends on the first: for that which does not exist of itself certainly does not understand of itself, since nothing can have being where Being itself is not. Both of these, therefore, happen to the angel insofar as he is a multitude. It remains that his liberation and perfection must come from the unity approaching from above. But God is unity, from whom being, life, and all perfection are derived for the angel. Just as there is a twofold imperfection (as if a twofold multitude), let us understand a twofold approach of unity so that both may be perfected. The first is that by which he is a raw and formless essence, devoid of life and being. This is the **formless and empty earth** <margin>Formless earth</margin> which God also created, lest perhaps you should believe, as some have believed, that only the *forming* of essence belongs to the Creator, and not also its *creation*. Together with the earth, He created heaven—that is, the act of that essence and the participated unity in the multitude, which is Being itself—so that it is as if the creation of heaven and earth were the same, as an embrace of equals and of two natures coming together toward the same thing with a similar bond. Nor do we speak out of harmony with the ancients when we call Being itself—the participation in divinity—"heaven," since **Xenophanes** <margin>Xenophanes</margin> called the archetypal world a "sphere," and the **Saracens** <margin>Saracens</margin>—and indeed our own people—call God a "circle."

## Chapter Two.

Through what we have said, the angel has now perfectly attained his nature and intellectual property. Nevertheless, he does not yet have that by which he may fulfill his duties—namely, of understanding and contemplating—unless he is first clothed by God with **intelligible forms** <term>Intelligible forms: The spiritual "blueprints" or ideas that allow an intellect to perceive and understand reality.</term>. Therefore, **darkness was still upon the face of the abyss.** <margin>Darkness</margin> The **abyss** <margin>The Abyss / Why "upon the face of the abyss" and not "above the abyss"</margin> is the intellectual property that penetrates and searches all deep things. Darkness is over this until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual notions by which it sees and contemplates all things. It is written, however, "upon the face of the abyss," not "above the abyss," because the same place holds both darkness and light. Now the light—that is, the intelligible forms—occupies the "face," which refers to the outermost parts of the angelic intellect, because these are accidental qualities and do not belong to his essence itself. What comes in between before the darkness is driven away and the light arises, he immediately adds, saying: *And the Spirit of the Lord hovered over the waters.* <margin>Spirit of the Lord</margin> What else should the **Spirit of the Lord** be if not the **spirit of love**? For we do not call the spirit of knowledge the Spirit of the Lord in such a proper sense, since knowledge sometimes leads away from God, but love always leads toward God. Unless this Spirit is carried over that abyss, light will not be made. For just as the eye will not be filled with light unless it is turned toward the sun, so the angel is not filled with spiritual light unless he is turned toward God. This movement of conversion is not, nor can it be, anything else in the angelic nature than the movement of love. Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was...

...the loving spirit is over the abyss—that is, over the angelic intellect (for love follows upon intelligence)—by which, while the mind of the angel is moved and excited, it is turned toward God. God said, **"Let there be light,"** <margin>Let there be light</margin> and light was made in the angel—the light, namely, of intelligible forms. And there was "evening and morning, **one day**" <margin>One day</margin>; for as **Averroes** <margin>Averroes</margin> <note>original: "Auerrois" — Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western Scholasticism.</note> proves, a more perfect unity is formed from the intellect and the thing understood than from matter and form. As the same author affirms, and as **Moses the Egyptian** <margin>Moses the Egyptian</margin> <note>original: "Moſes egyptius" — Better known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> also writes, this is found to be far more true in angels than in man. Leaving aside their specific arguments, let this reason suffice for us: that the angelic species are joined to the mind in an individual bond, not as a wandering or metaphorical connection—as happens in the human intellect—but united by perpetual ties.

### Chapter Three.

We have seen the nature of the angel created by God, and the same nature turned toward God by the spirit of love, then illustrated and perfected by him with the light of intelligible reasons. Let us now see in what order the angelic hosts are distinguished among themselves. We read that the **firmament was placed in the midst of the waters**, <margin>Firmament in the midst of the waters</margin> where three angelic hierarchies are indicated to us (for we shall always call them by that customary term). The first and the last of these are designated by "waters": the first by the **waters above the heavens**, <margin>Waters above the heavens</margin> and the last by those which are **below the heavens**. <margin>Waters below the heavens</margin> The middle hierarchy, dividing the two, is called the **firmament**. <margin>Firmament</margin> All these things, if we examine the nature and offices of the three hierarchies, could not better harmonize with the doctrine of **Dionysius**. <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century theologian whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* defined the nine choirs of angels into three triads.</note> The supreme hierarchy, since—as he writes—it is vacant for contemplation alone, is deservedly figured by the waters which are established above the heavens; that is, above all earthly or celestial action concerning mundane things, and they praise God incessantly with a perennial sound. The middle order, however, since it is delegated to celestial duties, certainly could not be more fittingly signified than by the firmament—that is, by the heaven. The last hierarchy, although by nature it is above every body and above the heaven, nevertheless cares for those things which are below the heaven. Since it is divided into **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**, all the operations of these are concerned only with those things that are sublunary: the Principalities concern republics, kings, and princes (as we learn from Daniel); the Archangels concern mysteries and sacred ceremonies. The Angels attend to private matters, and individuals are assigned to individual men. Rightly, therefore, this sub-celestial host is figured here by the sub-celestial waters. This host presides over things that are fluid and falling, and it is subject to that order which is occupied with celestial things.

### Chapter Four.

What it means, however, for the **waters which are under the heaven to be gathered into one place** <margin>Collection of the sub-celestial waters into one place</margin> would perhaps be doubtful, unless **Paul** <margin>Paul</margin> declared it to us. It is for man's sake that they are sent to us, appearing now in rest, now to us while we are awake, in various forms, places, and times. How this opinion is to be accepted we shall finally know only when we observe in what way that which Moses says is true: namely, that the waters were gathered into one place. And let us hear the Father saying: "Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which God has blessed." # FOURTH EXPOSITION ON THE HUMAN WORLD, THAT IS, ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

### Preface to the Fourth Book.

After we have shown that enough has been treated by the Prophet concerning all parts of the world and concerning every nature—celestial, angelic, and corruptible—it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again in terms of man. We shall prove by the matter itself that there is no discourse in this entire work which, just as it dealt with the three worlds discussed above, does not also embrace hidden meanings and the highest truths regarding the nature of man. We will do something no less worthwhile if we are diligent in explaining this fourth interpretation than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and how necessary self-knowledge is for a human being (to pass over the Delphic inscription <margin>The Delphic inscription</margin> <note>The famous Greek motto "Gnothi Seauton" (Know Thyself) inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note>) has been so demonstrated by Plato in the *First Alcibiades* <margin>Plato</margin> that he left nothing for those coming after who might try to bring something new to this subject. Indeed, it is a wicked and reckless pursuit for one who is still ignorant of himself—still not knowing whether he can know anything at all—to yet boldly seek knowledge of things that are so far removed from him. Let us return, therefore, to ourselves, and let us see (as the Prophet says) what great things God has done for our soul. Lest perhaps, if the soul should be less diligent in recognizing its own self, it might hear the Father saying in the *Song of Songs*: "If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful of women, go out and depart, following the tracks of your flocks." <note>Song of Songs 1:8. In this allegorical tradition, the "flocks" represent the lower, animalistic passions.</note> You see what punishment awaits us for our self-ignorance. <margin>Triple punishment for self-ignorance</margin> First, we must depart—namely, from the Father—which departure is followed by disinheritance; and what could be more unfortunate? Second, we must go out: that is, out of ourselves. <margin>Above self</margin> For the mind that does not see itself is not at home within itself. But whoever goes out from himself is torn apart from himself; <margin>Away from self</margin> what could be more bitter? Third, we must walk in the tracks of our flocks: <margin>Below self</margin> that is, after the tracks of the beasts which are within us, of which we shall say enough in the exposition; what could be more miserable? What more despicable and contemptible than to become the servants of beasts over whom nature had appointed us as leaders? Therefore, let us proceed not after the tracks of brutes but after the tracks of Moses, and enter into our very selves; let us enter the inner chambers of the soul, with the Prophet himself opening the way for us, so that in ourselves we may happily recognize both all the worlds and our Father and our homeland.

Before we proceed to a more accurate exposition following the order of the prophet’s words, it is necessary to first say a few things about the nature of man and briefly define certain terms, so that the meaning of the whole may afterward be more clearly understood. Man consists of a body and a **rational soul**. The rational soul is called "heaven." For Aristotle calls heaven an animal moved by itself, and our soul (as the Platonists prove) is a substance that moves itself. Heaven is a circle, and the soul is likewise a circle; indeed, as Plotinus writes, heaven is a circle precisely because its soul is a circle. Heaven moves in an orbit; the rational soul, by transferring itself from causes to effects and returning again from effects to causes, revolves in the circle of reasoning. If these points had to be explained individually for those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato.

<margin>Spirit</margin>

The body is called "earth" because it is of an earthy and heavy substance. For this reason, Moses writes that being made from the ground <note>original: "humo" — the Latin root for *homo* (man) is *humus* (earth or ground), a common etymological connection in Renaissance thought.</note> gave man his name. But between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the soul, there was a need for a middle bond to join together such distant natures. To this task was assigned that thin and spiritual "little body" <note>original: "corpusculum" — in this context, it refers to the "pneuma" or medical spirit, a subtle material substance that carries the soul's commands to the limbs.</note> which both physicians and philosophers call the **spirit**. Aristotle writes that this spirit is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds proportionately to the heavens. 

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
This is called **light**, a title that could not better suit the opinion of philosophers and physicians, whose common consensus is that it is a most brilliant substance, and that it delights in, is nourished by, and is recreated by nothing more than light. Furthermore, just as all the power of the heavens (as Avicenna writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so all the power of the soul—which we have called heaven—namely, all the power of life, motion, and sense, flows and is poured into this earthly body (which we have called earth) through the mediation of the lucid spirit. 

Let us now descend to the words of the prophet. In his work, we see first the creation of heaven and earth—that is, the extremes of our substance: the rational power and the earthly body. Finally, when **light** is made—that is, the lucid spirit is added—they are so united that from "evening" and "morning"—that is, from the body’s nocturnal nature and the soul’s morning nature—there is one man. And since (as we have shown) all vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this light, the earth was rightly "empty and void" before the birth of light. For the earth could not share in the benefits of life and motion from its own "heaven" except through light as a messenger. For this reason, he immediately added the cause of this emptiness: namely, that darkness was still upon it because the light had not yet arisen.

Even Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> in his books *On the Trinity* <note>Augustine’s *De Trinitate* (c. 399–426 AD) is a foundational text of Western theology that explored the "psychological trinity" of memory, understanding, and will within the human mind.</note> seems to follow this distinction when, disputing about our mind, he divides it into two portions. However, those who write more accurately about the senses, reason, and intellect, place Intellect in the mind, Reason in speech, and Sense in the appetite of desire. These three are proper to humans, and from them other animal diversities arise. 

When Intellect dominates Reason, and Reason dominates Sense, then humans rule both themselves and all things most justly. But if Sense is preferred to Reason, and Reason to Intellect, then confusion and perturbation arise in the human, so that he is no longer a "man," but a certain monster in whom the order of justice is perverted by the appetite of cattle and wild beasts. 

For even here, the author understands "cattle" and "wild beasts" as human affections and appetites which adhere most closely to reason. # Chapter One

Now, about to speak of the angelic nature—which is pure intellect—let us first conceive in the mind that minds are like eyes. For what the eye is in bodily things, the mind itself is in the spiritual genus. Even if the eye possesses some light by the mixture of its own innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the duty of vision, in which it observes the colors and differences of things. Nor is it for that reason "not sight" by its own nature, even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that which has been allotted the nature of seeing and is "sight" by the reason of its essence is that which can see once light is received. 

Let us consider these same things in intellects: Intellects are eyes; intelligible truth is light. And the intelligible intellect itself, since it is innermost, has some light by which it can see itself, but it cannot see the rest. Truly, it needs the forms and ideas of things, by which—as if using rays of some invisible light—the intelligible truth is undoubtedly discerned. Nor should it be said (as we declared by the example of the eye) that they are not "intelligent" by nature and have only received an intellectual property by accident, sharing the same condition as our own souls. 

From this flows the opinion of those who judge the name "intellect" to be unworthy of God. Because if we take "intellect" like an eye which sees not from itself but by participation in light, and since God is light (for truth is light), and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, God does not need this operation, for He is light itself. He is as much further removed from ignorance of all things than the angels are, as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. 

But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not undergo the composition of incoming light. <margin>Angels consist of act and potency</margin> From this comes the common proverb that angels consist of "act and potency" <note>original: "ex actu & potentia." In scholastic philosophy, "act" is the realization of a thing's essence, while "potency" is its capacity to become or receive something else. Only God was considered "Pure Act," without any potentiality.</note>, though the dispute is anxious over what that "act" is, what that "potency" is, and what the reason for their composition might be. Likewise, we consider what Averroes the Arab <margin>Averroes the Arab</margin> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an influential Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval Western thought.</note> intended when he said that both intellects—the one which is in act and the one which is in potency—exist in all intellects short of God. But the common opinion, however it is understood, suffices for us regarding this passage. 

Moses reveals to us all these things we have said on the first day of creation. For he divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—namely, the nature of "act" and the nature of "potency." Moreover, just as the same thing has different properties, so it has different names. Wherefore this same "act"—while taken as the virtue granting sight to the eye and as the fulfillment of potency—is called "heaven," because its relationship to potency is the same as heaven's relationship is to earth. Again, because the angel is in need of light and cannot perform its own duty of understanding by itself, it is figured by "the waters": a body capable of light, yet by its own nature shining not at all. There is also another reason for the similarity, because that act of potency which...

# Chapter Two

Closest to this world is the celestial world. Its primary property is that it is the interval between both worlds: the "intelligible" world <term>intelligible: the realm of pure thought and spirit, beyond the reach of the physical senses</term>, of which we have just spoken, and this "sensible" world <term>sensible: the physical world we perceive through our five senses</term> which we inhabit. Nor can we more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than if we express the extremes by which it is enclosed, since a middle nature is tempered by the extremes. Therefore, Moses opens to us the greatest knowledge concerning the condition of heaven when he says that the middle heaven is placed "between the waters and the waters"—that is, between the angelic and the corruptible substances—not so much by reason of location as by reason of essence. Now, we have already said that by "waters" we should understand "forms," which are closest to potential (as if to "earth") and which perfect the essence. However, just as the "earth" of the angels is one thing and the "earth" of the elements another (because the potential in each is different), so too the nature of the "waters"—that is, the forms—is different in each. Between these, the heaven is truly in the middle: on one side divine life, on the other physical embodiment; here incorruptible substance, there visible substance; here firmness of essence, there change of place; here whatever is simple and uniform, there whatever has variety, mixture, and dissimilarity. Thus it has been allotted by the disposing providence of the Artisan <note>original: "opificis." A reference to God as the Divine Architect or Craftsman, a common image in both the Bible and Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>.

# Chapter Three

After these things, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the "gathering of the waters into one place" and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it does not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that indicates more clearly that there are laws implanted in the elements by an intelligent cause—by which they are both ruled and held in their places—beyond the inclination of their corporeal and brute nature, than these barriers of the waters. By these the ocean is restrained, whose impulse would otherwise carry it over the entire circuit of the earth. Just as fire rests upon the whole of the air, yet, as if warned by a schoolmaster's rod, the sea pulls back its foot; nor does it put itself forward further than our safety and the life of all living things requires. ### Chapter four.

After he dealt with the celestial and elemental sphere, and thereby with the entire integrity of the corporeal universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and citizens (if I may call them that) of this worldly city; beginning with the celestial ones, of whom we must speak first as if they were the senate and governors of the city, and then of the terrestrial ones as if they were the commoners and the people. ### THE SIXTH EXPOSITION ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH ONE ANOTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.

->**Preface to the Sixth Book.**<-

<note>A large decorated initial "D" depicts a figure, likely representing the Creator or a philosopher contemplating the divine unity.</note> **GOD** is a unity so distinguished by a trinity that He does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is in the creature a manifold <margin>Vestige of the Trinity</margin> **vestige of the divine trinity**. We shall bring forward here only this one point, which as far as I know has been cited by no one else: that whatever unity we see in created things, we find it divided by a triple logic. <margin>Triple unity in things</margin> 

For first, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one with itself, and is consistent and coherent within itself. Second, there is that unity by which one creature is united to another, and by which, finally, all parts of the world are one world. The third, and most principal of all, is that by which the entire universe is one with its Maker, like an army with its leader. This threefold union is present in every single thing through its own one simple unity, derived from that One which is both the First One and the Triune and the One at the same time: I mean from the **Father**, the **Son**, and the **Holy Spirit**. <margin>Father, Son, Spirit: The root of all ordered love</margin> 

For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity upon all; the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and couples all things to one another; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back to God, joins the whole work to the Maker with the bond of charity. But just as God is more intimate to us, so is He more "one" to us than we are to ourselves. Again, since every single thing is more tightly joined to itself than to other parts of the world, we are taught the order of universal charity if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature: first we shall love God Himself above us and above all things; in the second place, ourselves; third, our neighbor. 

Our Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the presumed author of Genesis.</note> said enough about that unity by which each thing is one with itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Concerning that unity by which we are united to God, it will be dealt with in the next treatise, where we shall discuss the height of happiness. What remains is that unity by which the diverse parts are coupled together in a mutual covenant, which is what we must deal with at present.

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of man to the "Sixth Exposition" of the creation account, where Pico della Mirandola explores the "kinship" or interconnectedness of all parts of the universe. # **Chapter One.**

After we have seen the distinct natures of things and arranged them—so to speak—in their separate stations, <note>original: "stationibus," referring to the specific "ranks" or "levels" of being discussed in previous sections of the *Heptaplus*.</note> we must not believe that the universe becomes one from all these things only because the individual parts are contained by other individual parts according to the condition of their nature (as we showed above). The prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note> also wished to indicate in his narrative how many modes there were by which the natures of things might be joined together. He does this not only to call us to this scholarly <term>curious understanding|In the Renaissance, "curious" (curiosa) implied a deep, meticulous, and specialized inquiry into the secrets of nature.</term> but also to instruct and demonstrate to us by what path and reason we might be joined to those things which are better than ourselves.

As I was reflecting, before approaching the explanation of the words, on how many modes of connection either exist or could be imagined by which things might obtain an affinity or a bond with one another—and as I ran through all the dogmas of the philosophers over which I have labored since I was a boy—no more than fifteen genera <note>original: "genera," meaning categories or classes of connection.</note> occurred to me. Then, approaching Moses, I saw them indicated by him so clearly and so aptly that I believe no one could be better instructed concerning them anywhere else.

# **Chapter Two.**

<margin>The essence of the thing to which it belongs</margin>
<margin>The property of the essence</margin>
<margin>Form: to the Subject</margin>
<margin>The transmuter: to the transmuted</margin>
<margin>Art: to the matter</margin>
<margin>Heaven: Earth</margin>
<margin>Earth: emptiness</margin>
<margin>Abyss: Darkness</margin>
<margin>Spirit of God: waters</margin>
<margin>Light: bodies</margin>

Immediately, therefore, on the first day, I know not whether more briefly or more clearly, he encompasses five modes by which something can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its **essence**, or it is a **property** of the essence; or it exists within it as a **form in a subject**; or it reaches it either as a **transmuter** <note>an efficient cause or agent that changes something else.</note> to that which is transmuted, or as **art** to the matter subjected to it. Similarly, we read in Moses five pairs, as if compared and connected to each other: **heaven and earth**; **earth and emptiness**; **abyss and darkness**; the **spirit of God and the waters**; **light and bodies**.

First, therefore, the "empty and void earth" <note>original: "terra inanis & vacua" — Genesis 1:2.</note> designates for us the first mode of connection, since the earth—that is, matter—is by its own nature empty unless it is filled from elsewhere by forms. The second mode is indicated by the "darkness upon the face of the abyss." For the abyss, by its own nature, is neither luminous nor dark; yet darkness follows its nature unless the approaching light puts it to flight. In the same way, the darkness of privation <note>a philosophical term for the absence of a quality that should be present.</note> follows the formlessness and emptiness of matter until the arriving species <term>species|In this context, "species" refers to the specific "form" or "intelligible essence" that gives matter its particular identity.</term> expels them. The third mode is shown by the light that rose upon the bodies. For light is in them as a **form in a subject**. 

The fourth mode is **heaven and earth**, since heaven does not inhere in the earth as a form or an accident <note>a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a stone.</note> exists in the thing it perfects; rather, it is joined to it as an efficient cause to the patient <note>the "patient" is the thing that receives the action of the agent.</note> and as a transmuting cause to the body that is transmuted. The example of the last mode is the **spirit of the Lord** which is "carried over the waters." For the Artificer—the Wisdom of the Lord and the spiritual nature—is entirely separated from the commerce of the body; it is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than **art**, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to the mortar, wood, and stones.

Again, consider this sequence of reasoning: the earth is empty of itself and possesses its own "domestic" darkness; then, it is joined most closely to light through light; to heaven through heaven; and through heaven to spiritual substance. But let us see how these things relate to us. The **earth** is the earthly body, empty and void of life and sense; upon it is **darkness**—death, torpor, ineffectiveness, immobility, and lack of sensation. **Light** is the life which enlivens, excites, drives, moves, and [fills it with] sense...
