->### **Chapter Three.**<-

Let us examine what Moses intends in the following: we will see ten other modes suggested by him, in which we may understand a mutual alliance between things. Besides those mentioned, there are these again, which we will list: since either a thing is a **part** of another, or an **effect**. If it is a part, it is either an inseparable part of its whole—as the sun, moon, and stars are in the firmament—or separable, like the parts of water from the integrity of their own element, into which they have flowed together. If it is an effect, it either sprouts from an internal <term>seminal reason|In Neoplatonic philosophy, "seminal reasons" (rationes seminales) are the formative principles or "seeds" implanted in nature by God that allow things to grow from within.</term>, as plants sprout from the earth—yet fixed to their parent and connected by natural bonds and ligaments—or it consists and is fused from its own principles, like a mixture of elements. In this way, the bodies of animals are made from water and earth. Or it has an external cause, which can be divided in three ways: into the efficient, the exemplary, and the final cause. We have examples of these three from Moses: when God creates and brings man into being (the efficient cause); creates him in his own image as a model (the exemplary cause); and the beasts are subject to man and made for man as for an end (the final cause).

->### **Chapter Four.**<-

We have spoken of the part and the effect, and by the same reasoning, of the whole and the cause. For these relations correspond to each other. But we have not yet fulfilled all the kinds of kinship. For regarding cause, there remains that species of affinity where a secondary cause obeys and is joined to a primary one; just as when God produces, the waters produce. <note>Refers to Genesis 1:20: "Let the waters bring forth..."</note> These do so first because they are the proximate cause, but only as God commands, because the primary cause <margin>Primary cause</margin> <margin>influences more</margin> <margin>than the secondary.</margin> flows more than the secondary. Similarly, there is a secondary end attached and annexed to the principal end—which Moses wisely signifies by saying the stars were placed to shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth. For the good of lower things is not the primary end of celestial things. Instead, they intend first to shine for themselves; then, finally, to illuminate us also. For this reason, we read in <margin>Homer</margin> Homer that both the dawn and the sun rise first for the immortals and then for mortals to bring light. <note>Pico is likely referencing the opening lines of the Odyssey, Book 3, or the Iliad, Book 11, where the sun rises to bring light to gods and men alike.</note> Besides all these, man is related to man and lion to lion; yet a lion is neither a part nor an effect of a lion unless it was sired by it. This the prophet <note>referring to Moses</note> signifies when he gathers and unites the fish, the birds, and the beasts of the earth together. There is a final reason for affinity: that which is the **middle** of nature relative to the extremes. For man is suited to man and animal to animal because they share the same essential reason, either specific or general. But the "middle" is not the same essence as the extremes, but is tempered in some way from them; it differs from both while communicating with both. This was indicated to us by Moses when he places the firmament as a middle among the waters, dividing the super-celestial waters from the waters under the heaven; there he sufficiently reveals the nature of the "middle," just as we abundantly declared in the preface of the first book and the second chapter of the fifth.

<summary>Pico identifies and explains various modes of universal connection (affinity) found in Genesis, including part/whole relationships, cause/effect, and the role of "middle" natures that bridge extremes.</summary>

We are warned from this very point what we must do: that we may be united to better natures, in which the whole power and summit of our happiness is placed. For the first day also teaches us that light then first arose when the night was driven from the waters, when the spirit of the Lord hovered over them. From this is signified that saying of James: *Every best gift is from above, from the Father of lights.* <note>original: "Omne optimum donum desuper esse a patre luminum." See James 1:17. Pico argues that all human wisdom and virtue are gifts from God, not inherent human achievements.</note> Even if I do not mention our own Christian authors, Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the importance of theurgy, or ritual acts, to achieve union with the divine.</note> confirms this so strongly that he wishes human nature to promise itself nothing, not even anything mediocre, from its own power unless it is aided by a greater—that is, a divine—power.

If this is true, and proven not only by our own writers but also by the philosophers, then certainly all our zeal ought to be focused on this: that having turned toward higher things—which happens through sacred religion, through mysteries, through vows, through hymns, prayers, and supplications—we may seek strength from there for our weakness. Hence, Platonic and Pythagorean disputations, begun with sacred prayers, end in the same. Regarding these, Porphyry, Theodore <note>Likely Theodore of Asine, a student of Iamblichus.</note>, and all the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of the Platonic Academy in Athens.</note> confirm with one voice that nothing is more useful, or rather more necessary, for man. We read that the Brahmans of the Indians and the Magi of the Persians never attempted anything unless prayer was first sent ahead. 

I bring these testimonies of the nations for this reason: so that those who have been persuaded by an evil demon to believe the pagans rather than the Church might at least learn from those in whom they place faith. They should learn that it is neither a laughable, nor useless, nor unworthy thing for a philosopher to take up labor—and indeed a great and assiduous one—in sacred prayers, in mysteries, in vows, and in hymns to be sung continually to God. If this practice helps and suits any kind of men especially, it is particularly useful and fitting for those who have devoted themselves to the study of letters and the leisure of contemplation. For them, nothing is more necessary than that they purify with integrity of life those eyes of the mind which they repeatedly fix upon divine things. They must illuminate them more abundantly with light sought from above through the <term>staff of prayer|original: "ferulam orationis." The 'ferula' or giant fennel stalk is a classical symbol of a conduit or support, perhaps alluding to Prometheus bringing fire to humanity.</term>, and being always reminded of their own weakness, say with the Apostle: *Our sufficiency is from God.* <note>original: "sufficientia nostra ex deo est." See 2 Corinthians 3:5.</note>

### **Chapter Six.**

<margin>A deeper mystery</margin>

Again, let us examine what the arrangement of the water and the earth teaches us. Let us learn from the earth that we will not produce the fruit for which we labor unless we repress the onslaught of flowing and decaying matter that invades us. We must drive away and expel from our seats the whirlpools and torrents of pleasures rushing into us like waters. Let us learn from the waters that they were not considered suitable for procreating fish until they were gathered into the single integrity of their whole element. For neither will we be able to bring forth into the light any offspring worthy of our divinity <note>Pico often refers to the "divinity" of the human soul as its capacity to mirror and return to God.</note> if we are torn apart and distracted toward diverse things, and if we are not carried with all our gathered forces toward a single intention.

Here also a deeper mystery is contained: just as for drops of water there is this happiness, that they may reach the ocean where there is the fullness of waters, so our happiness is that the portion of intellectual light which is in us [should reach] the first...

### **Chapter Seven.**

But the greatest point of all is that which the doctrine of the firmament signifies to us: where we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit of the higher waters except by the mediation of the sky, which is placed as a medium between them. Thus we should set before our minds that the coupling of extremes cannot happen except through that nature which, being the medium between extremes, embraces both within itself. Therefore, it conveniently unites those extremes among themselves because it first united them within itself through the property of its own nature. 

We are reminded here of that great sacrament which is foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Hebrews, but to us is the power and wisdom of God: <note>original: "gentibus stultitia hebreis scandalum nobis dei uirtus & sapientia est." This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:23-24. Pico is applying the cosmological structure of the "firmament" to the theological role of Christ.</note> that man cannot be joined to God except through Him who, <margin>Man cannot be joined to God except through Christ, God and man</margin> having joined man to God within Himself, has been made the true mediator. He is thus able to connect men to God so that, just as in Him the Son of God put on man, so through Him men may become the sons of God. 

If what we say is true—that extremes are not coupled to each other except through a medium, and that which is truly called a medium is that which has already united the extremes within itself—then surely if that ineffable dispensation occurs in Christ alone (so that the Word became flesh), then Christ alone is also He through whom flesh can ascend to the Word. Nor is there (as John correctly wrote) <note>Pico attributes this quote to John, but it is found in the speech of Peter in Acts 4:12.</note> <margin>John</margin> any other name under heaven in which it is necessary for men to be saved. Let those who say they believe in Christ take diligent note of this, yet believe that a common religion—either their own or that into which each was born—is sufficient for attaining happiness. <margin>Paul, Christ</margin> Let them believe not me, nor these arguments, but John, and Paul, and Christ Himself, who said: *I am the way.* and *I am the door; he who does not enter through me is a thief and a robber.* <note>See John 14:6 and John 10:1-9.</note>

->**THE SEVENTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING HAPPINESS WHICH IS ETERNAL LIFE.**<-

### **Preface to the Seventh Book.**

If we have completed the order and nature of the levels of the whole world in the finished sixth exposition as if in six days, it remains that in this seventh treatise—as if in the Sabbath of our commentary—we should treat the Sabbath of the world and the rest of the creatures whose nature we established in the preceding parts. That is, we shall treat their happiness; or (to say it more correctly), let us listen to Moses as he speaks as a true prophet of all future things. 

Now, there is one kind of happiness (as the theologians preach) <margin>Twofold happiness</margin> which we can attain through nature, and another which we can attain through grace. They call the former "natural" and the latter "supernatural." Concerning the first, that is, natural happiness, enough has been said by Moses, since once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. It remains, therefore, for him to teach concerning the second, exhibiting himself as a prophet rather than a teacher; for when Moses wrote, grace did not yet exist, but it was to come.

But since I seem to see certain pseudo-intellectuals—or should I rather call them scoundrels and rascals—who call themselves philosophers when they are nothing of the sort, immediately laughing at both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales, I wished to create a brief dispute with them on this matter as a preface to the seventh book. This task is both useful to all in its own right and very necessary for the work we have undertaken, where we may clearly prove that the opinion of theologians stands firm, supported by the deepest roots of philosophy.

<margin>How true and stable is the opinion of theologians concerning supernatural happiness</margin> I define happiness in this way: the return of each thing to its own principle <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "principle" refers to the source or origin from which a thing originates; Pico argues that true fulfillment comes from returning to that source.</note>. For happiness is the supreme good, and the supreme good is that which all things desire. Now, that which all things desire is that very thing which is the principle of all things, as Alexander of Aphrodidias <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD) was a celebrated commentator on Aristotle.</note> <margin>Alexander</margin> testifies in his commentaries on the *First Philosophy* and as the Greek interpreters <margin>Greek interpreters</margin> attest in their works on Aristotle’s *Ethics*. Therefore, the end of all things is the same as the principle of all things: the one God, almighty and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be imagined. Hence, two primary names are given to Him among the Pythagoreans: <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> namely, "the One" and "the Good." <margin>Two names of God</margin> He is called "the One" because He is the principle of all, just as unity is the principle of all number; He is called "the Good" because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness.

<margin>The root of double happiness</margin> If we are a little more discerning, we can now see the reason for a double happiness. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this first Good. Created things can attain this Good in two ways: either in themselves or in God Himself. For this Good is both exalted above all things, dwelling in the depths of its own divinity, and is also found diffused through all things. In the former, it exists more perfectly; in the latter, less perfectly, according to the condition of the things that participate in it. Whence (as the poets write), "Jupiter is whatever you see," and "all things are full of Jupiter." <margin>Poets</margin> <note>original: "Iuppiter est quodcunque uides: & Iouis omnia plena sunt." This combines a thought from the poet Lucan with a famous line from Virgil’s *Eclogues*, suggesting God's presence is woven through all creation.</note> Therefore, since every nature has God within it in some way—because it possesses as much of God as it possesses of goodness (and all things which God made are good)—it follows that when a nature possesses its own being, perfected in every part, <margin>What natural happiness is</margin> it has attained itself and thus attains the God within itself. And if the attainment of God is, as we have proven, happiness, then that thing is in some way happy in itself. This is **natural happiness**, which different things have received as a greater or lesser lot according to the diversity of their natures.

Fire is a thing lacking a soul, yet it participates in God in many ways. <margin>In what way fire participates in God</margin> For first, it *is*, and everything that *is* participates in God, who is Being itself. Likewise, insofar as fire is a certain species and an "act," <term>act (actus)</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to a thing's realization or its functioning state, as opposed to mere potential.</note> it is similar to God, who is the first species and the first act. While fire produces fire, it imitates divine fecundity; while it contains itself within the boundaries of its sphere, it imitates justice; while it serves us, it imitates beneficence, according to the measure of its own nature. When fire performs these things, having attained its own perfection, it is happy insofar as it is capable of happiness. Plants are happier, for they possess life in addition; animals are happier still, for they have also received the lot of cognition. As they find more perfection, so they find more of the divinity within themselves.

<margin>Man is in the best condition of all mortals</margin> Man is in the best condition of all mortals: just as he excels others in nature, so he excels them in natural happiness, being endowed with intelligence and freedom of the will—special gifts most conducive to happiness. The angelic mind is supreme among creatures, both in the nobility of its substance and in the attainment of its end, of which it is the greatest participant because it is both joined and closest to Him. But...

<meta>This page continues the preface to the Seventh Book of the Heptaplus. Truly, as we said above, through this [natural] happiness, neither plants, nor beasts, nor man, nor angels reach God (who is the supreme good) in God Himself, but rather reach Him in themselves. <margin>On the imperfection of natural happiness / The opinion of the philosophers concerning happiness</margin> Therefore, according to the capacity of their various natures, the character of happiness varies step by step. For this reason, the philosophers—who spoke only of this [natural] happiness—placed the happiness of each thing in the best operation of its own nature. Regarding the angels, whom they call "minds" and "intellects": even if they admitted that their highest perfection was to understand God, they still established no other knowledge of God than that by which the angels know themselves; thus, they understand only as much of God as is represented of God's nature within their own substance.

Concerning man, however, although different thinkers have held different views, they all kept themselves within the narrow bounds of human faculty. <margin>Academics / Al-Farabi / Averroes / Avicenna / Abubacher / Alexander / Platonists</margin> They defined human happiness either in the search for truth itself—as the *Academics* <note>The Academics were followers of the school of Plato, who at certain periods emphasized the search for truth over the claim of possessing it.</note> did—or rather in its attainment through the study of philosophy, as *Al-Farabi* <note>Al-Farabi (c. 872–950) was a renowned early Islamic philosopher who integrated Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note> said. *Averroes*, *Avicenna*, *Abubacher* <note>original: "Abubacher"; refers to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajja, known in Latin as Avempace.</note>, *Alexander*, and the *Platonists* seemed to grant something more, fixing our reason in the "intellect which is in act" <note>A technical term in medieval philosophy for the "Active Intellect," a higher state of consciousness or a cosmic mind that enables human understanding.</note> or in some higher power related to us as its end; but not even these thinkers lead man back to his own beginning nor to the supreme good.

I neither reject nor despise these disputes and opinions of theirs, provided they profess to speak only of natural happiness. For it is certain that through such happiness, neither man nor angels can be raised higher than what these philosophers say. <margin>Man cannot be joined to God by his own powers</margin> This is proven especially by this reasoning: since anything relying on its own strength cannot rise above itself (otherwise it would be more powerful than itself), surely nothing striving for happiness by its own means will be able to attain anything greater or more perfect than its own nature.

But let the philosophers tell me: if this is the only happiness in things, why do even they admit that among animals, only man is born for happiness? <margin>He argues for supernatural happiness</margin> Since things other than man also reach their own ends, we might say that the happiness of other creatures is less than that of man; but how shall we defend the idea that they have *no* happiness at all? Indeed, since other creatures below man never stray from the end established by nature, while man almost always goes astray, the human condition will seem the most unhappy of all unless man can boast of some other privilege.

Let us hear, therefore, the sacred *theologians* <margin>Theologians</margin> reminding us of our dignity, and of the divine goods offered to us freely by the most generous Father; let us not, I pray, be cruel to our own souls and ungrateful toward God the Maker by rejecting them. We said above that the height of happiness lies in the attainment of God, who is the supreme good and the source of all. <margin>The difference between supernatural and natural happiness</margin> This attainment can happen in two ways: either we reach God through His creatures (in whom God shares Himself) or we reach God in God Himself.

We have likewise shown—and shall show—that created things cannot reach this latter state [supernatural happiness] by their own powers, but can only approach the former [natural happiness]. <margin>Natural happiness does not possess the character of true happiness</margin> If we pay attention, the former is a shadow of happiness rather than true happiness, just as the creature in whom you reach God is not the supreme goodness itself, but only a thin shadow of that divine goodness. Add to this that through natural happiness, things are restored to themselves rather than to God; they have not achieved a return to their own source, but only the preservation of their own being. True and perfected happiness, however, leads us back and draws us away to gaze upon the face of God—which is "every good," as He Himself said—and to a perfect union with that Principle from which we first flowed forth. Toward this, the angels...

<margin>Who are capable of supernatural happiness and how</margin> They can indeed be raised up, but they cannot ascend by their own power. This is why Lucifer sinned, saying: "I will ascend into heaven" <note>original: "Ascendam in caelum." A reference to Isaiah 14:13, where the King of Babylon/Lucifer expresses the pride of wanting to reach God's level by his own will.</note>. Toward this supernatural happiness, man cannot walk on his own; he can only be drawn. Hence Christ, who is happiness itself, said of himself: "No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him" <note>John 6:44.</note>. But the beasts and those things below man can neither go to it nor be drawn to it. Therefore, only man and the angel were made for that happiness which is true happiness.

<margin>An example of both types of happiness in bodies</margin> A vapor can rise on high, but only if it is attracted by a ray of the sun. Conversely, a stone or any bulky substance can neither admit the ray throughout itself nor be lifted up by it into the heights. This "ray," this divine power, this influx, we call "grace," because it makes both man and angel pleasing <term>gratos<note>Pico is playing on the Latin linguistic connection between "gratia" (grace) and "gratos" (pleasing or grateful).</note></term> to God. 

The philosophers have a clear example of this teaching in physical bodies. For some bodies are moved in a straight line, while others are moved in a circle. Straight motion, by which the elements are carried to their own proper places, represents that happiness through which things are established in the perfection of their own nature. Circular motion, through which a body revolves back to the same point from which it departed, is the most expressive image of true happiness, through which the creature returns to the same Beginning from which it had first proceeded. 

But see how all things agree on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle. Similarly, only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. For the elements to complete their movements, they need no power other than the impulse of either heaviness or lightness implanted in them from their origin; just as for natural happiness, each thing is carried by its own impulse and its own power. 

But the celestial bodies, although suited for circular motion, are not sufficient in themselves to complete this movement; instead, they have need of a divine Mover who may turn and revolve them. Finally, those bodies are so perpetually fit for rotation that they do not *produce* it, but rather *receive* it. It happens no differently for us and for the angels. For we are such by nature that we cannot turn ourselves around and reflect ourselves back [to our source], but we can be turned around by the moving power of grace and be reflected into God. 

Hence the saying: "Those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God" <note>Romans 8:14.</note>. He said "those who are led," not "those who lead." In this we differ from the heavens: they move by the necessity of nature, but we move by our own freedom. For the moving Spirit beats constantly upon your soul. If you refuse to listen <note>original: "ob audias." Pico likely uses this to mean hearing "against" or ignoring the call.</note>, you are left to yourself, to your own sluggishness and your own weakness, wretched and unhappy. If you admit the Spirit, you are immediately full of God and carried back through the circle of religion to the Father and the Lord, to possess life forever in Him—in whom you were always "life" even before you were created. 

<margin>The summary of true happiness</margin> This is true happiness: that we may be one spirit with God; that we may possess God in God, not in ourselves, knowing just as we are known. For He knew us not through us, but through Himself; so also we shall know Him through Him, and not through ourselves. This is the whole reward; this is eternal life; this is the wisdom which the wise men of the world did not know: that we are brought back from all the imperfection of multiplicity into unity through an indissoluble bond with Him who is Oneness itself. 

<margin>Christ</margin> For this happiness Christ prayed to the Father in this way: "Father, grant that just as I and You are one, so also these may be one with us" <note>John 17:21.</note>. <margin>Paul</margin> This is what Paul hoped for, saying: "I shall know not in part, but just as He is" <note>A variation on 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note>; and since he hoped for this, did he not rightly say: "Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?" and desire to be dissolved so that he might become one with Christ? <margin>The fall of the demon</margin> From this happiness the demon fell, because...

He wished to ascend to that [happiness] rather than be carried to it; and therefore he lost that which he would have possessed if he had remained <note>Pico is continuing the discussion of Lucifer, who tried to reach divine heights through his own pride rather than through God's grace.</note>.

From this root, the fate of infants who died before being initiated is made known. <margin>The lot of infants who die before being initiated</margin> Namely, they remain within themselves: neither stripped of their own natural goods, nor enriched by divine ones <note>Pico refers to the "Limbo of Infants," a theological concept where those who die without baptism (initiation) do not suffer the pains of hell but do not enjoy the supernatural vision of God, remaining instead in a state of natural happiness.</note>. For us, we must fall into one of two states: either the greatest misery or the greatest happiness. Since one who is not yet initiated and is himself the cause of not receiving the "mover" <term>motorem<note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "Mover" is the force that initiates motion; here, Pico uses it to describe God or Grace moving the soul toward salvation.</note></term>, not only makes himself immune to grace but also vitiates <note>To vitiate is to spoil or impair the quality of something.</note> his own nature. To the integrity of nature belongs this: that it should seek the recognized Spirit and not refuse it. Beyond doubt, a nature cannot be upright if it either rejects or despises the hope of a greater good set before it.

Therefore, after Christ has been made known, if any do not "put on Christ," they are deprived not only of the first happiness but also of the second—that is, they lose their natural rights. For to be unwilling to receive grace belongs only to a nature that is corrupt and failing. Just as we who live under the Gospel receive Christ—the power and wisdom of God—into ourselves, because we love and hold onto him as already given to the human race, so too did the Fathers under the Old Law receive him, since they both believed in his future coming without doubt and hoped for it eagerly, desiring it with ardor.

But just as they received him not as present but as future, so they did not experience the fruit of the indwelling Spirit as present until after he arrived. When, after that ineffable sacrifice was performed on the altar of the cross, and Christ descended to them, they were moved by him as their "mover" <note>This refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," the tradition that Christ descended into the Limbo of the Patriarchs to liberate the righteous souls of the Old Testament.</note> in a whirlwind moment toward liberty, and were carried up to the level of the highest happiness.

Religion promotes, directs, and impels us toward this happiness, just as we use philosophy as our guide toward natural happiness. But if nature is the foundation of grace, <margin>Philosophy is the beginning of religion and does not separate man from religion</margin> then surely philosophy is the beginning of religion; nor is that true philosophy which separates man from religion. Rightly, therefore, we too—following Moses, after we have philosophized for six days about nature—will speak on the seventh day about supernatural happiness, devoting ourselves to divine things.

### Chapter One.

As we have shown, two natures are capable of this supreme happiness: the angelic and the human. <margin>Angelic and human nature are capable of supreme happiness</margin> The former is called "heaven," the latter "earth," because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. And there is no need to say more about heaven, because [Moses] was going to write a law not for angels, but for men. Therefore, descending to men, he says: *The earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep* <note>Genesis 1:2.</note>.

God does not create emptiness, nor does he create darkness; but the earth, he says, *was* empty and there *was* darkness. He does not say these things were created, but that they existed. Why this was said will become clear as soon as we understand what this emptiness and this darkness are. Human nature—which is called "earth" when compared to the angels—right from the beginning (because it sinned immediately) was empty and void of original justice, and its "face"—that is, its reason—was covered by the darkness of sin. God did not do these things; rather, they were caused by the malice of man, who willfully deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him.

Thus the state of corrupted nature is described by the prophet <note>Referring to Moses as the prophetic author of Genesis.</note>; [and we shall see] in what way it was then [restored] by God through Abraham, through Moses, through the prophets, and finally through the Only-Begotten [Son].

## Chapter Two

<margin>The Mosaic Law</margin> The Law followed him, which is deservedly called by the name "Firmament" <note>The "Firmament" refers to the sky or expanse created on the second day of Genesis (Gen 1:6-8).</note> at its very beginning, by this very fact which we are now discussing: announcing to us the works of God's hands (as David sang: *and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands* <note>original: "et opera manuū eius annuntiat firmamentū"; Psalm 19:1.</note>). Therefore, the Law was given through an angel to Moses, confirmed by the word of God; it discriminated even more than the previous light between the nations and the Israelites—that is, between piety and impiety—just as the "waters above the heavens" were divided from the "waters which are under the heaven." <margin>Jeremiah</margin> Now, the Jews are called "waters above the heavens" because they alone (as Jeremiah says <note>Jeremiah 10:2: "Do not learn the way of the nations; do not be terrified by signs in the heavens."</note>) do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear. They do not worship the stars or the sky, but they both recognize and, having recognized, worship and venerate the Author and Lord of the stars and the sky. The nations, however, by a contrary reasoning, are "waters under the heaven," since they adore and worship the demons who inhabit the murky air (which region is above the waters) and they make the visible sky, the stars, and the planets their gods and lords.

## Chapter Three

It was to be, however, that unless some greater power and mercy of God stood in the way, the "waters which are under the heaven"—that is, those serving idols—would invade and occupy the whole earth. Thus the infection of the entire world from the first stain, and the empire and right of Satan the Avenger over us (guilty as we were of the ancient offense and subject to the punishment of this kind of servitude), demanded it. But the always beneficial and saving providence of God willed that one part of the earth, even if small, should be free from the injury of the waters, as much as the laws of justice allowed. This is called Judea, the Land of Promise, because it was promised by God to Abraham and his posterity.

...[they worshipped the true God] and cultivated the true religion: but it was incipient and imperfect until he should come who is the **way, the truth, and the life.** <note>original: "via veritas & vita." For by that same reasoning, it would have been much more necessary for fish, birds, and all the adornment of the elements to be made before the sun, lest they be believed to have been made by its power. Moses would therefore have left a suspicion: that even if the sun's light had not been necessary for producing plants (being imperfect things), it was nonetheless needed for producing animals, which are more perfect. For it follows that if more perfect things had come into the light without the sun's help, those things which are less perfect could also be made without it. However, the reasoning is not reciprocal: it does not follow that if those things which are more ignoble were made without it—such as plants, the most humble <note>original: "despicatissimum," meaning least regarded or most basic in the hierarchy of life.</note> kind of living things—then every kind of animal nature could also have been produced without its intervention.

Therefore, the author’s [Moses’s] purpose is more truly investigated through what we have said. Similarly, if someone considers the living things related to the waters that dwell in the waters, he will see that one kind rather than two ought to have been referred to them, and two kinds to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. And beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal; it is in no way an aquatic one.

### Chapter Six

The resolution of the question which has long tormented the interpreters of this book is also manifest from this: <margin>Why it was not said on the second day "that it was good"</margin> Why was it not said on the second day: *and God saw that it was good*? If we say what is usually said—that it was done because the work of the waters was not completed on that day, but on the third, when the waters which are under the heaven flowed together into one place—it will seem that the question has hardly been fully satisfied. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the firmament, which was made firm in the middle place between the waters. On that day, there was both the making of the firmament, when God said, "Let there be a firmament," and the distinction of the waters, when he said, "and let it divide the waters from the waters," which was quite complete. However, the collection of the waters which is called the sea, and the revealing of the earth, and the production of plants, just as they have the character of another work entirely, so they were completed on another—that is, the third—day to which they belonged. 

Therefore, a reason must be sought from a deeper mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) prefigures the Law. <margin>A paradoxical dogma of the ancient Hebrews</margin>

Let us take, for example, the first small part of the Book of Genesis, namely from the beginning up to the place where it is written: *And God saw the light, that it was good.* <note>Genesis 1:4.</note> All that scripture is joined together from one hundred and three elements <note>The author uses "elements" to refer to individual Hebrew letters.</note>, which, arranged in the way they are there, constitute the words we read, presenting nothing but the common and trivial. <margin><unclear>Bark and Marrow</unclear></margin>

But if we take those same elements, pulled apart once the words are broken down, and correctly join together the words that can be fashioned from them according to the rules they themselves hand down, they say that—if we are capable of such enclosed wisdom—wonderful and most secret dogmas concerning many things will shine forth to us. If this were done throughout the whole Law, then finally, from this correctly established position and connection of the elements, all doctrine and the secrets of all the liberal arts <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy) were the foundation of classical and medieval education.</note> would be brought to light. 

I said, however, *if we are capable of such enclosed wisdom.* For it can happen that while we are breaking down and reassembling these words, many terms and complex sequences of speech may be produced which teach and signify great things; but unless someone has already obtained knowledge of that subject elsewhere, he will not understand what they signify. <meta>This page transitions from the abstract philosophical and Kabbalistic discussions of the previous page to a direct, personal address. Pico della Mirandola is here dedicating his "Apologia" (his formal defense) to his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, following the controversy surrounding his 900 theses in Rome.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI, GREETINGS.

I have dedicated my **Apology** <note>original: *Apologiam*; a formal defense of his ideas, written after several of his 900 theses were condemned by a papal commission.</note> to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, so that—I call God to witness—I might offer a work not because I deem it worthy of such a great man, but because it is owed to you by that same right by which I have long understood that I owe all my things to you. For you should be most firmly persuaded of this: that whatever I either am or am to be in the future, it is yours, Lorenzo, and shall always remain yours hereafter. I say less than I would wish, and these words are altogether too cold to sufficiently express what I feel: namely, with what love, with what faith, and with what respect I honor you, and have honored you for many years now. I am moved both by the many kindnesses you have bestowed upon me—which clearly testify to your most loving spirit—and by those gifts of yours, not so much of fortune as of the soul; those same rare and indeed peculiar virtues of yours which your own modesty does not permit me to recount at present. 

I return to the **Apology**: I ask that you receive it with a cheerful countenance. It is indeed a meager gift, but truly a significant testimony of my loyalty and respect toward you for all time. If it should happen that you set aside for a moment the great affairs with which you are always most busily occupied to touch upon this work, remember that this is a work produced in haste <note>original: *properatum*; Pico wrote the Apology in a matter of weeks to defend himself against charges of heresy.</note> rather than one highly polished, and that the subject matter of the work had to be taken from the judgment of others, not my own. I did not dedicate it to you so that you might recognize in me an excellence of talent or learning which I do not possess, but so that I might know—for I shall say it again—that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your greatness.

## THE APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

When I had recently come to Rome, I kissed the feet of the Supreme Pontiff, **Innocent VIII** <margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff.</margin>—whose name is most well-deserved because of the innocence of his life—according to the custom of the Church. At the same time, so as not to depart from my established practice of always composing or treating something regarding literary matters, and to perform a task to the best of my ability that was worthy of the city of Rome, pleasing to a Christian prince, and useful to myself and to scholars, I proposed **nine hundred questions** <note>original: *nōgentas... questiones*; these are Pico's famous "900 Theses," intended to cover all branches of knowledge and find a common truth between them.</note> concerning divine and natural things. These I was prepared to answer in a public assembly of the most learned men. 

Hardly had they appeared in public when, among some who might have approved at least of my talent or learning or my study of the liberal arts, there arose a manifold crowd of detractors. And indeed, one could see the various distastes, the sneering, the censures, and all the differing judgments of every individual, as always happens when we attempt something new and not trivial. Nevertheless, there were about five principal points which these whisperers, one after another, condemned in me. For some carped at philosophy and letters altogether—even so that they might appear to be "know-it-alls"—sometimes adding that Adam was cast out of paradise because he wished to make himself equal to the gods through the **knowledge of good and evil** <note>A reference to the Fall of Man in Genesis, used by Pico's critics to argue that seeking deep knowledge is a sin of pride.</note>. By a similar example, they argued that those who wish to know more than is fitting should be banished from the court of Christ. Others did not so much disapprove of philosophy as of this very kind of disputing and this practice of publicly debating about literature, suggesting it was done for **display** <note>original: *pompā*; meaning ostentation or showing off.</note> rather than for...

For at this age—having not yet reached my twenty-fourth year <note>Pico was born in 1463; he was 23 when he published the 900 Theses in late 1486.</note>—I did not hesitate to propose a disputation in the most celebrated city [Rome], in a vast assembly of the most learned men, concerning the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines. Many accused me—calumniating that this was done superfluously, ambitiously, and beyond my strength—not only because it was in Rome, but because I was a young man and was going to dispute so great a number, namely, nine hundred questions. Among those who professed the study of wisdom—that is, the study of theology—there were some who, not content with perhaps lighter insults, proclaimed me to be not merely bold, rash, or boastful, but a magician, an impious man, and a new <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A leader or founder of a heretical movement.</note> in the Church of Christ.

I was (I call God to witness) long in doubt whether I should refute these objections or if they should rather be passed over in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent. First, that I, abhorring both contention and quarrels, have always loved the peace of the soul and the tranquility of a most placid life, which my studies have provided for me; nor do I hate any task of writing more than that which is established in dispute and bitter altercation of any kind. Indeed, I have never considered it the part of a good man or a philosopher to return an injury or an insult any more than to inflict one. The second reason was this: I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff—whose memory I must always worthily celebrate—and of many from the most holy <term>Apostolic Senate</term> <note>The College of Cardinals.</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can and should never forget. It seemed I could easily ignore the hatred and insults of wicked men; and indeed, as for the rest, I was of the opinion that I should consider them unworthy of any response.

But in the case of the single charge of heresy leveled against me, I feared that if I did this [remained silent], I would seem to acknowledge a crime that I did not refute. Moreover, **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), a monk and translator known for his work on Origen and his eventual conflict with Jerome.</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to follow Christ’s example by patiently enduring insults; but he who bears or ignores a mark of heresy is not a Christian. And our **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), the primary translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, with the greatest possible effort of mind, exclaims in a most clear voice: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under suspicion of heresy." <note>original: *Nolo in suspitione hereseos quemquam esse patientem.*</note> Therefore, Jerome does not want me to keep silent, and by his authority, he draws and compels an unwilling and idle man to write. Therefore, if there are those who perhaps wish I would stay silent, let them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to be silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace?

Therefore, at his persuasion—indeed, his compulsion—I have undertaken to write a brief **Apology**. I do so not to tear down or accuse anyone, but so that I may rightly excuse myself from the great crime of impiety which is unjustly cast against me. This, I pray, my detractors will endure with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. Let them endure it, I say, so that I—who was born a Christian of Christian parents, who bear the banner of Jesus Christ on my forehead, and who would gladly die for the faith of Christ—may exclaim, as if with **Paul**, while they listen with an even mind: "I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note>, no heretic. But I worship Jesus and carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world." <note>A paraphrase of Galatians 6:14: "May I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."</note> Finally, since I [cannot claim] for myself those distinguished titles of either sanctity or wisdom...

<meta>Pico continues his defense of his nine hundred theses. On the previous page, he addressed his love for philosophy; here, he explains why he chose to engage in such a massive intellectual debate and why he refuses to follow just one school of thought.</meta>

...[I knew] this kind of battle—namely, literary ones—to be unique in that winning is found in being defeated. Thus it happens that even the weakest person can and should, by right, not only not refuse such battles, but seek them out of their own accord. For truly, he who yields receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; for through the victor, he returns home wealthier—that is, more learned—and better prepared for future battles. Inspired by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared to enter into such a serious contest with the strongest and most vigorous of all. 

Whether this was done rashly or not, one could judge better by the outcome of the battle than by my young age. It remains for me to respond to those who are offended by the sheer number of the topics proposed, as if this burden sat upon their shoulders and not rather upon mine alone, however much labor had to be exhausted <note>original: *exanclandus*, a term often used for draining a vessel or enduring a hardship.</note>. 

<margin>Cicero</margin> It is surely unbecoming and too peevish to wish to set a limit on another's industry, and, as Cicero says, to desire moderation in a matter that is better the greater it is. If I were to satisfy them, I do not see why something that is praiseworthy when performed in ten questions should be considered blameworthy when performed in nine hundred. If I were to fail, they would have grounds to accuse me if they hate me, or grounds to excuse me if they love me. 

Since in a matter so serious and so great, it was more worthy of pardon than accusation for a young man of slender talent and meager learning to have failed; indeed, as the poet says: "if strength fails, the daring will certainly be praised, and in great things, to have willed is enough" <note>This is a reference to the Roman poet Propertius.</note>.

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a way that is not superfluous, but necessary; which they themselves, if they consider my method of philosophizing, must clearly admit, even if unwillingly. 

<margin>Thomas, Scotus</margin> For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the "families" of philosophers—namely to Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the champion of Scholasticism.</note> or Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, another major figure in medieval philosophy.</note>, who are now most often in people's hands—can indeed test their learning even in the discussion of a few questions. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them, lest—as a defender of a private dogma—I should seem bound to one while neglecting the rest. It was impossible, even if only a few things were proposed from each, for there not to be a very great many when all were brought forward together.

<meta>Pico continues his argument for the universality of truth. Having previously justified his study of diverse traditions (Latin, Arabic, and Greek), he now details his specific project: synthesizing these disparate voices into a unified "concord" and introducing his own original philosophical contributions, specifically through the use of mathematical symbolism.</meta>

Just as a husband hates barrenness in his wife, surely the divine mind—entwined and associated with the soul for so long—hates a soul that is unfertile even more, for a far more noble offspring is desired from that union. Therefore, not content with common doctrines, I have added many things from the ancient theology of **Hermes Trismegistus**, <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom a body of secret, mystical "Hermetic" wisdom was attributed.</note> many from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** and of **Pythagoras**, and many from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews**. We have also proposed for debate many things discovered and meditated upon by ourselves concerning natural and divine matters.

We have first proposed a harmony <note>original: "concordiam"</note> between **Plato** and **Aristotle**, <margin>The harmony of Plato and Aristotle</margin> which many before this time believed in but no one has sufficiently proven. <margin>Simplicius</margin> **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher; his project to harmonize Plato and Aristotle was cut short by his execution.</note> among the Latins promised he would do it, but he is never found to have performed what he always wished to do. <margin>Augustine</margin> **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note> among the Greeks made the same profession; would that he had fulfilled his promise as well as he made it! <margin>John the Grammarian</margin> **Augustine** also writes in the *Against the Academicians* that there were several who attempted to prove the same thing in their most subtle disputations: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is one and the same. Likewise, **John the Grammarian** <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator; he argued that those who see contradictions between the two thinkers merely misunderstand Plato's figurative language.</note> says that only those think Plato and Aristotle differ who do not understand Plato’s words; yet he left the proof of this to posterity. <margin>Note</margin> We have further added several passages in which we assert that the opinions of **Duns Scotus** and **Thomas Aquinas**, and several in which the opinions of **Averroes** and **Avicenna**, which are thought to be discordant, are in fact in harmony.

In the second place, we have set forth our own reflections on both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, <margin>New dogmas devised</margin> as well as seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas. If anyone holds these, he will be able—unless I am mistaken—to resolve any question proposed concerning natural and divine things by a reasoning far different from the philosophy that is taught in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. <margin>Note</margin>

Nor should anyone wonder that I, in my first years, in my tender age—during which it was hardly permitted, as some boast, to read the commentaries of others—wish to bring forward a new philosophy, whether to praise it if it is defended or to condemn it if it is rejected. Finally, since these discoveries are ours and our own writings, they <note>the critics</note> should judge the merits or demerits of the ideas rather than counting the years of the author.

There is, besides that, another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced. <margin>New institution of philosophizing through numbers</margin> This was indeed an ancient practice observed by the early theologians, <margin>Plato</margin> especially by **Pythagoras**, by **Aglaophemus**, <note>A legendary teacher of Pythagoras in the Orphic tradition.</note> by **Philolaus**, by **Plato**, and the earlier Platonists. But in this time, like other noble things, it has withered away through the neglect of those who followed, so that hardly any traces of it can be found. <margin>Aristotle</margin> **Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>original: "Epimonide"; a dialogue often attributed to Plato's student Philip of Opus.</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the chief and most divine is the science of numbering. <margin>Abunafar</margin> Likewise, asking why man is the wisest animal, he answers: because he knows how to count. **Aristotle** also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. <margin>Avenzoar</margin> **Abunafar** <note>Al-Farabi, the famous Islamic philosopher.</note> writes that it was a saying of **Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr, though here Pico may be citing a more mystical Babylonian tradition.</note> the Babylonian that "he knew all things who knew how to count." <margin>Plato</margin> These things can in no way be true if by the art of numbering they understood that art in which merchants today are most skilled. **Plato** himself testifies to this, warning us with a raised voice not to understand this "divine arithmetic" as the "arithmetic of merchants." To put this matter to the test, I have publicly promised to answer seventy-four questions—considered primary among the physical and divine sciences—using numbers. We have also proposed magical theorems, in which we indicate that magic is of two kinds. <meta>Pico continues his defense of "natural magic," contrasting it with demonic sorcery. Having established that the term "magus" originally referred to a worshiper of the divine, he now elaborates on how this true magic acts as a servant to nature and a tool for religious devotion, before transitioning to his second major topic: the secret Hebrew tradition of Kabbalah.</meta>

[margin: Note,]
Natural magic is so abhorrent to the demonic arts that when it is called to the rites of evil demons, it claims it would be more fitting for those demons to come to it than for it to approach them. And rightly so. For as the former art renders a man subject and enslaved to wicked powers, so this natural magic makes him their prince and master. Finally, that former practice cannot claim the name of art or science for itself. This latter magic, full of the highest mysteries, encompasses the deepest contemplation of the most secret things and, ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. Calling forth into the light—as if from hiding places—the virtues scattered by God's kindness and sown throughout the world, it does not so much perform miracles as it zealously assists nature as she performs them. Having scrutinized more deeply the consensus of the universe—which the Greeks more expressively call *sympathy* <note>original: "συμπαθειαν" (sympatheian) — the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the cosmos are interconnected and "feel" for one another.</note>—and having gained an insight into the mutual connection of natures, this magic applies to each thing its own native charms, which the magi call *iynxes* <note>original: "ιυγγεσ" (iynges) — derived from the Greek word for the "wryneck" bird; in magical tradition, these were spinning wheels or charms used to attract or bind cosmic influences.</note>. Thus, it brings out into the public view, as if it were the craftswoman herself, the miracles lying hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God. And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magus marries the earth to heaven—that is, he joins lower things to the gifts and virtues of higher things. Thus, just as the former art appears monstrous and harmful, so this natural magic appears divine and beneficial. Primarily for this reason: the former art, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; but this latter art excites in him such admiration for the works of God that 

[margin: What most
promotes the
religion of God]
charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God’s wonders. Not only the famous teachers of the Hebrews write of this, but also from our own writers, Ezra, Hilary, and Origen. They write that Moses received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity written in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. He was commanded by God to publish the Law to the people, but he was neither to commit the interpretation of the Law to writing nor to make it public. Instead, he was to reveal it only by word of mouth, with a great religious oath of silence, first to his successors and then to the leading priests in turn. And rightly so. For it was enough for the common people to recognize through simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all; and to be instructed by divine and salutary precepts for living well and happily in the worship of true religion. But the more secret mysteries, hidden under the outer shell of the Law and the rough covering of words...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's complex theological defense regarding how Christ’s soul was "present" in Hell. He is moving from a general discussion of heresy into a technical scholastic debate about how spirits (which have no bodies) can be said to be in a physical "place."</meta>

it is granted that being located or moving locally does not belong to [a spirit] except by reason of its operation. Therefore, I say that to have descended into hell or to have been in hell locally seems not to have belonged to Christ except by reason of His operation; so that, although the soul of Christ was truly and essentially present in hell, His substance itself was not the reason for that presence, but only His operation. 

<margin>A twofold opinion of those who posit that separate substances exist in a place through a transitory operation.</margin>

In order that these words may be more fully understood, it should be noted that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that <term>separate substances</term> <note>Scholastic term for beings without bodies, such as angels or the soul after it has left the body at death.</note> are not in a place except through a "transitory operation" <note>An action that passes from the doer to an external object.</note>. 

For some say that to incorporeal substances, by reason of their substance, no "place" is owed in any way. Just as a substance itself is never truly white or black, so according to them, it can not unreasonably be said of it that it is not in a place and is nowhere, just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. 

<margin>The first opinion.</margin>

As for the authorities of Scripture which seem to assign a place to angels when they say they are in heaven or are sent to this or that place, these should be understood as follows: not that they are here or there (since they are not properly in a place), but that they operate here or there, or begin to operate where they were not operating before. These thinkers rely heavily on the words of <margin>Gregory of Nyssa</margin> Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century theologian and Church Father.</note>, who says that while we ought to say the spirit "operates here," we improperly say it "is here." And so this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separate soul can never be said to be present to this place or that, except in a "negative" sense—meaning it is "not distant." But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere, that is the same as saying it operates or has operated somewhere. 

They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from bodily things. Because we see that bodies cannot act unless they are present (at least according to common opinion), we conclude that for incorporeal things, wherever they operate and where their operation is found, there also their substance is locally present. They conclude finally that it is a dullness of mind and a lack of imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a real being and yet not be in a place. They argue it is a frivolous argument to say that "being" presupposes "operating," for while it is true that a non-being cannot operate (since an agent must be in act), it is not true that operating in a place presupposes being in a place. This is because the operator may be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more applicable to it than whiteness or blackness. 

Those who hold this view would say that the soul of Christ, when separated from the body, according to its substance, was neither in hell nor outside of hell, but was truly nowhere. It is said to have been in hell because it operated in hell; and it is said to have been principally in that part of hell where it principally operated. Although many <term>doctors</term> <note>Specifically "Doctors of the Church" or high-ranking university theologians.</note> hold this opinion regarding the manner of being present in a place, I nevertheless do not hold it, nor have I followed it in my conclusion. Instead, I held the one I will immediately subjoin.

<margin>The second opinion, which the author held.</margin>

There is, therefore, another opinion which says that a separate substance—such as an angel or a soul not united to a body—is indeed truly in a place. It is truly present locally in a "definitive" way <note>original: "definitive"; in scholastic logic, this means a spirit is present in a specific space because its power is limited to that space, even though it doesn't have physical dimensions like a body.</note>, just as a bodily thing is locally present in a "commensurative" way <note>original: "commensurative"; this means the object's physical size exactly matches the space it occupies.</note>. 

<margin>The difference between this opinion and the opinion of the Scotists.</margin>

In this, this path agrees with the common path of Duns Scotus <note>A major 13th-century philosopher-theologian whose followers were called Scotists.</note> and all the Scotists. But they differ in this: the Scotists say that the definition and limitation of the essence—and ultimately the intrinsic determination of its substance—is the reason for a separate substance being in a place. However, this opinion which I have followed in my conclusion says that although a bodily substance is "commensuratively" in a place, the reason for its being in a place in such a way is not its "substantiality" but its "quantity," which is extrinsic...

external to the nature of its own substance. Thus, although an incorporeal substance may truly be "definitively" in a place and locally present, the reason for it being in that place is not its own substance, but rather its 

<margin>Declaration of the opinion</margin>

operation passing from itself to the outside. I judge that this opinion should be understood in the following way; and so understood, I judge it not only to be non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. This view holds that even if the finiteness or limitation of a <term>separate substance</term> <note>A being without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note> is the reason why it is not everywhere—or the reason why, if it is in one place, it cannot be in another place entirely at the same time by its own nature—nevertheless, its substance is not the reason for it being "simply" in a specific place. Here, "operation" refers to every relationship to a body or place that functions as an active or passive action, distinct from the way a physical object is present in a location. Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in hell only through His "effect," since He was not there except according to His soul. According to this opinion, one must say that just as it does not belong to a physical substance to be anywhere except through its physical dimensions, so it did not belong to that soul [of Christ] to be in hell (where He is believed to have been) except through His effect and operation. 

Consider the "reason for presence" for the souls of the <term>holy patriarchs</term> <note>The righteous figures from the Old Testament believed to be waiting in Limbo for Christ's arrival.</note>: their relationship to that place was a type of "transitory operation," specifically their detention and binding to that place until the door was opened by the Redeemer and they were led out. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his thesis. The previous page ended mid-word; the text here completes the word "arguments" and begins listing objections to Pico's view that a spirit’s presence in a place is defined by its actions (operations) rather than its essence.</meta>

...arguments <note>Completing the word "arguments" from the previous page.</note> which I have heard against this opinion. First, it is argued by the 204th Parisian Article <margin>Arguments against this opinion</margin> <note>Referring to the Condemnations of 1277, a list of 219 theological propositions forbidden by the Bishop of Paris to be taught at the university.</note>, which states that to say the substance of an angel is not in a place without an operation is an error. Second, it is argued because it is possible for a <term>separate substance</term> <note>A being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note> to perform no external operation. Given this <margin>First</margin> <margin>Second</margin> situation, one must ask whether that substance is somewhere, nowhere, or everywhere. It cannot be "nowhere," because even in this state it remains a part of the universe, and so it would be true to say that it is "in the world." It cannot be "everywhere," because that is a property <margin>Third</margin> unique to God. Therefore, it must be "somewhere." ...is present in a place unless it acts upon something or is acted upon by the place or by a thing existing in that place. <note>original: "Egidius"</note> **Giles of Rome** <note>A famous 13th-century theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> and many others say that one should not worry about those articles, because they were made without summoning all the doctors of Paris, but rather at the request of certain authorities. Whatever the case may be regarding this, I wish to say two things: First, that Article 218 supports our position no less than Article 204 might seem to oppose it. Second, that it is certain—and even the Parisians themselves admit this—that those articles do not bind all the faithful, nor are we required to believe them except insofar as they rely on Holy Scripture or the determinations of the universal Church. Hence the **English** scholars are accustomed to say that "those articles do not cross the sea" <note>A common medieval expression meaning that the local rulings of the Bishop of Paris did not have legal or theological standing in England.</note>; and so we, if one may joke in so grave a matter, can say that they "do not cross the Alps." Therefore, even if my conclusion were against such an article, those who were condemning me should remember that they erred entirely in their condemnation; for they claimed my conclusion was against the **Apostles' Creed**, when they ought to have said it was against the **"Parisian Creed"** <note>original: "simbolum Parisinum." Pico is using biting sarcasm here, suggesting his accusers have elevated local school-rules to the level of fundamental Christian dogma.</note>—and even that is false, as we have shown before.

It seems to me, however, that the true understanding of those articles is this: in Article 204, if it speaks of "operation" in the sense commonly accepted as described above, the intention is that even if all operation were excluded, the finiteness or limitation of a <term>separate nature</term> <note>An entity like an angel that exists without a physical body.</note> would still be the reason why it is not "everywhere," or the reason why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another whole place by its own nature. In Article 218, I believe the intention is that the substance (or the finiteness of the substance) is not the reason for an angel "being in a place" in a simple sense. By explaining the articles in this way, there is no contradiction, and the articles understood thus are not only not against my position, but they totally confirm it on both sides, as is clear from the explanation of the position set forth above.

To the **second argument**, many respond by granting that it is possible for an incorporeal substance to exist without an external "transitive operation" <note>An action that affects something outside the agent, like pushing a chair.</note>. Given this, the argument seems to suggest that one of three "inconveniences" (logical absurdities) must follow. The **first** is that, since the substance is a "part of the universe," it would be absurd for it to be "nowhere" in the universe. To this, they would say that the arguer uses the word "part" equivocally. For if by "part of the universe" one means something that has a determined position in the universe, they would say that an angel—whether acting or not acting—cannot be called a "part of the universe" in that sense. But if one means being a "part of all beings"—that is, one among the entities and natures of the universe—then they grant that it is a part of the universe, and indeed one of the most noble. But from this, it does not seem to follow that it must have a fixed position or a definition tied to a place.

The **second inconvenience** is that it cannot be said to be "everywhere," because that is unique to God. To this, it is said that to be "everywhere" in the way God is said by theologians to be everywhere by His essence—namely, through His power and presence—is unique to God and can belong to no created nature. However, whether "being everywhere" (meaning being here or there indifferently, or being everywhere by "non-distance"—that is, truly being according to substance without being distant from any place) is repugnant to a creature, you may hear **Henry of Ghent** <note>A major late 13th-century philosopher known as the "Solemn Doctor."</note> in his *Quodlibeta* (VII, question 9), speaking thus: In a creature, a **double limitation** can be understood. One is in its nature and essence, by which it is finite and contained within certain bounds; in this sense, only God is unlimited and infinite in nature. Another limitation of nature can be understood which is a limitation to **position**, by which it is so finite and contained within certain limits that it must be somewhere, and not "nowhere" nor "everywhere"; but rather, it is "so much here" that it is "not there," or even if it is not determinately here or there, it is still under the requirement of being either here, or there, or somewhere. This limitation belongs to the category of "Where," and every creature differs from God by that first limitation of nature...

To this third point, I say that their argument proceeds from a lack of full understanding of our position. For the position regarding the <margin>Operation</margin> operation through which an incorporeal thing is said to be located does not understand <margin>taken in two ways</margin> "operation" only as an external local motion or a real alteration—as we also touched upon in the response to the first point in the explanation of the Parisian article. These are the words of Thomas, verbatim. 

From these words, the response to the argument is clear: although angels have no operation toward the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens.</note> that constitutes local motion or real alteration, they nevertheless have something that functions by way of a "passing operation," such as presiding over it or something similar.

For when the essence of an angel is called "finite," "end" is taken as the limit of its essence and power—just as a definition is called a "term"—and not for the end of a physical dimension. A place, however, is called finite according to the three dimensions of quantity. An "end" in these two different senses has no shared measurement or proportion. Therefore, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence should be limited by the boundaries of a place. These are the literal words of Thomas.

From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, that Master is crude indeed, for he called his crude proof a "demonstration." Regarding the other reasoning concerning a "point," I say that it is even cruder than the first reasoning. For a point is a thing in the category of quantity, having a position by its very nature. For we know from logic that a sequence is not valid when it proceeds from the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent <note>A logical fallacy known as 'denying the antecedent.' Example: 'If it is a dog, it has four legs; it is not a dog, therefore it does not have four legs'—this is false because cats also have four legs.</note>. And so, although it is true that 'that which does not exist is nowhere,' it does not follow from this that 'that which exists is somewhere.' And although this does not follow from the words themselves, there are many who say that everything that exists is in some place, using the following reasoning: everything that exists is a particular thing; a particular thing is 'here and now'; and what is 'here and now' is somewhere; therefore, everything that exists is somewhere. Furthermore, everything that exists has a definite essence, because it is confined within its own limits; and what has a definite essence is defined in a place; and what is defined in a place is in some place."

Whatever is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it exists; however, an intelligence <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "intelligence" refers to a purely spiritual being, such as an angel or a disembodied soul.</note> by its own nature is not in a place, nor subject to any spatial distinction. <meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his eleventh thesis regarding Christ’s descent into Hell. On the previous page, he began to define the terms of his argument, specifically addressing the nature of spiritual "intelligence" and how it relates to physical space. He now moves into a technical linguistic and theological analysis of the word "presence."</meta>

...**presentially** <note>original: "presentialiter"; Pico is completing the sentence: "it is not required by faith to believe that Christ was presentially in Hell."</note> Christ was in [Hell].

For it must be noted that to be **presentially** <note>original: "presentialiter"</note> in a place signifies a specific mode of existence. When we speak of **presence** <note>original: "presentia"</note> or consider the **presence** <note>original: "presentiam"</note> of a spiritual substance, we are discussing its **presentiality** <note>original: "presentialitatem"</note>—that is, the specific way a spirit is said to be "at" a location.

Theological tradition often debates how a soul, which has no physical dimensions, can have **presentiality** <note>original: "presentialitas"</note> in a physical location like Hell. If we refer to Christ as being **present** <note>original: "presentem"</note> there, we must be careful with our definitions. The nature of his **presentiality** <note>original: "presentialitatis"</note> is fundamentally different from the way a physical body occupies a room. In the absence of a physical **presence** <note>original: "presentie"</note> of substance—since the soul is incorporeal—we instead look to the **presence** <note>original: "presentiam"</note> of his power and divinity. 

Therefore, while one might say he was **presentially** <note>original: "presentialiter"</note> there, it was by way of his divine authority and the spiritual effect of his triumph over death, rather than by being spatially enclosed or contained by the geography of the underworld.

<note>Pico is navigating a dangerous theological path. He is trying to uphold the Apostles' Creed—which says Christ "descended into hell"—while simultaneously applying Aristotelian logic, which suggests that only physical bodies can have a "place." By arguing that Christ was present "by effect" rather than "by substance," he hoped to satisfy both logic and dogma.</note>

It is in this specific sense that we must interpret the word **presentially** <note>original: "presentialiter"</note> whenever it is used by the holy doctors of the Church to describe this mystery.

<summary>Pico defines the technical term "presentially" to argue that Christ’s descent into Hell was an exercise of spiritual power rather than a physical or spatial movement of his substance.
