<meta>Pico continues his argument that his views are not only defensible but often align with various, sometimes contradictory, positions held by Thomas Aquinas himself. He transitions into a formal logical defense of his thesis regarding Christ's descent into hell.</meta>

And in the *Questions on Boethius' De Trinitate*, he follows the path of the Commentator regarding **indeterminate dimensions** <note>original: "dimensionibus indeterminatis"; a philosophical concept regarding the potential extension of matter before it receives a specific form, often associated with Averroes ("the Commentator").</note>. In the *Summa*, however, he holds that the soul of Christ was totally and in all respects like the soul of a comprehensor, and that it was due to a **divine dispensation** <note>original: "dispensatione divina"; God's providential arrangement or special exception to the natural order.</note> that the soul did not transmit the gifts of clarity and **impassibility** <note>original: "impassibilitatis"; the quality of being unable to suffer or be affected by external force.</note> to the body. Likewise, regarding the knowledge of Christ, he feels one way in his [earlier] writing and another in the *Summa*; and so it is with many other matters, in which it can be seen that he followed diverse opinions in different places. 

Because if these men contend so strongly that the opinion concerning the mode of being in a place through "operation" is also the opinion of Thomas, they will have nothing more against me except that my opinion on the manner of Christ’s descent is all the more probable and less to be judged heretical, insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of Saint Thomas. For this reason, however, I marvel even more that my conclusion was condemned by these masters. <margin>Note.</margin> Before they judged this conclusion heretical, I had not only clarified my intention to them in these words, but I had even dictated it to be written down and noted, saying thus: 

"Let no one understand me to say by this conclusion that the soul of Christ did not descend to the underworld, nor that the soul of Christ was not in hell during the **three-day interval** <note>original: "intriduo"; referring to the three days between the Crucifixion and Resurrection.</note>; on the contrary, I confess both. But I say that neither **local motion** <note>original: "motus localis"; physical movement from one place to another.</note> nor being located anywhere is appropriate for any **separate spirit** <note>original: "spiritui separato"; a soul existing apart from its body.</note>, as the soul of Christ then was, except by reason of its operation." 

I pronounced these precise words and no others, word for word, for them to note as a brief declaration of this conclusion. <margin>He argues against his opponents.</margin> How they could thereafter still judge as heretical that which they could now hold as Catholic, I do not see. 

And so that I may show briefly, by recapitulating through the mode of argumentation, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are themselves erring in the faith, I argue as follows: One who posits a conclusion that is heretical in itself can be accused of heresy insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But one who posits my aforementioned conclusion cannot, by its very assertion, be accused of heresy; therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not heretical in itself. They hold the major premise as granted. [For example], if proposition **A** is such that one cannot be accused of heresy, then even one positing proposition **A** cannot be accused. But one who posits everything that follows from the assertion of my conclusion in the way it was posited by me cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, one positing the proposition itself, as I have posited it, cannot be accused. 

I prove the minor premise thus: The contradictory of this statement—*the reason for being in a place (that is, here or there) for separate substances, in the manner declared above, is "operation" and not the "limitation of nature"*—is not a matter of faith. Likewise, the contradictory of this statement—*it is not permitted to argue from a whole **copulative** <note>original: "copulativa"; a logical proposition joining two parts with "and."</note> to one of its parts*—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—*If someone, having put forward some negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some Doctor with a proposition such as the word "as," it can be held as much **determinatively** <note>original: "determinative"; as a specific definition or restriction.</note> as **relatively** <note>original: "relative"; in relation to something else.</note>, because it can just as well be equivalent to the phrase "in the manner that" as to the word "that"*—is similarly not a matter of faith. Finally, the contradictory of this statement—*through the "common path" in theological matters, we can appropriately understand the path which is commonly held in the university*—is similarly not a matter of faith.

<summary>Pico points out inconsistencies in Thomas Aquinas's works to show that his own views are not uniquely controversial and provides a formal logical defense of his thesis on Christ's presence in hell as being defined by "operation."</summary>

...the university in which, at the time of the speaker, the study of theology most flourishes is not a **matter of faith** <note>original: "de fide"; a doctrine that must be believed as part of the Catholic faith.</note>. And the contradictory of this statement—that in the University of Paris it is now commonly held that the **limitation of nature** <note>original: "finitatio naturae"</note> is the **reason for the locatability** <note>original: "ratio locabilitatis"; the philosophical explanation for how a non-physical being can be said to be in a specific "place."</note> of a **separate substance** <note>original: "substantiae separatae"; a being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note>—is not a matter of faith.

Then the argument follows: If the contradictories of these statements are not matters of faith, it follows that to propose, believe, and dispute these statements is not in itself heretical or against the faith; nor can one who proposes, holds, and disputes them, either **disjunctively** <note>using "or"</note> or **conjunctively** <note>using "and"</note>, be accused of heresy. But from these statements, when posed together and conjunctively, the position of my conclusion follows exactly as it stands; therefore, one posing my conclusion exactly as it stands cannot be accused of heresy.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of Christ's presence and movement, transitioning from the general problem of how non-physical substances occupy space to the specific theological mystery of Christ’s descent into hell following his crucifixion.</meta>

The argument proceeds thus, and it seems that Christ, according to his soul, did not descend to hell <note>original: "ad infernum"; referring to the "Harrowing of Hell," the belief that Christ visited the underworld between his death and resurrection.</note> because the same finite thing cannot be in different places at the same time. But the soul of Christ, since it was a finite creature, was immediately after death in paradise with the soul of the thief, to whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise" <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note>. Therefore, at least at that time, he could not have been in hell. Also, those things which Christ did and suffered in his assumed [human] nature were ordained for human salvation. But it would not have profited this salvation for Christ to descend to hell, because through the passion which he sustained in this world, he liberated us from all guilt and punishment; therefore, it seems that Christ did not descend to hell. 

->On the contrary<- 

is what is said in the Creed <note>original: "simbolo"; referring to the Apostles' Creed, a foundational statement of Christian belief.</note>: "He descended into hell" <note>original: "descendit ad inferos"</note>. And the Apostle says in Ephesians 4: "But what does 'he ascended' mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?" <note>original: "descendit ad inferiores partes terre"</note>. The Gloss <note>original: "glo."; the *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard collection of biblical commentaries used by medieval scholars.</note> says: "that is, to hell." 

I respond <note>The "Respondeo" is the central part of a scholastic argument where the author provides their own resolution to the problem.</note> that since it is an article of faith that Christ descended to hell, and this cannot be understood by reason of his divinity (by which he is everywhere) nor by reason of his body (which was in the tomb), it remains that it must be understood by reason of his human soul. This being supposed, two things must be seen: first, by what manner the soul of Christ descended to hell; and second, to which hell he descended. 

Regarding the first, it should be known that since a separated soul <note>original: "anima separata"; a human soul that has been disconnected from the physical body by death.</note> is not a body, nor a power within a body, it cannot be said that Christ's soul descended to hell by that kind of motion or descent by which physical bodies move. 

<margin>How angels move to a place</margin> 

Whether it is by the kind of motion by which angels move is not clearly evident. For angels are said to move from place to place insofar as they operate successively in different places. A separated soul, however, is not said to have any operation regarding a place or regarding a body existing in a place because, since by its nature it is determined to a specific body, it cannot move or act upon another except through its own body; but it lacks that body while it is separated. Therefore, the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of an operation it has regarding a place or a body existing in a place. 

Nevertheless, this notwithstanding, a separated soul can be said to have descended to hell in two ways. 

<margin>The soul descends to hell in two ways.</margin> 

One way is according to **deputation** <term>deputation: a legal or divine assignment to a specific state or place.</term>. And in this way, the souls of the damned are said to descend to hell absolutely <note>original: "simpliciter"</note>, because they are absolutely assigned so that, once the body is resumed [at the resurrection], they are in hell; because of this, they are said to be where they are absolutely assigned. However, the souls of the holy fathers <note>The "Holy Fathers" refers to the righteous people of the Old Testament who died before Christ's redemption.</note> are said to be in **Limbo** <term>Limbo: from the Latin 'limbus' (edge), a place for those who died in friendship with God but could not enter Heaven until Christ opened the way.</term> or to have descended to Limbo because of a deputation that is not absolute, but conditional: that is, they would remain there after resuming their bodies unless they were liberated by the Redeemer. However, Christ's soul is not said to have descended to hell in this way—that is, by deputation—because all such assignment is due to contracted or committed guilt, which was not in Christ. 

In another way, the soul of Christ can be said to have prepared to descend to hell according to **effect**. And in this way, the soul of Christ is said to descend to hell because of a double effect he had upon those who were in hell. One effect was the showing of the divine vision <note>The "Beatific Vision," or seeing God face-to-face.</note> which they lacked, to which the passion of Christ related by way of merit. And because all merit depends principally upon the act of the soul, therefore this effect is attributed to the soul as the principal source of meriting. Likewise, by **appropriation** <term>appropriation: attributing a quality to one person of the Trinity or one part of Christ that actually belongs to his whole person.</term>, just as Christ was blessed according to his soul, so according to his soul it is attributed to him to have been the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a being in **potency** <term>potency: the capacity or potential to reach a state.</term> be reduced to **act** <term>act: the full realization or reality of a state.</term> by that which is already in act. Another effect was, according to some, toward whom...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into how Christ’s soul could be present in multiple locations—specifically hell and paradise—simultaneously after his death. It addresses the philosophical mechanics of spiritual movement and the definition of "place" for non-corporeal entities.</meta>

The soul of Christ behaved directly in the manner of an agent, namely, to illuminate the souls of the holy Fathers who were in Limbo and regarding the mysteries that fall under revelation. For according to Dionysius <margin>Dionysius</margin> in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on the hierarchy of angels and divine names were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>, Christ according to his soul has the task of teaching angels; and by reason of this double effect, it can be said that the soul of Christ descended to hell. 

This is confirmed by a threefold reason. The first <margin>First reason</margin> is because to be moved or to descend belongs to the separated soul <note>The "separated soul" refers to the human soul after it has been detached from the physical body by death.</note> not in the manner of the motion of bodies, but in the manner in which it belongs to a spiritual spirit to be moved. For other spiritual substances, such as God and an angel, it does not belong to them to be moved from place to place by a motion that exists subjectively within them, but through the effect they have in other things; therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to the separated soul and belonged to the soul of Christ. 

The second reason <margin>Second</margin> is this: Christ is said to have descended into hell so that he might illuminate the souls of the holy Fathers to see God. At the same instant in which Christ died, the holy Fathers saw God. However, in that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in hell through physical motion. Therefore, he did not descend there through a motion that was in itself, but through the effect he had on others. 

Likewise <margin>Third</margin>, just as in those three days <note>The "triduum" refers to the three-day period between the Crucifixion on Good Friday and the Resurrection on Easter Sunday.</note> the soul of Christ is said to have been in hell with the souls of the holy Fathers, so in those three days (or part of those three days) he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief. To whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise" <note>original: "hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note>. But this cannot be understood regarding a physical location acquired through motion, since according to those who hold that a spirit is in a place definitively <term>definitive presence: when a spirit is present in a location through the application of its power rather than being physically contained like a body</term> and moves from place to place, the same spirit cannot be in multiple places nor be moved simultaneously by multiple motions tending toward multiple places. Therefore, it must be understood according to the effect. 

But if someone says that "paradise" is spoken of in two ways <margin>Paradise is spoken of in two ways</margin>: In one way as a physical place, namely the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most spiritual part of the heavens in medieval cosmology.</note>, and in this way the soul of Christ was not in paradise except after the Ascension <note>The text uses "assumptionem," but in this context refers to Christ's return to heaven.</note>. In another way, "paradise" is called the vision of the divine essence, and thus the soul of Christ was in paradise from the instant of conception, and the soul of the thief was there on the very day of the Passion. By this manner it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been in paradise so-called (that is, that it saw God) and to have been locally in hell. 

If such a thing were said, it is not valid, because just as "paradise" is spoken of in two ways, so is "hell." For in one way, "hell" is called a place corresponding to the depths below the earth <margin>Hell is spoken of in two ways</margin>. In another way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with the soul of Christ in paradise except because, by the merit of Christ's Passion, the soul of the thief saw God, so the soul of Christ is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen Fathers in hell except because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and thus were said to be in hell—were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. 

Therefore, both ought to be understood equally according to the effect, and not according to the location or local motion that was subjectively in the soul itself. However, although this might be said with probability and also seems sufficiently to preserve the article of faith and the word of Scripture, yet because divine power is not comprehended by human reason, it should not be stubbornly asserted that the soul of Christ could not have descended to hell by another way unknown to us. 

Regarding the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once definitively or circumscriptively <term>circumscriptive presence: being physically contained by surrounding space, as a body is</term>, and in this way it is not claimed that the soul of Christ was in paradise and in hell at the same time. But according to the effect, nothing prohibits the same finite thing from being said to be in several places when the effects are compatible and simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. Thus, the soul of Christ is said to have been in paradise and in hell at the same time because, by his merit, the soul of the thief saw

<meta>This page continues the argument that while the Bible is perfectly consistent, even the most revered Church Fathers (the "Saints") frequently disagree with one another. ...confirms. Likewise, Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, says that the saying of the psalm <note>Psalm 19:4</note>, "their sound went out into all the earth," etc., and that word of Christ, "this gospel shall be preached in the whole world," were completely fulfilled by the apostles. Augustine, however, in his letter to Hesychius <note>The transcription says "Exitium," likely a scribal variant for Hesychius, to whom Augustine wrote regarding the end of the world.</note>—with whom Origen agrees in his commentary on Matthew—holds that this is not yet completed. Likewise, Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, holds that angels existed for many ages before the visible world and served God; Ambrose also holds this in his *Hexameron* <note>term: Hexameron (The "Six Days" of creation in Genesis)</note>. Augustine, however, in his commentary on Genesis, holds that they were created at the same time as the empyrean heaven. Likewise, Jerome, in the prologue to the Book of Wisdom, holds that the book belongs to Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note> and is not to be counted among the sacred scriptures. Augustine, however, in the third book of his *Retractions*, shows that he once held it was published by Jesus son of Sirach, which he retracts there; and although he does not state who published it, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, he numbers it among the sacred books.

Likewise, Jerome, in his book *Hebrew Questions*, says that God had established paradise before he made heaven and earth, because of what is written: "God had planted paradise from the beginning." Augustine, however, in his literal commentary on Genesis, interprets "from the beginning" to mean on the third day. Likewise, Augustine, in the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, asserts that Peter's entire denial took place in the courtyard of Annas, and that the things said there after Jesus was sent to Caiaphas were said by way of recapitulation. Jerome, however, in his commentary on Matthew, seems to suggest that Peter denied Him in the courtyard of Caiaphas. Bede, in his commentary on Luke, seems to agree with him. Likewise, Jerome, regarding that passage in Habakkuk, "your eyes are pure," denies that individual angels are assigned to <note>original: "praepositos"</note> individual physical creatures; but Augustine, in his *Eighty-Three Questions*, holds that they are. Origen and John Damascene agree with him. Likewise, Jerome, regarding that passage in Jonah, "Take me up and cast me into the sea," says that it is lawful to perish by one's own hand where chastity is endangered; Augustine, however, in the book *The City of God*, affirms the contrary.

Finally, many such things are found where the holy doctors <note>original: "sancti doctores"</note> wrote contrary views among themselves while keeping the faith intact. But not everything comes to mind for one in great haste; nor could this work be elaborated by me with more exact diligence, because I wanted to immediately counter the disease of unjust infamy coming my way. Intending to write elsewhere on this matter, so that with greater leisure and care I may add more and perhaps better things. I will add, however, what now occurs to me from Jerome's letter to Augustine, where he says: "Nor should you wonder if in your books, and especially in the exposition of the scriptures which are most obscure, some things seem to deviate from the straight line <note>original: "recta linea"</note>." He continues: "And I say this not because I judge certain things in your works as blameworthy; for I have never devoted effort to reading them, nor is there a supply of these copies among us, except for the books of your *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the Psalms. If I wished to discuss these, I would not say—by me, who am nothing—but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks, I would show that these deviate." Thus he said. Just as they disagreed with one another, so we can dissent from them in many things, provided the faith and the truth of scripture and the determination of the holy church are preserved.

The third proof is taken from the special prerogative of sacred scripture and the decrees of the universal church, to which alone we grant the excellence of infallible truth. Hence Augustine, writing against Jerome in a letter to him, says: "For I confess to your charity that I have learned to defer this fear and honor to those books of scripture alone which are now called canonical, so that I believe no author of these..."

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense against charges of heresy. Having previously argued that ambiguous propositions are common in academic dispute, the author now draws upon the highest authorities of the Church—Gregory the Great, Jerome, Ockham, and Augustine—to prove that the "true" meaning of a statement lies in the speaker’s intention, not merely the literal surface of the words.</meta>

<margin>Gregory</margin> **Gregory** says that we should not always understand words exactly as they seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous; rather, we must return to the intention of the speaker. And Gregory says that often, while the strict property of words is being observed, the sense of truth is lost. Furthermore, Gregory in the twenty-sixth book of the *Moralia* <note>Gregory the Great’s *Moralia in Job*, a foundational medieval work on ethics and biblical interpretation.</note> states: "One ought not to consider the words, but the will and the intention," because the intention should not serve the words, but the words should serve the intention.

<margin>Jerome</margin> And **Jerome**, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, testifies that the Gospel is not in the words of the Scriptures, but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the **marrow** <note>original: "medulla"; this refers to the inner core or spiritual essence of a text.</note>; not in the leaves of speeches, but in the root of reason.

<margin>Ockham</margin> For this reason, **Ockham**, in his *Dialogue*, proves the falsity of this common proposition: "words are to be received not from the opinions of individuals, but from common usage"—specifically in the second part. For he says that in ambiguous and multifaceted words, one must not resort to common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speakers. And so, when there is ambiguity in the teaching of someone speaking or writing, one must similarly return to the speaker's intention so that he may explain himself and express the true sense which the <term>force of the words</term> <note>original: "vis uerborum"; the range of meaning that the literal language can legitimately support.</note> allows. Nor is he to be rejected unless it can be proven that such a true sense is contrary to his other sayings or irrelevant to his purpose. The same Doctor <note>Referring to William of Ockham, the "Invincible Doctor."</note> says that even in simple speech, one must return to the intention of the speaker and stand by his interpretation, unless it is certain—or may be probably or strongly presumed—that he used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end.

<margin>Epilogue</margin> From all of these points, I conclude that **I have not erred**, for I—with a formal declaration—put forward a multifaceted proposition during a dispute to be clarified. Such a proposition cannot produce any sense that has not already been held by some doctor who has not been rejected, or who has not yet been declared as such by the Church. Rather, **those who have erred** are the ones who judged a proposition to be simply heretical, even though it possesses a Catholic sense permitted by the force of the words, and despite the fact that this Catholic sense had already been declared to them by the person proposing it. Even if they had made their judgment before I declared my sense, they might perhaps have erred more excusably; however, because they are truly learned, they were capable of recognizing through their own knowledge that the proposition had a double meaning. Noting this, they should not have simply condemned it, but rather should have interpreted it in its good sense.

<margin>Augustine</margin> For **Augustine**, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage in Matthew, "judge not and you shall not be judged," says: "In this place, I think nothing else is commanded except that we interpret in the better part those deeds which are doubtful as to the spirit in which they were done." For concerning neutral deeds, which can be done with either a good or an evil spirit, it is rash to judge—especially to condemn. Therefore, let us understand that what Augustine says about things that are *done* applies equally to things that are *said*. Thus, applying Augustine's sentence to speculative matters, we conclude that in these sayings which can have both a good and a bad sense, it is rash to judge—and especially to condemn.

# SECOND QUESTION CONCERNING THE PUNISHMENT FOR MORTAL SIN.

Now, the second conclusion which those men condemned is this: **for a mortal sin of finite duration, an infinite punishment according to time is not owed, but only a finite one.**

And because, when I set down this conclusion in my little book, these words were prefixed: "Unless there were the sayings of the saints <note>original: "dicta sanctorum"; referring to the authoritative writings of the Church Fathers.</note> which in the manifest expression of their speech seem to say the opposite, I would firmly assert the conclusions written below. However, I assert that they are probable and can be reasonably defended." The first of these is this: *Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.* The second is this: *for a mortal sin of finite duration, etc.*

A certain master, holding a dispute with me concerning this conclusion, said: "What other testimony do we seek that your conclusion is heretical, since you yourself clearly say it is against the sayings of the saints?" For he argued: it is against the sayings of the saints, therefore it is heretical. I showed him then, as I will also show below, how my conclusion was in no way repugnant to the opinions of the saints, and how those words were to be understood. But even if it had been the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the saints, how much his logic would be worth—and how unworthy it would be of a doctor of theology, as he boasts himself to be—can be clear to anyone from what was said above regarding the first conclusion.

I know what I might say here about this master. For he is the one who so often sent letters back to our country about me, promising, as it were, a trophy and a triumph. But I wish first to declare that the conclusion itself is Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" means "orthodox" or "in accordance with universal Church teaching."</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all doctors, despite the fact that the masters who interrogated me judged both the conclusion itself and the responses I gave them to be false, erroneous, and heretical. I call this conclusion "mine" because if you take it in a sense other than that which I intend through it, then it is no longer my conclusion which I proposed. For a <term>multifaceted proposition</term> <note>original: "propositio multiplex"; a statement that can have several different logical meanings depending on how terms are defined.</note> consists of many propositions. Then I wish to declare that my responses themselves are also of such a kind, always declaring my meanings—that is, those I intend by them—as the force of the words permits.

<margin>What he is about to do regarding the declaration, and in what order</margin>
<margin>A multifaceted proposition</margin>
<margin>The first thing to be noted regarding sin</margin>
<margin>Turning toward</margin>
<margin>Turning away</margin>
<margin>The second thing to be noted</margin>
<margin>The time of the way and of the end</margin>

For the declaration of the conclusion, therefore, five things are to be noted. **First**, it must be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: the **turning toward** <note>original: "conversio"; the act of the will focusing on a created thing instead of God.</note> a created good, and the **turning away** <note>original: "aversio"; the act of the will rejecting the Creator.</note> from the unchangeable and uncreated good. In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all doctors. In the second way, sin is a finite evil according to the "common path." And because the turning toward a created good—which the sinner misuses by sinning—belongs to the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is **intrinsically** a finite evil. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it **extrinsically** infinite, because it is called an infinite evil only insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good. And therefore, it remains only that it is an extrinsic and objective infinite evil.

**Second**, note that by "time" we can understand only the <term>time of the way</term> <note>original: "tempus viae"; the period of a person's life on Earth while they are still a "wayfarer" capable of change.</note>. In this way, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to time, since the "time of the way" for any wayfarer is not only finite in duration, but even brief. In another way, we can understand by "time" the time of the way and of the end <note>original: "tempus viae & termini"; "termini" refers to the state of the soul after death (the end of the journey).</note> and...

<meta>The author continues his systematic defense, now breaking down the definitions of "sin" and "being owed" to prove his conclusion aligns with orthodox theology despite his critics' claims.</meta>

<margin>Third point.</margin>
<margin>Mortal sin is understood:</margin>
<margin>For the act.</margin>
<margin>For the guilt.</margin>
...it is understood in this way in the conclusion, and thus something can endure in a person for an infinite time, as is evident. **Third**, note that **mortal sin** can be understood in two ways. In one way, it refers to a forbidden act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, it refers to the <term>guilt</term><note>original: "reatus"; in scholastic theology, this refers to the state of being liable to punishment that remains after the sinful act is over.</note> left behind by the aforementioned forbidden act or the said omission of an act. Indeed, this guilt is called "sin" in many places of Holy Scripture, and by such sin someone is called a sinner even when the act of sinning (in the first sense) has ceased or passed. 

From this third note, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although in one who is damned for mortal sin, the sin itself for which he is damned might eventually end—regarding the intrinsic entity of the act itself, which is called "sin" in the first sense—it does not, however, end regarding the guilt. Indeed, if it ended in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to him. Thus, the sin to which infinite punishment is owed is infinite in duration regarding its guilt. 

<margin>Fourth point.</margin>
<margin>"To be owed" is understood in two ways.</margin>
**Fourth**, it must be noted that **"to be owed"** is understood in two ways, or it can be understood in two ways that some punishment is "owed" for a sin. In one way, something is said to be owed to someone because it will actually be rendered to them at some time. In this sense, it is said reasonably and according to Catholic teaching that for a sin of finite duration—regarding both the intrinsic entity and the guilt—an infinite punishment in duration is *not* owed. It is in this sense that the present conclusion is understood: that for a sin of finite duration, [infinite punishment] is not owed, etc. For every sin to which punishment is "owed" in this way (that is, for which an infinite punishment will actually be rendered at some time) is, in the aforementioned way, infinite in duration. 

The conclusion also has another Catholic sense: namely, that an infinite punishment in duration is never "owed" (in the sense that it is rendered) to anyone unless he is finally impenitent and ceases to repent without end for that sin which he omitted or committed in life. Thus, for a temporal sin in the aforementioned way, infinite punishment is owed if the sinner does not return to justice. 

<margin>The punishment which God seeks from a sinner, and what it consists of.</margin>
For just as repentance ends sin regarding its rejection <note>original: "deacceptatiōem"; the state of being unaccepted or rejected by God's grace.</note>—following the saying: "at whatever hour the sinner shall groan [in repentance]," etc.—so impenitence regarding a sin perpetuates that sin in guilt and rejection unto infinite punishment. Thus, infinite punishment is never owed to anyone in that first sense unless they have a sin that is infinite in duration. For the **punishment** <note>original: "Vindicta"; while often translated as vengeance, in this context it refers to the restorative justice or penalty God requires to balance the moral order.</note> which God seeks from a sinner is that the sinner return voluntarily to his duty of obedience, grieving for his contempt; otherwise, he will be tormented as long as he remains in that state of will. 

<margin>Note: A common distinction regarding this word "owed."</margin>
<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
In another way, it can be understood that something is "owed" to someone because they are worthy of it through merit or demerit, and it will be rendered to them if they die in that state. In this sense, for a mortal sin of finite duration, infinite punishment *is* owed, because whoever sins mortally for the space of one hour is worthy of infinite punishment, and it will be rendered to him if he finally departs this life in that state—even assuming he has no other sin that is infinite in duration. This distinction of the word "owed" is in frequent use among theologians. 

Hence, according to this wording, the Doctors say that for the <term>foreknown</term><note>original: "prescito"; referring to those whom God knows will ultimately be lost.</note>, an act of merit performed while he is in a state of grace does not "owe" him eternal life, if we take "owed" in the first sense, because it will never actually be rendered to him. Similarly, it is said that for the <term>predestined</term><note>original: "pđestinato"; those God knows will ultimately be saved.</note>, while he is in a state of mortal sin, eternal punishment is not "owed," because it will never be rendered to him, given that the sin will be ended and he will not die in it, but in grace. From the aforesaid, it is clear that my conclusion has a Catholic sense even according to the usual way of speaking of Catholic Doctors; nor should it have been condemned as heretical, false, and erroneous, since its opposite is rather the false position.

...and erroneous. This opinion not only appears not to be heretical, but is so Catholic that no one, if they are a Catholic well-practiced in the Sacred Scriptures, can rightly and reasonably deny it.

<margin>that it is not heretical</margin>
That the proposition itself, by the force of its terms, conveys this meaning is evident. For the proposition says: **To a mortal sin of a finite time, an infinite punishment is not owed in terms of duration.** In this proposition, I take "to be owed" <note>original: "deberi"</note> to mean that which will eventually be paid off, which has already been shown above to be a very common usage among the Doctors of the Church. And I take "sin" to mean the offense and the guilt. This interpretation is not only not improper or abusive, but is frequent in Sacred Scripture. 

<margin>Master of Sentences</margin>
For after the **Master of Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> inquires in the second book whether, when the act of sinning passes, the sin remains in the one who sinned until he repents, he responds thus: "It must not be ignored that sins exist in a person in two ways: in the act, and in the guilt." 

<margin>Durandus</margin>
<margin>Sin is finished in two ways</margin>
**Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a prominent philosopher and theologian.</note> also says in the same place that sin is understood to be ended in two ways: in one way, by the cessation of the act alone; in another way, by the dismissal <note>forgiveness</note> of the sin. 

<margin>Thomas</margin>
That guilt is also sometimes expressly called "sin" is stated by **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential scholastic philosopher.</note> in the same place, saying: "Guilt, standing between the fault and the punishment, takes on the name of both extremes." In this way, "sin" is also understood in the passage: *Redeem your sins with alms* <note>original: "peccata tua elemosinis redime"; from the Book of Daniel 4:24.</note> and so in many other passages of Scripture. 

If, therefore, both the sense of the proposition is Catholic and the use of the terms in the proposition is Catholic and highly approved, why was there any reason to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical? 

<margin>Responses which the author had given</margin>
Now I come to my responses. First, I said that if someone persists only for a finite time in mortal sin, he will not be punished except for a finite time.

### THIRD QUESTION ON THE ADORATION OF THE CROSS AND IMAGES

The third conclusion which they condemned was this: **Neither the cross of Christ nor any image is to be adored with the adoration of *latria*** <note>original: "latrie"; in Catholic theology, "latria" is the highest form of worship reserved for God alone, as opposed to "dulia" for saints or "hyperdulia" for Mary.</note>, **even in the manner that Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> proposes.**

This conclusion, which was condemned by those men, I believe not only to be Catholic but even truer than its opposite, which is this: **The cross of Christ and images are to be adored with *latria* in the manner that Thomas proposes.** For it seems to me that the opinion of Thomas on this matter is less reasonable than the opinion of Durandus <margin>Durandus</margin>, Henry of Ghent <margin>Henry of Ghent</margin>, John of Guarra <margin>John of Guarra</margin>, Robert Holcot <margin>Robert Holcot</margin>, Peter of Aquila <margin>Peter of Aquila</margin>, and many others whom I follow in this conclusion. So that this may be made clear, I will first set forth the opinion of Thomas, which I do not hold. Then, I will set forth the opinion of the Doctors whom I do follow. From these it will be evident that the determination of those masters regarding my conclusion—besides being neither right nor just—presupposes the total opposite of what I intend in the conclusion. 

Thomas says, therefore, that because (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*) the movement of the soul toward an image is twofold: one toward the image itself insofar as it is a certain thing; the other toward the image insofar as it is an image of another. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement, by which something is moved toward the image as it is a certain thing, is distinct from the movement toward the thing of which it is an image. The second movement, however, which is toward the image insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as that which is toward the thing. 

And therefore he concludes that although adoration is not owed to the image of Christ as it is a certain thing in itself, nevertheless, as it is an image, the same reverence is owed to it that is owed to Christ himself, which is the adoration of *latria*. This is the manner of Thomas, which to other Doctors rightly seems foreign and dangerous. For the image itself, even as an image, is thus distinct from the thing imaged; for as such, it is referred to the thing imaged as to something distinct from itself. Wherefore, even if as such it terminates the adoration of *latria*, it seems to follow that something other than God will be adored with *latria*, which is absurd. 

Nor can it be said, as Capreolus <margin>Against the response of Capreolus</margin> says, wishing to save Thomas's statement, that the image itself is not adored separately, but the image and the thing imaged are one total object of adoration. Because either the image itself (which is a relative created being) is one part of this total object, or it is not. If it is not, then it should not be said that one total object is made from those two, because from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, though one of them is more principal. If it is [a part], it follows that some created thing of the category of relation will, at least partially, terminate the adoration of *latria*. 

Which certainly seems "badly Catholic" to say, all the more because not only can this not be said of a created thing, but even the Persons in the Godhead, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal terminus of adoration. <margin>Against the foundation of the opinion</margin> Moreover, Thomas's foundation seems hardly effective. For when the Philosopher says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imaged is the same, he does not understand it as meaning that the soul says that the image, as image, is the same as the original <note>original: "exemplari"</note> and thus whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other; rather, the Philosopher only intends this...

...that the recollective movement by which the soul is moved toward an image—insofar as it is an image—is also directed toward the thing imagined. But the idea that every movement of the soul (and especially of the will) is identical toward the image and the thing imagined is in no way what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> intended. This is evident from a similar case, even according to the way of speaking used by Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> himself. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same when the will is carried toward an end <note>a goal</note> and toward the means to that end when it desires them for the sake of the end. And yet, even according to him, it is certain that the movement is "enjoyment" <term>fruitio; the delight in something for its own sake</term> as it reaches the end, but it is "use" <term>usus; the handling of something for the sake of another</term> and not enjoyment as it reaches the means to the end.

<margin>The opinion of other doctors</margin>
<margin>The harsh opinion of Durandus.</margin>
Therefore, it seems to other doctors that we should in no way say that we adore an image of Christ—even as an image—with the adoration of *latria* <note>original: "latrie"; the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note>. This is because, in that capacity, it is a created thing not united to the divinity; and what is more, in that capacity, it is merely a relational entity. For this reason, Durandus says that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is adored with *latria*"—is false in its proper sense. However, it has an improper sense that is true, which is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross or as present in the cross (just as a thing imagined is present in its image), is adored with the same adoration as if he were present in himself. And according to this sense, I also grant this proposition: "The cross is adored with the adoration of *latria*." This, then, is what Durandus says: that it is adored "recollectively." 

<margin>The opinion of Robert Holcot, Henry, John of Guarra, and Peter of Aquila.</margin>
Robert Holcot intends the same meaning when he says that the more proper way of speaking is to say, "we adore *before* the cross" rather than "we adore the cross." Finally, Henry of Ghent and John of Guarra intend the same meaning when they say it is adored "by accident" <note>meaning indirectly or by association rather than by its own nature</note>. Peter of Aquila says the same. Truly, that which Henry and John of Guarra add—who speak more completely on this matter—is this:

<margin>What Henry and John of Guarra add</margin>
They say that that honor is owed to an image "by accident" (or recollectively) which is owed "by itself" to the thing imagined or remembered. It is certain, however, that there is nothing to which *latria* is owed by itself except the Triune God, and Christ on account of the unity of his person with God; but an image cannot be God. It remains that if there is any image to which *latria* is owed by accident and recollectively, it must be the image of Christ. Truly, because such an image principally represents the humanity of Christ to us, and only secondarily his divinity, it seems that primarily such honor is owed to it by accident as is given by itself to the humanity of Christ. But the humanity of Christ, taken by itself, is adored only with *hyperdulia* <note>the highest form of veneration given to a creature, specifically the human nature of Christ or the Virgin Mary</note>. Therefore, such an image primarily deserves only the adoration of *hyperdulia* by accident. Secondarily, however, it will also deserve the adoration of *latria* by accident in the way already described, because the image also secondarily represents and brings to our memory the divinity of Christ himself. 

<margin>The opinion of Francis of Mayronnes and the Scotists</margin>
<margin>The opinion of Thomas is somewhat dangerous in this matter</margin>
In this, Francis of Mayronnes and all the Scotists <note>followers of Duns Scotus</note> agree with Henry, for they say that *latria* is not owed to the humanity of Christ. Because Thomas seems to hold the opposite regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, he would perhaps also dissent from Henry in this case. Indeed, the opinion of Thomas—as Francis says in the third book—is somewhat dangerous, and in this matter of adoration, his path does not seem to me to be very safe. For he went so far as to say, in the third book of the *Sentences*, that even the physical cross of Christ on which he hung, even as an inanimate thing, was owed some adoration. And yet we know, according to all theology, that that which cannot be a subject capable of holiness or virtue cannot be the goal of our worship.

### FOURTH QUESTION: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED BY GOD

The fourth conclusion condemned by those men is this: **"I do not assent to the common opinion of theologians who say that God can assume <term>suppositare|The technical act of God taking a created nature (like humanity) into His own divine personhood, as in the Incarnation</term> any nature whatsoever, but I concede this only regarding a rational nature."**

By this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume any nature. Rather, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: *God can assume any nature whatsoever.* There is a great difference between these two intentions. Even if such a thing were possible according to the absolute power of God, a proposition that—literally speaking <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis"</note>—merely denies a positive, explicit assent to that specific statement does not detract from God's omnipotence, nor does it, by its literal wording, smack of any heresy.

The reason is this: not every faithful person is bound to assent explicitly and specifically to all things possible according to God's absolute power, or to profess these things explicitly. Instead, it is sufficient to believe certain such things generally and implicitly, provided one does not stubbornly disbelieve anything. Therefore, not without a certain mystery <note>The author implies he chose his words with deliberate care to avoid a legal trap</note>, I did not frame my conclusion in these terms: "God *cannot* assume any nature," but rather in these: "I do not assent to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature." 

From this conclusion, by the force of the words, it cannot be inferred that God is unable to do this. Nor can it be said that I asserted this in the conclusion—neither in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second part, from which it only follows that a concessive act <note>an agreement or "yes"</note> is held only regarding a rational nature specifically and in particular. I therefore deny that there is in me a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: *God can assume any nature.* And I can reasonably deny this. First, because even if the opposite were true, since it can remain unknown to us in a specific and explicit way, it seems I am not obliged to believe it explicitly. Second, and most importantly, because it is not easy to disprove or defeat that assertion ("God cannot," etc.) by claiming it detracts from God's omnipotence.

<margin>Henry of Ghent</margin> This is strongly confirmed by the authority of the solemn doctor **Henry of Ghent**, who, after having held the opposite opinion—namely, that any nature could be assumed—later leaned toward the view that only a rational nature can be assumed. For Henry writes as follows: <margin>Henry's words</margin> "Regarding the possibility of the nature to be assumed, there is no doubt whether God can assume to Himself any 'assumable' nature. Therefore, the whole difficulty of this question turns on the 'possibility' of the nature being assumed." <margin>The first position which Henry cites</margin> On this, there are two solemn positions. For the more common and solemn position says (and I myself was once accustomed to assent to it somewhat): "Any nature subsisting in creatures can be assumed." These thinkers hold that a certain nature might be "elevatable" even if the power corresponding to it is not "elevatable"—which does not seem to me to be a position that can be reasonably held.

One way is natural and in a manner congruent with nature. The other way is voluntary and in a manner exceeding the limits of nature. <meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding whether God can unite Himself to non-rational creatures. He is building a philosophical case that a thing’s existence is defined by its ability to act (operation), and therefore, a nature without intellectual "operation" cannot be "assumed" by God.</meta>

...the two things. But no creaturely nature is capable [of this union], nor can it be capable of God’s indwelling to receive within itself the aforementioned primary operation of God in a manner fitting to nature, unless it is also capable within itself of the second operation. This is because no creature can exist through its substance if it cannot also perform some operation through its power. For, according to <term>the Philosopher|Aristotle: Medieval scholars referred to Aristotle simply as 'The Philosopher'</term> at the end of the fourth book of the *Meteorology*: <note>original: "oīa ope determinātur & sunt pp suas operationes"</note> "All things are determined by their operation and exist for the sake of their operations; and they exist as long as they can perform their own proper operations; and when they cease to be able to perform their proper operations, they simultaneously cease to exist." <margin>The Philosopher</margin> As <term>Damascene|John of Damascus: An 8th-century Syrian monk and influential theologian</term> says in the same place in chapter 17: "An intellect that is foolish and deprived of knowledge will never exist. <margin>Damascene</margin> For if it is incapable of operation and movement, it is entirely non-existent." By this, he clearly suggests that if the substance of the intellect itself could not be elevated through the intellect, it would not be "assumable," nor would man himself be. For he would not be a man, according to what he [Damascene] states previously in the same place: "Since man is a rational, intellectual being, how then was God made man if he had assumed flesh without a soul or a soul <note>original: "anoin. i. sine intellectu"</note> without an intellect?" For this is not a man. 

Therefore, similarly, no creaturely nature is capable, or could be capable, of the <term>circuminsession|circuminsessio: Typically refers to the mutual indwelling of the Trinity, but here used for the intimate union of God and a created nature</term> of God—to receive within itself the aforementioned primary operation of God above the limits of nature—unless it is also capable within itself of the second operation. However, it is not capable of the second operation except through the powers of the intellect and the will; therefore, etc. 

For this reason, although the argument of <term>Augustine|Saint Augustine of Hippo</term> touched upon in the first reason does not hold regarding its logical form, <margin>Augustine</margin> it nevertheless does not fail in any matter but that it follows: if this nature (for example, of a man) is capable of being elevated according to its essence, it must necessarily also be elevated according to its power. And if it is not elevated according to its power, it is not elevated according to its essence. Just as it follows: "If the soul of <term>Fortis|A specific person named 'Fortis' used as a logical example</term> is immortal, then every man's soul is immortal; and if not every man's, then not Fortis's." This is because the same principle of immortality or mortality exists in all. And therefore, such an argument holds well by reason of its subject matter, just as if it held according to the logical form of the argument, which in truth holds by virtue of the form—namely, by looking at the common principle that applies to any nature, such as the immortality of the soul. For that principle is the same in every soul.

Let us therefore look at the possibility and impossibility of this "assumption" <note>The theological act of God taking a nature to Himself</note>. On God's part, as we said, there is no doubt [of His power]. But because the nature of the recipient is unknown to us, the understanding of the truth in this question is difficult for us. This pleases me more. 

Holding this opinion for the present, I say in response to the first opposing argument: the incorporeal nature of the rational soul or an angel, and in man the nature of the body insofar as it is ordered toward the soul (as that which can be perfected is ordered toward its perfection, and in which the soul performs its intellectual operation more effectively when all accidental hindering dispositions are removed from it than when it is separated), is the recipient [of God], so that the whole composite of body and soul with its intellect is the "susceptible" thing. The body is susceptible through the mediation of the substance of the soul and in relation to that substance of the soul, as the soul itself is the intellectual power. Thus, in no way can that in which there is no intellectual power be susceptible to this union. And I include under "intellectual power" all that in which the essence of the <term>Image|Imago Dei: The 'Image of God' found in rational creatures</term> principally consists, existing in the substance of the soul...

...so that nothing is capable of receiving [this union] except by reason of the image of God which is in it, whether through <term>circumincession|The Latin 'circumincessio' (Greek: perichoresis) refers to the mutual indwelling or 'interpenetration' of the divine and human natures</term> or according to substance and power together, as in Christ alone; or according to power alone, as in all those where this very image of God is, as it were, reprinted by its <term>prototype|The original pattern or 'first-type' from which a copy is made; here, God is the prototype and the human soul is the image</term>, just as a coin receives its form from the die <margin>Damascene</margin> by which its own image was impressed upon it. <meta>This page continues the defense of Henry of Ghent’s position regarding which natures can be "assumed" (taken into union) by God. It addresses potential counter-arguments, specifically focusing on God's omnipotence and the state of Christ’s body in the tomb during the three days (Triduum) between his death and resurrection.</meta>

...neither Robert of Orford <margin>Robert of Orford</margin> nor Bernard of Auvergne <margin>Bernard of Auvergne</margin>, both of whom I have seen reciting the opinion of Henry, ever judged it to savor of heresy or to be heretical. So that they may not seem to have acted irrationally in this, I wish briefly to set forth the manner in which Henry seems to defend his position.

There are, however, two principal arguments against Henry <margin>Two arguments against Henry</margin>. The first argument stands on this: that in God is the whole ground of substantializing <note>original: "rō substantiandi"; the power to give a nature its own existence or subsistence</note>, because He is the fullness of all being. Therefore, it seems that He could substantialize and <term>supposit|To 'supposit' (Latin: suppositare) means to give a nature its own distinct existence or personhood. In the Incarnation, the Divine Word acts as the 'suppositum' or person for the human nature.</term> any nature whatsoever. The second argument is that during the <term>Triduum|The three days between Christ's death and resurrection</term>, God suppositated the body that was in the tomb, which was not then rational <note>Because the soul was separated from the body after death</note>; and just as He suppositated it for those three days, He could have suppositated it for however long He had wished. 

These are the two principal foundations of the opposing opinion; and Henry himself, as was seen in the recitation of his opinion, brings these against himself. To the first argument, as we have seen <margin>Solution to the first</margin>, he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and the whole ground of substantializing and suppositing is most fully found in Him. But this is not the total cause of the <term>assumability|The inherent capacity of a created nature to be united to a divine Person</term> of any nature; rather, it is a co-cause. For unless He were the one "assuming," He could not assume. But beyond this, something is required in that which is assumed by which it is "assumable"; and this is the ground of the "image" <note>The *imago Dei*, or the capacity of the soul to reflect God</note> and, ultimately, a supernatural aptitude for elevation to <term>beatific operation|The soul's highest activity: seeing and enjoying God in heaven</term>. Since this is found in the intellectual nature alone, it seems fitting that it alone is assumable; for it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be elevated to the "second act" <note>the activity or operation of a thing</note> also cannot be elevated to the "first act" <note>the existence or being of a thing</note>. 

From this response, Henry seems to wish to preserve the idea that nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence. While the opponents claim that because this power exists in God, He must be able to "supposit" in this way, Henry also attributes all that power to God. He does not deny that the ground of what is required on the part of the one assuming <note>God</note> exists most fully in God so that He might assume any nature. Rather, he says that the irrational nature itself is not assumable, not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the deformed deficiency of the irrational nature. 

To the second argument, it seems many things can be said <margin>A manifold solution to the second</margin>. First is the response of Henry <margin>First</margin>, who says that He assumed the nature of that body insofar as it was ordered toward the intellectual soul; by reason of this ordering, even the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial <note>serving as a tool</note> and preparatory sense. And so that a more complete answer may be given, it should be said that when it is said that nothing can be assumed by God except an intellectual nature, it is understood that nothing besides it can be assumed in such a way that it is the "primary assumed thing" and a complete and adequate "assumable" object. The body during the Triduum was not assumed in that way, as is clear, but only as a part of the rational nature which was the total and primary object assumed.

Furthermore <margin>Second</margin>, perhaps someone might say that this body was not properly said to be "suppositated" during the Triduum, because it is not a nature capable of being suppositated by its own <term>suppositum|A distinct individual substance or person; the 'subject' that performs actions</term>. Whence it could consequently be said, not improbably, that to terminate the dependency of the nature of this body is not the same as to "supposit" it; otherwise, anything that terminates the dependency or leaning of a part would "supposit" it, which is not said. And thus, although the Word <note>The Second Person of the Trinity</note> terminated that dependency of the body during the Triduum (which the whole humanity would have terminated), and by virtue of this, the body in the Triduum communicated to Christ its <term>idiom|A technical term (Latin: 'idioma') referring to the properties or attributes of a nature</term> of "lying in the tomb," nevertheless He did not properly "supposit" the body in the same way He would supposit a human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate to Christ that "idiom" of "being a body" in the Triduum in the same way the human nature had communicated to Him (and still communicates to Him in a concrete sense) the "idiom" of "being a man."

->**FIFTH QUESTION CONCERNING NATURAL MAGIC AND THE CABALA OF THE HEBREWS**<-

$\quad$ The fourth conclusion condemned by these men was this: **There is no science that makes us more certain of the divinity of Christ than magic and Cabala.**
$\quad$ In explaining this conclusion, I stated that among those sciences which are "sciences" in such a way that they do not rely on revelation—neither in their methods, nor their principles, nor their conclusions—there is none that makes us more certain (in the way that humanly discovered sciences can provide certainty) than that "Magic" which is part of natural science, and that part of "Cabala" <note>Pico is referring to 'Natural Magic'—the study of the hidden powers in nature—and 'Cabala,' which he viewed as a mystical ancient wisdom that could prove Christian truths using Hebrew tradition.</note> which is a science and not revealed theology. These masters claimed that my explanation did not match the intent of the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the conclusion, strictly speaking <term>de uirtute sermonis|by the virtue of the words</term>, was false, erroneous, and heretical. Let us look, I pray, at how many things in their condemnation are themselves worthy of being condemned. First, let them tell me how my explanation could possibly be more suited to the purpose of my conclusion's words. For what does that explanation do other than explicitly define the weight of every single term placed in the conclusion? <margin>First</margin> For there, I first set forth what I mean by "science" when I say "no science," and what I mean by "certifying," and what I mean by "magic" and "Cabala." I do not see what else remains to be explained. Second, I wish to show that the literal phrasing is not only not false or heretical, but that the opposite of my claim is actually false—and, according to their own logic, totally heretical. <margin>Second</margin> For the said conclusion is a negative statement that can be broken down into three categories: either some science other than magic and Cabala certifies the divinity of Christ; or magic and Cabala do not certify it; or magic and Cabala certify us more than any other non-revealed science. This disjunction is true and Catholic <note>meaning 'orthodoxy' or 'universally accepted truth' in this context</note> because at least one of its parts is true. Thus, it is already clear that strictly speaking, it is not false. But it is clear that its opposite, according to them, would be heretical. For the opposite of "no non-revealed science etc. more certifies" is this: "Some non-revealed science more..."

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense in his Apology. He is arguing that his use of the word "magic" should not cause a "scandal" (stumbling block for the faithful) because he distinguishes between "natural magic"—which is a form of science—and "evil magic," which involves demons.</meta>

...cannot be, or that a scandal could arise through the ambiguity <note>original: *equivocationem*</note> of this name "magic." I have distinguished it in such a way that by rejecting that superstitious and diabolical magic and approving this natural magic, it can serve not as a cause for scandal, but rather for the edification of the simple-minded.

Among these people, I have seen many who—hearing that the **Magi** came to worship Christ <note>A reference to the Three Wise Men in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> and believing that this name "Magi" signifies nothing other than "necromancers" <note>term: *necromancer*; historically used here to mean any sorcerer who deals with evil spirits or the dead.</note>—take this as an argument that magic is not prohibited [Marginal note: Note] nor against the faith of Christ, since the first worshipers of Christ himself were practitioners of magic. It is useful, therefore, to have taught the faithful so that when they hear the word "magus," they do not always understand it to mean a worshiper of demons. 

And when they hear that among the Persians, the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence because of their learning and wisdom, they should know that those men were philosophers, not necromancers. For all nations have always pursued and detested necromancers—as beings destructive and harmful, indeed pestilential to the people—casting them out and holding them in ill repute. 

Similarly, when they read that **Albert** [Marginal note: Albert] <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous Dominican friar and scientist who was often (sometimes falsely) associated with magical experiments.</note> spent much time on "natural magic" among his experiments, they should understand this does not refer to prohibited magic; otherwise, they might devote themselves to evil by following the example of such a great man, presuming that what was permitted for him must also be permitted for them.

Therefore, our magical conclusions remove scandals from the minds of the faithful rather than creating them. For if they ever read in the works of the Doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," the authoritative theologians of the Middle Ages.</note> that "all magic is prohibited," they will immediately understand from the reasons for the prohibition that those authors are speaking only of the magic that has commerce with demons, and that they intend to say nothing concerning natural magic. 

Moreover, as **Hilary** [Marginal note: Hilary] <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent Latin theologian.</note> says, "the understanding of words must be taken from the reasons for speaking them." <note>original: *intelligentia dictorum ex causis assumenda dicendi*</note> But if they wish to return to the literal force of the words, they can know from logic <note>original: *dialectica*</note> that the negation or distribution of a term with multiple meanings does not negate or distribute it for every possible category collectively. 

Therefore, since this term "magic" has multiple meanings <note>original: *equivocus*</note> referring to both the superstitious and the natural, a general label applied to it [such as "all"] does not apply to every possible meaning together. But from the statement that "all magic is prohibited," it will only be understood that all types of superstitious magic—which are all grouped under one name and one logic—are meant. For many types of magic are indeed prohibited, and all these things are clear and lucid even to those who are only moderately learned.

In no way, therefore, should my magical conclusions have been suspect to these masters. For as I stated in my first conclusion, I refute all magic prohibited by the Church—damning and detesting it—and protesting that I speak only of natural magic. I declared this even more explicitly through a specific conclusion, stating that through this magic we perform nothing except by activating or uniting natural virtues. 

For thus says conclusion 11 of the *Magical Conclusions*: "The wonders of the magical art exist only through the union and activation of those things which exist in nature seminally and separately." And it is the same as what I said in the 13th conclusion: that to perform magic is nothing other than **to marry the world.** <note>term: *to marry the world* (original: *maritare mundum*); a famous phrase by Pico suggesting that the "magician" or scientist joins the hidden powers of the heavens to the objects of the earth to produce wonders.</note>

Moreover, I intend for the aforementioned specification and restriction of my intent—applying it to natural magic within the *Magical Conclusions*—to be applied to every individual conclusion. Thus, when I speak of the activity of characters and figures in a magical work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. For it is evident according to all philosophers that they possess such power, both in their manner of acting and in their capacity to be acted upon. And although according to the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> they are of far less activity and power than are quali...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his theses, specifically moving from the general concept of "natural magic" to the specific Pythagorean doctrine of numbers. He is arguing that numbers possess inherent power and that this belief is not heretical, but supported by the Church Fathers.</meta>

Pythagoreans [speak of] material properties. However, the Pythagoreans—whose philosophy I call **"secret philosophy"** <note>original: *secreatiorem philosophiam*</note> in my twenty-fourth conclusion because it is less known and less in use than [ordinary philosophy]—would say that just as mathematical things are more **formal** <note>In this context, "formal" refers to the "Form" or essence of a thing, which the Pythagoreans believed was rooted in number.</note> than physical things, they are also more **actual**. And just as they are less dependent in their being, so also are they in their operation. 

And so I spoke of their "greater power"; although the disagreement between the Pythagoreans and the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who generally viewed numbers as abstractions rather than active forces.</note> is indifferent to the faith, nevertheless I did not speak of it as something true in itself and absolute, but as a consequence of the **secret philosophy of the Pythagoreans**, to be understood in the manner aforesaid. It is also their opinion that among all mathematical things, numbers are more actual as they are more formal. Among odd numbers, they value the **three** <note>original: *ternarium*</note>, because it is the first odd number, and the first in any genus is the most perfect in that genus. Among even numbers, they value the **ten** <note>original: *denarium*</note>, which is "every number," as is evident. For beyond it, we count only by repetition <note>Ten was seen as the "Decad," the container of all numbers before the cycle starts again at eleven.</note>. 

And this is what I intended by what I said concerning the **three** and the **ten** in natural magic. Furthermore, Catholic doctors also attribute efficacy and power <note>term: *virtutem*; "virtue" here means an inherent efficacy or spiritual force, not just moral goodness.</note> to numbers, for both good and evil. 

Hence **Hilary** <margin>Hilary</margin> <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian.</note>, in his commentary on the Psalms, inquiring why the order of the Psalms is not according to history—but often a Psalm that was composed earlier is placed later in the order—says this: 

"It should not be ignored that among the Hebrews, the number of the Psalms is indistinct and they were written without a note of order. For **Ezra** <note>original: *Hesdras*</note> did not mark them there as first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth; but they were mixed into one without any prescription of order. For Ezra—as ancient traditions tell—collected them into one volume and recorded them, though they were uncomposed and scattered according to the diversity of authors and times. But the **seventy elders** <note>A reference to the translators of the Septuagint.</note>—who, according to the tradition of Moses, remained in the synagogue for the custody of the law and doctrine—when the task of translating the whole law from the Hebrew to the Greek language was mandated to them by King Antiochus, understanding the **powers** <note>original: *virtutes*</note> of the Psalms through spiritual and celestial science, reduced them into number and order. They assigned each to its specific number according to its efficacy and the completion of its perfection, arranging the order of these perfect and efficient Psalms." 

Thus speaks Hilary, word for word. From which it clearly appears that number gives power and efficacy. 

**Jerome** <margin>Jerome</margin> also, in his work *Against Jovinianus*, says that the number **twenty** is ill-omened <note>original: *infaustum*</note>, as it was the number [of years] Jacob served, and the price for which Joseph was sold, and the number of gifts Esau received. And in the same place he praises the number **ten**, saying he has spoken of its praises often. And in the same book, chapter eight, he says that on the second day [of Creation] it was not said, "and God saw that it was good," because the number **two** <note>original: *binarius*</note> is evil. 

Indeed, from the number two he takes an argument against those who marry twice; and for this reason he says all **unclean animals** entered Noah's ark by twos, while those that are clean entered by sevens. You will find similar things a hundred times in <margin>Basil, Nazianzen, Ambrose, Origen, Augustine, Rabanus</margin> **Basil**, **Nazianzen**, **Ambrose**, **Origen**, **Augustine**, and others. Furthermore, **Rabanus**, a distinguished doctor of the Church, composed a special book on the powers of numbers. You will always find the ecclesiastical doctors observing the properties of these numbers everywhere, and sometimes...

### Main Text

...of the Hebrews <note>original: *Hebraeorum*</note>, but also of our own doctors <note>theologians or teachers of the Church</note> as I shall show below: that besides the Law which God gave to Moses on the mountain, and which he left in writing contained in five books, there was also revealed to the same Moses by God Himself a true exposition of the Law, with a manifestation of all the mysteries and secrets which were contained under the bark <note>original: *cortice*; a common metaphorical term in medieval and Renaissance thought where the literal text is the "bark" or "husk" that protects the "pith" or inner spiritual meaning</note> and rough face of the words of the Law.
