<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of the Kabbalah. He has just argued that the secret tradition was committed to writing by Ezra to prevent its loss during the exile. He now transitions into explaining how this Jewish mystical tradition aligns with Christian theology and how it can be used in interreligious debate.</meta>

...revealed to his other successors. Whence it also received the name so that it was called "Kabbalistic" <note>original: *cabalistica*; the word Kabbalah literally means "received tradition."</note>, and in the time of Ezra it was redacted into many books, which are called the books of the Kabbalah. These books I have acquired for myself at great expense—for the Hebrews do not wish to share <margin>Note</margin> them with us Latins. Since I have read them through diligently, finding there many things—indeed almost everything—in harmony with our faith, it seemed to me that Christians might have a means by which to pierce the Jews with their own weapons, since the authority of the Kabbalists, whom they hold in great honor and reverence, cannot be denied by them.

Furthermore, it should be known that this exposition of the Bible <margin>Note</margin> corresponds to the method of interpreting the Bible which among us is called "anagogical" <note>In Christian theology, the anagogical sense is the highest level of interpretation, looking toward the spiritual or eternal fulfillment of a text.</note>. For just as among us there is a fourfold method of interpreting the Bible—literal, mystical or allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—so it is also among the <margin>The fourfold method of interpreting the Bible among the Hebrews is just like it is among us.</margin> Hebrews. The literal is called *Peshat* <note>original: *Pesat*</note> among them; this is the method held by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famed commentator.</note>, Kimchi <note>original: *Chemoy*, likely David Kimhi</note>, and others like them. <margin>Peshat.</margin> <margin>Rabbi Solomon</margin> The allegorical is called *Midrash* <note>original: *Midras*</note>. Whence you will often hear among them *Midrash Ruth*, *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: *Midrastillym*; the Midrash on the Psalms</note>, *Midrash Qoheleth* <note>original: *Midras coeleth*; the Midrash on Ecclesiastes</note>; that is, an exposition through Midrash—a mystical interpretation of Ruth, the Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and so on for others. <margin>Midrash.</margin> And this method is followed mostly by the Talmudic doctors. The tropological <note>The "tropological" or moral sense focuses on how one should act.</note> is called *Sekhel* <note>original: *sechel*; meaning "intellect" or "reason."</note>, which is followed by Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: *Abraā abnazara*</note>, where he does not interpret literally, and Levi ben Gershon <note>original: *leuibengerſon*, also known as Gersonides</note>, and many others, and above all Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note>. <margin>Sekhel.</margin> <margin>Abraham ibn Ezra.</margin> <margin>Levi ben Gershon.</margin> <margin>Rabbi Moses the Egyptian.</margin> The anagogical is called Kabbalah. <margin>Kabbalah.</margin> And this is because that exposition, which is said to have been delivered by the mouth of God to Moses and received through succession in the aforementioned manner, almost always follows the anagogical sense. Which is also the most sublime and divine among them all, leading us upward from earthly things to heavenly things, from the sensible to the intelligible, from the temporal to the eternal, from the lowest to the highest, from the human to the divine, and from the bodily to the spiritual.

And from this it follows that the most powerful arguments against the Jews are found there. Because the discord that exists between them and us—as is most clear from the letters of Paul—depends chiefly on this: that they follow the "letter that kills," while we follow the "spirit that gives life" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>. Let it suffice to have declared this now with a single example. <margin>Example</margin> For when it is promised to them in those prophecies that the Messiah will deliver them from captivity and lead them into the promised land and into Jerusalem, and they shall rejoice and be gathered in the Temple: they, understanding these things literally as referring to a worldly captivity and to a promised land which is the terrestrial Judea, and similarly to a material city of Jerusalem and a temple, cannot believe that He was the Messiah through whom they were cast out of that promised land, the city was destroyed, and the temple was demolished. But if they were willing, along with the Kabbalists, to understand those things anagogically by interpreting the Scripture as referring to the heavenly Jerusalem, to a spiritual captivity, and to the heavenly land of the living, they would necessarily recognize and confess that He was the true Messiah, through whom almost the entire world was liberated from the hand of the demon whom they served through idolatry.

That this would be the principal effect of the coming of Christ is the firm opinion of the Kabbalists themselves. Thus it would be recognized concerning all other matters, if the proofs of my Kabbalistic conclusions were seen, that there is—one might say—hardly any article of faith in which the <margin>Note</margin> Jews would not be compelled to agree with us through the authority of the Kabbalists. But immediately these "Fathers" <note>Pico is likely referring to the conservative ecclesiastical authorities who opposed his 900 theses.</note> rise up and ask: "Why then do all the Jews not become Christians?" and "Why did Augustine, Jerome, and the other doctors of the Church make no mention of this doctrine?" I marvel at the wisdom of these Fathers. And I ask them to tell me whether the miracles of Christ were true, or falsely fabricated by our people. If they say they were true, let them also tell me: why then were not all the Jews made [Christians by those miracles?]

...are Christians. For even if we assume that the Kabbalists themselves write the very same things that Augustine writes, there should be no doubt that the miracles of the living Christ, performed daily before their eyes, were of greater efficacy than the authority of any author, however authentic they might be in their eyes. 

Let it be known, however, that the Jews are forbidden from reading those books before they have reached the fortieth year of their age. And if they ever read them and do not believe—just as they did not believe in Christ himself whom they saw—I say with Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253) was an early Christian scholar and theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Scripture.</note> that they have become like those who "read and do not understand; they read and do not believe." For their foolish heart was darkened. And just as Paul speaks concerning those utterances of God—which we have declared above to be this Kabbalistic tradition—in this manner: "For what if some of them did not believe? Has their unbelief nullified the faith of God? Far from it. For God is truthful, but every man is a liar." <note>Pico is quoting Romans 3:3-4 to argue that the truth of a tradition isn't diminished just because its original keepers reject it.</note> So let us also say: what if many do not believe? Does their unbelief nullify the truth and nobility of this science? Far from it. 

Christians are especially worthy of this science, because just as it is a spiritual law rather than a carnal one, so we are spiritual Israelites, not carnal ones. Moreover, the spiritual law pertains to him who, according to Paul, is "a Jew in secret" <note>original: *in abscondito*; a reference to Romans 2:29, arguing that true faith is internal/spiritual rather than just external/legalistic.</note>, not to him who is one outwardly. 

As for the fact that the doctors of the Church are said to wonder why they never made mention of this doctrine, we have sufficiently shown above that Hilary, Origen, and Ezra—and alongside these, Paul and the Gospel—recall this science. It must also be noted that you will never, or very rarely, find any of our doctors—I speak of the ancients—citing any of the Hebrews by name. Instead, you will see them speaking only in general terms, saying: "Thus the Hebrews say," or "This is the opinion of the Hebrews." Indeed, I do not remember finding this but once in Origen, who cites the patriarch Huillus <note>original: *Huillum*; likely referring to Hillel II, a 4th-century Jewish leader known to Christian scholars.</note>, his contemporary. Therefore, it is no wonder if you never hear the authors of the Kabbalah cited by them by name.

But when we see our doctors so rely on the testimony of the Hebrews that, as our Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who studied with Jewish rabbis.</note> says: "When they wish to prove what they say—especially Eusebius, Origen, and Clement, and many others—they always refer back to the Hebrews," saying: "A Hebrew related it to me," "I heard from a Hebrew," or "This is the opinion of the Hebrews." And Jerome himself even calls them "masters," saying: "This is the opinion of the masters" <note>original: *magistrorum*</note>. There is no doubt that he understands them to be the teachers of the Kabbalah, which can be demonstrated by clear reason. 

For the entire school of the Hebrews is divided into three sects: the Philosophers, the Kabbalists, and the Talmudists. It is not to be believed that the Talmudists were cited by our ancient doctors. Firstly, because Clement and many others who cite the Hebrews lived before the composition of the Talmud itself, which occurred more than five hundred years after the death of Christ. Secondly, because the Talmudic doctrine was entirely fabricated against us by the Hebrews themselves, already fighting against Christians; therefore, our ancestors would not have shown such honor to that doctrine as to consider anything said by them to be firm, even when corroborated by the testimony of the Jews. 

Likewise, it is certain that they do not cite the Philosophers, because those who began to explain the Bible according to philosophy began only a short time ago. For the first was Rabbi Moses of Egypt <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher who reconciled Aristotelian logic with Jewish law.</note>, in whose lifetime Averroes of Córdoba <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval thought.</note> flourished; and three hundred years have not yet passed since the death of Averroes. It remains, therefore, that this Hebrew doctrine which the doctors [cite as ancient and authoritative must be the Kabbalah]...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his Kabbalistic and magical theses. He is narrowing his focus to define what "true" Kabbalah is, distinguishing it from both the general use of the term and the superstitious practices of his contemporaries.</meta>

<margin>
The first and true Kabbalah
</margin>

<margin>
The Hebrews have honored two sciences with the name of Kabbalah.
The Art of Raymond
</margin>

Catholics, following the testimony of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420) was the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible; Pico uses his authority to justify studying Hebrew traditions.</note>, grant and approve so much of that which our own doctors admit and believe: that it was revealed by God to Moses, and from Moses passed down through a succession of other wise men. This is the method of transmission that is called **Kabbalah**, which I often see designated by our own authors when they say, "as the ancient tradition tells." This is the **first and true Kabbalah**, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to make explicit mention. It is this Kabbalah that I use in my conclusions, which I have set forth specifically against the Hebrews to confirm our own faith. I do not know how these masters could consider them suspect in the faith.

However, because this method of "delivery by succession"—which is called <term>Kabbalistic<note>Derived from the Hebrew root QBL, meaning "to receive."</note></term>—seems to apply to every secret and mystical matter, the Hebrews have usurped the term. They call any science they consider secret and hidden "Kabbalah," and any bit of knowledge obtained through an occult path is said to be held "by way of Kabbalah." Generally, they have honored two sciences with this name. One is called the <term>Art of Combination<note>original: "ars combinandi"; this refers to the Jewish practice of *Gematria*, *Notarikon*, or *Temurah*, where the letters of the Torah are rearranged to find hidden meanings.</note></term>, which is a way of proceeding through the sciences. It is something similar to what our people call the **Art of Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher who developed a "Great Art" using moving paper circles to combine philosophical concepts, hoping to prove Christian truths through logic.</note>, though they perhaps proceed in different ways. 

The other science concerns the powers of superior things that are above the moon, which is the supreme part of <term>Natural Magic<note>In the Renaissance, "Natural Magic" was considered a legitimate science involving the study of the hidden properties of plants, minerals, and stars, distinct from "black magic" or demon-summoning.</note></term>. Both of these are also called Kabbalah among the Hebrews for the reason already mentioned, and I have also made mention of both in my conclusions. For that "Art of Combination" is what I call the **alphabetical revolution** in my conclusions. And this second science, concerning the powers of superior things, can be understood in one way as a part of natural magic, and in another as something distinct from it. It is this which I speak of in the present conclusion, saying that it aids us in the knowledge of the divinity of Christ in the manner already declared. 

And although the name "Kabbalah" might not fit these two sciences by its primary and proper definition, it can nevertheless be applied to them metaphorically. But just as in the past, <term>Magi<note>Originally referring to the Zoroastrian priests of Persia, the "Wise Men" of the Nativity.</note></term> were simply called wise men, until <term>Necromancers<note>Those who attempt to communicate with the dead or summon demons.</note></term> and diabolical men—falsely claiming the name of "wise man" for themselves—called themselves "Magi," so too have some among the Hebrews. These men, promising divine things through false and vain superstitions (indeed, in truth differing almost nothing from necromancers), claimed they possessed the secret names of God and powers by which they could bind demons and perform miracles, and they claimed that Christ performed miracles by no other way. These men falsely claimed the name of **Kabbalists** for themselves, saying their art was that "true Kabbalah" which God revealed to Moses. This is just as the necromancers say they received their incantations and brutalities from Solomon, Adam, or Enoch. 

This "falsely named Kabbalah" I have not only not approved in my conclusions or followed, but I have expressly rejected it. I placed a special conclusion directly against it, which states that the miracles of Christ could *not* have been performed by way of the Kabbalah <note>Pico is defending himself against charges of heresy by arguing that Christ's miracles were truly divine, not the result of the magical techniques his critics were afraid of.</note>. Let these words suffice for the present conclusion, which would otherwise require a special book. If we wished to declare exactly what natural magic is and what Kabbalah is, it is enough here to have shown that nothing is contained in them that repugns the Catholic and Orthodox faith.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola distinguishes the "true" Kabbalah—a divine tradition revealed to Moses—from the "false" Kabbalah used by superstitious practitioners and necromancers. He argues that his use of these traditions is intended to prove Christian truths and is entirely compatible with Catholic doctrine.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his Kabbalistic theses to his defense of his sixth "conclusion" regarding the Eucharist. He is responding to the Papal commission that condemned several of his 900 theses as heretical or erroneous. Here, he navigates the dangerous theological waters of how Christ is present in the bread and wine.</meta>

### SIXTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.

**S**hould the common path be held regarding the possibility of <term>suppositation<note>From the Latin *suppositatio*; in scholastic theology, this refers to a Divine Person (like the Word) taking a nature (like humanity or, in this hypothetical case, bread) into a personal union.</note></term> with respect to any creature, I say that without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ, or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," it is possible for the body of Christ to be on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament. Let this be said speaking of what is **possible**, not what **is actually the case**. By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that the bread is not converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ is actually in the sacrament—as it was in fact instituted by Christ—or that the actual truth of that sacrament is the presence of Christ's body alongside bread that has been assumed or "suppositated" by the Word. I explicitly reject these claims as actual facts at the end of the conclusion where I state it is "spoken of the possible, not of what is." Here, I want the term "possible" <note>original: "ly possibile"</note> to refer not only to the preceding statement about the assumption of bread by Christ, but also to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist and even to the sacrament itself; indeed, even to the presence of the body of Christ together with the assumed bread. It might not be strictly necessary that, by virtue of this assumption of bread by the incarnate Word, the body of Christ (which He already assumed from the Virgin) would be present with the bread. Nevertheless, it is possible that it would be on the altar together with the bread if the bread were assumed by Christ.

I speak, therefore, in the present conclusion about a *possible* sacrament, its *possible* truth, and the *possible* presence of Christ's body together with this "assumable" bread. Therefore, I marvel that the present conclusion has been condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as it is *now* instituted—which is what they claim I am speaking about. However, I explicitly profess in the conclusion to be speaking of a *possible* sacrament and its *possible* truth. Let them, therefore, consider the words of the conclusion more attentively before they condemn a conclusion that so explicitly refutes the meaning they are condemning. Indeed, let them consider that their own determination can hardly be defended from error; for if it were the case that the conclusion intended to uphold the truth of the sacrament according to Christ's institution (as the Church holds), then, as they say, it would be not only erroneous but simply heretical.

But if the meaning of the conclusion is the one I have explained, it is not only *not* erroneous in the faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite. For many things are heretical concerning what is the case, yet the opposite of those things concerning what is *possible* would be heretical. For example: to say that "the Father is incarnate" is heretical in terms of what is the case; however, to say that "the Father *could* be incarnated" is not only not heretical, but it is heretical to claim the opposite <note>Pico argues that denying God's power to do something (even if He hasn't done it) limits His omnipotence, which is itself a heresy.</note>.

<margin>
Question
</margin>

Let these things suffice for the declaration and defense of the conclusion. But for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving my conclusion aside, let us see whether it is true that the body of Christ could be on the altar through another mode than the conversion of bread into Himself. Specifically: through the sustenance of the "bread-ness" in the divine <term>Person<note>original: "supposito"; the underlying substance or "personhood" that supports the various natures.</note></term> together with the assumed humanity, so that there would be one Person in three natures: namely, divinity, humanity, and "bread-ness." By reason of the Person, each nature—taken in its concrete form—would be predicated of the other in relation to that Person. There would be a <term>communication of properties<note>original: "comunicatio idiomatum"; a theological principle where the attributes of both the divine and human natures are ascribed to the one Person of Jesus (e.g., "God died on the cross"). Pico is extending this logic to his hypothetical "bread nature."</note></term>: "God is bread" and "man," and vice versa. And "Christ as man" is on the altar just as "Christ as bread" is on the altar, and so on. And this would be "sacramentally," or by virtue of the sacrament, if power were given for this purpose.

<summary>Pico defends his thesis on the Eucharist by arguing that while the Church's doctrine of transubstantiation is factually true, it is logically possible for Christ to have remained present alongside the bread through a hypothetical "triple nature" (God, Man, and Bread). He accuses his critics of failing to distinguish between a discussion of God's absolute power and a discussion of established Church dogma.</summary>

...divinely by the sacramental word. Nor should we concern ourselves with whether this word—"This is my body"—would be sufficient for this by the aforementioned power, or whether something else would be required.

And first, an argument is made for the affirmative side—that this position should be held—because it seems that John Damascene <margin>First argument</margin> <note>John Damascene (c. 675–749) was a Syrian monk and Church Father whose writings on the nature of Christ and the sacraments were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> holds this as a matter of fact: namely, that this <margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin> sacrament exists through "assumption" <note>In this context, "assumption" refers to the Divine Word taking a nature into union with itself, just as it took on human nature in the Incarnation.</note>. For he says: "And now you ask how the bread becomes the body of Christ, and the wine and water become the blood of Christ? <margin>Damascene.</margin> I say to you, the Holy Spirit comes upon them and performs that which is beyond reason and intellect. The bread and wine are assumed." And further in the same place: "And just as in baptism—because it is human custom to be washed with water and anointed with oil—God joined <note>original: "iugauit"</note> water and the grace of the Holy Spirit and made it the bath of regeneration; so also, because it is human custom to eat bread and drink wine, God joined His divinity to them and makes them His body and blood." And further in the same chapter, speaking of this sacrament of the altar, he says: "Isaiah saw a coal; but a coal is not simple wood, but wood united to fire. So also the bread of communion is not simple bread, but bread united to the divinity."

Furthermore, Dionysius <margin>Dionysius</margin> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century mystical theologian whom medieval scholars often confused with a contemporary of St. Paul.</note> in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* calls this sacrament an "assumption." If these Doctors seem to say that this is how things *actually* are, then much more so can the position be held regarding what is *possible*.

Second, it is argued <margin>Second argument.</margin> that according to Augustine in his letter to Volusianus: "In miraculous things, the entire reason for the deed is the power of the Doer." To restrict this miraculous sacrament to a determined mode of defense—one that is not expressly found in the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church—is to restrict divine power to the capacity of our intellect. This is dangerous and goes against what Augustine says in the same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be a wonder; if an example is provided, it will not be singular. Let us grant that God can do something that we must confess we cannot investigate."

Third, it is argued <margin>Third argument.</margin> that any position whose opposite is not clearly established by the sayings of the Saints can much more easily be held as a possibility. But the opposite of this—namely, that the "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitas"; a technical term for the essential substance or nature of bread.</note> remains on the altar substantiated by a divine "suppositum" <note>A "suppositum" is the underlying personhood or individual "subject" that possesses a nature. Pico is arguing the Word could "own" the nature of bread as its own subject.</note>—is not clearly excluded by the sayings of the Saints. This is proven because the statement of Gregory <margin>Gregory</margin> <note>Pope Gregory the Great (d. 604).</note> in his Easter homily—saying that "the species and likeness are terms for the things that were there before, namely bread and wine"—is explained by those holding this opinion to mean they were "alone" before, but now they are not "alone" because the body of Christ lies hidden there.

Likewise, the statement of Ambrose <margin>Ambrose</margin> <note>St. Ambrose (d. 397), Bishop of Milan.</note>—that the power of God, which creates creatures from nothing, here "changes" the creatures—and other statements saying that bread and wine do not remain after the consecration but are "converted," would be explained thus: the bread does not remain *as it was bread* (meaning as its own independent thing), even though the "bread-ness" is the same, because it now has a different "suppositum" (the Divine Word). There is a great difference between saying that the nature of bread remains "hypostatized" <note>United into a single person or "hypostasis."</note> in a divine subject, and saying that the nature of bread remains in its own independent subject. In this second way (the independent way), there would be no "communication of properties" <note>original: "cōmunicatio ydiomatum"; the theological doctrine that the attributes of both natures (divine and human, or here, divine and bread) can be predicated of the one Person of Christ.</note> which occurs in the first way. However, I believe these authorities are entirely against those who claim this is the *actual* fact, rather than just a *possibility*.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding Pico’s sixth conclusion. ...let there be two underlying subjects <note>original: "supposita." In scholastic theology, a *suppositum* is the individual "person" or "subject" that possesses a nature. For example, in Christ, there is one person (the Word) and two natures (human and divine).</note> of Christ and of the bread. This view indeed posits that whatever is under the sacrament is to be adored with a single adoration on account of the unity of the person.

### Second Argument against the Position <margin>Second position</margin>
Secondly, it is argued that in no way can it be maintained that Christ's body can be on the altar by that method. Because when it is asked whether the body of Christ can be on the altar, etc., it is not understood as the "body" which Christ *is* (where "body" is taken as a genus <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category, like "animal" or "substance." Here, the author distinguishes between Christ *being* a body in a general sense and the specific physical *part* of him that is his flesh.</note>), but it is understood as the "body" which is a *part* and is not predicated of "man" directly. For such a body, which is a physical part, does not share the properties <note>original: "idioma." This refers to the "Communication of Idioms," a doctrine explaining how properties of the human and divine natures are shared by the one Person of Christ.</note> of the co-assumed nature with the person, nor vice versa.

For although God is man and vice versa, yet God is not the "head of Christ," and vice versa. And although Christ as man is everywhere by reason of his person <note>original: "suppositi"</note>, nevertheless the "head" of Christ the man is not everywhere, because the parts of the assumed nature do not share their properties with the person, nor are they predicated of it, or vice versa. Therefore, even if "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitas"</note> were assumed by the Word together with "body-ness" <note>original: "corporeitate"</note>, it would still not be said that the "body of Christ is bread," or that "the body of Christ is on the altar" just because the bread is on the altar; though it could be said and verified that the bread is the "body" which Christ *is*, according to how "body" is taken as a broad category or genus.

That it is not understood otherwise in this question and in the sacrament is apparent: first, because "body" as a genus, which is predicated directly of Christ, is not called "the body of Christ," just as the animal or man that Christ is, is not called "the man of Christ" or "the animal of Christ." Second, because the form of words in which this sacrament was instituted is this: **"This is my body."**

Now it is clear that the truth of that word is not maintained concerning "body" as a genus. For the "animal" which is predicated of me directly is not "my animal," but the animal that I *am*. Third, because if the consecration had occurred during the three days of Christ's death <note>The "triduum," the period between the Crucifixion and Resurrection when Christ's soul was in Hell and his body was in the tomb.</note>, there would have been on the altar not "body" as a genus, but "body" as a part only. For "body" as a genus is an animated body, which it was not then. Therefore, the body of Christ as it is asked here and as it is dealt with in the sacrament is the body as a part only, which is not predicated of bread or God or man. For it does not share the properties <note>original: "idiomata"</note> of the other natures. Therefore, it would not be true to say that the body of Christ was on the altar in the aforementioned way by reason of the bread or the person.

### Third Argument <margin>Third</margin>
Furthermore, even if it were said that by reason of the said sustaining in one person the bread were the body, it does not follow that where the bread is on the altar, there the body of Christ is; rather, the bread on the altar would be the body of Christ in heaven. Just as during the three days of death, the soul and body were sustained in the person of the Word, yet the soul was not for that reason in the tomb with the body, nor was the body in hell with the soul.

### Fourth Argument <margin>Fourth</margin>
Furthermore, if this sustaining were to occur, it would terminate in that in which we say the conversion of the bread terminates—namely, the body of Christ. But the sustaining of a foreign nature cannot terminate in a physical part. For this sustaining is proper to the uncreated person <note>The Divine Word</note> alone according to the common way. Therefore, the sustaining of "bread-ness" cannot occur in a person of another nature in this sacrament.

### Fifth Argument <margin>Fifth</margin>
Also, it is argued thus: because according to the aforementioned mode of sustaining "bread-ness" in the Word along with the body of Christ assumed long ago, the body would not *begin* to be on the altar, but something new would begin to *be* the body of Christ. But if it does not begin to be there, having not been there before, it follows that it will not be on the altar.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic disputation against the "Eucharistic assumption" theory. While the previous page addressed the second through sixth counter-arguments, this page details the seventh, eighth, and ninth arguments, focusing on the metaphysical impossibility of a creature assisting in the union and the practical sacramental consequences regarding the nature of the bread after consumption.</meta>

### Seventh Argument <margin>Seventh.</margin>
The Word cannot assume the nature of bread <note>original: "paneitatem," a scholastic term referring to the essential "bread-ness" or essence of bread.</note> while it exists in its own individual subject, because this would be to destroy the nature of bread rather than to assume it. Furthermore, it appears that no power can be granted to the Word regarding the union of the bread-nature to the Word. This is because the assumption of the nature of bread into the subject of the Word is of greater difficulty than creation itself. This is because the divine being is more distant from the nature of bread (to which the divine is said to be communicated in this assumption) than "being" is from "non-being." And yet, the power to create cannot be communicated to a creature, whether by its own operation or by cooperation with God. Therefore, neither can such power be granted for the purpose of <margin>Confirmation</margin> assumption. This is confirmed by the authority of Saint Thomas <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas, likely in the *Summa Theologiae*, Part III.</note> in the third part, who says that a creature cannot cooperate toward the union of natures in one person.

### Eighth Argument <margin>Eighth.</margin>
Furthermore, if that position were granted, after receiving the sacrament, the priest would no longer be fasting <note>In Catholic tradition, the "Eucharistic fast" required the stomach to be empty of physical food before and during the reception of the Host. If the bread remained "physical food" because it was assumed by Christ, it would technically break the fast upon consumption.</note>, and there would not be spiritual food alone present, but also corporal food. This is contrary to the dignity of the sacrament.

### Ninth Argument <margin>Ninth.</margin>
Likewise, Christ would be "laying something aside" after he had assumed it into the unity of his person. This is because he would be assuming the nature of bread, which he would then lay aside once the bread is converted into his physical limbs <note>original: "converso in membra." This refers to the digestion and assimilation of the bread into the body.</note>.

<meta>This page continues a technical scholastic defense of the "impanation" theory. It addresses objections regarding the breaking of the fast and explores the metaphysical relationship between Christ's body and the substance of bread using analogies of accidents and subjects.</meta>

...[taken] by way of physical food, and with the intention of eating, would break a fast. But because the priest does not consume [the host] by way of physical food, but by way of a sacrament, the fast is not broken. It would be similar if the substance of the bread remained; even then it would not break the "fast of nature," provided it were not consumed by way of physical food.

<margin>First response to the ninth [argument].</margin>
Regarding the saying that Christ does not set aside what he once assumed: this is said by presupposing that he is only held to have assumed human nature, just as in fact he assumed only that. However, he could assume another nature and later set it aside.

<margin>Second. Another question.</margin>
It can also be said that if "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitas"; the essential substance or "whatness" of bread.</note> were assumed by the Word, it would never be set aside by the Word of its own accord or on its own part. However, it might be set aside "by accident" due to the condition of the nature assumed—with its natural defects—because of the corruption of that assumed nature, just as he set aside his humanity during the three days <note>The *Triduum*, the period between Christ's death and resurrection when his soul and body were separated.</note>.

<margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
But again, let us inquire through disputation whether it can be maintained that the body truly exists on the altar without the conversion of the bread into it. It seems so, because just as color is sustained in a substance (as in a subject) by means of another accident—for example, a surface—it is not that the surface is the actual subject of color (for one accident is not the subject of another, because, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says, a quality is not a quality), but rather because color does not exist in a subject except in relation to a surface.

In this same way, "bread-ness" can be sustained in the Word by means of the body. This does not mean the body is the immediate sustainer and life-giver of the assumed bread-ness while the Word is the primary one. Rather, it means that bread-ness is not sustained in the person <term>supposito</term> <note>The "suppositum" is the individual person or substance that underlies the natures; here, the Divine Person of the Word.</note> of the Word except in relation to the part that is Christ's body. God can establish this order among "assumable" natures, even if they do not have that order in their own nature, just as he can take away from some things the natural order they have between themselves—such as the link between heat and the act of heating in the "furnace of the Chaldeans" <note>A reference to the biblical story of the three youths in the fiery furnace, where the fire existed but miraculously did not burn them.</note> and in many other instances.

Therefore, just as color—because it exists in a substance in relation to a surface—is spoken of in relation to the surface as an accidental quality (by saying "the surface is colored"), so "bread-ness," which is a substance, will be spoken of in relation to the body of Christ as a substantial quality or by way of "whatness" <term>quid</term> <note>The "quid" or "quiddity" refers to the essential definition of a thing.</note>. Thus, one would say "the Son of God is bread" and vice versa. Just as humanity is predicated of the person <term>supposito</term> in its "whatness" by saying "the Son of God is man" and vice versa, so because God is man and vice versa, they share their properties <term>idiomata</term> <note>The *communicatio idiomatum*, where properties of the human and divine natures are attributed to the one Person.</note>: where God is, there the man is. The same logic applies to the surface and the white color, and thus to the bread and the body. For if the bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar.

<margin>Ancient theologians.</margin>
Perhaps it should be said differently: that assumed natures have the "mode of an accident," as the ancient theologians used to say, insofar as they are added to a person <term>supposito</term> who already exists in actuality. They do not "make" the person, but are rather "made" to exist through the person. Just as among accidents one is found to be the "subject" of another (though not the ultimate one)—as we say the power of the soul is the subject of virtues and habits insofar as it is sustained by the soul, and similarly a surface is in some way called the subject in respect to color—so, although one assumed nature cannot of itself and primarily sustain another nature, nevertheless, insofar as it is united to the Word and sustained in it, it can sustain another in itself. It can have the mode of a "subject," as it were, in respect to that other, and that other a mode of "accident" in respect to the first. This is only in this regard: that one is sustained in the other as it is united to the Word and sustained by him. For if the person <term>supposito</term>...

<meta>This page continues the technical scholastic debate regarding the theory of "impanation." The author is exploring how the Word (Christ) can grant subsistence to the nature of bread through the mediation of his own human body, using the philosophical relationship between subjects and accidents as a primary analogy.</meta>

...[Christ] does not give subsistence <note>original: "substentificat"; the act of providing an underlying foundation of existence for a nature.</note> to the assumed nature except by reason of his own infinite being, to which he draws the nature that is united and associated with him. To whatever nature he communicates his infinite being, he also communicates the power to allow another nature, united to it, to subsist. Thus also a substance, insofar as it draws an accident to its own being—because an accident is not a being except in that it is "of a being" <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea that properties like "redness" only exist because they belong to a "thing" like an apple.</note>—gives that accident the power to sustain another accident coming to it, just as an act comes to a potentiality, within itself and in its own being. 

Therefore, the Body, taken as a part, being united to and sustained by the Word in its being (which is the being of the Word communicated to it), can give subsistence within itself to the nature of bread that is capable of being assumed and which possesses the mode of an accident. For this is presupposed: that just as God gives to accidents the mode of substance <note>A reference to the Eucharist, where the "accidents" (taste, smell, shape) of bread remain without their original substance.</note>, so he can give to "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitati"; the essential quality of being bread.</note> the mode of an accident by sustaining it in something else which stands toward it as a subject. Regarding this, it makes no difference whether the subject is "perfect in species" or not—for sometimes the subject of an accident is "imperfect in species," such as a head or a hand.

Just as God produces some creatures immediately and others through the mediation of others, and just as he terminates some creatures in himself as an end by means of others, so also can the Word terminate in himself (as the sustaining individual or "suppositum" <note>term: "suppositum" (an individual person or thing that exists in its own right, not as a property of something else).</note>) some creature through the mediation of another. And just as the creatures through which God produces things are called "producers," and those through which he terminates things are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so the creature through which the Word gives subsistence to another in himself shall be said to "give subsistence." 

By reason, therefore, of such sustaining in the body of Christ as in a quasi-subject and immediate foundation, it shall be said in concrete terms: "**the bread is the body**" and vice versa, just as "**the Son of God is man**" and vice versa. They will communicate their properties <note>original: "ydiomata"; a theological term referring to the "Communication of Idioms," where the properties of the divine and human natures are predicated of the person of Christ.</note> to one another in the manner mentioned before, like a surface and a colored object. For "bread" stands for that which sustains "bread-ness," just as "white" stands for that which sustains whiteness. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For as the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Topics*, "white" is a body having such a color. 

<margin>Damascene.</margin>
John Damascene says in Book III, Chapter 11: "God is he who has the divine nature, and man is he who has the human nature," and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference to something being "white" whether the thing in which the whiteness is sustained is perfect in species or not, so it makes no difference to something being called "bread" whether that which is the immediate foundation of the bread-ness is perfect in species, imperfect, a nature, or a part of a nature.

<margin>Against.</margin>
**Against this:** Because an assumed nature (or a part of an assumed nature) does not have the character of a "suppositum," nor does it have the "being of subsistence" in itself. For although the being of the Word is communicated to it, nevertheless, insofar as it belongs to the nature, it is not the "being of subsistence," but the "being of existence" in another. Therefore, the assumed nature, as it is united, cannot sustain another nature in itself, nor draw it to the person, since it does not itself have the character of a "suppositum."

<margin>Response.</margin>
**Response:** If this conclusion holds, would it not also conclude that a surface cannot sustain color in itself? For the "being of subsistence" regarding a substance, when communicated to an accident, becomes the "being of existence" [in another], and thus a surface could not be the subject of color because the surface itself is an accident. Must we not say that the being of the Word, as it belongs to the assumed humanity in relation to the Word, is the "being of existence" (in another), but as it belongs to that same humanity in relation to "bread-ness," it is the "being of subsistence"? However, as it belongs to the *last* assumed nature, it is "being of existence" simply, just as might be said of a surface.

<margin>Against again.</margin>
But against the aforementioned, it is argued again: a nature is immediately united to the person...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the Eucharist, specifically transitioning from the defense of the "assumption" theory (where Christ assumes the bread) to the arguments against it, citing the influential (and often controversial) theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain.</meta>

...the state of being a <term>suppositum</term> <note>A "suppositum" is a technical term for an individual, self-subsisting subject—essentially what makes a thing an individual "it" or "person."</note> to a new existence of a <term>suppositum</term>. When things are "assumed," that which simply ceases to be is **annihilated**. Thus, its reproduction would be a new creation, and [the concept of] **annihilation** is entirely irrelevant to this, whether it is proposed that something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it; this is because [succession] is entirely extrinsic to the thing which ceases to be. 

### Conversion
However, that which is **converted** is that which remains according to its essence, but having lost its own existence as a <term>suppositum</term>, it passes into the existence of another <term>suppositum</term> and truly becomes that <term>suppositum</term>. This is the true definition of conversion, in which two things are understood in the converted object: 

<margin>The definition of conversion.</margin> 
First, that it remains in its essence (by which it differs from the **annihilated**); and second, that it becomes something else by reason of its <term>suppositum</term> (by which it differs from the **unconverted**). And while it becomes something else, it lets go of the nature of its own <term>suppositum</term> (by which it differs from the **assumed** <note>In an "assumption," a nature is typically taken up without necessarily losing its own character, whereas in "conversion" or transubstantiation, the bread is thought to become Christ entirely.</note>). 

However, by holding to the common mode of conversion <note>i.e., the standard doctrine of Transubstantiation.</note>, the bread is not "converted" but **annihilated**. Those who wish to maintain that it is a conversion and not an annihilation seem to satisfy with words rather than with reality. Whence many from that path have conceded that it is an annihilation, etc. 

### Arguments for the opposing (True) side
<margin>Arguments for the opposing true side.</margin> 
On the other hand, it is argued for the "true side" that the opinion claiming the sacrament of the Eucharist is actually brought about through the **assumption of "bread-ness"** <note>original: "assumptionem paneitatis"; the theory that Christ's divine personhood takes on the nature of bread.</note> is inconvenient and irrational. 

<margin>Durandus’s first argument.</margin> 
First, **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a Dominican philosopher known as "Doctor Resolutissimus" for his independent and often skeptical approach to standard church authorities.</note> argues thus: that it is ridiculous for a single nature—or rather many natures—to be assumed by the **Divine Suppositum** <note>The person of Christ.</note> every day and then be laid down every day. This is what would happen if the substance of the bread were assumed anew in this sacrament: for there would be as many "assumptions" as there are consecrations, and as many "layings down" as there are consumptions of the sacrament. 

**Response.** 
But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not demonstrate the falsehood of the premise. 

<margin>Second [argument].</margin> 
Second, it is argued that it seems impossible for such an **assumption** to take place through some **created medium**, as the aforementioned opinion proposes. This is because that medium would have to act either as the **efficient cause** of such an assumption or as the **terminating cause**; but nothing created can relate to an "assumption" in either of these ways. 

The minor premise is proved: for it is clear that nothing created can be the **efficient cause** of such an assumption, because such an assumption happens because a thing loses its own natural mode of being and puts on a foreign one. It seems no one can do this except the **Author of Nature**, who alone instituted the natures of things. Thus, He alone seems able to change them. This argument of Durandus perhaps shows that a created thing cannot be the *principal* efficient cause. 

**Response.** 
By the same logic, it seems that nothing created can **terminate** <note>In this context, "terminate" means to be the final ground or subject that supports the nature being assumed.</note> such an assumption, because it cannot be granted to any nature that which is above nature and the entire course of nature. This [above-natural act] is the act of giving subsistence to another nature that is by its own birth meant to subsist in itself. Perhaps this erroneous opinion mentioned above would believe it could avoid this through certain previously stated points. Indeed, a falsehood is not always easily convicted of its own falsity by evident reasons. So weak is the light of our intellect, being as it is the lowest in the order of intellectual natures. 

<margin>Third [argument].</margin> 
Furthermore, Durandus argues as follows: whatever the case may be regarding the proposal of such an **assumption**, it is nonetheless entirely inconvenient that it should happen through a "body as a part." 

### The Body
<margin>As a part.</margin> 
For a body is never taken as a "part" of human nature when one posits only a single form in a man. Since it cannot name matter alone, but must necessarily name the composite of **matter and form** giving it "corporeal existence," it is necessary that the **"human body"** refers to the **whole** reality and not a **part**. 

<margin>As a whole.</margin> 
Although, according to reason, it can name a "part" because the soul gives all...

The text transitions from logical definitions of "body" to specific arguments by the theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain regarding the nature of Christ's blood and the necessity of its union with his divinity for the sake of salvation.</meta>

perfections which lower forms provide. And therefore, if one considers a composite of matter and the form which is the soul, insofar as it gives only bodily existence, and compares it to the same composite insofar as through the soul it has not only bodily existence but also sensation, life, and reason—then in the first way, "body" is taken as a part, and in the second way as a whole. But since this difference is only one of reason <note>A "difference of reason" means a conceptual distinction made by the mind, rather than a physical or "real" difference in the object itself.</note>, it does not serve the purpose of those who claim a real assumption of the bread by means of the body acting as a part. For a conceptual difference contributes nothing to the reality of a physical assumption. 

<margin>Response</margin>
Whatever the effectiveness of this reasoning may be against those who posit only one form <note>Referring to the "uniquity of forms," a major debate in medieval philosophy about whether a human has one soul/form or multiple forms for different functions.</note>, <margin>Fourth</margin> it is clear that it does not proceed against those who do not hold to a single form. 

Likewise, he [Durandus] argues as follows: This position fails in that it posits that through such an "assumption," the body of Christ taken from the Virgin is in this sacrament through a <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "communicationem ydiomatum"; a theological principle where the attributes of one nature (like humanity) are spoken of as belonging to the other nature (divinity) because they are joined in one person.</note> because one thing is predicated of the other. For by the same reasoning that the body of Christ would be in the sacrament of the altar through the assumption of the substance of bread, the blood would be in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of wine. But this is not true, as will be proven. Therefore, etc. 

The premise is proven because if Christ’s blood were in this sacrament by the assumption of the substance of wine—just as it is posited of Christ's body by the assumption of the substance of bread—then it would follow that just as the bread is assumed by means of the body (which belongs to the unity of the assuming <term>suppositum</term> <note>A self-subsisting individual; here, the Person of the Son of God.</note>), so wine would be assumed by means of the blood belonging to the unity of the assuming <term>suppositum</term>. 

Now, it is established that the blood of Christ does not belong to the identity of the <term>suppositum</term> of Christ, since blood is not yet under the "human form," but is a humor <note>In medieval medicine, blood was one of the four humors; the author argues it is a fluid in the process of being converted into flesh, rather than being the "person" itself.</note> on its way to conversion so that it may come under the human form. Therefore, it cannot be assumed by the <term>suppositum</term> of Christ by means of blood, unless perhaps it were said that in every consecration of this sacrament there were an assumption of Christ's blood immediately, and through that blood, an assumption of the wine. And thus every day there would be an assumption of a new nature—namely, blood—without any relationship to the assumed nature of the bread (which others deny), and through this, there would be an assumption of wine. 

<margin>Response</margin>
But in this matter, many would perhaps not only reject Durandus’s reasoning, but would rebuke him no less than the aforementioned opinion—namely, concerning his claim of the non-assumption and the lack of a <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The union of divine and human natures in the person of Jesus.</note> of the blood of Christ shed on the cross and presented in the sacrament. For it seems that according to this view, that blood would not have been a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race, since it would not have been personally united to the divinity. 

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Wherefore Saint Thomas, in his *Quodlibetal Questions* (Book 6, Question 6), says: "The blood of Christ shed in the Passion sanctified the human race," according to that which is written in the last chapter of Hebrews: <note>original: "Hebreorum ultimo"; referring to Hebrews 13:12.</note> "Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate." Also, the humanity of Christ had salvific power from the power of the Word [the Son of God] united to it, as <margin>Damascene</margin> Damascene says in his third book. <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian often cited in these debates.</note> Hence it is manifest that the blood shed in the Passion, which was most especially our salvation, was united to the divinity, and therefore it was necessary that in the Resurrection it be joined to the other parts of his humanity, etc. Thus he [Thomas] spoke. 

<margin>Another argument of Durandus</margin>
Durandus continues against the aforementioned position because the body of Christ is on the altar (or in the sacrament of the altar) through the true existence of its nature, and not solely because of the "communication of properties" as this opinion posits. This is evident because this always refers to the same numerical thing that preceded it. But Christ, in instituting this sacrament, said: "This..."

<meta>This page continues the technical critique of the "assumption theory," which proposed that the Second Person of the Trinity assumed the nature of bread in the Eucharist, much like he assumed human nature in the Incarnation. The text moves from general logical definitions to specific scriptural and scholastic arguments by theologians like Durandus of Saint-Pourçain and Peter of Palude.</meta>

The words of Luke 22: *This is my body which is given for you*, etc. And *This cup is the new testament in my blood which is shed for you.* <note>original: "uerba Luce.xxii. Hoc est corpus meum quod pro uobis tradetur &c. Et hic calix i meo sanguine qui pro uobis effundetur." This is the foundational scriptural basis for the Eucharist.</note> Therefore, that same specific body which was later given to the apostles in the sacrament to be eaten—the body that was given to be crucified—was not of the nature of bread, but was a body belonging to the nature of humanity. Therefore, the body given to the apostles in the sacrament of the altar was truly of the nature of humanity; and by the same reasoning, in our sacrament, the body of Christ belongs to his humanity and is not present there merely through a <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "cōmunicationē ydiomatū"; a theological concept where attributes of one nature are applied to the person because of the union of natures.</note> resulting from the assumption of "bread-ness" <note>original: "paneitatis"; the essential nature or "what-it-is-to-be" bread.</note>.

<margin>Removal of an objection</margin>
Now, if someone should say that a relative term refers to the same underlying subject <note>original: "suppositū"; the individual person or substance that "holds" the natures.</note> but not the same nature—and thus it could truly be said, when pointing to the assumed bread, "This is my body which shall be given for you," because it is the same subject that has the assumed bread-nature and the later-given body-nature; and thus the same subject was first pointed out and then given, even though under different natures—this does not hold up. Because when it is said "This is my body," the word "body" cannot be taken there to mean the subject possessing bodiliness, but rather for the nature possessed, as is indicated by the possessive pronoun <note>In Latin, "meum" (my).</note> added to it when it is said "my body," meaning "this is what I have." But perhaps this argument would have greater force among grammarians than among theologians.

<margin>Response. Another argument of Durandus.</margin>
Furthermore, he [Durandus] argues thus: the aforementioned "assumption" is not sufficient for the body of Christ to be on the altar either really or according to the communication of properties. Not really, because the assumption of two natures by one subject is not enough for one nature to be wherever the other is. For if the person of the Son had from the beginning assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and of Paul in Judea, it would not follow that wherever Peter was, Paul would be, and vice versa—except in regard to the subject who is predicated of both and of whom both are predicated concretely. Similarly, even granted that the person of the Son assumed both humanity and bread-ness, it does not follow that where the nature of bread is, there the nature of humanity must be. Nor could it be said by reason of the subject that "where the bread is, there is the body of Christ" because of the communication of properties; for according to that opinion, the name of the subject does not receive the predication of the assumed bread nor the parts of the body. For it is not true to say, according to those thinkers, that the Son of God is "bread" or a "body" which is a part; therefore, by reason of a common subject, one cannot be predicated of the other so as to say one *is* the other, or one is *where* the other is. 

Nor is it similar to the case of the tooth of an Ethiopian and its whiteness <note>This was a standard example in medieval logic to discuss accidental properties: an Ethiopian is black, but his teeth are white. It tests how we apply descriptions to parts versus wholes.</note>, where the tooth is called "white" and the white thing is called "the tooth," and where one is, the other is, because they are one in their underlying subject and consequently indistinct in subject and place. But this cannot be said of the human body and the assumed bread-nature. 

<margin>Response. First argument of Peter of Palude.</margin>
Whatever may be the case regarding this argument, it is true that while it does not follow by necessity, it follows by possibility, etc. Peter of Palude <note>A prominent 14th-century Dominican theologian and Archbishop of Jerusalem.</note> argues thus: He would either assume the substance of the bread with its <term>accidents</term> <note>Physical properties like color, weight, and shape.</note> or without them. Not without them, because that is impossible; for that which cannot be made or sustained on its own by any power (such as a relation or something of that kind) cannot be assumed on its own. A physical substance cannot exist without "quantity" <note>original: "quantitate"; here meaning spatial extension or size.</note>, because quantity or shape is its own limit and proper attribute—though many would deny this. If, however, he assumed it with the accidents, then he would not be in the altar sacramentally, but locally through the quantity associated with the assumed substance.

<summary>This page presents scholastic arguments refuting the "assumption theory" of the Eucharist, using logical proofs from Durandus of Saint-Pourçain and Peter of Palude to show that Christ's presence must be a change of nature, not merely a shared subject.</summary>
<keywords>Eucharist, assumption theory, Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, Peter of Palude, communication of properties, bread-ness, accidents, sacramental presence, medieval logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "assumption theory" of the Eucharist. Having previously addressed scriptural arguments, the text now focuses on scholastic objections from Peter of Palude and the counter-arguments involving the "Thomists" (followers of Thomas Aquinas) and John of Damascus.</meta>

on the altar. Nor was it moved from there locally, as it was in the womb by its <term>quantity</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, "quantity" refers to the physical extension or dimensions of a body in space.</note> along with the humanity assumed there. And perhaps this concludes that it is not there sacramentally in the way the Thomists <note>Followers of the theology of St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> say, <margin>Response.</margin> namely through "conversion." They say that the body is not there through its own quantity, but through the quantity of the bread; however, if it were to assume the bread, it would then appear to be there through a quantity that is its own. This "mode" of the Thomists, however, is not held by many. 

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, Peter <note>Likely Peter of Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian.</note> argues that "body" cannot be understood as a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category (like "animal") that includes various species.</note> but only as a "part," because a genus is not predicated possessively of its inferior member, in the way a part is of a whole. For instance, when I say "my humanity" and "my hand," I do not say "my animal" or "my man" regarding myself. This is also apparent in the consecration of the blood, where it is said, *This is the chalice of my blood* <note>original: "hic ē calix sanguinis mei"</note>. "Blood" is not an <term>equivocal</term> term <note>A word with multiple meanings.</note> referring to both a genus and a part, as "body" is, but is only taken to mean a part. 

Therefore, granted that the "body" which is Christ through "assumption" would be on the altar by the power of the sacrament, it would nonetheless not be the "body of Christ" which is a part, except through natural <term>concomitance</term> <note>The doctrine that because Christ is living, his body, blood, soul, and divinity are always found together.</note>. This is because through "assumption," a union would not occur between the natures, but only in the <term>person</term> <note>original: "persona"; the underlying subject or "suppositum" that holds the natures.</note>. Hence, through that assumption, it would happen that the bread would be the body which is Christ, <margin>Response.</margin> but not the "body of Christ," just as the divinity is not currently the humanity. Enough has been said about this above, namely concerning the body as a part and the body as a genus. 

<margin>Third.</margin> Third, he argues that just as the assumed human body of Christ was not meant to be corrupted or to decay, neither in its substance nor its quantity, so too the bread ought not to decay if it were assumed. <margin>Response.</margin> Perhaps, however, this similarity does not hold by necessity. 

<margin>Response to arguments for the opposite side.</margin> To the arguments for the opposing side, regarding the authority of [John of] Damascus, <margin>To the first.</margin> it is said that just as it is established that the water of baptism is not assumed into the unity of the divine person <note>original: "suppositi diuini"</note>, nor is the grace of the Holy Spirit united to it so that they make one person, so similarly the bread and wine are not assumed into the divine person, nor is the divinity joined to them in a unity of person. But just as the water there is assumed as a permanent matter of the sacrament, so the bread and wine are taken as a "transient" matter. This is because the matter of the sacrament is converted into the body of Christ, and consequently is said to be united in some way to the divinity—not through "assumption" while the nature of the bread or wine remains, but through <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>The change of the whole substance of bread into the substance of the Body of Christ.</note> into the previously assumed humanity. 

This is clear from what follows, where it is said: *just as naturally, through eating, bread and wine and water (through drinking) are transformed into the body and blood of the one eating and drinking, and it does not become a different body than before; so also the bread of the proposition, and the wine and water, through the change and arrival of the Holy Spirit, supernaturally pass into the body and blood of the Lord, and therefore they are not two, but one and the same.* <note>original: "quemadmodum naturaliter per comestionem panis... transit in corpus domini & sanguinem & ideo non sunt duo sed unum & idem." This is a paraphrase of John of Damascus's "De Fide Orthodoxa."</note> From these things, it appears that it is not the intention of Damascus that the substance of the bread and wine remain and are assumed by the divine person, but rather they pass into the body and blood of Christ and are thus united to the divinity. 

<margin>Objection.</margin> However, those people persist, asking: how can that which is "annihilated"—that is, truly ceases to be in itself—be united? And they persist with that analogy of the coal, in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood but wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread but united to the divinity. <margin>Solution.</margin> And it is said that the coal and the fire are not one in person; however, one passes into the other along with its corruption. Thus, the bread of communion is not one in person with the divinity, but through its ceasing-to-be, it passes into the body of Christ which is united [to the divinity].

Defense of Origen

### SEVENTH QUESTION: CONCERNING THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.

In the third book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note>, it is said that faith concerning the body of Christ, all the sacraments, the "keys" of the Church, and all such things is included in the article of faith regarding the effect of grace, which is "the Holy Catholic Church," and so on. Regarding the confession of Berengarius <margin>Regarding the confession of Berengarius.</margin> <note>Berengar of Tours (d. 1088) was a theologian who famously doubted the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist and was forced to recant.</note>, it must be said—as the Gloss <margin>Gloss.</margin> <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard collection of biblical and legal commentaries.</note> says there—that unless you understand Berengarius’s words soundly, you will fall into an even greater error than he himself held. Therefore, Peter of Palude <margin>Peter of Palude.</margin> <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and Archbishop.</note> says that when it is said "the body of Christ is broken," it must be explained to mean that it remains under the <term>species</term> <note>In Eucharistic theology, "species" refers to the outward appearances of bread and wine (taste, smell, shape) that remain after the substance has changed.</note> which are broken, so long as it remains in any part. <margin>Note.</margin> Furthermore, Peter adds these words: "Thus I say that God could *assume* the bread and wine just as he could *convert* them, and that he could have instituted words which, upon being spoken, would result in an 'assumption,' just as now, upon the speaking of these words, a 'conversion' follows. However, he did not give this power to these words; nor could the meaning of the moderns be saved if an 'assumption' took place without a 'conversion.'" These are his words. These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is *possible*, not about how things actually are.

Regarding the point <margin>To the other point.</margin> that whenever two things are identical in their <term>suppositum</term> <note>The "suppositum" is the individual substance or "person" that underlies various properties. The author is arguing about how two things can be in the same place.</note>, wherever one is, the other must be: it is said that this reasoning holds only for those things that are in a place <term>accidentally</term> <note>In scholastic logic, something is in a place "accidentally" if its location isn't part of its essential definition (like a person in a room).</note>. It is otherwise for those things that are in a place by their own nature. <margin>To the last point.</margin> When it is said that "the bread is the body of Christ" or "the body of Christ is the bread," these cannot be verified unless the bread remains; it must be said that this is to be explained as: "where the bread was, there the body of Christ now is." And let this suffice for the dispute on this question. From all of this, I hold those things which are consistent with my declaration of the conclusion explained above. Those things which are dissonant, I judge should be rejected and condemned.

->**SEVENTH QUESTION: CONCERNING THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.**<-

**It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe that he is damned.**

These masters have said that this conclusion is rash, reprehensible, "savoring of heresy," and against the determination of the universal Church. I, however, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct, and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church. What is more, even if everything they bring against me were true, it still could not be said that this conclusion is heretical or "savors of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles.

1. In the first, we will see whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion regarding matters of faith. <margin>Seven articles: how to proceed in the declaration of the conclusion.</margin>
2. In the second, granted that he did write such things, whether he wrote them dogmatically (as fixed doctrine), as a personal adherence, or merely as an inquiry.
3. In the third, granted that he adhered to them, whether he sinned mortally in writing them such that he could be called a heretic. <margin>For the first article.</margin>
4. In the fourth, granted that he wrote them and erred in doing so, whether he ever repented for such things. <margin>Rufinus, Jerome, Augustine.</margin> <note>Rufinus and Jerome were famous 4th-century scholars who had a bitter falling out over whether Origen was a saint or a heretic.</note>
5. In the fifth, granted that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe he is damned or saved.
6. In the sixth, what should be judged from the text of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen.
7. In the seventh, how much the determination of the Church binds our belief in this matter.

It focuses on the famous dispute between St. Jerome and Rufinus regarding whether Origen’s works were corrupted by heretics.</meta>
