<margin>On the controversy of Jerome and Rufinus regarding the first article.</margin>

<margin>Pamphilus the Martyr.</margin>

<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Jerome</margin>

<margin>Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea.</margin>

(he deplores the dissension between them) God had granted that, being most closely joined and intimate friends, they might together lick the honey of the holy scriptures. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in the books of Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a prolific early Christian scholar whose works became highly controversial centuries after his death, leading to the "Origenist Crises."</note> were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they do not represent Origen’s true mind. Jerome feels the contrary.

But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—saving the faith and the full satisfaction of all those things which we are bound to believe as a necessity for salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies for which Origen’s sin is proven (and consequently his condemnation) were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely imposed upon him by perfidious heretics corrupting his books.

On this side, there is first the authority of Pamphilus the Martyr <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a scholar and martyr who was a great admirer of Origen.</note>, whose book is said to be a defense of Origen, in which the most glorious martyr—using the very words of Origen recited from his own books—shows that he thought in a Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox teaching of the Church as opposed to heretical sects.</note> manner regarding those things in which he is accused of being a heretic.

Jerome, however, denying that this book belongs to Pamphilus, speaks thus in his *Apology* written to Oceanus and Pammachius <note>Oceanus and Pammachius were Roman aristocrats and friends of Jerome who kept him informed of the theological disputes in Rome.</note>: "If you say that his books were violated by the enemies of Origen so that he might be defamed, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under the name of Pamphilus, which might claim him from infamy by the testimony of a martyr?" From these words, it seems sufficiently noted that Jerome considers both positions probable, implying that just as Rufinus cannot be proven wrong that those books were corrupted, neither can Jerome be proven wrong that the book is not truly by Pamphilus.

And further below, Jerome adds: "The very name of an 'apology' shows an excuse; for nothing is defended except that which is under accusation." But perhaps someone might say then: "Since Jerome himself marks this very treatise in which he writes these things with the title of 'Apology'—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen’s learning but not his dogma—he likewise shows himself to be guilty of a crime, since nothing is defended unless it is under accusation." Thus, no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a just accusation.

But let us now see by what conjectures Jerome is moved to believe the book is not by Pamphilus. The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (d. 339 AD), the famous "Father of Church History."</note>—those six books which he wrote in favor of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that Pamphilus wrote no work of his own. For thus says Jerome in the first book against Rufinus, addressed to Pammachius and Marcellus: "Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, once the standard-bearer of the Arian faction <note>Arianism was a major heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ. Jerome is accusing Eusebius of being a leader of this movement.</note>, wrote a very wide and elaborate work of six books in defense of Origen; and by many testimonies he approved that Origen was a Catholic according to him—that is, according to us, an Arian <note>original: "iuxta nos Arianum esse." Jerome is using sharp irony here, suggesting that what Eusebius calls 'orthodox' is actually heretical Arianism.</note>. You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr [Pamphilus]."

And Jerome continues: "If that is Pamphilus’s book, which of the six will be the first of Eusebius?" And further: "Likewise Eusebius, the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus, wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he says of Pamphilus: 'He himself wrote nothing at all of his own work, except for letters which he perhaps sent to friends.' So far did the defender of Origen and the praiser of Pamphilus lower himself in humility, saying that Pamphilus composed nothing at all, not even any of his own speech; and he said this after Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you might have no refuge [to claim he wrote it] after the books published by Eusebius..."

<meta>Continuing the discussion from the previous page regarding the dispute between Jerome and Rufinus over the orthodoxy of Origen. ...that Pamphilus had written, and so on. What will the letters of Bishop Theophilus <note>Theophilus was the Bishop of Alexandria (385–412 AD) and a fierce opponent of Origenism.</note> <margin>Theophilus the Bishop.</margin> and those of Pope Anastasius <note>Pope Anastasius I (reigned 399–401 AD) condemned the works of Origen.</note> do, which pursue the heretic throughout the whole world? Since your book, published under the name of Pamphilus, fights against their letters. And in his second book, Jerome writes thus: <margin>Pope Anastasius.</margin> "When, nearly ten years ago, my friend Dexter—who served as the Praetorian Prefect—asked me to weave together for him an index of the authors of our religion, I placed this work among the other commentators, believing this book to have been published by Pamphilus, just as it had been circulated by you and your disciples.

But since Eusebius himself says that Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters, etc., and the first book of the six volumes of Eusebius contains the same things and the very same words which were forged by you under the name of Pamphilus, it is clear that you wished to disseminate this book for this reason: so that you might introduce heresy under the mask of a martyr. Since you have also perverted many things even in that text which you pretend is by Pamphilus, and it reads one way in Greek and another way in Latin." 

Furthermore, in the responsive apology to Oceanus and Pammachius <note>Oceanus and Pammachius were Roman aristocrats and friends of Jerome who alerted him to Rufinus's translations of Origen.</note>, in which he shows that he [rejects] the doctrine of Origen and

<meta>Continuing the scholarly debate between Jerome and Rufinus regarding the authorship of the "Apology for Origen." Jerome argues that Pamphilus the Martyr wrote nothing but letters, implying the defense of Origen was a forgery by Eusebius or Rufinus himself. This page offers a point-by-point rebuttal to Jerome's claims.</meta>

->->**Concerning the book of Pamphilus the Martyr**<-<-

Therefore, it cannot be easily understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could also be read in the first book of Eusebius’s work, unless perhaps they shared some common points regarding Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a hugely influential but controversial early Christian theologian whose orthodoxy was fiercely debated in the 4th and 5th centuries.</note> that were not relevant to the specific point of this conclusion. Nor does it seem as marvelous as Jerome wonders that Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote similar things; for, as Jerome himself says, they were companions <note>original: "contubernales," meaning they shared a life and library in Caesarea.</note>. Eusebius could have repeated things he had read in Pamphilus’s writings in his own books, or, as happens every day, he could have discovered and thought of them himself through a similar movement of the mind. And so much for the first book of Eusebius.

Now, Jerome says that Eusebius writes in his *Life of Pamphilus* that, out of humility, Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work except for letters. He adds that Eusebius—a defender of Origen and a praiser of Pamphilus—says this. Perhaps Rufinus would respond that this does not do much to hinder his own case. 

<margin>First.</margin> First, because that little treatise of Pamphilus tends more toward the brevity of a letter than toward the magnitude of a formal book. 

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, because that short defense <term>Apology<note>From the Greek 'apologia,' a formal speech or piece of writing defending a person or doctrine.</note></term> for Origen perhaps cannot rightly be called a "proper work," since Pamphilus does not dogmatize there; rather, he does not treat any general question at all, but only deals briefly with a particular man—that is, Origen. Whether his books were corrupted or not is not the same as composing a "proper work," nor is it a matter of his humility to avoid the name of an author when he is merely providing support. 

<margin>Third.</margin> Third, it is possible that this book never came to the notice of Eusebius, both because of the small size of the book and because of the author's own humility, which Eusebius himself cites—writing nothing grand and hiding those thin and tiny things he did write rather than showing them off. 

<margin>Fourth.</margin> Fourth, Rufinus will say it is even possible that Eusebius, as a defender of the Arian treachery <note>Arianism was a Christological heresy that claimed Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father. Eusebius of Caesarea was often accused of leaning toward this view.</note>, did not merely wish to hide the book of the martyr—which deprived his sect of Origen's testimony—but also acted through this indirect testimony of his so that posterity would believe it was not by Pamphilus. Therefore, when Jerome says "defender of Origen" as if to strengthen his own argument—saying Pamphilus wrote nothing, etc.—it is actually more against him than for him. For since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could rightly be suspected in this matter, as I have said. 

But why labor over these points? How can Jerome prove at all from Eusebius’s testimony that the *Apology for Origen* is not by Pamphilus, when Eusebius himself, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that a defense for Origen was written by the holy martyr Pamphilus?

When Jerome then adds, "What will the letters of Bishop Theophilus do? What of Pope Anastasius?" and so on—perhaps Rufinus would say that Pamphilus’s book does not fight against their primary intention. For their purpose was to root out those most wicked heresies and poisonous dogmas, whoever they belonged to, from the world. This pertained to the faith and to the confirmation and stabilization of the Church. These most religious pontiffs would have cared little whether those doctrines were Origen's (as was believed by many) or not. Indeed, it might have been desirable and most acceptable to them if it could have been proven by certain and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were not believed by Origen; for this would be done for the faith, not against the faith—against the heretics, and not for the heretics.

<meta>Continuing the debate between Jerome and Rufinus over the authorship of the "Apology for Origen." This page presents Rufinus’s hypothetical rebuttal to Jerome’s claim that the book was not written by the martyr Pamphilus, but was a forgery or an error Jerome once shared.</meta>

They relied not a little on the testimony of so great a man, who was so highly praised by Catholics, and they defended their own error with his authority. Therefore, Pamphilus’s book would contend against those letters [of Jerome], if the heresies of which they accused Origen were excused within it. However, this is not the case if every effort is made in that book to ensure that the supporters of those heresies are deprived of such a good patron, whom they follow if they follow those letters. It is certain that they follow him only as the heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> of their own trusted opinion. Moreover, to those things which Jerome brings forward in his second book, one might perhaps respond in this way:

First, when he says that he himself once believed and even wrote that it was Pamphilus’s book, before he read in Eusebius that Pamphilus had written nothing, and so forth. From this statement of his, Rufinus might perhaps argue against him thus: "O Jerome, if you once both believed and wrote that the book of Pamphilus you read was indeed by Pamphilus: Tell me, I pray, did you recognize the things you were reading in it as lies and heresies or favors toward heresy? Or did you instead see them as true or probable things that in no way harmed the Catholic faith? If they were false and heretical, how could you be led to believe the author of the book was a Catholic martyr, about whose testimony and words no one could suspect anything sinister without it being a disgrace? But if they were both Catholic and, in short, worthy of a Christian martyr, why do you now condemn these same things and call them fabricated and spread abroad for the purpose of introducing heresies? And briefly, why do you now judge as unworthy of a martyr those things which you then judged worthy of a martyr? For they are the same things you read now as those you were reading then—setting aside, as we might say, the title of the author. Let us consider the things themselves that are said there in defense of Origen on their own merits. If they are bad, why did you then judge them to be the work of a holy martyr? If they are good, why even now, regardless of whose they are, are they not accepted as good?"

"Furthermore, how can you say, O Jerome, that I distributed the book to introduce heresies? For in that book nothing else is being done (as was also said above) except that the heretics may not be able to strengthen themselves by Origen’s testimony; this serves to uproot heresy, not to spread it. Besides, this book is found not only in Latin but in Greek. I, Rufinus, made the Latin version by translating it from the Greek. Who published the Greek if not Pamphilus? Certainly not I, Rufinus—at least according to you, who accuse me of ignorance of Greek literature—could have written a book in such eloquent Greek that it equaled the style of Eusebius. If someone else is put forward, Jerome responds that it belongs to Didymus or someone else."

Rufinus would then press: "Whoever that other person may be, I, Rufinus, will no longer be held guilty of this crime, but another. And if Didymus is a liar, then according to you, Didymus is a deceiver—your own teacher, O Jerome, whom you called both a 'seeing prophet' and the 'eye of the bride' <note>original: "prophetam uidentem & oculum habentem ſponſe." Jerome famously praised Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a renowned Alexandrian theologian, despite Didymus’s later association with Origenism.</note> in reference to the Song of Songs, and an apostolic man in your own books. He is the liar, I say, who published the Greek version by falsely ascribing it to Pamphilus—not I, who, having found the Greek under the title of Pamphilus, communicated it to the Latins by translating it under the same author’s title. Nor should it be a wonder to you that I believed Didymus in this matter, since you believed him in the explanation of the Scriptures."

As for what Jerome says—that it is one way in the Latin and another in the Greek—Rufinus would say: "Why do you not bring forward the passages, O Jerome, that were badly translated? Is it so that I cannot defend myself from blame? You act just as you did when Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who famously corresponded and sometimes disagreed with Jerome regarding his new translation of the Bible from the Hebrew.</note> wrote to you that certain things in your translation from the Hebrew were condemned, yet he did not specify the passages."

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen’s orthodoxy, transitioning from general claims of textual corruption to specific theological rebuttals regarding the Trinity and the ultimate fate of the devil.</meta>

Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist—they deny that the Son of God should be professed as God, lest they seem to profess and speak of two gods. And what will they do with this passage of the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in Romans 9:5: "Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever."</note> in which Christ, through whom all things were made, is clearly described as being God over all? But they do not notice that those who hold this view do so because, just as the Lord Jesus Christ was not called the "one Lord" in such a way that God the Father is not also called Lord, so also He did not say God the Father was "one God" in a way that the Son should not be believed to be God. For the Scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God.* <note>Psalm 100:3.</note> However, both are one God, because there is no other beginning of divinity for the Son than the Father; rather, as Wisdom says, the Son is the "purest emanation" <note>original: "purissima manatio," a reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 7:25, describing the relationship between the Father and His Wisdom/Son.</note> of that one paternal fountain. Therefore, Christ is God over all things—those things, without doubt, which we mentioned a little earlier: over principalities, and powers, and virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. Now, He who is over all things has no one above Him; for He is not *after* the Father, but *from* the Father. This same thing concerning the Holy Spirit must also be understood as the Wisdom of God, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,* and that which contains all things has knowledge <margin>Note.</margin> of the voice. Therefore, if the Son of God is said to be "over all things," and the Holy Spirit is remembered to "contain all things," while God the Father is He "from whom are all things," the nature of the Trinity and the single substance <term>substance: the underlying essence or "stuff" that makes God what He is, shared equally by Father, Son, and Spirit.</term> which is over all things is clearly demonstrated. These are the words of Origen, translated literally.

And elsewhere, regarding that passage of Paul, *How shall they preach unless they are sent?* <note>Romans 10:15.</note> he says: "For there are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not sincerely and not completely, as is the case with all heretics. They announce the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but they do not announce them well or faithfully. For they either wrongly separate the Son from the Father, saying the Father is of one nature and the Son of another <note>A reference to Arianism, which claimed the Son was a created being lower than the Father.</note>, or they wrongly confuse them, making God a composite of three or merely a threefold naming." <note>A reference to Sabellianism or Modalism, which claimed Father, Son, and Spirit were just three different "masks" worn by one person.</note> "But those who announce good things well will give to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the properties belonging to each; yet they will confess that there is no diversity in substance or nature." These are Origen's words.

What could be more orthodox <note>original: "catholicum," meaning in agreement with the universal Church's teaching.</note> or more clearly expressed than these words? It is necessary, therefore, that if anything is found written differently in the books of Origen, it is not Origen’s, but the work of heretics who, through the corruption of his books, wished to have Origen as a patron <margin>Defense regarding the second heresy which was charged against him.</margin> for their own error. 

Concerning the second heresy <note>The "second heresy" refers to the belief in *apokatastasis*, the idea that all creatures, including the devil, will eventually be saved.</note>, however, there exists such clear testimony that, in my judgment, <margin>Origen himself denies it and asserts the opposite.</margin> it can hardly be denied. For in his own letter, even according to the translation of Jerome—who makes mention of that letter—Origen expressly denies that the devil can <margin>Origen's dialogue.</margin> ever be saved. He says that not even a madman could say such a thing. Furthermore, there exists a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a follower of the Valentinian doctrine <note>Valentinianism was a major Gnostic movement that Origen frequently argued against.</note>. This Candidus charged Origen with that very error, and Origen refuted it and denied that he held such a view. And regarding that passage of Paul, *Have they stumbled so as to fall?* <note>Romans 11:11.</note> Origen speaks thus, looking back at that fall of which Christ said, *I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.* He denies that Israel has fallen [permanently]. For their conversion will occur at the end of the age, when the fullness [of the Gentiles] has entered, and then "all Israel will be saved." But for that one who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be no conversion, not even at the end of the age. These are Origen's words. This also applies to that heresy attributed to him, which claims the Spirit does not understand the Son, and the Son does not understand [the Father]...

...[lest the title of] Father be falsely attributed to him. This is clear from what he himself says concerning that passage of Paul: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!* <note>original: "O altitudo diuiciarum sapientiæ & scientiæ dei." Romans 11:33.</note> For he says that he calls this "depth of God" inscrutable to every creature, but he could not say such things about the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is because the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: *Father, all mine are yours, and yours are mine.* <note>John 17:10.</note> And concerning the Holy Spirit, Paul himself declares, saying: *No one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him; so also no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:11.</note> Therefore, when Paul says, *Who has known the mind of the Lord?* <note>Romans 11:34.</note> he is speaking of creatures; but Origen excepted the nature of the Trinity from this statement.

There seems to remain one heresy attributed to Origen: <margin>Regarding the heresy of the creation of souls.</margin> namely, in his opinions concerning the soul—that they were created from eternity and fall from heaven into bodies. And concerning the soul, Origen himself writes in his commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to Titus <margin>Defense against the objections.</margin> that he can establish nothing from Church dogma except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will receive punishments for evil and rewards for good. 

He says he affirms only these things about the soul because evident testimonies for them are found in the Scriptures. Regarding other questions about the soul, however, he says he states what seems more probable to him, proceeding by way of inquiry rather than by definitive assertion, because nothing has been determined about those matters in Church dogma. However, that which seemed more likely to Origen—that souls were created before bodies and lived in the heavens—is something all <note>This refers to the controversial doctrine of the "pre-existence of souls," which suggested souls existed in a spiritual state before falling into material bodies as a result of a primordial cooling of their love for God.</note> agree was his view. 

And Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD) was a monk and historian who translated many of Origen's works into Latin, often attempting to soften Origen’s more controversial ideas to prove his orthodoxy.</note> in his apology to Anastasius, <margin>Rufinus</margin> Bishop of the city of Rome, after relating three opinions concerning the soul, says at the end: "But as for me, having read these individual views, I say before God as my witness that until the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question, but I leave it to God to know what is the truth, and to whom He himself deigns to reveal it. However, I do not deny that I have read these individual views, and I confess I am still ignorant, except for what the Church clearly hands down: that God is the creator of both souls and bodies."

...[the question of the soul's origin] was only determined much later than that time. Indeed, this was not only true in the time of Origen, but even in the time of Augustine—who lived two hundred years after Origen—there had still been nothing definitively settled by the "Catholics" (that is, by the universal Church) concerning the soul. <margin>Augustine lived 200 years after Origen and was also doubtful in his opinion concerning the creation of the soul.</margin> For Augustine himself was doubtful in his opinion regarding the soul, as is clear from his letter to Jerome. He wondered "whether individual souls are created for individuals" <note>original: "an singule singulis creentur." This refers to the doctrine of Creationism—that God creates a new soul for every birth—which eventually became the standard view.</note> as orthodox tradition now holds. Because of this opinion, it seemed to Augustine that it would follow that God was unjust, or whether they were propagated from that one soul which was made in Adam by God—others then following "soul from soul" just as "body from body." <note>This "soul from soul" theory is known as Traducianism, suggesting that the soul is passed down from parents like biological traits.</note> Nor should you believe that Augustine doubted this matter only in his youth; for even in the first book of his *Retractions*—which was among his final works—he still doubts this question. <note>The *Retractions* was a work written at the end of Augustine's life where he reviewed and corrected his previous writings.</note> He writes as follows in the first book: "Without controversy, therefore, God is a certain original region of happiness for the soul; He did not indeed beget the soul from Himself, but founded it from no other thing, just as He founded the body from the earth. But as to its origin—how it comes to be in the body—whether it comes from that one soul which was first created when man was made into a living soul, or whether individual souls are similarly made for individuals, I did not know then, nor do I know now." These are Augustine’s words verbatim. From this, it is clearly evident that Origen can in no way be called a heretic on account of the aforementioned erroneous opinion concerning the soul.

<margin>The second proposition: Saint Thomas.</margin>
The second proposition I state is this: that if it is true what Thomas [Aquinas] says in his *Quodlibets* <note>original: "in quolibetis." Basil the Great.</margin> The faith of Rufinus is even said to have been proven by prisons and exiles in the holy Alexandrian church during the time of the persecution by heretics. Indeed, it is better to believe the words of Origen himself, especially since in many other matters that pertain even more to the substance of the faith, we do not approve of Jerome. This is seen in the matter of the legal ceremonies, and it is also pious not to believe Jerome where he calls the commentaries of Ambrose on Luke "trifles" <note>original: "nugas." Jerome was famously sharp-tongued and often insulted his intellectual rivals.</note> and calls Ambrose himself now a "raven," now a "little crow." <note>original: "nunc coruum nūc corniculā." Jerome was accusing Ambrose of "stealing" ideas from Greek writers like a bird stealing shiny objects.</note> It is also seen where he condemns Ambrose’s book on the Holy Spirit, saying that he had "seen good Greek works made into bad Latin ones," and where he taxes Basil the Great for pride, and where he says in the letters of Augustine that he has read certain heretical things. Thus, perhaps in this matter too, one might prefer to believe that the things demonstrating Origen to be a Catholic are genuine, and those proving him a heretic are forged and adulterated—to not adhere to the latter is neither impious nor does it appear ruinous to the faith. Rather, the defense of Origen seems to confirm the faith by taking away the "patronage" and testimony of Origen from the heretics, rather than weakening it. This is according to what is written in the book of Pamphilus in these words: "They ought to have contemplated how much material for laughter they provide to the heretics when they see those whom they think to be the assertors and defenders of Christian dogma now being refuted and repelled by their own people; the heretics rejoice as if in a civil war <note>original: "velut ciuili bello."</note> over an attack on a man whom they themselves could not defeat in a hostile manner." ...of the church, even Jerome and later figures who held this view, argued that those heresies were not from the mind of Origen but were falsely ascribed to him by heretics. Therefore, Aymo, one <margin>The words of Haymo in testimony of Origen.</margin> of the noble and ancient doctors of the church, in his book *On the Memory of Christian Affairs*, speaks thus: "I would certainly say of Origen—a man so illustrious, of such extremely abstemious life and most chaste, of distinguished doctrine and pure, clear speech—saving the faith of the fathers, that he did not write these things at all. These things were said regarding the first article to be examined and investigated: whether those opinions of Origen were heretical or not. In this matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church before the judgment and reasons of all others.

Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused because, if he wrote anything that is not accepted by Catholics, <margin>Regarding the second article.</margin> he proceeded in those writings neither dogmatically <note>original: "dogmatice." To write dogmatically is to present an idea as an established, unchangeable truth of the faith.</note> nor assertively, but always doubtfully and inquisitively. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Therefore, just as in the books of Augustine *On Genesis* there are many things which are not accepted, they are nevertheless excused by us because, as he himself says in the book of *Retractions*, more things in that book were "sought after than found." <note>Augustine’s *Retractions* was a late-life work where he corrected his own earlier errors, showing that even great saints could be "inquiring" rather than "dogmatic."</note> So too there can be many things in the books of Origen that are to be rejected and condemned; yet because he spoke them not by determining them but by inquiring into them, he should not for that reason be called a heretic. Heresy is properly defined as a dogma asserted against the express truth of either Scripture <margin>Heresy properly defined.</margin> or the determination of the Church.

That Origen always spoke in this [inquisitive] way is clear from many places. <margin>Note.</margin> For even after a disputation on the soul, he says: "Let these things, according to our opinion, not be dogmas but only matters of inquiry and put forward so they would not seem entirely unaddressed." And elsewhere, <margin>The words of Origen.</margin> speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith," and so on. And further down: "A threefold suspicion is therefore suggested to us concerning the end, from which the reader may inquire which is true and better." Then he subjoins three opinions regarding the resurrection. And in the preface to his books on Genesis, he says: "If something profound should occur to be said about this, it must indeed be spoken, but yet not affirmatively." And further: "Regarding great things which are above us, we do not ignore our ignorance." 

And in the second book on the *Epistle to the Romans*: "Let these things be said by us on this condition: that if anyone says something better and more reasonable, those things should be held rather than these of ours." And in the fourth book: "These things, as far as we were able in matters so arduous and difficult, have been brought forward. If anyone should consider the zeal of our mind, he might embrace them; but if he wishes to note the infirmity of our perception, we ask for pardon, and we gladly yield to him who is able to discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let he who reads prove which of these more agrees with the apostolic sense, and let him hold that." And in the fifth book: "These things in the meantime were able to occur to us in this present place. If anyone perceives anything better, let it not be a burden to disregard these and look to those." 

And what is more, if the book *Periarchon* <margin>The book *Periarchon*.</margin> <note>original: "Periarchon." This is the Greek title of Origen's famous work *De Principiis* or *On First Principles*.</note> is read, we will see that he proceeds in this order: first, he places those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in the Scriptures, and in those, he did not deviate at all from the Church. Other things he says are <margin>Regarding the third article.</margin> doubtful to him, and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting for all of them that only that truth is to be received which in no way contradicts apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas.

Regarding the third article, which is as it were a confirmation of the second, I say this proposition: that if there is someone holding an <margin>Note this proposition.</margin> erroneous opinion about matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided there is no stain in his will, but a firm purpose to always believe in conformity [with the Church]...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, transitioning from a discussion of the universal church's judgment to the specific theological argument regarding the distinction between intellectual error and the "stain" of the will.</meta>

...of the universal church.

<margin>Blessed Cyprian</margin> From this proposition, I infer the following regarding Origen’s case: even granted that Origen may have held many—indeed, very many—erroneous opinions regarding the faith, if there was precisely no stain in his will <note>original: "voluntate." In scholastic theology, a distinction was made between the intellect (which might be mistaken) and the will (which chooses to persist in error). Without a "stain" or malicious intent in the will, an error of the mind was not considered a damnable heresy.</note> in any way, it cannot be used as an argument that his soul is damned. 

<margin>Note.</margin> The argument proceeds thus: either no matter how great an error regarding any matters of faith might be in a person's intellect—provided there is no stain in the will—it does not impede their salvation; or no matter how small an error is, regarding any matter at all, it does impede salvation; or perhaps some errors impede it and some do not. If even a great error does not impede salvation <note>That is, if the error is purely intellectual and not a willful rejection of known truth.</note>, then even though Origen erred in many things, and even in the most fundamental <term>articles of faith<gloss>The core, essential doctrines of Christianity.</gloss></term>, nevertheless, if his will was well-disposed and in no way stained, it in no way impeded his salvation.

<summary>This passage argues that Origen's salvation is not jeopardized by his intellectual errors, provided his intent (will) remained pure and free from the sin of heresy. It establishes a logical framework for distinguishing between accidental error and willful defiance of doctrine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of Origen, specifically addressing the claim that he erred in fundamental matters. It builds on the previous page's distinction between intellectual mistake and the "malice of the will."</meta>

Concerning Origen, because Origen erred in fundamental matters: for however great an error might be, as long as it is only an error in the intellect and there is no malice in the will, it does not seem that one who errs in such a way sins mortally <note>original: "peccet mortaliter." In Catholic theology, a mortal sin is a grave violation that destroys charity in the heart and turns the soul away from God, as opposed to a venial sin.</note>. Wherefore, since we do not read that there was such malice in the will of Origen—even granted that he may have erred even in the principal mysteries of the faith with a most grave error, and one deservedly condemned by the Church—it cannot be proven that he himself is damned in his person and in his soul.

But if someone should say that there are many levels of propositions to be believed, besides this level of propositions—namely, those determined by the Church—and that even if there is no stubbornness <term>pertinacity<gloss>The willful and obstinate persistence in an error regarding the faith; in canon law, this is what transforms a mistake into heresy.</gloss></term>, it is nevertheless a sign of stubbornness to assert anything whose opposite the speaker is bound to hold and believe with explicit faith. And that error is not only mortally culpable because of stubbornness, but is also sometimes blamed on account of negligence in...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen’s orthodoxy. Having previously discussed the vast number of works attributed to Origen, the author now addresses the specific circumstances under which some of his more controversial or "erroneous" writings were produced and eventually published against his will.</meta>

...that he [Origen] dictated to Ambrose <note>This refers to Ambrose of Alexandria (died c. 251), a wealthy friend and patron of Origen who provided him with secretaries and stenographers to record his teachings. He is distinct from the more famous St. Ambrose of Milan.</note> certain things in earlier years, before he had yet discovered anything of the truth, which were to be communicated to Ambrose alone in private and not published for the general public. These were matters that Ambrose did not yet know to be fully secure or in harmony with apostolic truth. Ambrose, however, brought those things—originally issued in secret—into the public eye. Afterwards, once the Catholic truth had been discovered by Origen (who was by then sixty years old), he began to write boldly and publicly as a Catholic. He was deeply grieved that those things he had written for Ambrose's private use had already been published by him. To clear his own name, as can be gathered from the words of Jerome and Eusebius, he wrote to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome <note>Pope Fabian (reigned 236–250), to whom Origen reportedly wrote a letter defending his orthodoxy.</note>, providing testimony of his Catholic faith and explaining the series of events: namely, that the writings found under his name from earlier times were not written to be published. He himself had been doubtful about whether they were Catholic or not. But Ambrose had published them. Indeed, this is what Jerome says: 

<margin>Jerome</margin> Origen himself, in the letter he writes to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, expresses regret for why he wrote such things, and he shifts the blame for his rashness onto Ambrose, who brought into the public those things that had been issued in secret. 

Eusebius, however, when recounting what Origen wrote after his sixtieth year—after he had numbered the book *Against Celsus* <note>Origen’s most famous apologetic work, written to defend Christianity against the pagan philosopher Celsus.</note> and the twenty-five books of commentaries on Matthew and the twenty on the Prophets—adds: "He also wrote to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, and to many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith." So says Eusebius. Therefore, let it be true that before his sixtieth year, Origen was doubtful about many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he communicated many things in writing to Ambrose in secret, which he then held not as firm beliefs but as investigative inquiries, and which are now not to be accepted by Catholics. Thus Jerome speaks the truth: that the things found in many of Origen's books which are not Catholic are indeed Origen's, because they were truly dictated by him—though not as things believed, but as things sought after rather than discovered. Consequently, they should not be blamefully attributed to Origen, who later discovered the Catholic truth; in these works, many things were also devised by heretics, according to Rufinus. We can also accept this as true because Origen himself complained about this very thing while he was still alive. 

Let it be true, then, according to Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (and approved by Jerome as true), that Origen does not claim as his own works—that is, those in which he says something definitively and with adherence—except those which he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it be true also, according to Jerome, that he repented of the things written earlier that were rashly published by Ambrose, and consequently that he died a Catholic. Thus, not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but even according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe that he is 

<margin>Regarding the fifth article.</margin> damned. Regarding the fifth article, I say this proposition: no matter how gravely someone sins mortally in life, and even if it is certain that he sinned mortally, unless it is certain 

<margin>First proposition.</margin> regarding his final impenitence <note>The state of refusing to repent for one's sins up until the very moment of death.</note>, it is rash to truly assert that he is damned. The truth of this proposition is evident from the common opinion of all the doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church" or authoritative theologians.</note> who agree with said proposition. From this proposition, I infer two 

<margin>First corollary proposition.</margin> corollary propositions. This is evident because, while a mortal sin has been committed, that fact alone does not constitute the entire case upon which eternal damnation follows. Rather, beyond the sin, one must also establish and be certain of...

...concerning final impenitence. Nor do I firmly deny that it should be believed he is in hell; I have to show you his repentance. But you, who assert that he is damned, have to provide proof of his impenitence. On this point, the saying of Henry of Hesse <note>Henricus de Langenstein (1325–1397), also known as Henry of Hesse, was a prominent German theologian and mathematician.</note> carries much weight, who in his exposition on the third chapter of the book of <margin>Henry of Hesse</margin> Genesis says these formal words: "If the argument of certain people were effective—by which they persuade us that someone is damned, as they do concerning Solomon, because the Scripture commemorates his sin and makes no mention of his justice or his repentance—then the first man [Adam] would be proven damned by his sin just as the first angel [Lucifer] was." Thus says Henry. For nowhere is mention made of the repentance of Adam, but only of his sin. Similarly, in Judges chapter 8, we read of the sin of Gideon <note>Gideon was a judge of Israel who, after a great victory, made a golden ephod that became an object of idolatry (Judges 8:27).</note> and not of his repentance; and yet he is well believed by the doctors [of the Church] to be saved. And you can see that by this same argument, certain people were erroneously deceived into saying that Moses was damned, because his sin at the waters of contradiction <note>original: "in aquis contradictionis." This refers to the waters of Meribah (Numbers 20), where Moses struck the rock in anger.</note> was read, and nothing of his repentance was explicitly held. And yet God said to Joshua: "Moses my servant is dead" <note>original: "Moyses servus meus mortuus est." This title "servant of the Lord" implies a state of grace and salvation.</note>.

The <margin>Second corollary proposition</margin> second corollary proposition is this: no one can be certain that anyone is damned to hell unless they have this from a special revelation of God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except He who knows the secrets of the heart, and him to whom He wished to reveal them. For since no one is so certain of the state of another as he is of himself—because "no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," as is said in 2 Corinthians 2—and since a man cannot be certain of himself "whether he be worthy of hatred or love," as is said in Ecclesiastes 9, how much more shall he not be able to be certain regarding another, unless he has a special revelation regarding this?

From this principal proposition, with its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even granted that Origen sinned mortally by erring in those matters, nevertheless, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an entirely rash judgment and is to be rejected. Since, therefore, we cannot be certain of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and highly reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God saved him—a man of such and so great knowledge. Regarding <margin>The words of Jerome</margin> whom Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), who was initially a great admirer of Origen but later became one of his harshest critics during the Origenist controversies.</note> says in his preface to the Song of Songs: "While in other matters he surpassed all others, in this he surpassed himself." And concerning him, this is verified: "The King has brought me into his chamber." And elsewhere, wishing to imitate Origen in part, Jerome says: "Whom, after the Apostles, <margin>Origen Adamantius</margin> no one but the unskilled denies was the master of the churches." And elsewhere: "Origen labored with such great toil over the scriptures that he justly received the name *Adamantius*" <note>Adamantius means "Man of Steel" or "unbreakable," a nickname referring to Origen's tireless work ethic and the perceived strength of his arguments.</note>. He is condemned by Bishop Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Alexandria (died 232 AD), who originally supported Origen but later presided over the synods that condemned him and stripped him of his priesthood.</note>, with the exception of the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia. Even the city of Rome itself consents against him; it gathers a senate not because of the novelty of his dogmas, not because of heresy—as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him—but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge." Why I have written this, and dictated it quickly with unpolished speech by the small flame of a poor lamp, you can understand if you think of the Epicureans and Aristippians <note>Followers of Epicurus and Aristippus, here used as archetypes for those who prioritize pleasure or worldly reputation over truth, or perhaps those who are envious of intellectual excellence.</note>. O ingenious reader, pay diligent attention, and through these points understand for yourself those things which I do not explicitly state. In the preface to his *Hebrew Questions* <note>Jerome’s *Hebraicae quaestiones in Genesim* is a 4th-century work focusing on the Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> speaking of this same man, Jerome says: <note>original: "hoc unum dico q̃ uellem cum inuidia noĩs eius habere etiam ſciam ſcriptu/rarũ."</note> "I say this one thing: that I wish I had his knowledge of the Scriptures, even if it came with the envy attached to his name," valuing as naught the images and shadows of ghosts whose nature is said to terrify children and chatter in dark corners. I pass over what Jerome proclaims about him elsewhere: that he trampled upon avarice; that he castrated himself out of zeal for God <note>According to tradition, Origen took the "eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven" passage in Matthew 19:12 literally as a young man.</note>—though not according to knowledge; and that he toiled day and night in the explanation of the Scriptures, through which those who clarify them shall have eternal life, as the Wise Man says. And, as is written to Vigilantius, he explained the obscurities of the prophets and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and Old Testaments. I pass over that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was barely far from the merit of martyrdom. For Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History," who wrote extensively on Origen.</note> says that even as a young boy, he burned with such great ardor for attaining martyrdom that he would voluntarily thrust himself into dangers. Later, in the time of the **Decian persecution** <note>The persecution under Emperor Decius (r. 249–251 AD) was the first empire-wide organized effort to suppress Christianity.</note>, he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and torments unheard of in all ages. Indeed, Eusebius says he was harassed by a thousand deaths so that the one death he longed for might not reach him—the persecutor acting with the greatest effort to ensure that neither his destruction was granted nor his pain ceased. See how little he lacks of the praise of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples achieved under his leadership and encouragement. I say again, he was surely little far from the praise of martyrdom; rather, he earned a merit almost equal to it.

For Augustine also says in the book *On the Good of Marriage* <note>original: "de bono cõiugali"</note> that the merit of martyrdom is not unequal in John [the Evangelist], who did not suffer death, and in Peter, who did. Note these words of Augustine well. Thus, just as John—though he did not pass by the sword—was nevertheless ready to sustain martyrdom when he was sent into the vessel of boiling oil, so too was Origen. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nevertheless ready; indeed, he was most greedy to undergo it. He suffered so many torments, as Eusebius says, that he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one. This is what Bernard says in his sermon on the holy martyrs: that there is a **triple martyrdom**. There is a martyrdom of will only, a martyrdom of work only, and a martyrdom of both work and will. John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of will only, to whom it was said, as to his brother: "You shall drink of my cup" <note>Matthew 20:23.</note>. Concerning this, Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and a famous martyr himself.</note> says: "In the servants of God, among whom martyrdom is contemplated and the mind is conceived as dedicated to the good, it is crowned by God the judge." For it is one thing for the mind to lack martyrdom, and another for martyrdom to lack the mind. Therefore, if the mind of Origen never lacked martyrdom and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how can we not believe him to be crowned by God the judge, if the martyr Cyprian does not lie? And if he is damned, who, I ask, damned him to the death of Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna (hell)</note>? Was it Jesus Christ, for whom he wished to die so many times? Rather, just as Augustine says of Cyprian himself—that the blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him—so too regarding Origen. We piously believe that the blood of martyrdom, poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly over his celestial soul burning with zeal for God and charity, washed away every stain of heresy. We say with David: **Blessed is Origen**, who, even if he sometimes went into the counsel of the erring, nevertheless did not stand in the way of sinners through impenitence, and never sat in the chair of pestilence through pertinacity, but his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night. **Blessed is Origen**, whose iniquities were forgiven through baptism, and whose sins were covered through repentance, and to whom the Lord did not impute sin because of martyrdom. Finally, such a great and such a...

Even if this man sometimes erred regarding the mysteries of faith out of a defect of intellect rather than any malice of the will, let us believe that he was not abandoned by the Lord at his end. Instead, through the visitation of His most clement mercy, let us believe he was illuminated regarding those secrets of faith in which he may have erred, and was called back from an erroneous way to the way of salvation. And I understood this in my short response when I previously said: since he was not found to be obstinate <term>pertinax: the legal and theological requirement for a belief to be considered formal heresy is "obstinacy," or a refusal to be corrected by the Church</term>, it is likely to believe that God saved him. That is, by visiting him with the visitation I mentioned, God most mercifully placed him in a state worthy of salvation and, by illuminating him regarding the secrets of the faith in which he erred, called him to a saving repentance for them.

Whether this actually occurred or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed from above. But to believe that it was so, rather than otherwise, seems more consistent and thus more reasonable to anyone considering the acts and life of Origen. For it is also reasonable that in doubtful matters, one should always adhere to the more favorable side. And let these words be spoken so that they may be valid even if Origen’s repentance were not established; however, we have already very clearly shown above, through the testimony of the most blessed Jerome, that it was indeed established.

Regarding the sixth article, I say that it does not <margin>Regarding the sixth article.</margin> seem credible that the Church ever determined that the soul of Origen was damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition with two arguments. The first argument is this: <margin>First argument.</margin> concerning that which cannot be determined with certainty except through rashness, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the Church. But concerning this question of whether Origen is saved or damned, neither side can be determined except rashly, at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the Church on this matter. The major premise is well-known, and to believe the opposite would be injurious to the Church—namely, to believe that it could judge anything ill-advisedly or rashly.

The minor premise is evident from the articles stated above. This is confirmed <margin>Confirmation</margin> because the Church could not be made certain of the damnation of Origen except through a special revelation made concerning him; but of such a revelation having been made, no mention is found anywhere. Therefore, etc.

The second argument is this: <margin>Second argument.</margin> if there is anything that might persuade one that the Church determined Origen’s damnation, it is certain texts of the decrees <note>Specifically, the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of canon law for the medieval Church.</note> which seem to suggest this to those who interpret them in a crude manner. These are the texts they usually bring forward: First, in the 15th Distinction, the chapter *Sancta Romana Ecclesia* <note>original: "di. xv. c. ſancta Ro. eccleſia"</note>, as written by Pope Gelasius: "Likewise, we accept for reading some of Origen’s small works which the blessed Jerome does not repudiate; but all the rest, along with their author, we say are to be rejected." And the gloss <term>gloss: a marginal or interlinear commentary on a legal or biblical text</term> on that passage: "Since he was damned, are not his writings also?"

Also, in the section *De hereticis* ("On Heretics"), the chapter *Fraternitatis*, where it is written: "Since Celestinus and Pelagius were damned in the Synod of Ephesus <margin>Synod of Ephesus.</margin>, how can their chapters be received when their authors are damned?" From these authorities, some believe that the damnation of Origen’s soul to hell is proven.

But I say that nothing more is established by the preceding points except that the Church condemns the opinions and dogmas attributed to Origen as heretical, and thus condemns and detests him as one who put forward such dogmas—intending nothing at all regarding the salvation or damnation of his soul. ...because it does not belong to the Church to damn or save the souls of men. That pertains only to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. Therefore, it is ridiculous if, when one reads in the decrees "We damn Origen," one explains it to mean: "that is, we damn his soul with the damnation of hell." And this is also clearly evident from the manner of speaking of <note>Pope</note> Gelasius himself, who says that "we say his remaining works, along with their author, are to be rejected." For this word "to reject" <note>original: *renuere*</note> can in no way imply what they [the opponents] intend; rather, the Pope intends nothing other than this: namely, that his works are not accepted as authentic in the Church, nor is he himself likewise received as an approved doctor whose words are to be believed in the Church. Even if the Pope had not only said "we reject" but also "we damn," it would be of no help to them, because we are also accustomed to say, "In this point, Scotus damns Thomas; Hervaeus damns Scotus," <note>A reference to the sharp intellectual disagreements between scholastic theologians like Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, and Hervaeus Natalis.</note> and so with the rest. In such expressions, we must always understand "damnation" as referring to the doctrine and not the soul, according to the customary and proper way of speaking.

<margin>Secondly, he argues against them.</margin>

Secondly, I argue against them from the gloss <note>a marginal commentary on canon law</note> which they cite, which says: "If he is damned, are not his writings also?" I ask them, therefore, if this logical sequence holds: "Origen himself is damned, therefore his writings are also damned." How is the term <term>ly: a technical term in scholastic logic used to designate a specific word being analyzed</term> "damned" taken in the first part? If it is taken to mean "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher," then I have proven my point. If, however, it is understood as "damned in his soul with the damnation of hell," then the logical sequence is worthless. For it is possible for many doctors, whose writings are Catholic and are read daily as Catholic works, to be in hell; because it is possible for someone to err in nothing regarding the faith, but to think correctly about all the articles of faith, and yet be in another mortal sin and die in it. And the damnation of a soul is entirely irrelevant to the damnation of a doctrine, because the former pertains to the malice of the will, while the latter pertains to a defect of the intellect. Therefore, neither does it follow that "This man is in paradise, therefore his sayings are

Catholic." This is both because, as was said above, the Church is neither accustomed to nor able to damn men in their souls, and because we must understand the judgment to be about that which was previously questioned and disputed. But in that Synod, as is clear from the acts of the council, the question was not whether the souls of Celestius and Pelagius were in paradise or in hell, but rather whether their sayings and dogmas were Catholic or not Catholic. Therefore, we must understand the judgment to be about this: that is, about the truth of their dogmas and about the approval or rejection of those authors specifically as teachers of such dogmas.

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense against ecclesiastical overreach, transitioning from the specific case of Origen's salvation to a broader theological and psychological argument about the nature of belief and the limits of Church authority in defining new dogmas.</meta>

They should take care not to establish new things to be believed by the faithful on their own authority, nor determine them to be matters of faith. And they should listen to that prohibition of the Lord in the fourth chapter of Deuteronomy: "You shall not add to the word that I speak to you." <note>original: "Non addetis ad uerbum quod ego loquor uobis" (Deuteronomy 4:2). A common scriptural warning used by reformers and scholars to argue against the expansion of Church dogma beyond Scripture.</note> This saying condemns not only those who, by their own authority, add new things to be believed on top of previous ones, but also those who reject Catholic truth as if it were heresy.

## EIGHTH QUESTION: ON THE FREEDOM OF BELIEF.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion for its first part. Aristotle.</margin> Just as no one holds an opinion <term>precisely</term> <note>original: *precise*; in scholastic logic, this means "exclusively" or "only"</note> because they want to hold that opinion, so no one believes something to be true precisely because they want to believe it so.

<margin>Proof for the second part. Augustine.</margin> From this conclusion, I infer the following as a corollary: It is not within the free power of a person to believe an article of faith is true whenever they please, and to believe it is not true whenever they please. Those masters <note>The author is likely referring to the university censors or inquisitors who condemned his work.</note> judged that this proposition and its corollary were erroneous and <term>smacking of heresy</term> <note>original: *heresim sapiens*; a technical theological grade of suspicion for a statement that sounds heretical even if it is not explicitly proven false.</note>. I, however, consider the main conclusion to be not only Catholic but most true, and far truer than its opposite. And I say the same regarding the corollary, if it is understood correctly; its meaning, if taken according to my intent, is not to be understood in any way other than how it follows from the main conclusion of which it is the corollary. 

<margin>Pierre d’Ailly. Heinrich von Oyta. Henry of Hesse. The University of Paris.</margin> Moreover, that the conclusion is not only Catholic but also most true is clear. For regarding its first part—which is that no one holds an opinion precisely because they want to—Aristotle supports this in the second book of *On the Soul*, in the text of the commentary numbered 253, where Aristotle places a difference between imagination and opinion. <note>Aristotle argues that while we can imagine anything we like at will, we cannot "opine" (hold a settled belief) at will, because belief requires a sense of truth or evidence.</note> This sentiment of Aristotle has not only never been rejected but has instead been unanimously approved by all our theologians. 

<margin>Declaration of the corollary proposition.</margin> The second part of the conclusion—which states that no one believes something to be true precisely because they want it to be true—is found in several places in the works of Augustine, who says quite often that one cannot believe by <term>free choice</term> <note>original: *libero arbitrio*</note>, that is, by the mere command of the will without the persuasion of reason or a motive. This entire conclusion of mine—which summarily holds that when a doubtful proposition is presented, the mere apprehension of the terms and a mere command of the will are not enough for someone to believe or disbelieve it—is held by Pierre d'Ailly, Heinrich von Oyta, and Henry of Hesse. <note>These were prominent 14th and 15th-century "nominalist" theologians associated with the University of Paris.</note> And when I was in Paris, almost the entire University of Paris held this view. Since many Catholic doctors hold this to be so true that they consider the opposite to be impossible, I have yet to read a doctor who contradicts this opinion. 

The corollary proposition should not be understood or accepted in any other way than with the restriction or determination placed in the preceding statement: namely, that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true whenever it pleases and to believe it is false when it pleases. That is to say, the intellect does not believe <term>precisely</term> because it pleases the will that it should believe. Such an understanding of one proposition through another linked to it is not unusual; indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the letter is often taken from what precedes or follows it, which is especially the case here.

<margin>Something is said to be in the liberty or free power of the will in two ways.</margin> In the first way, something is in the power of the will because once the <term>apprehension</term> <note>original: *apprehensio*; the basic mental grasping of the meaning of a sentence before one decides if it is true.</note> is present in the intellect, and with no other act of the intellect required, it is within the commanding power of the will to simply produce that act of belief. <margin>First.</margin>

<margin>Second.</margin> In the second way, something is said to be in the free power of the will because, once all other things required for that act are present, the will has the power to bring it into being or not. The will is not forced into this act even when everything else is in place. In this way, the act of believing an article is in the free power of the will. This is the intended meaning of the corollary proposition; and from what has been said, anyone who has understanding can recognize that those masters did not do well to say absolutely that the statement was erroneous and "smacked of heresy."

Moreover, that the opinion of those doctors whom I follow—namely, those who say that the mere understanding of terms combined with the pure command of the will is not enough to cause the <term>assent of faith</term> <note>The mental "yes" given to a religious truth.</note>—is probable and reasonable can be clearly seen. <margin>Augustine.</margin>

<margin>It is argued first.</margin> And first, it is argued as follows: It is not in the free power of a person to hold an opinion that something is one way or another just because they want to. Therefore, it is not in the free power of a person to believe something is one way or another just because they want to. The logic follows: because if something which seems more likely to be true [holding an opinion] is not in our power, then [believing] is not either. But it is "lesser" to adhere to something while having <term>fear of the opposite</term> <note>original: *formidine*; in scholastic logic, this is the intellectual anxiety that the opposite side might actually be the truth, which characterizes "opinion" as opposed to "certainty."</note> than to do so without such fear.

Therefore, the premise is expressed by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul*, in the text of commentary 153. And it is clear from experience: for anyone can experience in themselves that if a doubtful proposition is presented, if it is purely doubtful to them, they are not inclined toward either side of the opinion by assent until a new "appearance" comes to them—either through syllogistic reasoning, or intuitive knowledge, or the testimony of many, or the authority of the speaker, or something similar.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

<margin>Second.</margin> Second, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of a person to make something appear true to their own intellect, or to make it appear not true. Therefore, it is not in the free power of a person to believe something is or is not true in such a way. The logic holds, because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and <term>assent</term> to it while it does not actually appear true to them.

The assumption is proven because for this or that to "appear" a certain way to the intellect is for this or that to be represented a certain way to the intellect. And this cannot depend on the command of the will, because this appearance precedes the act of the will.

<margin>It is confirmed.</margin> This is confirmed because something appearing a certain way to the intellect happens because the object represented is such, and the evidence (or whatever it is that makes it credible or not) is such, and the intellect is such. But making an object be a certain way or making the intellect be a certain way is not within the choice of the will...

### QUESTION NINE ON ACCIDENTS IN THE SACRAMENT.

Whoever says that an accident <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color, taste, or shape) that can only exist by "inhering" in a substance (like bread or wood).</note> cannot exist unless it exists in a subject could still uphold the sacrament of the Eucharist while holding that the substance of bread does not remain. Because the "act" depends less on the "potentiality" than the other way around, it seems more feasible for "being" to exist without essence than the reverse.

Secondly, they show that this is not only possible but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the uncreated. Now, the essence of the bread and the essence of Christ's body agree in matter and category; hence, one can be converted into the other—even by nature, if the body were mortal. But the "being" of the bread does not share in matter or category with the substantial "being" of Christ's body, since that [Divine existence] is uncreated and divine, belonging to the Divine Person, as in Christ there is only one "being" of actual substantial existence. Therefore, it is impossible for the "being" of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

Thus, just as humanity could be assumed without its being being assumed (but rather remaining in the potentiality of matter), so the essence can be converted without the "being" being converted (but rather reduced to the potentiality of the essence). Though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are more easily spoken of than understood. <meta>This page concludes the discussion on the linguistics of the Eucharist—specifically whether the priest speaks as a narrator or in his own person—and begins a new inquiry into the nature of Christ's miracles as evidence of his divine nature.</meta>

...in such a way it will not be shed; therefore, those words are taken only in a **recitative** <note>original: "recitatiue." In medieval logic, this means the speaker is quoting words originally spoken by another (Christ), acting as a narrator rather than speaking in their own person.</note> sense. For what is recited but a voice brought forth by another, for which the voice of the person reciting stands in? For this reason, that voice—which recites another voice—must be understood **materially** <note>original: "materialiter sumenda." To take words "materially" means to treat the words as objects or quotes being repeated, rather than as a direct statement about the speaker’s current reality.</note>. 

Furthermore, even if these words were taken not recitatively but **significatively** <note>original: "significatiue." This would mean the words are intended to point directly to the immediate action of the speaker.</note>, it would imply that the blood of Christ is shed for others and not for the one performing the consecration. This is because the text says, "which will be shed for **you** and for **many**." If the priest were speaking for himself, it should instead say "which is shed for **us**," and so on. I do not say these things because I believe the opposing opinion cannot be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic but is also more probable than its opposite. 

From this, it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable. The opinion of the **solemn glossator** <note>A "glossator" was a scholar who wrote explanatory notes (glosses) on legal or theological texts. ...to humans, and indeed reason would be said to be in God only in an improper sense. If, indeed, it is inferred from the present conclusion that God is "improperly" said to understand (just as a comparison implies a baseline), let that consequence be accepted only in this sense: God is not called "intellect" according to the strict or specific definition of this word "to understand," etc., but according to the common and less strict way, as was clear from Dionysius's manner of speaking.

Truly, he who reads the booklet of propositions to be debated can be warned by the title itself; for while I distinguish those things said according to our own opinion from those of others, I do not propose the latter as my own or as true opinions, but as believed by those authors. Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are mine; and let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might think many things which are not ours.

Conclusion 16.
The manner of worshipping images and the cross proposed by Peter of Aquila, Henry of Ghent, John Guarra, Durandus, Robert Holcot, and commonly by all the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus. This group argued that images should not receive the same worship—*latria*—due to God alone, but rather a relative or secondary honor.</note> is more probable than the manner proposed by **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, who argued that the cross and images of Christ should be worshipped with *latria* because the movement of the mind toward an image is the same as the movement toward the reality it represents.</note>.

Conclusion 17.
Just because someone denies that images should be worshipped in the way Thomas proposes, it does not follow that they deny they should be worshipped in the way the Church proposes.

Conclusion 18.
Since in God there is the fullness of all being, God can—insofar as it depends on Him—**hypostatize** <note>original: "hipoſtatizare" — a technical term meaning to take a nature and give it a distinct personal existence, as when the Divine Word assumed a human nature in the Incarnation.</note> every nature.

Conclusion 19.
Regarding the question of whether an **irrational nature** <note>For example, a plant or an animal.</note> is—due to a defect in its own nature—incapable of being assumed into the divine nature in the unity of a **person** <note>original: "suppositum" — the individual substance or "personhood" that carries a nature.</note> (as Henry of Ghent believed), or whether it is not incapable (as the **common path** <note>original: "communis via" — the standard theological teaching.</note> holds), a Catholic may be so uncertain as to have no positive act of contradicting Henry’s opinion.

Conclusion 20.
A proposition denying assent to a certain statement does not, by the power of the words themselves, imply positive assent to the opposite statement. <note>This is a rule of formal logic: withholding belief in "A" does not automatically mean one is asserting "not-A."</note>

Conclusion 21.
All magic that is commonly called **necromancy** <note>original: "necromantia" — here referring to "black magic" or sorcery involving the conjuration of spirits.</note>, and absolutely any art or science—if indeed such things should even be called arts or sciences—that has any kind of pact or communion with demons in any way, whether explicit or implicit, whether as a primary goal or a secondary attachment, whether occurring before, during, or after, or in any way whatsoever, is a forbidden and superstitious thing, and is rightly condemned by the Church.

Conclusion 22.
That science which is rightly called the practical part of natural philosophy, and which is called **natural magic** <note>Pico distinguishes "Natural Magic" as a legitimate science that uses the hidden powers of nature (like magnetism or medicinal herbs) from "Necromancy," which relies on demons.</note> by William of Paris, Roger Bacon, and all the Greek authors, contains nothing in itself that is contrary to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

Conclusion 23.
There is no science—extending the name "science" to both revealed and non-revealed branches of knowledge—that can make us certain of the divinity of Christ, other than the teaching of the Gospel and the science of Christian theology.

Conclusion 24.
Among the non-revealed sciences—those discovered and acquired by human effort in all their parts—there is none that helps us more in knowing the divinity of Christ than that science <note>Refers back to "Natural Magic."</note> through which we learn what can be done by the power of natural agents, both **sublunary** <note>Earthly; literally "under the moon."</note> and heavenly, so that we may then understand from Christ’s works that He was truly the Lord and author of nature; for He performed, by His own power, those deeds which exceed the limits of all natural power, both heavenly and earthly.

Conclusion 25.
A believer is not obligated to use the term "science" in every instance of their speech as a general term covering both revealed and non-revealed sciences.
