### Conclusion 28.
Given the situation that either Origen never actually believed those opinions, but they were falsely attributed to him by heretics—as **Rufinus, Pamphilus, Methodius, Didymus, and Aymon** <note>A group of early Christian writers and defenders of Origen.</note> maintain—or if he did believe them at one time, he eventually repented of them in the end—as **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who was often a critic of Origen’s theology.</note> suggests—it is reasonable to believe well regarding the salvation of his soul; and we are not bound to believe the opposite as a necessity of salvation.

### Conclusion 29.
The act of believing is a free act.

### Conclusion 30.
The act of believing is not within human power in such a way that, when a purely doubtful proposition is presented, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other by the mere and sole command of the will.

### Conclusion 31.
A person who believes this proposition—that it is not within the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true when they please, or to believe it is false when they please—does not err in faith, provided the explicit sense of the preceding conclusion is allowed.

### Conclusion 32.
The **accidents** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color, taste, or weight) that exist only within a "subject" or substance. In the Eucharist, the accidents of bread remain while the substance changes.</note> in the sacrament of the altar exist in no subject.

### Conclusion 33.
It is possible by the absolute power of God for the **existence** of the bread to remain without its **essence**, and for the accidents of the bread to be supported by that existence; this assumes a real distinction between essence and existence.

### Conclusion 34.
Whoever believes this proposition—namely, that anyone who says an accident cannot exist unless it exists within the Eucharist could hold the sacrament even while holding that the substance of the bread cannot remain—as can be verified by what was said in the preceding conclusion—does not err in faith.

### Conclusion 35.
**Breadness** <note>original: "Paneitas" — a technical Scholastic term for the abstract essence or "bread-ness" of the bread.</note> does not remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist as if it were assumed by Christ, God and man, but through conversion passes into the essence of the body of Christ.

### Conclusion 36.
If one follows the "common path"—that God can assume <note>original: "suppositare" — a technical term meaning to take a nature into the unity of a divine person.</note> any nature—it is possible that Christ assumes "breadness" into the unity of the divine person. It is possible that through such an assumption, Christ is present on the altar where the bread is, such that without the conversion or annihilation of the "breadness," Christ is on the altar according to a possible truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist—not indeed the one instituted by Christ, but one that was possible to be instituted.

The miracles of Christ, as far as the deed performed is concerned, are proof that they were performed by divine power.

->### Conclusion 41.<-
The miracles of Christ, as far as the manner of performing them is concerned, are proof that Christ himself, when performing the divine power, possessed it from himself and not from elsewhere.

->### Conclusion 42.<-
God, in the most perfect mode of knowledge, knows both Himself and all things other than Himself.

->### Conclusion 43.<-
In God is every perfection, absolutely.

->### Conclusion 44.<-
If we use this term "intellectual" according to the manner of **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian. He argued that God is "beyond-being" and therefore beyond human categories like "intellect."</note>—meaning knowledge appropriate to the angelic nature, just as "rational" denotes knowledge appropriate to human nature—then we speak improperly when we say that God is "intellectual" or that he "understands."

->### Conclusion 45.<-
The soul, through that hidden act of understanding which is direct and permanent without the aid of the senses or the imagination, understands itself alone actually and distinctly.

->### Conclusion 46.<-
The soul, through its multiple and various other acts, understands various and multiple things other than itself.

->.·. THE END .·.<-

# Brief of Alexander VI, Supreme Pontiff, to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia.

### To our beloved son, the noble man Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola.
### POPE ALEXANDER VI.

**BELOVED** Son, greetings and apostolic blessing. We look after the peace and reputation of all Catholics as much as God allows, especially those whom nobility of birth, mastery of letters, and integrity of life and orthodox faith commend. <note>original: *Dilecte Filii salutem & apostolicam benedictionem*</note>. Some time ago, when you first presented yourself to our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Innocent VIII, and the Roman Court, you posted nine hundred conclusions in theology and other faculties to be publicly debated—as is the custom—with the permission of the aforementioned predecessor. You offered to maintain these under the correction of the Apostolic See. However, our predecessor understood from some that among those conclusions were several contrary to our faith and religion, being erroneous, scandalous, and ill-sounding <note>original: *male sonantes*. A technical ecclesiastical term for propositions that, while not explicitly heretical, offend the ears of the faithful or lead toward error.</note>, and suspected of unsound doctrine.

Desiring then to look after the integrity of the faith, lest the minds of the faithful—especially the simple folk who usually flock to such public debates—be corrupted, he commissioned several venerable brothers (then his, now ours) who were bishops and other professors of sacred theology and both branches of law <note>original: *utriusque iuris*. Refers to a doctor of both Canon Law and Civil/Roman Law.</note> named by him. He commanded them by a letter in the form of a Brief to examine the contents of said conclusions: whether any of them, by the force of their words, clashed with the Catholic faith, or savored of heresy, or were doubtful and ambiguous such that they could be drawn toward an erroneous meaning. They were to report back to our predecessor, as is contained more fully in the said Brief, so that with a faithful report in hand, he might provide the necessary remedy.

These bishops and professors reported to the same predecessor that certain conclusions seemed suspect to them and, as they asserted, savored of heresy. Nevertheless, you had published those conclusions only for the sake of scholastic debate and subject to the correction of the Apostolic See. You eventually professed that you would hold them only as our predecessor judged them, promising by oath to assent to whatever declaration he might make concerning them.

Afterward, our predecessor learned that you had published another "Apologetic" book <note>This refers to Pico’s *Apologia*, written in 1487 to defend his 900 Theses against his critics.</note> in which you interpreted and declared these same conclusions in a better and Catholic sense, explaining them through the understanding of sincere faith. To prevent the aforementioned propositions from corrupting the hearts of the faithful in any way, the same predecessor forbade the reading of the booklet of the nine hundred conclusions. However, he declared that you had not incurred any mark of disgrace regarding your reputation, as is more broadly contained in the same letters, the tenor of which we wish to be held as expressly stated here.

Later, however, because some suggested to the predecessor that under the pretext of this *Apologia* you had violated your aforementioned oath, he commanded you—then living in France—to be summoned to the Court. Having reverently accepted his orders, you set out on the journey to return to the Roman Court. When you reached Italy, you remained in the regions of Florence by the good pleasure of the predecessor himself. In the meantime, the aforementioned matters were brought to our notice, and we investigated the truth of the whole business.

This was established especially by the reports of our venerable brother Giorgio, Bishop of Albano and Lisbon, and our beloved sons Giovanni Battista Orsini (priest of the title of Saints John and Paul) and Francesco (deacon of Saint Eustace), Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. We specifically commissioned them to accurately inform themselves and report to us, bringing in our beloved son Paolo of Genoa, a professor of theology of the Order of Saint Dominic and Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace. <note>The Master of the Sacred Palace was the Pope’s chief theologian and domestic prelate.</note> They reported that nothing else was subsequently done, processed, or attempted against you, and that in the same *Apologia*, you had written to clear your mind before all people from any mark of suspicion regarding the orthodox faith...

You affirmed that you were continually awaiting the judgment and determination of that same predecessor and of the Apostolic See, to which you humbly submitted yourself; and you have persisted in your aforementioned promise and oath, just as you intend to persist and even now promise anew. Therefore, embracing with paternal affection your good and upright mind, the sincerity of your faith, and your devotion and obedience toward us and the Apostolic See—and considering that divine generosity has also distinguished you with various virtues—we hereby act for your greater security <note>original: *pro potiori cautella tua*. A legal phrase ensuring the subject is protected even if the legal necessity is debatable.</note>. 

We absolve you, and decree you to be absolved, from any guilt of perjury which you might have perhaps indirectly incurred by contravening your said oath in any way (the form of which oath we wish to be held as if fully expressed here). Furthermore, regarding the case of this commission against you and its individual status (which we also hold as if fully expressed), we call to ourselves any parts of it currently pending before any judges, even Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. 

By our own impulse <note>original: *motu proprio*. A legal term for an act taken by the Pope on his own initiative, without a formal request from another party.</note> and from certain knowledge, we extinguish this case. We declare that you, persisting in that same oath according to the form of the letters of our predecessor, have incurred no mark of ill-repute at all on account of the preceding events. We further declare that on account of the publication of your declarations and of your *Apologia* <note>Pico’s *Apologia* was his published defense of the thirteen disputed theses, which had previously caused further friction with the Church.</note>, or for any other reason, you have incurred no appearance or suspicion of heresy, nor any sinister mark, nor have you fallen into the crime of a true or feigned relapse <note>A "relapsed" heretic was someone who fell back into error after a previous recantation, a crime often carrying the death penalty in this era.</note>. Nor have you incurred the penalties or censures contained in law or otherwise against heretics or those suspected of heresy. 

By the same impulse, knowledge, and authority mentioned above, we decree and declare through these presents, strictly prohibiting and commanding by virtue of holy obedience the local Ordinaries, commissioners, and all officials—even inquisitors of heretical depravity—that they do not presume to molest or investigate you in any way on the occasion of the premises. We decree it null and void if anything to the contrary regarding these matters is attempted by anyone of any authority, whether knowingly or through ignorance; notwithstanding the premises as well as apostolic constitutions and ordinances and anything else to the contrary, even if they would require specific and individual mention here. 

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, under the Ring of the Fisherman <note>The official seal used by the Pope for briefs and private correspondence, depicting St. Peter casting a net from a boat.</note>, on the 18th day of June, 1493, in the first year of our pontificate.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA. ON BEING AND THE ONE, TO ANGELO POLIZIANO. <note>original: "De Ente et Uno." This is one of Pico's most famous works, written in 1491, attempting to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note>

## PREFACE.

[Large initial N] YOU WERE telling me in recent days about the discussion Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the effective ruler of Florence and a massive patron of the arts and philosophy.</note> had with you concerning Being and the One, when he disputed against Aristotle—whose *Ethics* you are publicly lecturing on this year—by relying on the arguments of the Platonists. And since those who think Aristotle disagrees with Plato also disagree with me—for I make the philosophy of both concordant <note>Pico was a "syncretist," meaning he believed that different schools of philosophy and religion ultimately pointed toward the same universal truths.</note>—you asked how Aristotle might be defended in this matter and how he might agree with his master, Plato. ### CHAPTER TWO, IN WHICH IT IS ASKED WHERE PLATO SPOKE OF BEING AND THE ONE; IT SHOWS THAT HIS WORDS FAVOR THE VIEW THAT THE ONE AND BEING ARE EQUAL, RATHER THAN THOSE WHO WISH THE ONE TO BE SUPERIOR TO BEING. <note>original: "Caput secundum in quo querit ubi plato de ente & uno sit locutus..." Pico is entering the core of the metaphysical debate: is God (The One) "above" existence itself, or are they the same thing?</note>

<margin>What should be thought of Plato’s *Parmenides*.</margin>

<margin>The usefulness of logic.</margin>

These are the arguments they lean upon. Before we dismantle them, it would not be out of place to bring into the open what Plato himself expressed on this matter. I find Plato discussing Being and the One <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note> in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics <note>Pico refers to the Neoplatonist followers of Plato who believed in a hierarchy where "The One" is the highest principle, even above "Being."</note> claim that in both works, Plato places the One above Being. 

However, I will first say this concerning the *Parmenides*: that in the entire dialogue nothing is actually asserted as a definitive truth. Furthermore, even if something were asserted, nothing can be found there so clearly that we could definitely attribute such a dogma <note>A fixed principle or set of beliefs held by a school of philosophy.</note> to Plato. Certainly, this book should not be ranked among his dogmatic works, since it is entirely nothing but a kind of dialectical exercise <term>dialectical exercise: a logical training method used by ancient philosophers to explore all sides of an argument and sharpen the mind, rather than to establish a final doctrine</term>. This is so far from my own opinion that the dialogue itself...

--- Page 203 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Pico is critiquing the Neoplatonist interpretation of Plato's *Parmenides*, arguing that the dialogue is a logical exercise rather than a statement of metaphysical dogma that places "The One" above "Being."</meta>

Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea, a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his paradoxes; he was a student of Parmenides.</note> had judged this a duty of old age. If we do not believe even these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself. We shall see that nowhere is anything affirmed as a certainty. Rather, everywhere it only asks: "If this were so, what would follow?" and likewise, "What if it were not so?" However, the Academics <note>Followers of the later Platonic Academy who leaned toward skepticism or the belief that the One is superior to all categories of existence.</note> snatched an opportunity for their own opinion regarding Being and the One from this source: because in the first position of this problem, Plato exercises himself to see if all things are one, what would then follow? He responds that it would happen that the One, which we posit to exist, would be indivisible, would be infinite, would be nowhere; and since he enumerates many things of that kind, he brings this up among others: namely, that it would follow that this "One" is not **Being**.

Take note, however: even if this were not a dialectical exercise, but a dogma regarding Being and the One were being handed down, consider how much these things differ: namely, to assert that the One is "above" Being, versus asserting that *if* all things are One, that "One" would not be Being. But enough about Parmenides.

Indeed, in the *Sophist*, Plato speaks more toward the opinion that the One and Being are equal <margin>What he says in the *Sophist* about Being and the One</margin> rather than the One being superior to Being. For I do not find where he explains that [superiority]. He signifies the other [equality] in many ways, such as through these words: "For considering it thus, you confess it is necessary that he who says *something* says *one thing*"; and shortly after, "but he who does not say *something*, must of necessity say nothing at all, not even *one thing*." These are his words. Therefore, in his view, "not one" and "nothing" are equal—indeed, they are the same—and likewise "one" and "something" are equal. After this, he likewise proves it cannot be said that "Non-being" is "One." And thus he concludes: "Being does not happen to Non-being; therefore the One does not happen to Non-being." But he speaks of the One which he had said before was equal to that which is "something." He seems, therefore, to hold it as confessed that the One is Being. But let it be; let us grant that Plato affirmed this—though he certainly affirmed it nowhere. Come, let us examine in what sense it could truly be said, first laying down the foundations of the Aristotelian opinion itself in this manner.

### Chapter three, in which he declares how "Being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to the One and encompassing all things. <margin>Being can be understood in two ways. He proves the term is rightly accepted in the way Aristotle accepted it. First testimony. Second: Simplicius defending Parmenides. Solution to the first argument of the Platonists.</margin>

This word, **Being**, about which there is doubt whether it is equal to the One, can be understood in two ways. The first is that when we say "Being," we understand everything that is "outside of nothing." Aristotle used it in this way when he made Being equal to the One. Nor did he use the word thus without reason; for as it is truly said: we ought to *think* like the few, but *speak* like the many. We think and hold opinions for ourselves; we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. Now, the common people and everyone from the public sphere understand "Being" in such a way that everything is called "Being" which does not lack existence, and which cannot truly be called "nothing." 

But even those who are considered the wisest among these very people who think otherwise, we find have used this word in this way. For Parmenides the Pythagorean, when he said "The One is that which is," he understood God. If we believe Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle who attempted to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him. As if he had said that all things are one! For they respond with one voice that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things—which he himself openly confesses elsewhere in his poems. But when he said "The One is that which is," he judged that the name of "Being" truly fits that [God] alone; and that what truly *is*, is the One alone, which One is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders and the Platonists, the One cannot be above Being unless it is above God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God is Being, that he grants the true name of Being to God alone.

[Marginalia:]
<margin>Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century. Pico cites him here because the Neoplatonists often used his works to support their views.</note></margin>

And so, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists occurs to us in passing. But also Dionysius the Areopagite—whom those who dispute against us claim as a supporter of their own opinion—will not deny that it was truly said by God to Moses: **I am who I am** <note>original Latin: "ego sum qui sum"; see Exodus 3:14.</note>. This we read in Greek as **I am the one who is** <note>original Greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν (*ego eimi ho on*)</note>, that is, **I am Being**. Indeed, when these very people say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to **Being**, just as "multitude" is opposed to the **One**, they will necessarily concede that whatever is not **Being** is nothing or non-being. Just as that which is not one is many or a multitude; therefore, if the same rule of speech is observed, they must admit either that God is nothing—a thought which the ears themselves dread—or that He is **Being**. 

In this way, when we take "**Being**," we establish that first <term>axiom</term> <note>Referring to the principle of the excluded middle in logic.</note> and universal pronouncement: that regarding any thing whatever, it must necessarily be said that it either is or is not...

<summary>Pico argues that God’s self-identification in Exodus as "I am" proves that the Divine is "Being," contradicting Neoplatonists who place the One above Being. He concludes that if God were not Being, He would logically have to be "nothing," which is an absurdity.</summary>

--- Page 205 ---
<meta>Continuity: Pico continues his reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle. Having previously argued that Being and the One are co-extensive, he now addresses the Neoplatonic claim that God is "above Being" and shows that Aristotle held a compatible view.</meta>

He is God, who is the fullness of all being: who alone exists from Himself, and from whom alone, with no intermediary, all things have proceeded into being. For this reason, we shall truly say that God is not a "being" but is "above being," and that there is something higher than being—namely, God Himself. Since the name of the "One" is given to Him, it follows that we must confess the "One" to be above being. 

<margin>Why God is called "One."</margin>

However, we call God "One" then, not so much stating *what* He is, but rather *how* He is all the things He is, and how other things come from Him. For "One," says Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose *Divine Names* Pico frequently references to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian theology.</note>, is what God is called because He is all things uniquely. Again, He is called "One" because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. 

<margin>How it could be said by Plato that the One is superior to being, if he indeed said this.</margin>

Therefore, if—as the Academics <note>The "Academics" here refers to the Platonists of the Academy.</note> wish—Plato affirms in the first hypothesis of the *Parmenides* that the One is superior to being, that "One" will be none other than God; and they themselves admit this, asserting by common consent that the first principle of all things is treated there by Plato. 

But someone might say that at least in this regard, Aristotle will be in discord with Plato: for Aristotle never accepts "being" in such a way that it is subordinate to the "One" and does not include God, whereas Plato does. 

<margin>Thus also by Aristotle, sometimes taking it so that God is not "being" but must be called "above being."</margin>

Those who say this have not read Aristotle. For he himself does this, and far more clearly than Plato. For in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* was traditionally called "First Philosophy."</note>, he says that "being" is divided into "being in itself" <term>per se</term> and "accidental being" <term>per accidens</term>. Since "being in itself" is divided into the ten categories <note>The ten fundamental classes of things (substance, quality, quantity, etc.) defined by Aristotle.</note>, there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not contained under this "being"; for He is neither "accidental being," nor is He contained under any of the ten categories into which "being in itself" is divided. 

Likewise, that division is common among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "covered walkways" (*peripatoi*) of the Lyceum.</note> by which being is said to be divided into "substance" and "accident." When this occurs, we understand "being" in such a way that God is above being, and is not categorized under being, just as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> teaches in the first book of his commentary on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>.

<margin>That Aristotle gave these two names especially to God: the One and the Good.</margin>

I will add this: that certain Platonists boast wrongly, as if they possessed a mystery unknown to Aristotle, when they say there are two proper names for God, namely "the One" and "the Good," and that thus the Good and the One are before being. For just as we have shown that it is not hidden from the Peripatetics how God can be understood as "above being," we can also show that Aristotle gave these two names—the Good and the One—to God above all others. 

For in the twelfth book of *First Philosophy*, after he has disputed concerning all being and the "separate intellects" <note>The "unmoved movers" or celestial intelligences in Aristotelian cosmology.</note>, he asks finally (as if having turned, after all else, to investigating the properties of God alone) whether, besides the "good" that exists in the universe of beings—much like the order in an army—there is some "separate Good," like the leader of this army. And he determines that this is so: that God is the Good. Consequently, in the same chapter, he proves His unity, citing—after powerful arguments—that line from Homer: **"Let there be one ruler, one king."** <note>original Greek: εἰς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἰς βασιλεύς (*heis koiranos esto, heis basileus*); quoted from the *Iliad* 2.204.</note> 

Where, then, is Aristotle false? Where is he in discord with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he think of God less honorably than is fitting?

### Chapter Five, in which he explains by what reasoning the Peripatetics ascribe many things to God which the Platonists deny of Him, and teaches in what way we ascend through four steps to the darkness in which God dwells.

<margin>That the first argument of the Academics must be resolved again.</margin>

Let us now resolve the arguments of the Platonists by which they contend—not in the way with which we agree, but absolutely against Aristotle—that the "One" is superior to "Being." Although the first argument was sufficiently resolved above (which said God is the One but not "being"), it would be worth the effort to digress further to show why many things are both truly affirmed and truly denied of God—not only by different schools like the Platonists and Peripatetics, but often by the same author. God is all things, and He is all things most eminently and most perfectly. This would not be so unless...

### Chapter Seven
#### in which he solves the third argument of the Platonists regarding multiplicity and shows that for those who say the "One" is something more common than "Being," something must be conceded which Plato denies.

<margin>Solution of the third reason.</margin>
<margin>Argument against the Platonists proving that, according to Plato, the One cannot be higher than Being.</margin>

They are greatly mistaken in their third reason. For multiplicity is not opposed to the One in the same way that non-being is opposed to being. The latter pair have a contradictory opposition; the former have either a privative or contrary opposition, about which the Aristotelians argue relatively in the tenth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>original: "prime philosophiæ." In this period, Aristotle's *Metaphysics* was commonly referred to as First Philosophy.</note>. But let them see what ruins they fall into—those who are called Platonists and say that the "One" is higher than "Being." It is certain that whenever two categories are so related that one is under the other as under something more common, it is possible for something to escape the scope of the lower category without escaping the higher. This is why the latter is said to be "more common" <term>common: In logic, a "more common" term (like "animal") covers a wider range of things than a "less common" term (like "human").</term>. An example is at hand: because "animal" is more common than "human," it can happen that something is a "non-human," which is nevertheless an "animal." By equal reasoning, if the "One" were more common than "Being," it could happen that something might be a "non-being" (or nothing) which was nevertheless "one." And thus, "one" would be predicated of non-being, a concept which Plato expressly refutes in the *Sophist* <note>In Plato's *Sophist*, it is argued that you cannot attribute "one-ness" or "many-ness" to that which does not exist, as it would lead to a logical contradiction.</note>.

### Chapter Eight
#### in which he declares how these four—namely being, the one, the true, and the good—are in all things that exist after God.

<margin>Followers of Avicenna. Averroes. Plato.</margin>
<margin>The order in these four.</margin>

The truest opinion, therefore, is that there are four things that encompass everything: being, the one, the true, and the good. This is true if they are understood such that their negations are "nothing," "the divided," "the false," and "the evil." To these four, two others were added—namely, "something" and "thing"—by later followers of Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath whose interpretations of Aristotle deeply influenced Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, who in many places interpolated the philosophy of Aristotle. From this, great battles were fought between them and Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was an Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" for his strict adherence to Aristotle; his followers often clashed with those of Avicenna.</note>; but as far as this matter is concerned, there is little actual discord. For they divide what is understood under the "one" into "one" and "something"—which does not differ from Plato, who in the *Sophist* enumerates "something" among these most similar terms—and they divide what is contained under "being" into "being" and "thing." 

But of these elsewhere. To follow what was begun: these four are in one way in God, and in another way in those things that are after God, since God has these from Himself, while others have them from Him. Let us see first how they are present in created things. All things that exist after God have an efficient, exemplary, and final cause: for all things are *from* Him, *through* Him, and *toward* Him. If, then, we consider things as they are established by God as the efficient cause, they are called "beings" because they participate in existence through His action. If we consider them according to their pattern—which we call the "Idea" <note>In the Platonic and Scholastic tradition, "Ideas" are the divine blueprints in the mind of God.</note>—according to which God established them (matching and responding to it), they are called "true." For a "true" image of Hercules is said to be that which is conformed to the real Hercules. If they tend toward Him as toward the ultimate end, they are called "good." If, however, each thing is taken absolutely according to itself, it is named "one." There is, moreover, this order, that...

<summary>Pico refutes the Platonic claim that "The One" is superior to "Being" by arguing that attributing unity to non-existence is a logical fallacy. He then introduces the four transcendentals (Being, One, True, Good) and explains how they manifest in created things through their relationship to God as cause and pattern.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the introduction to Chapter 7, Pico continues his argument that "the One" is not superior to "Being." He is now moving into a detailed defense of the "convertibility" of the transcendentals—Being, One, True, and Good—showing how they all coincide in reality.</meta>

First, let every single thing be conceived under the notion of being <term>notion of being: Latin *ratio entis*, the fundamental concept of what it means for something to exist</term>, since an agent <note>The "agent" here refers to the First Cause or God, who brings things into existence.</note> brings about each thing before that thing is anything in its own right; otherwise, it would not proceed from the agent according to the whole of what it is. 

From this it follows that there is nothing after God that we, in conceiving it, do not understand as: a being from another; a finite being; a participated being. "One" follows "Being." The third [property] is "Truth," because after a thing exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar <term>exemplar: the divine pattern or "Idea" in the mind of God according to which a thing is created</term> according to which it was formed. If it is found to be similar to that exemplar, it remains that it turns itself toward it through "Goodness," as toward something related and kindred. <margin>Plato.</margin>

Who does not see that these [Being, One, True, Good] are equal in their scope? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly also "One." For he who does not say "one" says nothing, as Plato says in the *Sophist* <note>original: "in sophiste." Referring to Plato's dialogue *The Sophist*, 237e, where it is argued that to speak of "that which is not" (non-being) is to say nothing at all, because "being" and "oneness" are linked.</note>. For whatever it is, it is undivided in itself and divided from others which are not itself. This is what we mean when we say "one," or to use Plato's words, it is "the same as itself and other than others," <margin>Truth is convertible with being.</margin> which he himself confirms in that same dialogue belongs to every single thing. 

It is also necessarily "True." For if it is a man, it is certainly a "true" man. It is the same to say "this is not true gold" as it is to say "this is not gold." For when you say "it is not true gold," <margin>Augustine.</margin> you mean this: it appears to be gold and is something like gold, but it is not gold. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine, defining what is "true" in his *Soliloquies*, says: "the true is that which is" <note>original: "uerū ē id qđ ē." St. Augustine, *Soliloquia* II, 5.</note>. This should not be understood to mean that "being" and "true" are the same [in concept]. For although they are the same in reality, they are different in reason and definition. Therefore, one should not be defined by the other, but Augustine wished to express this: that a thing is called "true" when it is that which it is called and said to be. Thus, gold is "true" when it is gold and <margin>The Good is convertible with being.</margin> nothing other than gold. This is what he meant by "the true is that which is"; those who do not notice this falsely accuse the definition. 

Similarly, a thing is also "Good," because whatever exists is good insofar as it exists. <margin>He disputes against Olympiodorus.</margin> In my opinion, Olympiodorus <note>Olympiodorus the Younger (c. 495–570), a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the Good is superior to Being because we can desire not to exist (to escape suffering), but we always desire the Good.</note> is far mistaken in believing he can prove that "good" and "being" are different things because we desire the "good" simply, but we do not desire "to be" simply, but "to be well." He argues that it can happen that if things go badly for us, we desire not to be. 

Leaving aside for now whether those who are in a bad and wretched state can seek "not to be" by a right and natural desire, he fails to notice that just as "being" is manifold, so goodness is manifold. For first, there is the natural being of things, such as "to be a man" for a man, "to be a lion" for a lion, or "to be a stone" for a stone; a natural goodness follows this being indivisibly. There are other types of being which can be called accidental <term>accidental: Latin *adventitia*, qualities like health or wisdom that are added to a person's basic existence</term>, such as for a man to be wise, to be beautiful, or to be healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are "beings" distinct from basic humanity, so they are different "goods." For the goodness of humanity, by which a man is a man, is one thing; the goodness of wisdom, by which he does not just emerge as a man, but as a wise man, is another. Just as these are different beings, so they are called different goods. 

Therefore, just as all things seek the "good," so all things seek "to be." First, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, since this is the foundation of the goodnesses that follow. All those other goods come to it in such a way that they cannot stand without it. For how will he be happy who does not exist at all? However, that goodness which they obtain when they first exist is not enough for them; rather, they desire to attain the others as well, which complete and adorn that first one. Just as we truly say that other goods are sought by them beyond that first goodness, so we can truly say that other ways of being are desired by them beyond the first "being"—because it is one thing "to be happy" and another "to be a man." And even if someone allows that one might not wish "to be" if they are not "happy," it does not follow (as Olympiodorus thinks) that the "good" is one thing and "being" another. Rather, it follows that the "being of a man" is one thing and "happiness" is another—and likewise, the goodness of a man is one thing, and the goodness of happiness is another.

<summary>Pico argues for the "convertibility" of the transcendentals, asserting that Being, One, True, and Good are identical in reality but different in conceptual definition. He specifically refutes the Neoplatonist Olympiodorus, arguing that the desire for "well-being" (happiness) over "simple being" does not prove they are distinct categories, but rather reflects different levels of existence.</summary>

...of which he does not want the first (that is, the primary one) unless it also possesses the second. The things we said above show that "the false" and "nothing" are the same. <margin>Evil and nothing are convertible <note>In medieval logic, "convertible" means two terms refer to the same reality; wherever you find one, you find the other.</note>.</margin> If we say that "evil" and "nothing" differ, both philosophers and theologians will protest. This refutes the madness of those who proposed two principles—one for good things and another for evil things—as if there were some creative principle of evil.

But to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it; nor can we take away from any thing its own natural unity without it ceasing to remain in its integrity. For the whole is not merely its parts, but that "one thing" which results from the parts, as **Aristotle** teaches in the eighth book of *First Philosophy*. <margin>Aristotle</margin> <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, which was historically called "First Philosophy."</note> Therefore, if you divide a whole into parts, the parts indeed remain, but the whole that was divided does not remain; it ceases to exist in reality <term>in reality: Latin *actu*, meaning "actually" or "in act"</term> and exists only in potential, just like the parts. Those parts, which were previously "in potential," then begin to exist "in reality"—for while they were in the whole, they did not have their own actual unity, which they only obtain for the first time when they subsist by themselves, separated from the whole.

### Chapter nine, in which he declares how those four properties are in God.

Let us examine again how these properties exist in God, in whom they do not exist by reference to a cause, for he has none. For he himself is the cause of all things and is from no one. <margin>e</margin> They can be considered in God in two ways: either insofar as he is the cause of others (a distinction that does not apply to created things in the present context, since God can exist without being a cause), or as he is in himself. 

Other things cannot exist unless they are from him. Therefore, we primarily conceive of God as the totality of all action, the fullness of being itself. An understanding follows from this: that he is "One" in such a way that even an opposite cannot be conceived. See how far they wander who invent multiple first principles or multiple gods! 

Immediately, it is also "most true": for what can he have that appears to be and yet is not, since he is Being itself? It certainly follows that he is also Truth itself, and he will also be Goodness itself. <margin>The three conditions of the Good according to Plato.</margin> For there are three conditions of the "Good," as **Plato** writes in the *Philebus*: it must be **perfect**, **sufficient**, and **desirable**. <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *Philebus* (20d), where he defines the criteria for the Good.</note> That which we conceive of in this way will be perfect because nothing will be lacking to him who is all things; it will be sufficient because to those who possess it, nothing will be lacking, for in it they will find all things.

<summary>Pico explains that Being, Truth, Goodness, and Unity are reflections of God's power, wisdom, love, and simplicity. He refutes Manichaean dualism by arguing that evil is merely a "nothingness" or a lack of being, and introduces Chapter 9 to describe how these attributes exist perfectly in God.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Having established that God is the supreme example of Being, Unity, Truth, and Goodness, Pico now explores how these four concepts relate to the Pythagorean "Tetrad" and transitions from abstract philosophy to practical morality.</meta>

...must be sought: because from Him and in Him are all things which can be sought for any reason. God is, therefore, the fullest **entity** <term>entity: the state of being a real, distinct thing</term>, the most indivisible unity, the most solid truth, and the most blessed goodness. This, if I am not mistaken, is that **Tetraktys** <note>original: *τετρακτυσ*. We even swear by those things which are holy, firm, and divine; and what is firmer, holier, or more divine than these? 

But if we assign these four names to God insofar as He is the **cause** <term>cause: the source or reason why something exists</term> of things, the entire order is reversed. For first, He will be "One," because He is understood first in Himself before He is understood as a Cause. Second, He will be "Good." Third, "True." Fourth, "Being." For since the cause which is called the **End** <term>End: the "final cause," or the goal for which a thing is made</term> is prior to the one that is the **Model** <term>Model: the "exemplary cause," or the blueprint in the mind of the creator</term>, and the Model is prior to the **Maker** <term>Maker: the "efficient cause," or the one who physically builds it</term>: for first we desire to have a place where we may be protected from the injury of storms; then we conceive the **Idea** <note>original: *ideam*. In Platonic thought, this is the perfect mental pattern of a thing.</note> of a house in our mind; and finally, we form that house out of matter by building it externally. Therefore, if—as we defined in the previous chapter—**Goodness** relates to the Final Cause, **Truth** to the Exemplary Cause, and **Being** to the Efficient Cause, then God, as Cause, will possess the character of Goodness first, then Truth, and finally Being. We touch upon these things briefly here, for they are otherwise pregnant with many great questions.

### Chapter Ten
### In which he turns the whole dispute toward the instruction of life and the improvement of character.

But let us take care lest we dispute for the sake of others rather than ourselves, and lest while searching into the highest things, we live in a lowly—that is, unworthy—condition. <margin>Note.</margin> It has been granted to us by heaven that we are able to track the very reasons of celestial things. We must, however, meditate assiduously on this: that our mind, to which even divine things are accessible, cannot be from mortal seed, nor can it be happy anywhere except in the possession of divine things. The more the mind raises and kindles itself toward the divine, setting aside the care for earthly things while it travels here like a stranger, the closer it draws to happiness. 

This present discussion seems to warn us above all that, if we wish to be happy, we should imitate God—the most blessed of all—by possessing unity, truth, and goodness within ourselves. <margin>Ambition disturbs the peace of unity.</margin> **Ambition** <margin>Ambition.</margin> disturbs the peace of **Unity**; it snatches the soul away from itself and drags and tears it into different directions as if it were a mangled thing. Who will not lose the splendor and light of **Truth** in the mud and darkness of **Pleasures**? <margin>The splendor of truth is obscured by pleasures.</margin> Most thieving **Cupidity**—that is, **Avarice**—steals **Goodness** from us. <margin>Cupidity takes away goodness.</margin> For it is the peculiar trait of goodness to communicate to others the good things you possess. Therefore, when **Plato** asked why God created the world, he answered himself by saying: "He was good." 

These are those three: the pride of life, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, which—as **John** <margin>John.</margin> writes—are from the world and are not from the Father, who is Unity itself, Truth itself, and Goodness itself. Let us flee from here, therefore—that is, from the world that is set in malice—and let us fly to the Father, where there is unifying peace, truest light, and the best pleasure. But who will give us wings so that we may fly there? The **Love** of those things which are above. What will take them away? The **Lust** for things upon the earth, which if we follow...

### FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONY OF FAENZA AGAINST THE LITTLE BOOK ON BEING AND THE ONE.

<margin>First objection.</margin> If any little book deserves to be titled *On Being and the One*, it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of being and the one. However, in this little work which recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several matters are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. Indeed, the main purpose of the author is to dispute whether, according to Plato, "being" and "the one" mutually follow each other, or whether, as the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the followers of Plato’s Academy, who often argued that the "One" was a higher principle than "Being."</note> think, the "one" is more common than "being." But this is not to treat of being and the one in themselves, but rather the mutual "conversion" <term>conversion: a logical term meaning that two terms are interchangeable in scope</term> of being and the one; and not even in an absolute sense, but only according to Plato. For even if some philosopher were to discuss only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not therefore be "disputing about the soul" in a general sense, but a treatise would be held specifically on the soul's immortality.

<margin>Second objection.</margin> Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics believe that God, according to Plato, is not truly and properly "being"; at which I, for my part, wonder greatly. For if he means all Academics or Platonists, as his phrasing seems to signify (otherwise he would not pronounce absolutely that "the Academics" feel this), it perhaps does not lack for falsehood. For **Themistius** <margin>Themistius.</margin> <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a statesman and philosopher who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle.</note>, an author of no small renown among the Platonists, testifies that the "Idea" which is the principle of things is, in Plato's opinion, truly and properly "being" and "the one." Indeed, most or all Platonists do not think the "Idea" is one thing and God the creator another.

<margin>Third objection.</margin> Continuing, he [Pico] says: "If it can be defended in any way that, according to Plato, the 'one' is more common than 'being,' it should be judged thus: those words," he says, "which in the Latin tongue are called 'concrete nouns'—such as white, shining, being—signify something external, by whose presence the things receive the name of the word." For indeed, whiteness is one thing, a white thing another; man is one thing, humanity another. Therefore, that will be called "being" in which the "to-be" <note>original: "esse". This refers to the act of existing.</note> is one thing and that which subsists is another. God, therefore, who is Being itself, cannot be considered "a being," but "the One," because he contains and encloses all things. But does not this kind of defense hold together poorly with itself? For...

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA<- <note>Antonio Faventino (Antonio da Faenza) was a Franciscan theologian and contemporary of Pico who provided a detailed critique of Pico's attempt to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note>

We interpret the free judgment of friends as hatred or grumpiness, but flattery as love and natural goodness. Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised even when unworthy, rather than being corrected when we deserve it, we are always laughed at and never deserve praise. 

See how much we err. For almost every praise is always useless, and often even harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Reproof is certainly always useful; if it is just, it leads to knowledge; if less just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. <meta>Continuity: Pico della Mirandola continues his response to critics regarding his work "On Being and the One." I do not doubt it. Finally, you contend that the divided is not the negation of the one, nor the false the negation of the true, nor evil the negation of the good. <margin>Solution to the fifth objection</margin> Indeed, regarding the oppositions of these things, I know that the controversy among great authors is not an easy one, and for that reason, I ended the book in which these matters were treated in passing with this closing statement. All of these things we touch upon briefly here; otherwise, they are the destiny of many and great questions. However, the things you object to do not move me at all to doubt that the opinion I followed is less probable or true.

You say that a Chimera <note>original: "chimeram" — In Renaissance logic, the Chimera (a mythical beast composed of different animals) was a standard example of an "impossible object" or a concept that exists in the mind but cannot exist in reality because its parts are contradictory.</note> is neither one nor divided. I, however, say that the chimera which we conceive in the mind does not exist precisely because the parts from which we understand it to be composed are divided in the nature of things, rather than united. And just as that thing "is not" if the parts from which it would be constituted are divided, so too that thing not only "is not" but cannot even exist if its parts are neither united nor able to be united by the force of nature. For this reason, we say a chimera not only does not exist, but we believe it cannot even be brought into existence, for no other reason than that it is not credible that the beasts from which we fashion it could ever come together into a single animal composition. 

Again, you insist that because the diameter [of a square] is incommensurable <term>incommensurable: a mathematical term referring to the fact that the diagonal and the side of a square cannot be measured by the same unit; Pico is using this to argue that some truths seem "divided" or paradoxical</term>, it is neither one nor divided. You are mistaken, in my opinion. For by the same reasoning that it is false, it is necessarily divided within itself. For a thing is detected as false to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. And what else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within oneself? Therefore, every truth is "one," because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every falsehood is "divided," because it fights with itself and is not coherent with itself. 

Many have believed that the false is the negation of the true <margin>Solution to the sixth objection</margin>, a fact which is certainly not hidden from you. Nor do the arguments you bring stand in the way. For as I said, we call that "false" which is not what it seems to be: just as "false gold" is that which appears to be gold, but nonetheless is not gold. However, although false gold is not only "not gold" but is also "something other" than gold, it happens to be something else besides gold only insofar as it is false; it is false because it is not the gold it appears to be. Therefore, it is false gold because it does not match the "Idea" of gold; but because it matches the Idea of brass or silver, it is not entirely false. It is only "false gold," just as it is not entirely "non-being" <term>non ens: a thing that has no existence whatsoever</term>; for although it is not this specific thing which is gold, it is nevertheless something else: say, brass, lead, or silver. 

But that which corresponds to no Idea at all <margin>What absolute falsehood is</margin> is entirely and absolutely false, just as it is also entirely "non-being"—such as the thing we call a chimera. See, therefore, how they proceed in a parallel course: non-being, the Divided, and the False; and how a chimera can properly be called "false," and every false thing can deservedly be called "divided."

Thomas.</margin>—this is also what Albertus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a prolific philosopher and the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> teaches when explaining Aristotle's *Categories*, and what your favorite Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). All of these things, I believe, have long been very well known to you.

### Response to the Second Objections.
#### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANTONIO CITTADINO.

Since my previous letter was far too brief, or certainly more obscure, in solving your questions concerning that little book I recently published, *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente et uno"</note>; for you repeat those same questions and doubt the same things about them. I will not deny that in my first letters certain things were omitted and received no response, lest I waste words on trivial matters; some things were treated briefly by me, as I believed matters should rather be indicated to a man of philosophy than explained in detail. Now, since you demand this of me, we shall pursue even the smallest details. Through each chapter of your questions, I will bid you remember those things we wrote before, and I will rouse you where it is necessary to a deeper understanding of them. Furthermore, since you have not yet touched the Platonic commentaries, nor—due to your lack of the Greek language—the Greek Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle’s philosophy. This, moreover, is what bothers you first: for what reason the Platonists place God *above* Being? For if God, as you say, truly *is*, then certainly He is truly and properly *being*, and is so called; just as someone who sits is truly called "sitting" because he sits. You add that if, insofar as He is an Idea, He is "being," then much more insofar as He is God will He be (and be called) "being." <margin>He reviews those things about which he [Cittadino] doubts again.</margin> Even if all Platonists do not concede that the "Idea" and "God" are the same thing, you say it is enough to oppose me if even a single author like Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–387 AD), a philosopher and statesman who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> did not say what I have attributed to the Platonists in common. <margin>Themistius</margin> 

Likewise, you cannot understand how I say God is called "the One," since by this name we signify not *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is. For if He is "One," you say, because He is uniquely all things, why should He not also be called "Being," since for the "One," to "be" is all that He is? For He is not called "One" because He alone is one. Therefore, He could equally be called "Being," even if He were not "Being" alone. These are the first things from which you cannot extricate yourself; but in a few words and just as...

Do you not see what is being said? That by the name of "The One," we do not indicate *what* God is, but rather *how* He is that which He is? <meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his philosophical theses against the critiques of Antonio Cittadino. That a falsehood is a falsehood in such a way is not false, but true; therefore it is not <margin>[Another solution]</margin> divided but one. You add that I am speaking falsely when I say that what is false contains a contradiction. Because there are many things that are false which, by the power of nature or man, could be true. 

But consider this: everything that is false, for as long as it is false, contains a contradiction. But just as some things are so false that they could become true, others are so false that they can never be true. So there are some things so contradictory and warring with themselves that they can never return to friendship and concord. Others hate each other in such a way that they can nevertheless return to favor. <margin>[Example]</margin> This will be made manifest by an example: for a man to be a lion is always false, because it always contains a contradiction; and just as it can never be reduced to unity, so it can never be reduced to truth. But for me to sit <note>Pico is discussing "contingent" truths—statements that are not inherently true or false until applied to a specific moment.</note> is neither true nor false. If, however, you add that "I am sitting while I am standing," immediately, just as you introduce falsehood, you also introduce a contradiction. For "me sitting while I stand" includes a contradiction; and as soon as it ceases to be false—for instance, when I begin to sit—at that same moment it returns <margin>[Another solution]</margin> from division to unity. 

Furthermore, the objections you raise regarding the opposition of the true and the false have already been resolved in the previous letter. For you say: "if the true is that which seems to be what it is, and the false is that which seems to be what it is not." Since there is no contradiction between "seeming to be what is" and "seeming to be what is not," <margin>[Another solution]</margin> falsehood would not be the negation of truth. But I do not define the nature of falsehood as residing in "seeming to be something that is not." Rather, I want its nature to consist in this: <margin>[Note]</margin> that it *is* not that which it is said to be. For "false gold" is false precisely because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of the false is concerned, it happens to either seem to be or actually be something other than gold. 

As for your claim that I have not resolved your argument by which you prove that good and evil are contraries, I will speak frankly: I did not think a solution was needed where there was no knot <note>original: "nodus," a common term in Scholastic logic for a difficult problem or entanglement in an argument.</note> to untie. The argument is of this sort: Good is to be sought. Evil is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, good and evil are contraries. Indeed, your reasoning seems so effective and of such great strength to me that it would prove to be contraries not only good and evil—about which someone might perhaps doubt—but even *being* and *non-being*, which everyone knows are contradictories <term>Contradictories: In logic, these are terms where one is the direct negation of the other (A and Not-A). Contraries (like black and white) are opposites that allow for a middle ground (like grey).</term>, to be contraries. For we would gather this: being is to be sought; non-being is to be avoided; seeking and avoiding are contrary motions; therefore, being and non-being are contraries. Either you must grant me that being and non-being are contraries, or I will not grant you that good and evil are <margin>[Another solution]</margin> contraries. 

But you will say another reason must be resolved. For "non-being" is not a genus <term>Genus: A general category in logic under which specific species are grouped.</term>. How then is evil "nothing," when Aristotle <margin>[Aristotle]</margin> says in the *Categories* <note>original: "predicamentis," referring to Aristotle's work *Categoriae*.</note> that good and evil are the genera of contraries? All the interpreters of Aristotle are full of solutions to this question, to whom I had referred you in my previous letter, lest I entangle both myself and you <margin>[Simplicius]</margin> in superfluous labor. To omit the fact that it does not displease Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), an influential Neoplatonist commentator who attempted to harmonize Plato and Aristotle.</note> that Aristotle spoke there according to the custom of the Pythagoreans—who establish two orders of things, one contained under "the good" and the other under "the evil"—certainly he [Aristotle] often uses examples in his logical commentaries based on the opinions of others rather than his own. I respond with what you could also have read in Simplicius: that good and evil are said to be the genera of contraries because one of the contraries always possesses the character of evil and deficiency; as...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic rebuttal of Antonio Cittadino. Having previously discussed the logic of falsehood and contradiction, Pico now addresses the metaphysical status of "evil," arguing against his opponent’s claim that good and evil are "contraries" (opposing forces that both exist) and insisting instead that evil is a "privation" (a lack of existence).</meta>

...black if compared to white and bitter if compared to sweet: For in this way all contraries are reduced to good and evil. Insofar as every defect has the nature of evil, which is why in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Latin: *physicae auscultationis*, referring to Aristotle's *Physics*.</note> it is said that contraries are always compared to each other according to the nature of the "better" and the "worse." But if evil is "nothing," it cannot be the contrary of good, since by nature both contraries must be *something*. And this is exactly what Thomas confirms there by the authority of Simplicius. See how far you wander astray: you believe that an opinion is confirmed by the testimony of Simplicius which Thomas actually refutes using Simplicius’s own testimony. Perhaps you would not have fallen into this error if you had ever actually read the book of Simplicius himself, in which no mention is ever made of a contrary opposition between good and evil. 

But if you should object to me by citing ophthalmia <note>A general historical term for inflammation of the eye.</note> or sickness—in which Thomas seems to acknowledge a contrariety—<margin>Note.</margin> I bid you to look more carefully into his words. For he does not say that these things *are* contraries, but that since they are privations <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a 'privation' is not a thing itself, but the absence of a quality that should be there—like blindness being the absence of sight.</note>, they are nevertheless sometimes *called* contraries. If you pay attention, you will see why he wishes this to be done: because evil itself is entirely ignorant of the properties of a "contrary." For he concedes that these things can, in a certain way, obtain the name of a "contrary" only insofar as they do not possess the nature of evil completely, but retain something of the goodness which they have not yet lost. 

Therefore, they are in some way "contraries" only because they are in some way not entirely evil. But if I were to present death or blindness to you, <margin>He argues against his opponent.</margin> I would ask whether these are "true evils" according to the opinion of Thomas, and again, whether they oppose each other by that type of contrariety which you describe. I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these things are evil, Thomas—in that very passage from which you bring forth testimony for your side—contends with great assertion that they can in no way be contraries in that sense of contrariety which you bring forward. By what logic do you affirm this as Thomas's opinion? You ought to have realized that what is conceded regarding certain "imperfect" evils—because of the mixture of goodness they still retain—must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself.

But I pray you, repeat the words of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" by medieval and Renaissance scholars.</note> more diligently, for they bear judgment against you, which is shown in this way <margin>h</margin>. Thomas openly says that "being" and "something" are said in two ways. One way is that which has the nature of some category; the other way is that which answers the question "is it?" Now, regarding God, one answers the question "Is there a God?" [by saying He is], and that response is not a lie; therefore, God is "being." If we must proceed further, let us say this without departing at all from Thomas: that to the question "is it?" the response is rightly given that "it is being." Therefore, that which truly and properly responds to the question of whether a thing truly and properly exists, is truly and properly "being." For just as that which simply *is* relates to that which simply *is*, so that which truly and properly *is* relates to that which truly and properly *is*. When asking if God truly and properly exists, one reasonably answers "God [is]"; therefore, He is truly and properly "being."

Furthermore, Thomas calls "something" <margin>i</margin> and "being" according to the first way that which answers the question "what is it?" But to one asking "what is it" that preserves and moves the world, and "what is it" that raises the dead, one reasonably answers "God." Therefore, in both the first and second way, God is "being" and "something" <margin>k</margin>. Furthermore, would you dare, following Thomas, to deny that God is "the Good" and "the One"? Since, therefore, the Good, Being, and the One are mutually convertible <term>Convertibility: The scholastic doctrine that Being, One, True, and Good are different names for the same reality viewed from different perspectives.</term>, how can it be said or imagined, according to Thomas, that God is not "being"?

But you, if I am not mistaken, seem to argue from these words in this manner: "Being" in one way signifies the nature of the ten categories; however, God is in no category, as Thomas himself testifies; therefore, God is neither "being" nor "essence." But you ought to have noticed (permit me <margin>l</margin> to joke) if the argument is effective...

[Marginal notes on the right:]

<margin>f</margin> You must admit this to be true unless you abandon your Thomas.

<margin>g</margin> These are the things which, if you had seen them before, perhaps you would not have erred.

<margin>h</margin> I marvel that you always insist on these same things; has it not been said a thousand times already that "being" can be understood such that it is said of God—namely, when it signifies that which *is*—but again, it can be understood such that it is not said of Him, as when it signifies "essence" as something distinct from "existence." <note>A classic Thomist distinction: in creatures, essence and existence are different; in God, they are identical.</note>

<margin>i</margin> See how much you are deceived. Evil, according to Thomas, is not such that we can answer "something" or "being" to one asking what it is; and yet, to one asking "what is sin?" we can answer that it is "an evil."

<margin>k</margin> When "being" is converted with "the good," it is not understood in the same way as when it is denied of God by Thomas.

<margin>l</margin> You joke against yourself; for this very thing is what I am saying, and I have emphasized it a hundred times: you either do not wish to or cannot understand that in the first way God is not "being," although in the second way—namely, when "being" is the answer to the question "is it?"—He is called "being." For I was saying that God cannot be called "being" in *every* way, but in *some* way, even according to Thomas. It is permitted, however, to argue thus, fellow father: God is not "being" in the first way, therefore in some way He is not "being."

Whence, adding an example, Thomas says: "and thus evil is, just as blindness is"; that is, "and thus evil is being, just as blindness is being." For in Thomas's writing, there is no difference in the word whether it is said "it is" or "it is being." 

But as for what he joins next, "that to be 'something' does not only signify etc.," he does not intend that one asking "what is the moon?" or "what is thunder?" is answered reasonably if it is said "it is being" or "something," as you seem to have thought—for such a solution is <margin>o You say nothing. For responding to the second argument, he says: 

"As it says in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, 'being' is said in two ways. One way according as it signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided into the ten categories; and in this way it is interchangeable with 'thing' <note>Original: *res*.</note>. And in this way no privation is being, whence neither is evil. In the other way, 'being' is said which signifies the truth of a proposition which consists in composition, the sign of which is this word 'is' <note>Original: *est*.</note>. And this is the 'being' that answers the question 'is it?' And thus we say blindness is in the eye, or any other privation. And in this way even evil is called being."

Since, therefore, there is no contradiction in "appearing to be what is" and "appearing to be what is not," I was proving that "falsehood" is not the simple negation of "truth" if your definition held firm.

...to conclude that God does not exist and gold does exist—for there is no contradiction in this, as theologians, philosophers, and logicians themselves aptly admit that it can be imagined. For it can be imagined that gold exists, yet God does not—nor even a First Cause or a First Being. For those who believe there are infinite^h worlds <margin>h Those who say these things and claim gold exists speak in contradictions and are ignorant of their own words.</margin>, or that the heavens are infinite in number, or other similar things, do not for that reason deny that the gold which is seen with the eyes and handled with the hands exists. Furthermore, whether it is a contradiction or not, the reasoning is not yet resolved. For I say this:^i <margin>i If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold and gold would not be gold; for the impossible gives birth to the impossible. <note>original: "impossibile enim impossibile parit." This is a logical principle stating that from a false or impossible premise, anything (including further impossibilities) can follow.</note></margin> If God did not exist and gold were present, gold would be gold, but it would not be **true** [gold]. Therefore, the formal definition of "truth" is not "to be that which it is." Just as it would not be a formal definition of man if I said: "If God did not exist and man were a rational animal," then man would not be nothing for that reason. For nothing can be deprived of its own definition, nor can a definition apply to anyone to whom the defined name cannot be fitted. 

<margin>g You love gold too much, my friend, when you grant it so much that you believe it could exist even if God does not.</margin>

Furthermore, you cannot deny that gold is "gold" by its nature before it fits the divine Idea;^k <margin>k This relation is not accidental (distinct from the gold), but substantial; see Henry of Ghent <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293) was a major scholastic philosopher who argued that things have a "being of essence" even apart from their actual existence, through their relationship to God's intellect.</note> regarding this, unless you feel it beneath you.</margin> for the absolute is prior to the relative. Therefore, even if gold is gold, it cannot be **true** unless, beyond the nature of gold, a certain likeness is added by which it corresponds to its own exemplar <note>The "exemplar" is the perfect blueprint or "Idea" of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note>—whether that likeness is one thing and gold another, or not; this is a separate question of its own. 

Furthermore, you seem to define "being" in this way: "Being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say that the definition by Augustine <note>Saint Augustine defined truth as "that which is" (Verum est id quod est) in his work *Soliloquies*.</note> must be completed in this way: "Truth is that which is itself," lest, if we said only "that which is,"^l <margin>l Everything that is, is this very thing which it is. Therefore every "being" is "true," and everything "true" is a "being." But they have different definitions.</margin> the definition of "truth" and "being" would seem to be the same. If, therefore, the definition of being is "that which is," by that same reasoning by which being is that which it is, it is also itself; therefore, by the same reasoning that something is a "being," it must also be "true"—which is completely false. 

Furthermore, if "truth" is "that which is," then blindness will be true, and death, and falsehood, and altogether non-being; for blindness is blindness, and death is death, and falsehood is falsehood, and even non-being is non-being. Any of these would be "true" without any intellect thinking of them at all. But if any of these is true, it must be "one." <meta>Continuity: Pico della Mirandola continues his rigorous critique of his opponent’s logic.
