[Left Margin - Bottom]

<margin>l It is one thing for blindness to be "true" <note>In a philosophical sense, "true" can mean "real" or "existing."</note> and another for blindness to be "truly blindness." Therefore, you labor in vain with many words to show that blindness is not "true."</margin>

[Left Margin - Bottom]

<margin>m That "I am sitting" is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting. To say that "I am sitting" is neither true nor false means that this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood for itself intrinsically, as necessary propositions <term>Necessary propositions are statements that must be true by their very nature (e.g., 2+2=4), unlike "contingent" ones like sitting, which change based on circumstances.</term> do. But since it can be true when I am indeed sitting, and false when I am not, it is indeterminate in itself. But without doubt, my dear friend <note>original: "mi compater" — literally "my co-father," a term of familiarity used between colleagues or peers.</note>, you must have an abundance of paper and leisure to stoop to discussing things known even to schoolboys.</margin>

[Main Body]

...to be false is not false, but is true, because it is not divided but one. But on the contrary, everything that is "one" is "good," and in the same way, "true." Blindness, however, is not only bad, but according to what you write, it is entirely bad and tastes of nothing good. It is the same with death. For you seem to call the nature of blindness and death an absolute nature of evil, unmixed with any good. Therefore, neither of these is "true," nor are they "one," especially when the soul is not thinking of them.

Furthermore, that which is true corresponds to an "Idea" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect, eternal archetypes of things. Evil or "privations" like blindness were often thought to have no such divine Idea.</note>; however, blindness and death have no Idea. Furthermore, if God did not exist, nor anything else capable of intelligence, nonetheless non-being would be non-being, and nothing would be nothing. For it must be either something or nothing. Certainly, it would not be "something," as is evident; therefore, it would be "nothing" and "non-being." It would therefore be exactly what it is now and what it would be then. If, therefore, "true" means "to be that which it is," then non-being and nothing would be "true." This cannot happen, for no Idea would correspond to them. Therefore, the formal definition of "truth" is not "to be that which it is."

Moreover, you attempt to defend what you previously said: that any falsehood contains a contradiction. You say that every falsehood contains a contradiction so long as it is false. You also add these words: "But for me to sit is neither true nor false." 

But if you were to add "I am sitting" while I am actually standing, you immediately bring in a contradiction along with the falsehood. For "I sit while I stand" contains a contradiction, and it is primarily defined as being false. Thus, when I begin to sit, that statement returns from a state of division to a state of unity. 

But I ask you to see if you are consistent with yourself. For you think "true" and "false" are opposed, not as opposites <note>original: "contraria" — things that can both be false at once (like "black" and "white").</note>, but as affirmation and negation. How then can a middle ground be found between them? Unless there is a middle ground between "yes" and "no." Furthermore, every statement is either true or false, unless you deny the first principle <term>The Law of the Excluded Middle: a fundamental rule of logic stating that for any proposition, either that proposition is true or its negation is true.</term>, which is that in any contradiction, one part must be true and the other false. How, then, is "your sitting" neither true nor false?

Indeed, I do not see by what reason you could defend this unless you abolish all philosophy and every concept of opposites. Furthermore, if every falsehood contains a contradiction so long as it is false, then the statement "God does not exist"—which is false—[would also contain a contradiction]...

...it will involve a contradiction so long as God exists in the nature of things.

If, therefore, God did not exist, it would not even be false that God does not exist, nor would it be a contradiction. If, then, "false" is the negation of the "true"—as you posit—it would be true that God does not exist if God were not to exist <insert>n</insert> <margin>n Good and evil are in actual things; falsehood and truth are in the mind. Therefore, a true proposition can signify an evil thing, even though the proposition itself, insofar as it is true, is to that extent good; and the thing itself, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent false. It is one thing to say, "That Judas sins is true," and another to say, "The sin of Judas is true."</margin>. Furthermore, in your previous letter you said that every falsehood is "divided" from itself <note>In scholastic logic, "divided" refers to a lack of internal unity or self-identity. If, therefore, not every falsehood involves a contradiction simply and absolutely, but only so long as it is false, then not every falsehood is simply and absolutely divided. For that to which the nature and cause of being does not belong, neither does that belong to it which is part of its definition; and if "being one" does not belong to it simply, neither does the other [division]. Therefore, not every falsehood is simply divided—which is a point that cannot be granted. For every falsehood is simply and absolutely false; therefore, it is simply and absolutely non-being. For both, as you posit, are interchangeable; by the same logic, it is simply "divided," if "divided" and "non-being" coincide <insert>o</insert> <margin>o "Every falsehood is divided," as we said in the previous book; but not every falsehood is equally false, and therefore not every falsehood is not equally "divided," as we said to you in the letters. For those things that are necessarily false and always false are not the same as those that are not necessarily false nor always false. Therefore, the former and the latter do not have the same character of division. See whether there is anything in these points that I should have been afraid to say, or that you can refute.</margin>.

Furthermore, every truth is simply "one"; therefore, every falsehood is simply "divided." For one is the negation of the other. Furthermore, if I show that every falsehood is absolutely divided, what reason was there for you not to dare to declare that every falsehood is indeed simply and absolutely divided, but only then when there is opposition? 

We demonstrate the "division" of falsehood in this way: "Socrates is sitting" <note>This is a classic example in logic: a statement that is true only if the physical reality matches the words.</note> is false [if he is standing]. However, "Socrates sitting" is not "Socrates sitting" [as a truth], therefore it is divided from itself. For if "Socrates sitting" is "Socrates sitting," and "sitting Socrates" is "sitting Socrates"—for both are linked—and if "sitting Socrates" is "sitting Socrates," then "sitting Socrates" is "Socrates"; therefore, by a simple conversion, "Socrates is sitting Socrates," therefore he is sitting, therefore he sits: which is false. <note>Pico is using a "reductio ad absurdum" argument here. He is showing that if you follow his opponent's logic to the letter, you end up proving things that are obviously false, like the fact that a standing man is sitting.</note>

By the same logic, I will prove that a chimera <note>A mythological beast; in logic, it represents an "impossible object" that can be thought of but cannot exist.</note> is not a chimera, nor that "a chimera to be" is "to be a chimera." For if a chimera exists, a chimera is an animal. For we understand a "chimera" to be an animal consisting of a goat and a stag <note>original: "ex hyrco... et ceruo." Usually described as lion/goat/serpent, but Pico uses "stag" here.</note>, or something of the sort. But if it is an animal, it can live and die: which we agree is impossible, since we posit that a chimera cannot be produced by nature, just as a "golden mountain" cannot be generated; furthermore...

<summary>Pico uses logical "wordplay" and the example of the chimera to argue that falsehood is a form of internal division and non-being. He mocks his opponent's rigid definitions by showing they lead to the "absurd" conclusion that if God didn't exist, His non-existence would be a "good" thing.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the debate between Pico della Mirandola and his correspondent regarding the nature of truth, being, and the definition of "the good." Pico is currently critiquing the opponent's logical consistency and their failure to resolve his previous arguments.</meta>

[Left Column]

p You should have explained how you have now solved it; for it is no marvel not to untie what has no knot <note>original: "non habet nodum" — a metaphorical way of saying a problem has no inherent difficulty or "snag."</note>. In this, therefore, you admit to me that you solved something in which there was no difficulty.

q Why are they not similar, since just as these have no force, neither do those? For if "the good," by the very reason it is good, is to be sought, and "the evil" to be avoided, and since fleeing and seeking are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove; yet for the proving of this, you have never spoken a single word, nor do you now. Rightly, then, I said there was no "knot" in your argument, because you assume what you are supposed to prove, but you in no way prove it, nor even attempt to prove it.

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

If a chimera <note>A mythological creature used in scholastic logic to represent something that cannot exist in reality.</note> is an animal, then some animal is a chimera; but no animal is a chimera. For every animal exists, and lives, and is simply a being and a "something." For that which does not exist is not an animal—unless used equivocally <note>original: "equivoce" — meaning the word is being used in a different sense than its proper definition.</note>. Therefore, a chimera is not a chimera. By the same reasoning, "to be a chimera" is not "to be a chimera." For if "to be generated" is "to be moved," then generation is motion. If, therefore, generation is not motion, then "to be generated" is not "to be moved." By equal reasoning, if "to be a chimera" is "to be a chimera," then a chimera is a chimera. For both are linked together; but a chimera is not a chimera, as has already been proven; therefore, "to be a chimera" is not "to be a chimera."

Furthermore, no chimera is a chimera; therefore it is true that "no chimera is a chimera"; thus it is false that "some chimera is a chimera." By the same reasoning, it will be shown that a vacuum is not a vacuum, because it does not exist; nor is blindness blindness, provided that nothing is blind. Nevertheless, "non-being" is always "non-being." For "not to be" is "non-being," and this is true, just as it is both true and necessary that a chimera "is not." Why then was it necessary to fear that you might be refuted if you had stated simply and absolutely that every falsehood is divided within itself? Therefore, there was no need to flee to a contradiction. 

Next, you candidly confess that my argument—by which I proved that good and evil are contraries to one another—has not been solved; but you say it remains unsolved because no "knot" was present in it. A clever excuse, by Hercules! <note>A common Renaissance exclamation of surprise or emphasis.</note> But it is a wonder that, if no knot was present, how you were able to "untie" the knot. The words of my argument, which were written to you in my first letters, are as follows: "The good, by the very nature through which it is good, is to be sought; the evil, however, is to be avoided. But to seek and to flee are mutually contrary, just as 'to gather' and 'to separate' are. Therefore, good and evil will be mutually contrary"—which Boethius also asserts in the *Categories* <note>original: "in praedicamentis." This refers to Aristotle's work on the basic classifications of being, which Boethius translated and which served as a foundation for medieval logic.</note>. 

But you respond thus: "to be" is to be desired; "not to be" is to be avoided; yet it does not follow that they are contraries. But I ask: does it seem to you that your argument is at all similar to mine? You might say it this way: "to be," by the reason through which it is "to be," is to be desired (that is, the proper nature of being is something to be desired), while "not to be," by its proper nature, is something to be avoided; therefore they are contraries. You will then have constructed your argument beautifully! For by this form we demonstrate that hot and cold, or white and black, are contraries. For the nature of the hot is to separate heterogeneous things <note>A standard Aristotelian definition: heat separates different substances, while cold brings them together.</note>, but of the cold, to gather them; so too the nature of white is to disperse the sight, but of black, to concentrate it.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola employs classical logic and Aristotelian definitions to argue that good and evil are true contraries, mocking his opponent's inability to deconstruct his proof. He uses the examples of chimeras and vacuums to explore how truth and falsehood apply to non-existent things.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique of his opponent’s logic regarding the nature of the Good. When you responded to my argument in person, you said that the proper definition <term>ratio: the essential nature or formal definition of a concept</term> of "the good" is not that it is something to be sought out <note>original: "expetendum" — that which is desirable or worthy of being sought as an end.</note>. This point is conceded by all philosophers, especially the Latins; even Aristotle, in the first book of the *Ethics*, says that they defined "the good" correctly when they said it is that which all things desire <note>original: "quod omnia appetunt" — a fundamental Aristotelian principle that defines "good" through its role as the object of desire or purpose.</note>. To those listening, your denial of this seemed strange.

And when the definition of "the good" was requested from you, you said that a thing is good for this reason: because it is ordered toward God. But I immediately interjected: "Therefore, God is not good." It was then said that God is not "good" [in the sense of a thing possessing goodness] but is rather *Goodness* itself <note>Pico is highlighting a scholastic distinction: created things are "good" by participating in God, but God cannot "participate" in Himself; He is the essence itself.</note>. I then added: therefore, there is some middle ground between good and evil, for God is not good, yet neither is He evil.

How, then, can it be defended that evil is merely the negation of the good, if a middle ground <note>original: "medietas"</note> is admitted? Furthermore, if evil is the negation of the good, then "evil" and "not-good" are one and the same; for there is only one unique negation for any one thing. It follows, therefore, that if a thing is "not good," it is "evil." Thus, it is gathered from the negation...

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on whether God can be called "good" if He is Goodness itself, Pico now addresses his opponent's interpretation of St. Thomas Aquinas regarding the nature of evil. The debate focuses on whether evil is a "contrary" to good (like black vs. white) or a "privation" (like blindness vs. sight).</meta>

Why, to explain yourself, you must pervert **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian whose definitions of good and evil were central to this debate.</note> entirely and devise for yourself I know not what "semi-full privations." You deny that Thomas there takes "privation" and "habit" <term>habitus: a state of being or the possession of a quality, the opposite of privation</term> in their proper sense when he says that evil is the privative opposite of good. Does he not, through the whole question, prove that **evil is nothing**? And for that reason, does he not conclude that evil is a **privation** and not a **contrary**? Or is a privation that is nothing a "semi-full privation"? We likewise say that **blindness** has the perfect character of evil, not because it takes away every good—for who does not know this?—but because it takes away that entire good of which it is called the privation; that is, it takes away **sight**, which inflammation of the eye <note>original: "ophthalmia"</note> does not do. These, therefore, are the evils which **Thomas** insists can in no way be called contraries, since they possess the true nature of evil. Therefore, he who says that evil, according to the opinion of **Thomas**, is a contrary, errs no less than that close friend of mine <note>original: "compater meus"</note> who used to say that **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> said things which he did not say.

<column-break/>

...and that good and evil are contraries to each other. But be careful that you do not err, you who have poorly weighed my mind or my words. The words written to you in the second letter are read in this sequence: "I say again and I approve that **good** and **evil** are contraries to each other; not indeed in the same way as white and black or hot and cold, which are all true qualities, but in the same way as **healthy** and **sick**, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar such things." Nor does **Blessed Thomas** deny this; rather, that most eminent man, in the first question *On Evil* <note>original: "de malo"</note> regarding the solution to the second argument, shows how good and evil—even if they oppose each other through the opposition of privation and habit—are nevertheless usually counted among the **contraries**. He confirms this by the authority of **Simplicius**. Remember, therefore, that **Aristotle**, in the *Categories* <term>praedicamentis: Aristotle's treatise on the classification of things and their relationships</term>, assigns four types of opposition. Also, remember that **Aristotle** separates these types from one another. Again, note that **healthy** and **sick** are numbered by him among the contraries. For this reason, therefore, by which **Aristotle** separates contraries from the other types of opposition, I affirmed that good and evil are contraries, and I confess it again. And this is what **Saint Thomas** said in the first question *On Evil*: that good and evil are contraries in the way that health and sickness are, but not in the way that **sight** and **blindness** are.

But you say: "I will show you that evil is entirely ignorant of the properties of a contrary." For although a certain evil might seem contrary to a certain good—such as "sick" to "healthy" because it leaves some good behind—I will nevertheless offer a certain evil that can in no way be opposed to a good by this reasoning: for example, **death** and **blindness**. But truly, I do not know if they are similar. For if you have read the words of **Thomas** more accurately, it can be clearly understood how neither blindness, nor death, nor any other evil can take away good entirely. Blindness indeed takes away sight, and entirely so; but it does not take away life or the body. Death indeed takes away life completely, but neither the body nor prime matter <term>materia prima: in Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical things</term>. What deceived you, therefore, is this: that blindness is the privation of sight, and death the privation of life; but it should not have been believed on that account that they are the privation of *the* Good <note>Pico distinguishes between the privation of a specific faculty (like sight) and the total absence of "the Good" as a transcendental category.</note>. Does **Thomas** not openly confess to you and say that evil is contrary to good just as "sick" is to "healthy," and not as "blindness" is to "sight"? Therefore, blindness, insofar as it is evil, leaves behind something of the good upon which it rests; but insofar as it is blindness, it permits nothing of sight to exist. What **Thomas** says—that good and evil are opposed like habit and privation—is most true; for in that place, **Thomas** properly calls them "habits"...

<summary>Pico argues against his opponent's interpretation of Thomas Aquinas, distinguishing between evil as a "privation" (like blindness) and evil as a "contrary" (like sickness). He asserts that even profound evils like death or blindness do not remove all "good" from a being, as they leave the underlying matter or body intact.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page where Pico criticized his opponent for misinterpreting St. Thomas Aquinas on the nature of evil, he now moves into a technical discussion of Aristotle's "Categories" and uses the logical example of a "Chimera" to demonstrate the absurdity of his opponent's position that evil is a positive "something" rather than a lack of being.</meta>

He calls them privations not only because they are perfect states <term>habitus: a stable quality or "possession" of a trait, the opposite of privation</term> or perfect privations—which are the only ones **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE). The text refers to his work "Categories," often called the "Praedicamenta" in Latin scholarship.</note> includes in the *Categories*—but more broadly, he pronounces all things to be opposed as state and privation where one is the state and the other is the privation, whether it be complete or semi-full. What I have said is confirmed by the authority of **Simplicius** <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 CE), a Neoplatonist whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Renaissance philosophers.</note>. 

**Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says that Simplicius, in his commentary on the *Categories*, states that those things are properly called "contraries" <note>Contraries are opposites that are both "something" (like black and white), whereas privation is the absence of something (like blindness as the absence of sight).</note> in which each side is a distinct "something." **Aristotle**, however, numbers "healthy" and "sick" among the contraries, but not "blind" and "seeing." 

<margin>Why then do you not frankly admit that you have erred? For it is no wonder; you are only human.</margin> Therefore, **Simplicius**, who interprets **Aristotle**, must provide the reason why Aristotle did not count all privations among the contraries. He cannot explain the reason except in the way already stated. Blessed **Thomas**, therefore, who says that Simplicius claims those things are properly called contraries of which each is "something else," must conclude from Simplicius (while explaining why "healthy" and "sick" are numbered among contraries but not "blind" and "seeing") that he is expounding Aristotle. Whether this is true or false is a matter of no importance that needs to be pursued here.

However, since in your last letters you seem to call "evil" (which you consider a negation of good) that which is *entirely* evil—and in the same way you ask about the "false" as a division of the "true" and the "one"—I wish to ask you: 

<margin>In that Chimera of yours, you are inventing many other chimeras <note>Here "chimeras" refers to mental delusions or false logical constructs.</note>.</margin> Do you think a **Chimera** <note>In logic, a "Chimera" is a classic example of an "impossible object"—it can be thought of, but it cannot exist in reality.</note> is "entirely non-being"? If you deny it, you must contradict yourself, for you previously said the Chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I shall proceed in this manner: "non-being" and "evil" are equivalents; therefore, "entirely non-being" and "entirely evil" are equivalents. But the Chimera is "entirely non-being," therefore it is also "entirely evil"—which cannot be the case. 

<margin>If a Chimera can be created by God, this power is not *in* the Chimera, but in God.</margin> For a Chimera does not imply a contradiction in its definition <note>Pico argues that while a Chimera doesn't exist, the concept of it isn't logically impossible like a "square circle."</note>; therefore, it *can* be created by **God**. What can be created can *exist*; and to exist <note>original: "esse"</note> is "good." Therefore, what can be created can be "good." Since the potential for goodness is itself good, the Chimera is not entirely evil. 

<margin>The notion that I form of a Chimera is good insofar as it is "something" in the mind; but the Chimera itself, insofar as it is "nothing," is likewise not good.</margin> Furthermore, the Chimera can be understood both by **God** and by us; it can therefore exist in our mind and soul. Therefore, it can exist in some way; and whatever can exist in any way participates in goodness. Thus, the Chimera is not entirely evil. 

Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is something to be avoided; but nothing can be avoided or shunned unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by **God**, who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, that every evil can be known in some way. But knowledge is a kind of good; therefore, to be "knowable" is also a good. For the potential for good is itself a kind of good. Moreover, **Aristotle**...

<margin>According to you, good and evil are contraries, and each of the contraries is something positive. Therefore, that which is good is something positive, and that which is evil is something positive. And according to you, "non-being" is good; therefore, according to you, "non-being" is something positive. And since "something" and "being" are interchangeable <note>original: "convertuntur," a logical term meaning the terms are co-extensive</note>, then according to you, "non-being" is a "positive being." See where your Chimera has led us!</margin>

<meta>Continuity: These objections continue the metaphysical debate from the previous page regarding the nature of God, existence, and essence. The discussion moves from the definition of "evil" as a privation to the technical distinction between "being" (esse) and "essence" (essentia), particularly how these terms apply to God versus created objects like stones or concepts like "Ideas."</meta>

### Fourth Objections.

It was not said that God is not a being <note>original: "ens"</note> because "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note> in God stands for His essence; 
but rather because His being is not different from His essence—which is a vastly different thing. Otherwise, the very being of a stone—which for the stone serves as its essence—would be neither a being nor good. For the being of a stone is not its essence <note>in the sense of a definition</note>, but is itself to it: both its own being and its own essence.

If, in the case of negations and privations <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should normally be present, such as blindness being the privation of sight</term>, one cannot ask "what" they are: 
Since they exist, it is not enough for formulating the question "What is it?" simply to know that the thing about which one asks exists. Rather, one must know more: both that it is, and that it is *something*. Therefore, to a person asking "What is it?", the answer "a being" or "something" is given ridiculously and irrationally—whether "being" is understood in the first sense <note>as a noun, a thing that exists</note> or the second <note>as a verb, the act of existing</note>. For if one asks what "sin" is, the question concerns the word <note>the name of the lack</note> rather than a physical thing.

If something is a being, then according to your position, it is a being because its "being" is a different thing from its essence. You say humanity is one thing, but a human is another; whiteness or "the white" is one thing, but a white object is another. Therefore, if an Idea <note>referring to the Platonic "Ideas" or archetypes</note> is a being, it will be a being only because the being of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. However, the Idea is God; therefore, the being of the Idea would be something different from God. <note>The author is pointing out a logical trap: if God is the ultimate "Idea," and Ideas must have a separate existence from their essence to be called "beings," then God would be divided against Himself, which contradicts the doctrine of Divine Simplicity.</note>

<summary>This page presents a series of logical objections regarding the relationship between "being" and "essence," arguing that in God, these two must be identical. It also explores the difficulty of defining "non-things" like sin or privation using standard categories of existence.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, essence vs existence, divine simplicity, privation, Platonic Ideas, scholastic logic</keywords>

--- Page 242 ---
<meta>Continuity: The author continues to address specific objections regarding the nature of being, evil as a privation, and the philosophical status of impossible things like the Chimera, while defending his interpretation of Aristotle against rivals who favor Simplicius over Boethius.</meta>

If indeed every human is, simply and absolutely, capable of laughter <note>original: "risibilis"; in medieval logic, the ability to laugh was considered a "proprium," a characteristic unique to and universal among humans</note>, there is no need to add a condition to restrict it by saying: "every human is capable of laughter as long as they are human." Nor should such a restriction be added because not all false things are equally divided, or even false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good.

How it may be concluded that good and evil are contraries will be easily established if you pursue the matter: if "seeking" and "fleeing" are contraries, the reasoning behind contrary motions will be sufficiently understood by you.

Why do you wonder if I say that the Latin scholars do not deny Aristotle—whom Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a Greek Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle</note> denies, but Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), the "Last of the Romans," whose translations of Aristotle were the foundation of medieval logic</note> does not? Is it because I do not imitate Boethius, or because I exalt the "barbarians" <note>likely a reference to the Scholastic philosophers, often called barbarians by Renaissance Humanists for their dry Latin style</note>? You call me a "strange man"; indeed, I might call you "wonderful," since while I imitate Boethius and set Simplicius aside for the moment, you think I despise Boethius and follow the barbarians.

If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that a Chimera <note>a mythical creature used in logic to represent an impossible object or a "non-being"</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if it were understood in what sense I called good and evil contraries—which you either do not yet wish to, or cannot, understand—you would have proved nothing regarding the Chimera.

You are greatly amazed that I call certain things "semi-full privations" <term>privation: the lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term> and you prove they are nothing in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore it is not a semi-full privation." But I, following your own argument, would say: sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing, and thus it is not a semi-full privation. Yet sickness is a certain kind of privation; therefore it is not a semi-full privation of either health or some good, but rather a full and perfect one. But that cannot happen; therefore, privations are "semi-full" or imperfect, such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, and blindness. Blindness is a perfect privation of sight, but an imperfect privation of the good; for it does not take away the whole good that exists in the one who cannot see.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves something of the good behind, then the Chimera—which is entirely a non-being and evil—also retains something of the good. But if it preserves something of the good, it is not entirely evil, nor entirely a non-being. Even if the power by which it could be created and exist is in God, and the notion by which it can be understood is in the mind, it does not prevent the Chimera from being "good" in potentiality and a "being." For it is the power of God, and the Chimera is one thing or another depending on the reasoning used. Nor do we deny that the Antichrist is good in potentiality, whose power to exist is partly in matter and partly in the heavens and in man. Furthermore, how is the Chimera—if all thought and the power of God are excluded for a moment—entirely a non-being and evil? For in order to be a "non-being," it certainly cannot be "evil." For evil is a privation that exists in a subject, which must necessarily participate in goodness; otherwise, it could not be a subject. For that which is entirely non-existent cannot act as a subject for anything.

You have not yet disproven what I said, and you confirm it with the authority of Simplicius, except that Simplicius does not say what you claim. But there was no reason to boast of this; for I did not say that Aristotle felt that everything that exists does so either through itself <note>original: "per se"</note> or by happenstance <note>original: "per accidens"</note>, nor did I falsely ascribe anything to the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> on that account.

Although every privation is a kind of negation, it is not yet established that there is not one kind of opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and habit <note>original: "habitus," meaning a possessed quality or state of being</note>. Nor is it necessary, if evil is the privation of good, for "evil" and "not-good" to be interchangeable.

Your defense, by which you wish to protect the idea that "God is not God"... I [submit] neither to the truth nor to the Blessed [Thomas]...

<meta>Continuity: The author concludes a complex logical debate regarding the nature of God, definitions, and the infinite, before transitioning into a new section mourning the death of his uncle, the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</meta>

I consider this to be consistent with Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose works on the "Divine Names" argued that God transcends all human descriptions</note>, for the blessed Dionysius never denied that God is God. But as the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian</note> interprets it, no name can fully explain the nature of God; nor does he think affirmations are applied to God for any other reason. You, however, say that if the name of God has a description, it has the nature of a definition <note>original: "rationem"; in logic, this refers to the defining essence or formal reason of a thing</note> rather than a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: let *a* be the definition of the name, and let it be said in this way: "God is *a*." For the definition of anything is predicated of that of which it is the definition. Therefore, by a simple conversion, "*a* is God." Thus, "God is God." 

Likewise, you say that when one asks whether God is something other than God or not, one must establish what is conceived by the name "God." Whatever else is given, you say, "I will call it God." For He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not a solution of this kind contradict itself? For if you admit a proposition of this sort—which is "God is above that which can be conceived"—do you not clearly affirm something about God? Let it be so, then, and let the definition of the name be "that which is entirely above all that can be conceived," and the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above everything that can be conceived; therefore, God cannot be conceived." Otherwise, the same thing would be above itself. Therefore, He could neither be loved nor worshipped <note>This is a classic theological problem: if God is completely beyond human understanding (unknowable), how can humans fulfill the religious obligations to love and worship Him?</note>.

Finally, you seem to think the power of gold <note>The author is likely critiquing an alchemical or metaphysical argument where the existence of a perfect material (gold) is used to prove the existence of a perfect Being (God)</note> is so great that, whether we wish it or not, by necessity of fact or mind, it drags God along with it in this manner: "Gold exists. Therefore, Being itself exists. Therefore, God exists." Likewise: "God is. Therefore, the infinite is. The infinite is; therefore, it is nothing." If you say "infinite being is," then "the finite is not," as if you were arguing: "the finite is not; therefore, it is nothing." Then: "the infinite is; therefore, the infinite is not," for you say the infinite destroys itself. Truly, I think if anyone had written such arguments to Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a famous Averroist professor at the University of Padua known for his strict Aristotelianism</note>, he would have answered nothing. Nor shall I oppose anything against them, lest I seem to doubt a matter that appears clearer to me than light. If you prove your "polishing" <note>original: "politionem"; likely a reference to a specific philosophical treatise or a rhetorical refinement</note> by these arguments, I truly fear you may lose your gold.

If you wish, reply something to these objections, my best friend, so that we may now bring an end to this disputation; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I have turned to these things out of hatred or ill-will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my Mirandolan companion <note>A reference to his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>. If you should ever care to put me to the test, you will find that I have told no lie.

->**GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO THE DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHER ANTONIO FAVENTINO, GREETINGS.**<-

<margin>q</margin>Although, upon the death of my uncle Giovanni Pico, all the vigor of my studies and the hope that had been almost entirely placed in him withered away—since I hoped while he lived that the study of philosophy might be recalled to its ancient purity, yet enriched with great resources; and that the Christian faith, having eliminated all errors and repelled heresies, might be fortified with the strongest towers against its enemies—nonetheless, I was not so dismayed in spirit that I did not labor with all my might to ensure that all the vigils and begun nighttime labors which flowed from that man (who is to be admired in literature everywhere) should not utterly perish. On this account, for myself and for our people...

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous philosophical debate, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola now describes his efforts to recover and publish his late uncle Giovanni Pico's papers, specifically his work "On Being and Unity."</meta>

Consulting for the benefit of all men, I hurried to Florence by the greatest journeys I could manage. I gave my effort by whatever means I could so that whatever had been noted by him—even if unpolished and unexamined—might be permitted into our possession. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if his wills <note>original: "tabule," referring to legal tablets or a testament</note> were not yet opened, nor the heir known, his chests were nonetheless such that we could inspect and turn over all his commentaries. We saw in those scattered paper volumes the man’s incredible diligence: universal reading, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Yet, in the arrangement of his writings, there was a lack of care not to be praised; everything was dissected and scattered here and there. But more on these things elsewhere.

While we were unfolding these works with diligent care, his little treatise *On Being and Unity*—published about four years before his death—fell into my hands, together with three letters written to him by you <note>likely addressed to Antonio Civitella or another contemporary critic/correspondent</note> concerning it, and their replies. Because of the novelty of the subject, I did not just read them, but drank them in, almost (as they say) devoured them. (For I had heard a rumor that this had been done, but I did not have sufficient proof of what weight they carried). I began to think and debate with myself whether I should give that work to the printers publicly alongside the other works I had collected and decided to publish, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more advisable if it went out into public attacked by obstacles <note>original: "offensaculis," meaning objections or points of stumbling</note> on one side and fortified by defenses on the other. After a long discussion of the matter, the latter opinion finally settled in my mind.

Indeed, meeting learned men, it would seem to carry marks of infamy if he did not only fear his accusers, but also did not dare to summon them to judgment, as if he had little faith in his conscience. Likewise, it seemed opportune that it should go accompanied by responses, as if with witnesses to defend the cause of innocence. I did not doubt that our plan would be praised by upright men, since I would have had to allow my deceased uncle—a man who surely deserved the most from me—to be defrauded of some part of his famous teaching by not publishing such a booklet, or, if it went out alone, to leave an opportunity for the most wicked vituperations to always accuse him by not calling into the forum those things which had been composed on both sides in many letters of objection and rebuttal. 

But when some letters were presented by our friend Christopher Saxolus <note>Christoforo Saxolo da Parma, a physician and humanist associate of the Pico family</note>, both a citizen and a physician, which signaled to us that you had fashioned a fourth letter on that business which lacked a response (as you said), the matter was called back into doubt. Again made of a wavering opinion, I thought the judgment must be weighed more exactly, since the last accuser pressed the case and there was no one to act as a defender. Then there came to my mind a certain title of undertaking a defense, though it was not easy to see how I might turn to protect that silence. On one hand, the man’s modesty and his kindness toward everyone moved my mind, as did the skill and sharpness of his genius in untying and washing away difficult knots and inexplicable riddles <note>original: "scyrpis," literally "bulrushes," referencing the proverb "nodum in scirpo quaerere" (to look for a knot in a bulrush), used for over-complicating simple things or solving complex puzzles</note> on the spot; so that I naturally judged that your last letter had not been safely delivered. I thought it was likely that he had replied. If, however, your letters were delivered to a faithful messenger, perhaps they perished on the journey through the negligence of the couriers (as often happens) or some other accident. It finally occurred to me in the untying of your prior questions that you had complained that you were often repeating the same things and often doubting the same things; for which reason I immediately ran through the headings of your entire controversy to see if anything could be found in the first responses which showed that the fourth letter was already sufficiently answered in part...

<meta>Continuity: Gianfrancesco Pico continues his address to Antonio Civitella, explaining his decision to publish his late uncle Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of the treatise "On Being and Unity" against Antonio’s previous criticisms.</meta>

This was done even before it was written. The matter succeeded according to my wish, and I found so much relevant to the proposed task that even if I have not responded with as many words as possible to the objections of your last letter, you may recognize through God’s help that the knots of those very objections are largely untied by the solutions to your prior questions. I have added many points sought from great authors as testimony; I would like you to believe I have done this for no other reason than to counter the judgments of the unrefined, those unacquainted with philosophy, and the malevolent. For if the rumor had reached them that you had sent a fourth letter to my uncle regarding that controversy to which he had not responded, they would have immediately passed judgment—as is the custom of babblers and the envious—that he had not cared to write back for some reason other than a just one. 

Otherwise, my dear Antonio, I would have very willingly omitted this undertaken work from the beginning. This was partly so that I would not seem to be initiated into controversies—which I abhor, even if I were pleading a most righteous case—and partly so that I might not deviate from the true path of philosophy. I began to travel this path after my time with horses and arms <note>Gianfrancesco refers to the traditional nobleman's life of military service before turning to scholarly pursuits.</note> (though I had smelled some "little flowers of literature" since I was a boy), under the guidance of my uncle Giovanni Pico and our friend Giovanni Mainardi. For the knowledge of nature should not lead us to sweat over literary struggles, but to recognize the Creator of nature Himself. Philosophical meditations should, of their own accord, always invite us to investigate the deepest meanings of the divine words. This is the goal of all studies; here the way to heaven is revealed to us, provided we do not cultivate these studies for the sake of capturing glory for ourselves, but so that we can both know our God more easily and love Him more fervently. Thus, we may more readily pursue what He commanded to be done and flee what He taught to be avoided. 

Here is the cause of this burden I have taken up and of my dealings with you, now explained; it is a most just cause, as you see. Therefore, I thought it right to offer these writings to you with a calm mind—and indeed, I thought I might use these works as messengers to confirm the goodwill already auspiciously established between me and you at Ferrara. For when I arrived there recently, you deigned to visit me with great kindness. During our talk about literature and my uncle’s death and his many works that were begun but not finished, you showed that you were so far from being offended by my opinion on responding to you and solving your arguments that you even praised what I was going to do. But now, approaching the business itself, let us first apply our hands to dissolving the first objection. It is of this sort:

<margin>The First Objection.</margin> It is not said that God is not "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> because "to be" in God stands for His essence; rather, it is because "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note> is not different from His essence, which is a far different thing. Otherwise, the very "being" of a stone (which is its essence) would be neither a being nor good; for the "being" of a stone is not an essence, but is both its own "to be" and its own essence.

<margin>A certain preface.</margin> To which I shall respond very easily. But I will first ask you to remember those things which were written by Pico himself for the sake of this matter, lest he seem to have uttered conflicting words. In that commentary *On Being and Unity* (which he also mentioned in the replies to your objections), he not only approved of Amelius, Iamblichus, Syrianus <note>These were Neoplatonist philosophers who argued that God/The One is "beyond being" and therefore cannot be called a "being" in the same way created things are.</note>, and many Platonists who said God is not "being," but throughout the whole treatise he mainly aimed to show—according to the dogma of both Aristotle and Plato—that God both truly *is* and is properly called <term>Being</term> <note>Giovanni Pico's project was "syncretism": proving that Plato and Aristotle actually agreed on fundamental truths, such as God being the ultimate Being.</note>. But he also showed there is a certain way of speaking which, if followed, would not be absurd.

<meta>Continuity: Gianfrancesco Pico continues his defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, against critics of "On Being and Unity." Having discussed how God relates to the concept of "Being" (ens), he now addresses the logic of inquiry: how we ask whether a thing exists and what it is.</meta>

...to have understood that a question can be formed to which an affirmative and correct answer can be given. First, if you think that a question cannot be correctly formed unless the matter being inquired about is of such a nature that a response can be provided through it, I do not agree with you. 

For it is Aristotle’s <margin>Aristotle</margin> opinion <note>Aristotle discusses this in his "Posterior Analytics," exploring how we can ask about the existence of things that might be fictional.</note> that one can inquire whether a "centaur" <note>A mythical creature, half-man and half-horse, frequently used in logic to illustrate things that have a definition but no physical existence.</note> exists or not; yet a centaur is not the kind of thing that allows the question "is it?" to be answered [affirmatively], since it is a mere fable, a mere figment of the imagination. 

In the same way, I also oppose your view if you believe that the person asking the question must already know the answer. For a person who correctly inquires "what a thing is" <note>original: "quid sit res"</note> does not need to know more—as we have shown—than the fact that the thing exists. Therefore, if someone knows a thing is "something" <term>aliquid; "something," a term used in logic to denote a subject of thought</term>, it is not a ridiculous answer to say it is "something" to a person who does not know and is asking about it. 

However, for those who ask what a thing is, I have not been accustomed to teach them simply that it is either "a being" <term>ens; "a being" or "that which exists"</term> or "something," so that we might provide a more complete answer. For even when they have established that the thing is indeed "something," they would still be searching for what *kind* of being it might be. Therefore, [one must] satisfy not only their explicit request, but also their desire for further investigation...

<meta>Continuity: Gianfrancesco Pico is continuing his technical defense of his uncle Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's treatise "On Being and Unity." He is currently addressing the metaphysical distinction between essence (what a thing is) and existence (that a thing is) in both created things and the divine "Ideas."</meta>

For even if in created things essence differs from being <note>original: "eſſe"; refers to the act of existing</note> in reality, it does not necessarily follow from this <margin>Peripatetics</margin> that whatever can in any way be called "a being" must be composed of essence and "being" (or existence) as if from <margin>Antipater</margin> parts. Therefore, in the case of the Idea <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal archetypes of all created things.</note>—which is the pattern for created things—essence and existence <margin>Posidonius</margin> do not coincide as things distinct in reality. However, we might say there is a "composition" in the Idea when we <margin>Seneca</margin> consider it as the "exemplary cause" of the essence and being (or the being and existence) found in created things. We apply this same sense of composition and distinction even to the simplest things; and we call it "according to reason" <note>original: "secundum rationem"; a conceptual distinction made by the mind rather than a physical split in the object itself.</note> when our intellect has fashioned it. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who famously walked while they taught.</note> very frequently employ this common view, which, as that author says, was repeated by Antipater, mentioned by Posidonius, and discussed in the letters of Seneca. For that reason, in this manner, we can say that an Idea is "composed" of essence and existence according to reason, and we can call it "a being." That is to say, we consider it the pattern for those creatures that are composed of a being and an essence that differ in reality. But we do not place such a composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the pattern for others, but as He is in the innermost sanctuary of His own divinity, enjoying Himself.

Fourth, you say that according to the definition of "denominatives," <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin> "one" is named from "unity." Yet, according to your position, God is called "one" based on a likeness to unity. Therefore, you argue that the predication by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, you think that when we say "God is one," we are signifying not *what* He is, but *how* He is; and since a "mode" or "how" belongs to the category of accidents <note>An "accident" in logic is a quality that can change without destroying the essence of the thing (like hair color), whereas "substance" is the core reality.</note>, the word "one" in God is not substantive. You suggest that perhaps I have not learned the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language, but that is not enough to defend the discipline of the Academics <note>The "Academics" here refers to the Platonic school of thought.</note>. However, the response is easy. For when it is said by the Platonists that the "one" which is predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative, it is correctly asserted. And again, when it is asserted that He is called "one" because He is like unity, this is not inconsistent. Nor can it be said for that reason that the term is not substantive. For even if a name is adapted to something because of a property or likeness to another thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive, provided it is accepted as a substantive name—one that signifies not as an attached quality <note>original: "per modum adiacentis"</note> but as something standing by itself. It is clear enough that the "one" predicated of God is understood not as an inherent quality, but as something standing by itself, so that it needs no proof. You have, therefore, a property from which the name is applied that does not take away its status as a substantive being. For your Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin>—or rather *our* Thomas <note>Refers to Saint Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian.</note>—both in other places and in the first part [of his *Summa Theologiae*], reports that the thing a name is intended to signify differs from the reason why the name was imposed. For example, he explains that this name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is imposed to signify that substance which is so-called, but it is named from a related property, namely, that which "hurts the foot" <note>A common medieval etymological pun: *Lapis* (stone) was thought to come from *laedere pedem* (to hurt the foot).</note>. Hence, in another place, he teaches that it is a custom used by grammarians to write that a name denotes "substance with quality." John Scotus <margin>John Scotus</margin> <note>Duns Scotus, another major medieval philosopher/theologian.</note> affirms this same thing in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*. Therefore, my dear Anthony, when we speak of "one" regarding God, we speak truly and use it as a substantive name, because we both conceive and predicate it in the manner of something "standing" <term>per modum stantis; a logical term for a word that functions as a noun/substance rather than an adjective</term>. Again, when we say it is imposed from a likeness to unity and its properties, we are following the truth.

He also defends the use of the term "One" for God, arguing that even if the word is derived from a "likeness," it functions as a substantive name describing God's core reality, not just a passing attribute.</summary>

<meta>Gianfrancesco continues his point-by-point rebuttal of critics attacking his uncle Giovanni Pico's work "On Being and Unity." The discussion shifts from the metaphysical "Idea" to the specific logical puzzles (sophisms) regarding God's existence as the foundation of all truth and the use of names like "Unity" for the Divine.</meta>

We approach as far as is permitted for us, because we use a suitable term to indicate that deity who is ineffably far above all created things; for He is the principle <note>original: "principium"; the source or beginning</note> of all things that are, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument concerning the mode <note>original: "modo"; the manner or category of existence</note>, which you claim belongs only to the category of accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size.</note>. Specifically, you ask how it is signified in the prediction "God is one" <note>original: "Deus est unus"</note> and whether the term "one" is used substantively when applied to God. <margin>A brief solution from the words of the uncle.</margin> If you consider the source from which the name originates and what it is attributed to denote, you can recognize the solution to your doubt even more briefly from the words of my uncle. He asks: "Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher.</note>, when—as you boast with a loud voice—you have never even read Dionysius or the Platonists?" But you should know that among the Platonists, the pattern of God is Unity; and for Dionysius, God is uniquely all things. No one could rightly desire a more straightforward solution. For when it is said that the pattern <note>original: "Typum"; the archetype or model</note> of God is unity, this refers to likeness and mode; but when it is said that God is uniquely all things, this refers to His substance. It has been asserted that these two are entirely the same. Furthermore, in the Greek language, which he knew well, the abstract can sometimes be signified by the same word as the concrete.

To offer a solution to your fifth doubt, many words are not needed. <margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin> He says: "If God did not exist, and gold were gold, then gold would also not be gold." You add these words: "Therefore, would it be gold? What if the definition of truth stands? It will be a truth corresponding to no Idea." <note>This is a logical "reductio ad absurdum." The argument is that without God as the source of truth, the very concept of "gold" becomes a logical impossibility or a contradiction.</note> Add, I pray, these few things which he said follow from his words, and you will recognize how it will be a truth corresponding to no Idea. What do I mean? That which is impossible. That is, an impossibility gives birth to an impossibility; and therefore, it is no wonder if from your impossible proposition you make whatever you wish follow. For if God did not exist and gold existed, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since from the impossible, the impossible is produced. Not only the dialecticians <note>Logicians who study the art of reasoning.</note> but also the theologians agree with this. For if you ask John of Baconthorpe <margin>John of Baconthorpe.</margin>—the Carmelite—whether it could be that gold exists and God does not, he will respond to you in the first book of his Sentences <note>A commentary on Peter Lombard's "Sentences," the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> that no thing whatsoever, of whatever kind it may be, can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is within the understanding of all things, you may gather whether it can be pronounced—even among novice logicians and beyond all controversy—that it is impossible for gold to exist and God not to exist. But we shall speak of this again at the end of the work, if you later consult the Cardinal of Cambrai <margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai.</margin> <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and philosopher known for his work on logic.</note>. You will hear a man practiced in every philosophy saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that from any impossibility, a contradiction follows.

In the sixth place, you said that if it were neither true nor false that "Socrates is sitting" <margin>Solution to the sixth objection.</margin>—as he had asserted because it was not a necessary truth—you could defend the idea that a negation or affirmation is not true in every case, since in some cases neither one nor the other has a necessary truth. Solving this objection, we respond that this statement—namely, that "Socrates is sitting"—does not, insofar as it depends on itself, necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood. Nor does it follow from this that an affirmation or negation is not true of any given thing. Nevertheless, if you understand it in the way he himself teaches...

<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his response to critics of his uncle Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically focusing on the logical relationship between truth, being, and the location of "good" and "evil" within the soul versus within physical reality.</meta>

<margin>The seventh objection and solution.</margin>

You could also deny that in any case an affirmation or negation is true in such a way that one part is necessarily true. For he says <note>The author refers to Aristotle's discussion on future contingents in *De Interpretatione*.</note> "that I am sitting" is always either true or false, because either I am sitting or I am not sitting. And yet that which is said—"that I am sitting"—is in itself neither true nor false; this means that this proposition does not, by its own nature, determine truth or falsity for itself, as necessary propositions do. But since it can happen that it is true when I am sitting and false when I am not sitting, it is in itself indeterminate toward either state.

Furthermore, you persist against some of his words concerning good and evil, truth and falsehood, which he had proposed would be found in things and in the soul, arguing in this manner: If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For a negation posits <term>posits: places or affirms as fact</term> nothing. How also is a chimera <note>original: "chymera"; a mythological beast made of different animals, frequently used in logic to represent a concept that can be thought of but cannot exist in reality.</note> both in things and in the soul? If it is entirely non-being and false, since you think non-being and evil are mutually convertible <term>convertible: terms that can be used interchangeably in formal logic, such as "Being" and "Good".</term>

But I pray you pay attention and notice that evil and good are declared to be in things for this reason: because they relate to things, just as truth and falsehood relate to the soul. For truth and falsehood are not in things, as <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle writes in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "sexto prime philosophie libro"; referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, but in the mind. Nor does it necessarily follow from this that a thing which is entirely evil is a "true thing." It also follows that if good and evil are in things, they cannot for that reason be opposed contradictorily; because the evil that is pronounced to be in things is not said to be in things so that it is understood as being some *thing*, but because it is attended to and considered regarding the things themselves. That is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections <note>In this period, "evil" was often defined not as a substance, but as a "privation" or lack of a good that should be there (like blindness is a lack of sight).</note> and it results in them being not good. A chimera, however, is not in things because it is entirely non-being and entirely evil; nevertheless, if it could be brought about by nature that it were a thing, it would also be good. But it is "false" insofar as it is nothing existing at all and corresponds to no Idea; nor do we affirm it to be in the soul, except for the notion of the chimera itself, which, as a certain thing, is both nothing and evil.

<margin>The eighth objection with its solution.</margin>

After this, you believed you could prove that blindness is true—which he had denied—and if he had said that blindness *is*, you argued in this manner: if "that blindness is blindness" is true, who would not see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing; for when blindness alone is posited, this—which is "that blindness is blindness"—is posited, and when it is taken away, it is removed. From where it is generated, and through itself, God also is "that God is God," the same in both cases, for both are eternal and the First Truth.

But I, my dear Anthony <note>Likely Antonio Pizzamano, a Venetian scholar and contemporary of the Picos.</note>, contend against this and deny that those things which you affirm are the same. For when one of those which you bring forward is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. For if blindness alone is posited without any intellect considering it, blindness will indeed exist, yet "that blindness is blindness" <note>Gianfrancesco is distinguishing between a thing (or a lack of a thing) and the logical proposition *about* that thing.</note> will not exist. On this account, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also resolved. For Socrates generates through himself, not "that Socrates is Socrates," since complex things <note>original: "complexa"; referring to complex propositions or mental compositions rather than simple substances.</note> are not generated. Even if I were to grant to you that they are the same, we still say that what you were concluding does not follow, on account of the different way of signifying—namely, complexly and incomplexly—since it would be of no sound value...

<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, addressing technical objections regarding logical structures, the nature of truth, and the distinction between a thing itself and the proposition that describes it.</meta>

This argument—that "blindness" and "for blindness to be blindness" are the same—is indeed true, but the former is true because the latter is true; for by the same logic it would follow that if this is a complex term, then the other must be as well. This is absurd, since "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex expression or some kind of enunciation. Therefore, it is one thing for blindness to be true, and another for the truth to be that blindness is blindness.

And although these points might suffice for my uncle’s defense, nevertheless, lest you believe that we lack further ways of protecting and defending his position, and so that a more complete response may reach you, I would have you know that I could have spoken according to the opinion of Gregory of Rimini <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin>. [Gregory] says that even if "blindness" being posited <term>posited: stated as an existing fact or premise</term> were to mean that "blindness is blindness" is also posited, it does not therefore follow necessarily that they are the same thing. For he denies this consequence and many others of this kind: "God exists, therefore for God to be is God." <note>original: "deus est ergo deus ē deū esse." This is a subtle point in Scholastic logic: Gregory of Rimini argued that the existence of a being is not identical to the mental or linguistic proposition stating that existence.</note> The Cardinal of Cambrai also <margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and logic expert.</note> denies all statements in which something is enunciated regarding an infinitive phrase taken significantly <term>significantly: when a word is used to refer to the actual object or reality it represents, rather than just the word itself.</term>; he asserts they are both false and incongruous, as is seen in his first book on the *Sentences*.

You complain next <margin>The ninth objection and the solution to the objection.</margin> that "the false" should not have been pronounced as "divided" under this condition: namely, "so long as it is false." You state this in these words: if every false thing is simply "divided" (which you do not deny has been proven), it shouldn't be doubted that a certain false thing is divided only with this condition: "so long as it is false." For if every man is simply and absolutely "risible" <note>original: "risibilis," meaning "capable of laughter." In logic, this was the standard example of a "proper" attribute of humans—only humans laugh.</note>, one should not need to add a condition to restrict it, saying: "every man is capable of laughter so long as he is a man." Nor, you argue, did the restriction need to be added because not all false things are equally divided or false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all beings are absolutely good. 

But weigh his words carefully, for through them you will be able to cast aside every doubt. He says: "Every false thing is divided, yet it is not false equally as it is false, because it would not be divided equally since those things are not equal falsehoods which are not necessarily and always false." And those things which are always and necessarily false are [distinguished from them]. Therefore, Antoni, that phrase "so long as" was rightly added because those things are not always and necessarily false which, even if currently false, can become true and united either by the work of nature or of an artist <note>The "artist" here refers to any human agent or "maker" who changes the state of things in the world.</note>—which you also admitted in your second objections. Truly, however, as long as they are divided, they remain false; whereas those things are always false which can never return into friendship <note>A poetic logical term for "agreement" or "composition" where terms fit together truthfully.</note>, as is seen abundantly in the response to the second objections. 

Nor does the similarity you draw between "beings" and "the capacity for laughter" help your case at all. For beings are always and absolutely good. Although they are not equally good and some participate in the nature of goodness more than others, they are nonetheless always and necessarily good; for insofar as they are beings, to that extent they are good, nor can they become non-beings and non-good unless they are reduced to nothing. But a "falsehood" or a "division" that exists in a complexion <term>complexion: the joining of a subject and a predicate to form a sentence.</term> can easily be changed from "divided and false" to "united and true." Therefore the comparison does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless divided insofar as they are false, un-united, and untrue. Add to this that this objection ought to have disturbed us very little; for who would doubt that a man (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) can be described as "being capable of laughter so long as he is a man"? Would learned men really disapprove of the phrase: "a man is capable of laughter as long as he exists"?

The tenth head of your objections <margin>Solution to the tenth objection</margin> brings nothing else against him except the claim that what you said could have easily been established if the logic of contrary motions had been sufficiently understood by him...

<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his argument from the previous page, where he challenged the notion that the psychological opposition of "seeking" and "fleeing" proves a metaphysical contrariety between good and evil. As that Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> of yours says—who is not only a Latin author but the chief among the Latins—he not only reports this but proves it. To him, we also add others, such as Giles <margin>Egidius</margin> in his second book on the *Sentences* <note>original: "sententiarum." This refers to the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages which scholars like Giles of Rome commented upon.</note> and many others, such as Burley <margin>Burleus</margin> and Esculanus <margin>Esculanus</margin>, who hold the same view. Moreover, John Duns Scotus <margin>Io. Scotus</margin>, in explaining Aristotle’s *Categories*, agrees with our opinion, saying that if the **good** is understood as being interchangeable with **being** <note>In scholastic philosophy, "good" and "being" were considered "transcendentals," meaning they refer to the same reality from different perspectives.</note>, then **evil is nothing**, and thus it is not a contrary to the good. For since both sides of a pair of contraries must, beyond dispute, be something positive, it is necessary that what is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is the character of evil—cannot be declared a contrary.

And although you have denied that evil is nothing, appealing to Thomas [Aquinas], he not only fails to support your opinion but refutes it abundantly. My uncle <note>Gianfrancesco refers to his famous uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> also sufficiently showed this in the margin of his third letter. Nevertheless, we do not think it out of place to touch upon a few points in passing to support my uncle's opinion and to show that not only was Thomas of the mind that evil was "nothing," but that in droves, many illustrious philosophers and theologians have wholeheartedly <note>original: "pedibus manibusque," literally "with feet and hands," a Latin idiom for total agreement or moving with all one's might.</note> descended upon this same view. 

We find Augustine <margin>Augustinus</margin>, when discussing the customs of the Manichaeans, saying that "no nature is evil." A little later, lest there be any ambiguity about what he understood by "nature," he added: "nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own kind." We have seen that Giles of Rome <margin>Egidius</margin>, in his first book of commentaries on the *Sentences*, left it written that evil, insofar as it is evil, is a **pure privation** <note>privation: the absence of a quality or "good" that should naturally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note> and not "something." He argued it can only be called "something" in the same way that "nothing" itself can be called "something"—namely, when both can be referred to by a name. 

In the second book of those same commentaries, he affirms that evil does not have—to use his words—a **quiddity** <term>quiddity: from the Latin "quidditas," meaning the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, and for that reason, the question "What is it?" cannot be answered regarding evil. He says there is nothing else to it than a name. He also interprets Aristotle’s words on the opposition of evil and good according to my uncle's mind, and agrees with the teaching of Simplicius <margin>Simplicius</margin> and other worthy interpreters of Aristotle. He declares that good and evil are not "proper genera" <term>genera: the plural of genus; the broad categories or classes used to organize knowledge</term>, but that other things should more properly be called genera of contraries. This is because one side of a contrary has the character of a positive thing, while the other does not; and no contrary, in and of itself, is "non-being," but rather possesses some nature and existence. 

Gregory of Rimini <margin>Gregorius ariminensis.</margin> testifies to this same thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences*: namely, that evil itself is not any **entity**—to use his own term—but pure privation. This same thing was felt by that man of most piercing intellect, Robert Holcot <margin>Robertus olchot</margin>, in the first question of his commentaries on the second book of theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged this same thing, whom bringing forward now might perhaps cause weariness to me in writing and to you in reading. It will be enough for the present matter to have listed these, especially since it will be necessary to speak of this again when resolving other objections where mention of evil is made. 

But to return to where we digressed: you seem to cite Boethius alone out of all the Latin authors against Simplicius and the other illustrious interpreters. If you deign to count only him among the "Latin expositors"—excluding all others—he will be the only one who will seem to support your opinion. Add to this that even he, if his mind is properly examined, does not protest against our view; he does not weigh this question exactly nor probe it with ultimate judgment, but only declares what Aristotle's words, strictly and narrowly understood, require—a habit that was very familiar to him.
