<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his philosophical discussion on the nature of evil. Having previously defined "privation" as the lack of a specific good, he now moves to distinguish between "particular evil" (a flaw in a real thing) and "absolute evil" (which he argues is total non-existence).</meta>

What is granted regarding certain imperfect evils because of the mixture of goodness they still retain must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself. And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, I will not be reluctant to explain the force of the distinction. 

<margin>Evil is understood in two ways.</margin>

**Evil** can be considered in two ways: first, **absolutely** and under its own proper character as evil—that is, insofar as it is **nothing**—and second, insofar as it is the **privation** of some good—that is, a **particular evil**. Evil understood in this second way leaves behind at least some subject <note>In philosophy, a "subject" is the underlying thing that possesses qualities. For example, in a "blind eye," the eye is the subject that still exists, even though the quality of sight is gone.</note> of goodness. This is not the case for the other kind of evil, which is entirely **non-being** and **nothing**, just as we speak of the **Chimera** <note>original: "chymeram." In Renaissance logic, the Chimera (a mythical creature) was a standard example of an "impossible object"—something that can be thought of but has no reality and cannot exist.</note>, since it does not refer to any subject or **habit** <note>original: "habitum." Here referring to a natural state or possession, like health.</note>. For this reason, it is called "wholly evil" by the absolute and unmixed nature of evil itself. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>

This is the evil—to use the words of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian Neoplatonist whose works on the "Divine Names" argued that evil has no independent existence but is a "lack."</note> in his book *On the Divine Names*—which, because it lacks a subject, exists in no way and nowhere, and is nothing. Indeed, although the Chimera might be called "good in potential" because of the power to produce it which resides in God, it nevertheless cannot be named as either a **being** or a **good**. 

For if this connection—namely, "something is good in potential, therefore it is good"—were valid, I think it would force the author to admit that all things which ought to be created by God do not happen by the force of nature, and even those things that have decayed <note>original: "corrupta sunt." In this context, "corruption" refers to the natural process of a thing breaking down or ceasing to be.</note> are both "something" and "not something." For if, according to him, they were both beings and good by the power of the Creator, then they would necessarily be "something," since "something" and "good" are interchangeable terms and cover the exact same ground. 

That something could not exist in this way, I shall argue as follows: **"Something cannot be made from nothing."** Before a Chimera is created, according to you, it cannot exist unless it is created; therefore, it is created from nothing. Therefore, before it was created from nothing, it was not "something." A Chimera can by no means be called a "being" because of the power to produce itself which exists in God. That power is so far removed that it can be called neither the Chimera nor anything intrinsic to the Chimera; indeed, they differ by an infinite distance.

<margin>Solution to the objections that were contained in the seventeenth place.</margin>
For this reason, my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> most correctly said that negation is a privation only insofar as privation is formally a negation. This is because privation in itself is a negation and a non-being, and it establishes nothing, as **Thomas Aquinas** proves in many places, most notably in his *Treatise on the Four Opposites*. Add, therefore, through the rule of contradictories, that "evil" corresponds to "non-being." Listen to the most celebrated theologian **Anselm**, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his book *On the Fall of the Devil*, uttering these words: "evil is nothing other than not-good," from which it is most firmly concluded that "evil" and "not-good" mutually follow one another.

...that God can truly be called "God." Likewise, according to the opinion of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher whose "negative theology" argued that we can only describe what God is *not*, rather than what He *is*.</note>, He is greater than any name—even this name "God"—just as was held in the book *On Mystical Theology*. He had said in another place that when, through this word "God," you conceive only that which is signified by the name, this word does not function as a **predicate** <note>term: "predicate" (Latin: *praedicatum*). In logic, the part of a sentence that says something about the subject. For example, in "God is good," "good" is the predicate.</note>. Instead, it stands for itself when it is the subject of the inquiry—namely, what can or should be declared about Him—rather than being something declared about another. 

For this reason, this was not unknown to Simonides <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by the Tyrant Hiero of Syracuse to define God, continually asked for more time because the more he thought about it, the more obscure the matter became.</note> when the Tyrant consulted him. When you likewise ask whether, if God cannot be called "God," He is something other than God, I ask you what you conceive by this word "God" that you declare regarding Him. If you conceive nothing, you would not err, because you would be saying nothing. But if you were to conceive something, you would be saying that God is something other than what you conceive; and you would be explaining the concept through this word "God" since He is above everything that can be conceived by us. This is his argument.

I believed it was clear to you from these words that here lies the truest resolution of your doubts on this matter. You, however, contend that Dionysius does not deny that "God is God." <margin>Dionysius</margin> Read, I pray, Dionysius in the final chapter of the book *On Mystical Theology* and his *First Letter to Gaius*, and it will become plain to you that God is greater than any name. Read him also in the second chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and you will understand that this divine man teaches us that the likeness of divine truth transcends all substance and life. No light can express it, and all speech, all mind, and all reason are, without any comparison, inferior to His likeness. 

From these points, I thought you could weigh my uncle's mind: namely, that in a certain way it cannot truly be said "God is God" <note>original: "deus est deus"</note> if the name "God," acting as a predicate, is intended to declare that which we attempt to conceive through the subject. It is not that it cannot be said in *any* way—just as it is said "God is good" or "God is wise." Other predications are also granted, of which the sacred books are full, in which something is stated about God in some manner. Yet, His nature is not explained by them, since He is infinitely distant from those concepts. My uncle taught this clearly enough in the fifth chapter of his book *On Being and the One*. He was not speaking about those words of Dionysius which are cited by Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, as you supposed, but about those cited just above.

Furthermore, John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century theologian.</note> writes in the first book of the *Sentences* of his theology that there are certain things said affirmatively about God which have the power of a "super-excellent negation." For example, if we speak of "darkness" in God, we do not mean literal darkness, but rather that He is "not light"—or rather, we say He is "above light" and "is light" only when we mean the absence of our limited concept of darkness. <margin>Jean Gerson, Chancellor of Paris.</margin> The most learned and devout Chancellor of Paris, Jean Gerson, treating this same opinion, says: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively about God includes some negation." And a little later, he says that for this reason, Dionysius denies that God is a "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> but affirms that He is "above being."

<margin>Giles</margin> Giles of Rome says in his first book on the *Sentences* that God is wise, but not in the way that we understand wisdom. Hence he says this is the reason why Averroes <note>An influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note>, in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, pronounces that these predications we attribute to God are similar to mathematical propositions. In the manner of mathematicians, the things we understand exist in reality, but not in the way we understand them—just as we understand a "line" that exists in physical matter, but we do not understand it *through the reason* of it being in matter. But why should I delay you with many words when I can make you certain of this truth we assert with only a few? Namely, that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different from what we conceive and state.

<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his philosophical defense of his uncle’s views on the nature of God. <margin>Christ
Dionysius</margin>

Jesus Christ himself—the power of God, the wisdom of God, and the Truth, as witnessed in the Gospel of John—says: "God is spirit." <note>John 4:24.</note> Yet Dionysius, in his book *On Mystical Theology*, when speaking of God and contemplating the ineffable Deity, removes many of the predicates that we attribute to Him, asserting that He is not even "spirit" insofar as we are able to know spirit. <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century philosopher whose "negative theology" argued that because God is infinite, human words like "good," "wise," or even "spirit" are inadequate to describe Him.</note> See, therefore, that Dionysius does not want the word "spirit" to be declared of God in the same way that we can understand spirit. Through these final words, he teaches his readers that it is true that God is spirit—so as to agree with the Gospel of Christ—and yet He is not spirit in the way we conceive of spirit. He does this so that we do not believe the nature of God can be truly expressed by us through any name.

Indeed, how great is the authority of Dionysius, and how highly his most sacred doctrines have been praised and celebrated by all the theologians who have attended the schools of Paris! <note>original: "parisiorum Gymnasia." This refers to the University of Paris, the premier center for theological study in the Middle Ages.</note> Although I thought this was not hidden from you, since your uncle, in his responses to your objections, hinted that during your disputation you did not very willingly admit the sayings of Dionysius, I want you to know that he was the most faithful disciple of the Apostle Paul in the faith of Christ. By Paul's help, God willed that he, having left behind the errors of the pagans, should both recognize and follow the truth, and be granted the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. I want you to know that Gregory <note>Likely Pope Gregory the Great.</note> spoke great things of his doctrine; that Pope Martin, in the synod celebrated at Rome against the heretics, did the same; and that Damascene <note>John of Damascus, a major 8th-century theologian.</note> and many others have extolled him with the highest praises. Though his books were hidden for a long time by heretics, so that they were kept from the minds of the faithful,

<margin>Constantine the Philosopher</margin>

there was the testimony of Constantine the Philosopher, who had committed all his books to memory. <note>Constantine the Philosopher, better known as Saint Cyril (the missionary to the Slavs), was famous in the 9th century for his mastery of Dionysian theology.</note> If Dionysius had been held in such regard by the many Fathers who fought great wars against the heretics and enemies of the holy Catholic Church, how much more quickly and easily they would have triumphed over their enemies—a feat they only achieved later with great effort and exhausted labor.

But when you intend to prove that God can be called "God" because of the **reasoning of the name** <note>term: "reasoning of the name" (Latin: *rationis nominis*). In logic, this refers to the definition or essence that a word is intended to signify.</note> which is predicated of the name, I say that you labor in vain, my dear Antonius. For you do not declare anything about God, but only about this name "God." To understand this more clearly, I will explain at length. For I ask you: what do you conceive through 'A', which you designated as the "reason for the name"? If you conceive nothing, you do not err (to use your uncle's words). If you conceive something, I ask again if you conceive it as that about which something can be declared. If you do so in this highest sense, you still do not err, because that 'A' will again take the place of the **subject**, not the **predicate**. <note>term: "subject and predicate". In the sentence "God is good," "God" is the subject and "good" is the predicate. Gianfrancesco argues that any concept we have of God acts as a new subject to be studied, rather than a final description of His nature.</note>

<margin>Apuleius
Plato</margin>

If you were to conceive that which is declared about Him, you would wander far astray, since God Himself is infinitely greater than everything you can conceive. Even the Platonist Apuleius, in his book *On the Doctrines of Plato*, calls Him "unspoken" and "unnamable." The words of Plato himself on this matter were rendered into Latin by Apuleius: "To find God is indeed not easy; to understand Him is impossible." <note>A famous quote from Plato's *Timaeus* (28c).</note> Let us say, therefore, that all affirmations about God are "improper," because whenever we wish not only to say but even to conceive something, He infinitely exceeds it. Furthermore, we are not only held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery, but even in the enjoyment of God itself—by which we are perfectly blessed in heaven—we do not have the faculty to **comprehend** God, but only to **apprehend** Him, to use the words of our theologians. <note>term: "comprehend vs. apprehend". In scholastic theology, to "comprehend" means to know something totally and exhaustively; to "apprehend" means to reach out and touch or know something partially. Even in heaven, humans cannot "exhaust" the infinite nature of God with their minds.</note>

<meta>Gianfrancesco Pico continues his defense against objections regarding the nature of God. Having previously discussed Pseudo-Dionysius, he now addresses the logical problem of how one can love or worship a God who is defined as being beyond human comprehension.</meta>

...it will be forgiven. Furthermore, you believe these following propositions conflict with one another: namely, that **God is above that which can be conceived** and that **something cannot be affirmed about God**. And you say that if this were the definition of the name—"above that which can be conceived"—then your argument would hold weight. 

But this is resolved: for when it is said that "proper" affirmations <note>A "proper" affirmation in scholastic theology is a statement that describes a thing’s essence exactly as it is, without metaphor or limitation.</note> cannot be brought forth concerning God, it is understood that no predicate can be found that represents the nature of God in its entirety. Indeed, this phrase—namely, "above that which can be conceived"—signifies nothing other than that God cannot be [fully] grasped by the mind and that what God is cannot be known. Therefore, these words do not say what God is, but rather that what He is cannot be known. They thus possess the power of negation rather than affirmation. 

But even if I grant you that they are affirmative, your argument will still not hold weight. Otherwise, if we were asked about some unknown thing that someone desired to know—questioning us about its essence—and we responded to the seeker: "It is that which we do not know, which we have not recognized, which we have not yet conceived in the mind, nor are able to conceive," his request would not seem to be satisfied. By perceiving this doctrine, he would not be able to state anything affirmatively about that thing, but only negatively. Unless, perhaps, someone could be found who could disclose to others what that thing was, which—as something utterly unknown to men and beyond the grasp of all thoughts—could not be known or conceived even by himself.

And so both Simonides <margin>Simonides</margin> <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC) was a Greek poet. According to a famous story, when the Tyrant Hiero asked him "What is God?", Simonides asked for a day to deliberate, then two, then four, eventually concluding that the longer he thought, the more obscure the answer became.</note> and the Tyrant who consulted him knew that the name of God represented the greatest possible thing; yet one of them desired to know what God was, and the other denied that he knew. 

Furthermore, you use such a logical connection: "God is above all that can be conceived, therefore God cannot be conceived; otherwise He would be above Himself. Therefore He can neither be loved nor worshipped." 

I respond that God can be conceived in His entirety, just as He is, only by Himself, and by no other intellect. Yet it does not follow from this that He cannot be loved or worshipped. For we conceive the Deity to be so great, endowed with omnipotence, surpassing His creatures in every way with infinite virtue, that we cannot conceive Him except from His effects <note>This is the "argument from effects": we cannot see God's essence directly, but we can know He is powerful or good by looking at the world He created.</note>. And stirred by this wonder and warmed into love for Him, we begin; we conceive the effects, and that He is the supreme good, and we wonder, and worship, and love. For when these things He made are perfectly known—to use the words of Themistius <margin>Themistius.</margin> <note>Themistius was a 4th-century philosopher and rhetorician who wrote famous commentaries on Aristotle.</note>—He turns the minds and faces of all toward the wonder and praise of Himself. 

Likewise, we read those things which have been revealed by God, and being endowed with His grace, we conceive through faith that which we cannot by nature conceive to the full. At the very least, it is necessary that we love Him above all things, so that at last, when the enigma of this flesh is broken <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in an enigma]; but then face to face."</note>, we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the highest joy of the whole man—which is our true happiness. 

Again, for us to love something, it is not necessary that it be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us; it is enough if we know that He exists, or that He is such a being, even if confusedly and obscurely, whether from faith or from His effects. Thus, even a modest preceding knowledge, of whatever sort it may be, is enough for us to love such a thing. For from those things which the soul knows, it learns to love the unknown, as Gregory says <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> also, in the "First of the Second Part" <note>original: "prima secunde." Referring to a specific section (the *Prima Secundae*) of Aquinas's *Summa Theologica*.</note>, proves that something can be perfectly loved even if it is not perfectly known, and proposes the example of God among others.

<summary>Pico argues that although God’s essence is beyond human conception, He can still be known and loved through His worldly effects and through faith. He refutes the idea that "unknowability" prevents worship, citing authorities like Simonides, Themistius, and Thomas Aquinas.</summary>

<margin>Reasons to show the point</margin>
For if the First fails, it is necessary that all those things which proceed from it perish, as is gathered from Aristotle’s eighth book of *Physics* <note>original: "physice auscultationis." This term refers to Aristotle's "Lectures on Nature."</note>. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
God, moreover, according to the testimony of the same philosopher, is the true principle from which all other true things exist; therefore, if God is removed, it is necessary for all true things to perish. But if true things tend toward nothingness, beings likewise are not saved from destruction, since they coincide with an equal scope <note>Pico is using scholastic logic: "Truth" and "Being" are convertible terms. <margin>Aristotle</margin>

<meta>The author, having discussed the upcoming publication of his debate with Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, now reflects on the limits of human knowledge and the virtue of intellectual humility before concluding the correspondence on a note of friendship.</meta>

& let us examine our thoughts with the greatest diligence: we Christians, when the poison of ambition creeps into the heart, which afterwards brings forth a deadly pride. From this it often happens that lovers of this wisdom in which we are daily occupied—swollen and puffed up by fleeting glory—completely neglect that wisdom which is begotten but eternal <note>The author distinguishes between "human wisdom" (secular philosophy/science) and "eternal wisdom" (divine revelation or the Logos).</note>, from which all this flowing and temporary stuff is derived. But let us see, I pray, from what we are lifted up in spirit, or why we esteem ourselves too much: for how small is our knowledge? Since we possess the smallest science of natural things, and those very things which we ignore—how many and how great they are—silently cry out that we profess or think ourselves learned in vain and falsely. Doubtless even a crude man, unpracticed or entirely ignorant of letters, a farmer, could ask many things placed before his sight and eyes about which an otherwise great philosopher would be unable to give a certain explanation. Indeed, in perceiving those very substances utterly separated from sensible matter, how far do we proceed in knowledge? We see them only with the bleary and owl-like eyes of the mind <note>original: "noctuinis mentis oculis." This is a reference to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, suggesting that the human intellect is as dazzled by divine truth as an owl's eyes are by the sun.</note>. But what shall we say of divine things, towards which we direct our sight—almost covered by the thickest clouds—panting and anxious not only to know them, but even to track them down while we are blinking and groping in the dark? Furthermore, have we not received this knowledge of things either from books or from a teacher? What need is there, then, to boast that we have learned the meditations of others, having drunk them in as if from someone telling a story? But it is a history of nature; yet one placed in bitter altercations through diverse studies and agitated by various opinions, and for that reason uncertain: which is revealed most clearly from the very name of "opinion." If we indeed obtain some little bit of knowledge from ourselves, what else is it, I ask, than a certain uncertainty wrapped in a thousand coverings and tangled in a thousand fallacies? I would pursue this business, being incensed against those who magnify these studies more vehemently than is appropriate, had I not treated this subject specifically in a long inquiry and dedicated a special booklet to it. For these reasons, I have decided to turn myself to the unfolding of those books whose propositions are foretold and honored, whose conclusions are gathered in an inexpressible syllogism and render the mind purified (if only we take care of it). But let there now be an end to this literary conflict, and now, to the letter itself. But see how different the effect has been of our controversy compared to others: when a dispute carried on by voice or writing is finished, hatreds and animosities are often practiced between those minds that were at odds; fraudulent wars are plotted, and detractions of honor and reputation gush forth from both sides. You indeed and our Pico were godfathers <note>original: "compatres." In the Renaissance, this term referred to spiritual kinship, such as the bond between a father and a godfather, which was legally and socially significant.</note> before the dispute, bound by this spiritual knot; nonetheless, the former concord of your souls has not been dissolved because of this. I, however, was known to you only by name while your uncle was alive, and you to me; this defense has caused a certain treaty of friendship to be struck between us. Take care that it remains stable while we are alive; and strive by whatever means you can so that, by living rightly and piously, it may persevere eternally after this death which we await. I too shall strive to do the same. In the meantime, do not be loath to experience with what love I pursue you: perhaps I shall provide more abundantly what you requested than I promised at the end of the defense. For there is nothing so difficult that I would not do for the sake of more readily deserving your favor (you, a most serious philosopher indeed). From the Citadel of Mirandola, January 4, 1496.

->### The Argument of Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, etc., regarding the Oration and Letters of his uncle, Giovanni Pico, etc.<-

Accept, reader, these labors of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola as well—works of "lighter care" <note>Gianfrancesco characterizes these works as "lucubrationes levioris curae," meaning minor works or products of "burning the midnight oil" that were not intended to be his uncle's primary philosophical legacy.</note> which perhaps he himself would not have published while living, nor would I have, unless urged by the frequent encouragements of celebrated men. You will first read a most elegant oration <note>This refers to the *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, originally intended to open a great debate in Rome in 1487.</note>, composed indeed with youthful spirit, but often admired by more learned men for its pinnacle of doctrine and eloquence. Do not let it trouble you if many things are seen at its conclusion which were also inserted into the preface of the *Apology* <note>original: "apologiae." Pico’s *Apology* was a legal and theological defense of thirteen of his 900 theses that had been challenged by a papal commission.</note>; since he published that work to the world but kept this one always at home, sharing it with no one except friends. You will see many dogmas of the ancients, previously hidden in riddles and the wrappings of fables, most ingeniously unlocked. You will see that attempt to show—with both strength and oratorical charms—how the "poetic theology" of the ancient sages served as a handmaid to the mysteries of our own theology <note>Pico was a pioneer in syncretism, believing that ancient pagan myths and "poetic theology" contained hidden truths that aligned with Christian revelation.</note>. Having unknotted certain complexities of both, he invites men to literary contests; for during that time, he was most frequent in these contests, which he later left behind as if they were mere playful battles and preludes to weightier studies. He then turned his mind to laboring on those things which I have now released and those I am to release in the future. You will also read several letters (for it would be most laborious to collect them all): some familiar ones written both during his tender youth and his more advanced years; others written after he dedicated his whole heart to God, filled with most holy admonitions. You will find that the former smell most abundantly of learning and eloquence; the latter you will perceive to taste of both sufficiently and, beyond this, to breathe most richly the love of Christ.

->### ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.<-

I have read, Most Reverend Fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdala the Saracen was asked what was to be seen as most admirable on this world-stage, he replied that nothing is more wonderful than man. This opinion is supported by that famous saying of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurii." Pico refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom the *Hermetic Corpus* was attributed.</note>: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." <margin>Hermes</margin> When I considered the reason for these sayings, I was not entirely satisfied by those arguments many people offer regarding the excellence of human nature: that man is the intermediary between creatures, familiar to the higher beings, <margin>The dignity of man</margin> the king of lower things; by the sharpness of his senses, by the inquiry of his reason, and by the light of his intelligence, he is the interpreter of nature; the interval between stable eternity and flowing time; and (as the Persians <margin>Persians</margin> say) the bond of the world, or rather its marriage-hymn; and, according to the testimony of David, "a little lower than the angels." <margin>David</margin> These things are indeed great, but they are not the principal reasons—that is, those which may rightly claim the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate living thing, and consequently worthy of all admiration; and what that condition is which he has received in the order of the universe, which is an object of envy not only to the beasts but to the stars and the minds beyond this world. It is a thing beyond belief and wonderful. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and esteemed a great miracle and a truly admirable living thing. But hear what this condition is, Fathers, and grant me your attention with kindly ears, according to your courtesy.

Now the Father Architect, God, had already built this world-house <note>original: "mundanam domum." Pico uses the metaphor of the universe as a house or temple designed by a divine architect.</note> we see, the most august temple of divinity, by the laws of secret wisdom. He had adorned the super-celestial region with minds <note>This refers to the angelic orders.</note>; He had animated the celestial spheres with eternal souls; He had filled the excremental and dross-filled parts of the lower world with a crowd of living things of every kind. But, when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there be someone to weigh the reason of such a great work, to love its beauty, and to admire its vastness. Therefore, when all things were now finished (as Moses and Timaeus <margin>Moses, Timaeus</margin> <note>Pico references both the Biblical account of creation and Plato’s dialogue on the origin of the universe, the *Timaeus*.</note> testify), He finally thought of producing man. But there was nothing left in the archetypes from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor in His treasures what He might bestow as an inheritance upon a new son, nor in the seats of the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. All places were already full; all things had been distributed among the highest, middle, and lowest orders. But it was not in the Father’s power to fail in His final birth, as if exhausted; it was not the part of His wisdom to have wavered in a necessary matter for lack of counsel. It was not the part of His beneficent love that he who was to praise the divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. At last, the best of craftsmen decreed that he to whom nothing could be given as his own should share in whatever had been private to each individual creature. Therefore, He took man as a creature of indeterminate image <note>original: "indiscretae opus imaginis." This is Pico’s core argument: unlike animals or angels, man has no fixed nature and can become whatever he chooses.</note> and, having placed him in the middle of the world, He spoke to him thus: "Neither a fixed seat, nor a face of your own, nor any gift peculiar to you, have we given you, O Adam, so that whatever seat, whatever face, or whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, you may have and possess them according to your wish and your judgment. The nature of all other creatures is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us. You, hindered by no such restrictions, shall determine your own nature for yourself according to your own free will, <margin>Free will in man</margin> in whose hands I have placed you. I have placed you in the middle of the world, so that from there you may more conveniently look around at whatever is in the world. We have made you neither celestial nor terrestrial, neither mortal nor immortal, so that you may, as if the voluntary and honorable molder and maker of yourself, fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer."

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that man's true dignity lies not in a fixed place in the hierarchy of being, but in the unique gift of free will, allowing him to choose his own nature and form. This celebrated opening of the "Oration" synthesizes Arab, Hermetic, Biblical, and Platonic thought to define man as the "molder and maker" of himself.</summary>

...you may shape and fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer. You shall be able to degenerate into the lower forms of life, which are the brutes; you shall be able, through the judgment of your soul, to be reborn into the higher orders, which are divine. O supreme generosity of God the Father! O highest and most marvelous happiness of man! To him it is granted to have whatever he chooses, to be whatever he wills. As soon as brutes are born, they bring with them from "their mother’s womb" <note>original: "ebulga matris," likely a corruption of *e vulva matris*.</note> (as Lucilius says) all that they will ever possess. The highest spiritual beings were, from the beginning or soon thereafter, that which they will remain for all eternity. But upon man, at the moment of his birth, the Father bestowed seeds of every kind and the germs of every way of life. Whatever seeds each man cultivates will grow and bear their fruit in him. If these are vegetative, he will become a plant. If they are sensual, he will become brutish. If they are rational, he will become a heavenly creature. If they are intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, not content with the lot of any creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he will become one spirit with God, in the solitary darkness of the Father <note>original: "solitaria patris caligine." This refers to the "Cloud of Unknowing" or the mystical state where the soul transcends all defined concepts to meet God.</note> which is set above all things, and he will surpass them all. Who would not admire this chameleon of ours? Or who could admire anything else more? Not without reason did Asclepius of Athens say that man was symbolized in the mysteries by Proteus, <note>Proteus was a Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note> because of his changing character and his nature that transforms itself. This is the source of those metamorphoses celebrated among the Hebrews and the Pythagoreans. For the secret theology of the Hebrews transforms the holy Enoch now into an "angel of the divinity" <note>The Hebrew text likely refers to the angel <unclear>Metatron</unclear>, into whom the patriarch Enoch was said to have been transformed.</note> and now others into different divine beings. The Pythagoreans transform wicked men into brutes and, if Empedocles is to be believed, even into plants. Imitating them, Muhammad often had this saying on his lips: "he who falls away from divine law becomes a brute." And rightly so. For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its mindless and insensitive nature; it is not the hide that makes the beast of burden, but its brutal and sensual soul; it is not the spherical body that makes the heavens, but its right reason; and it is not the separation from the body, but spiritual intelligence that makes the angel. If you see someone dedicated to his belly, crawling on the ground, it is a shrub you see, not a man. If you see someone blinded by the vain illusions of his imagination, like those of Calypso, <note>A reference to the nymph in the *Odyssey* who enchanted men and kept them from their true path.</note> and enticed by beckoning allurements, delivered over to his senses, it is a brute you see, not a man. If you see a philosopher discerning all things by right reason, তাকে venerate him: he is a heavenly creature, not an earthly one. If you see a pure contemplator, oblivious to the body, withdrawn into the inner reaches of the mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly creature; this is a more august divinity clothed in human flesh. Who would not admire man? For he is, not without reason, designated in the sacred Mosaic and Christian scriptures now by the name of "all flesh," and now by that of "every creature," since he fashions, builds, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and into the character of every creature. Therefore, Evantes the Persian, where he explains Chaldean theology, writes that man has no image of his own that is native to him, but many that are foreign and external; hence that saying of the Chaldeans: <unclear>Enosh</unclear> <note>Hebrew/Chaldean for "man" or "mortal," here used to emphasize man's shifting nature.</note>—that is, man is a creature of a varied, multiform, and changing nature. But why all this? So that we may understand that since we are born with this condition—that we may be whatever we want to be—we ought to take the greatest care of this: that it may never be said of us that, "being in a state of honor, we did not realize we had become like the brutes and the senseless beasts of burden." <note>A reference to Psalm 49:20.</note> But let us rather remember the saying of Asaph the prophet: "You are all gods and sons of the Most High." <note>Psalm 82:6.</note> Let us not abuse the most indulgent generosity of the Father, who gave us this free choice, lest we make for ourselves a harmful choice instead of a saving one. Let a certain holy ambition invade our souls, so that, not content with the mediocre, we may pant after the highest things and (since we can if we will) strive to reach them with all our might. Let us disdain the earthly...

...let us disdain earthly things <note>original: "Caelestia contemnamus." While *caelestia* usually means "heavenly," Pico uses it here to refer to the lower, visible heavens/planets, which are still part of the "world" to be transcended for the "ultramundane" or spiritual realm.</note>. Setting aside everything of the world, let us finally fly to the supramundane court closest to the most exalted divinity. There, as the sacred mysteries teach, the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones <note>In the traditional celestial hierarchy, these represent the three highest orders of angels, closest to God.</note> hold the highest places. But by what means, or what precisely must we do? Let us see what they do and what life they lead. If we live that same life (for we are able to), we shall perhaps have already equaled them. <margin>Seraph</margin> The Seraph burns with the fire of love <note>original: "charitatis igne." The name "Seraphim" was traditionally interpreted to mean "the burning ones," symbolizing their intense love for God.</note>; <margin>Cherub</margin> the Cherub shines with the radiance of intelligence; <margin>Throne</margin> the Throne stands firm with the stability of judgment. 

Therefore, if dedicated to an active life, we undertake the care of lower things with right judgment, <margin>Throne</margin> we shall be strengthened by the established solidity of the Thrones. If, resting from actions, meditating on the Creator in the work and the work in the Creator, we are occupied in the leisure of contemplation, we shall flash everywhere with Cherubic light.

<summary>Pico exhorts humanity to aspire to the highest angelic ranks—Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—by emulating their specific virtues of love, intelligence, and just action.</summary>

...we must strive to live this life with all our desire. ...me, and I will give you peace which the world and nature cannot give to you. <note>original: "dabo vobis pacem quam mundus et natura vobis dare non possunt." <margin>Friendship</margin>

Let us wish for this peace for our friends, and for our most excellent age; let us wish it for every house we enter and for our own soul, so that through it, the soul itself...

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page’s discussion on the soul’s ascent toward divine peace and angelic transformation, Pico now explains how the different branches of philosophy (moral, dialectic, and theological) correspond to specific "divine frenzies" and ancient mysteries that lead the soul to union with God.</meta>

<margin>Socratic frenzies</margin> 
Who would not desire—by setting all things aside, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body—to become a guest of the gods while still dwelling on earth? And, soaked in the nectar of eternity, who would not wish to be gifted with the prize of immortality, though still a mortal creature? Who would not wish to be so inspired by those Socratic frenzies <note>In Plato’s *Phaedrus*, Socrates describes "divine frenzy" as a gift from the gods that elevates the soul above ordinary human reason.</note> celebrated by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, that by the rowing of wings and feet, he might fly away from here—that is, from this world which is set in evil <note>original: "mundo qui est positus in maligno." A reference to 1 John 5:19.</note>—and be carried in a swift course to the celestial Jerusalem? 

Let us be driven, fathers, let us be driven by these Socratic frenzies which place us so far outside our own minds that they place both our minds and ourselves in God. We shall certainly be driven by them if we have first done what lies within us. For if through the strength of moral philosophy the power of our emotions has been so restrained by proper proportions that they harmonize with an unshakable accord; and if through dialectic <note>The art of logical reasoning and debate.</note> our reason has moved forward in rhythmic measure, then, gripped by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the celestial harmony with our innermost ears. 

<margin>Bacchus</margin> 
Then Bacchus, the leader of the Muses, <note>In this context, Bacchus (Dionysus) represents the "divine intoxication" or ecstatic joy of discovering hidden truths.</note> showing the invisible things of God to us as we philosophize through his mysteries—that is, through the visible signs of nature—will "inebriate us from the richness of the house of God." In that house, if we are faithful as <margin>Moses</margin> Moses was, most sacred Theology will approach and animate us with a double frenzy. For when we have been raised to her most eminent height, measuring from there all things that are, will be, and have been in the unchanging eternity, <note>original: "infectili... evo." Measuring time against the backdrop of the eternal "Now" of God.</note> and beholding their primeval beauty, we shall be the <margin>Phobean seers</margin> winged lovers of this Phobean <note>Belonging to Phoebe/Apollo, the god of light, prophecy, and the sun.</note> seer. Finally, stirred by an ineffable charity as if by a divine sting, and burning like flaming Seraphim <note>The "burning ones," the highest rank of angels characterized by their intense love for God.</note> outside of ourselves, filled with the divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but rather He who made us.

The sacred names of Apollo, if anyone explores their meanings and hidden mysteries, show clearly enough that this god is no less a philosopher than a seer. Since <margin>Ammonius</margin> Ammonius <note>Likely referring to Ammonius Saccas or Ammonius Hermiae, ancient commentators on Greek philosophy.</note> has sufficiently followed this path, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. 

But let three <margin>Three Delphic precepts</margin> Delphic precepts <note>The maxims inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> come to mind, fathers, which are absolutely necessary for those about to enter the most holy and majestic temple of the true Apollo (who illuminates every soul coming into this world): you will see that they warn us of nothing else but that we should embrace with all our strength this threefold philosophy which is the subject of our present dispute. 

First, that famous saying: "Nothing in excess" <note>original: "μηδεν αγαν" (meden agan).</note> rightly prescribes the rule and standard for all virtues according to the principle of moderation, which is the concern of moral philosophy. Then that other saying: "Know thyself" <note>original: "γνωθι σε αυτον" (gnothi seauton).</note> rouses and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the human being is the intermediate link and, as it were, the blending. For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as <margin>Zoroaster</margin> Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet and legendary founder of the Magi; Pico believed his teachings aligned with Plato.</note> first, and then <margin>Plato</margin> Plato wrote in the *Alcibiades*. 

Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, and already standing close to God, we shall address the true Apollo with the theological greeting: "Thou art" <note>original: "ει" (ei). According to Plutarch, this was the greeting used by initiates at Delphi to acknowledge the god’s eternal existence.</note>—calling upon him familiarly and therefore happily.

<margin>Pythagoras the wise</margin> Let us also consult the most wise Pythagoras, who was considered especially wise because he never deemed himself worthy of the name of "wise man." <note>Pythagoras is credited with coining the term "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) because he believed only God is truly "wise."</note> He first commands: "Do not sit upon a bushel" <note>original: "ne supra modium sedeamus." A Pythagorean "symbol" or riddle.</note>—that is, do not lose the rational part of the soul, by which it measures, judges, and examines all things, through lazy idleness. Rather, let us direct and stir it up constantly through the practice and rule of <margin>Explanation of Pythagoras's precepts</margin> dialectic. 

Then he will point out two things for us to avoid: "Do not urinate against the sun," and "Do not cut your nails during a sacrifice." But only after we have urinated away <note>A metaphor for purging the "overflowing" and fluid base desires of the body.</note> our flowing appetites for excessive pleasures through moral philosophy, and have cut away the "clippings of our nails"—the sharp outgrowths of anger and the stings of our spirits—then at last may we take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus, which we mentioned, of which the Sun is rightly called the father and leader of our contemplation...

<summary>Pico describes how moral philosophy, logic (dialectic), and theology correspond to the ancient "frenzies" and the Delphic/Pythagorean maxims. He argues that by purifying the soul and using reason, one can achieve a divine state of "intoxication" and union with God.</summary>
<keywords>Socratic frenzy, Plato, Delphic precepts, Pythagoras, Apollo, Bacchus, moral philosophy, dialectic, theology, self-knowledge, Seraphim</keywords>

...we may begin to devote ourselves to contemplation. <meta>Continuity: Having criticized those who treat philosophy as a commercial trade, Pico now defends his decision to engage in public debate (disputation), arguing that intellectual struggle is the true path to wisdom.</meta>

...you; but this is common to me along with Plato, with Aristotle, and with the most esteemed philosophers of every age. For them, it was most certain that nothing was more helpful for achieving that knowledge of truth which they sought than to be very frequent in the practice of disputation. For just as physical strength becomes firmer through gymnastics, so without doubt in this literary wrestling ring <note>The original Latin uses 'palaestra,' referring to the ancient Greek wrestling schools where athletes trained.</note>, the powers of the soul become far stronger and more vigorous. 

I would not believe that the <margin>Poets</margin> poets meant anything else by the famous weapons of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, often depicted with a helmet, shield, and spear.</note>, or that the <margin>Hebrews</margin> Hebrews meant anything else when they say that the serpent is a symbol of the wise <note>original: "ferpentem fapientum symbolum"</note>, except to signify to us that these most honorable types of contests are exceedingly necessary for attaining wisdom. 

From this, it perhaps follows that the <margin>Chaldeans</margin> Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and sages. Pico frequently draws on 'oriental' wisdom to support his arguments.</note>, in calculating the birth-chart of one who is to be a philosopher, require that Mars behold Mercury in a trine aspect <note>The 'triquetro aspectu' refers to an astrological trine (120 degrees), considered a harmonious and powerful alignment. Mars represents energy or conflict, while Mercury represents intellect and speech.</note>; as if to say that if you take away these encounters—these battles—all philosophy would become drowsy and sluggish. 

But truly, with those who say I am unequal to this task, the manner of my defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal to it, I may be seen as immodest and over-estimating myself; if I confess I am unequal, I seem likely to incur the mark of being rash and ill-advised. See what a tight spot I have fallen into, in what a position I am placed; I cannot promise things about myself without fault, nor can I soon fail to deliver them without fault. 

Perhaps I could also bring forward that quote from <margin>Job</margin> Job, that "there is a spirit in all men," <note>Job 32:8</note> and hear with <margin>Timothy</margin> Timothy, "let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12</note>; but I will say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing great or singular in me. While I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the noble arts, I neither assume nor claim for myself the title of "learned" man. Therefore, as to why I have placed such a great burden on my shoulders, it was not because I was unaware of my own weakness; but because I knew that in this kind of fight—that is, a literary one—it is a unique feature that to be defeated is a gain. For...

<summary>Pico defends the practice of public disputation as an essential "intellectual gymnasium" for the soul, drawing on Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean traditions to argue that wisdom is forged through mental struggle.</summary>

...if they were to consider the method of philosophizing, they must clearly and even unwillingly admit it is necessary. For those who have not devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian whose followers are called Thomists.</note> or to Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), the Franciscan theologian whose followers are called Scotists.</note>, who are now most frequently in people’s hands—can indeed put their own doctrine to the test in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so established myself that, sworn to the words of no one <note>original: "nullius uerba iuratus." Pico is referencing the Roman poet Horace: "I am not bound to swear allegiance to any master."</note>, I might pour myself through all the masters of philosophy, examine every page, and recognize every family. Therefore, since I had to speak concerning all of them—lest, as a defender of a private dogma, I should seem bound to one while neglecting the rest—even if only a few points were proposed from each, there could not fail to be very many points which were brought forward from all of them at once. Nor should anyone condemn in me the fact that I am carried as a guest wherever the storm may drive me. 

For it was once observed by all the ancients that, in unrolling every kind of writing, they would pass over no commentaries they were able to read. This was seen most especially in Aristotle, who for that reason was called by Plato "the reader" <note>original: "αναγνωστησ (anagnostes), i. lector." Plato reportedly gave Aristotle this nickname because of his voracious appetite for books at a time when philosophy was still largely oral.</note>. Indeed, it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single portico or academy <note>The "Portico" refers to the Stoics, and the "Academy" to the followers of Plato.</note>. Nor can one rightly select what is his own from all of them if he has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. 

Add to this that in every single family there is something distinguished that is not common to the others. And to begin now with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: There is in **John Scotus** something vigorous and analytical. In **Thomas**, something solid and balanced. In **Egidius** <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316).</note>, something polished and exact. In **Francis** <note>Francis of Meyronnes (c. 1285–1328).</note>, something sharp and keen. In **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280).</note>, something ancient, ample, and grand. In **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293).</note>, as it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. Among the Arabs, there is in **Averroes** something firm and unshakable. In **Avempace** and **Alfarabi**, something serious and meditated. In **Avicenna**, something divine and Platonic. 

Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, especially bright and pure. In **Simplicius**, it is rich and abundant. In **Themistius**, elegant and concise. In **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, the famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, seriously elaborated. In **Ammonius**, clear and graceful. And if you turn to the Platonists—to review a few—in **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and a diverse religion. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the barbarians. In **Plotinus**, there is nothing in particular to admire because he offers himself everywhere as admirable; the sweating Platonists can scarcely understand him when he speaks of divine things divinely, and of human things in a learned, indirect way far above man. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, luxuriating in Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him—**Hermias**, **Damascus**, **Olympiodorus**, and many others—in all of whom that "divine" element <note>original: "το θειον (to theion), i. diuinum"</note>, which is the particular symbol of the Platonists, always shines forth.

It happens, too, that if there is any sect which attacks truer dogmas and mocks good causes with the slander of wit, it confirms the truth rather than weakening it; and like a flame shaken by motion, it excites rather than extinguishes it. Moved by this reason, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as pleased some), but of every kind of doctrine, so that by this comparison of many sects and the multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "splendor of truth" of which Plato mentions in his letters might shine more clearly upon our minds like the sun rising from on high. What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely Albert, Thomas, Scotus, Egidius, Francis, and Henry—were discussed, while omitting...

<summary>Pico explains his syncretic philosophical method, arguing that a true seeker of truth must study all schools—Scholastic, Arabic, Greek, and Neoplatonist—rather than being bound to a single "family" or master.</summary>
<keywords>syncretism, Scholasticism, Neoplatonism, Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle, Plotinus, Averroes, eclecticism, splendor of truth</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Pico concludes his explanation of why he has studied every school of philosophy, moving from the specific names of thinkers (Aristotle, Plato, Averroes) mentioned on the previous page to the broader historical movement of wisdom from the ancient East through Greece to the Latin West.</meta>

...was being discussed by Greek and Arab philosophers? Especially since all wisdom flowed from the barbarians <note>Pico uses "barbarians" in the classical sense to refer to non-Greeks, specifically the ancient Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Egyptians, whom he believed possessed the original divine revelation.</note> to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. In this way, our own countrymen have always considered it sufficient, in their method of philosophizing, to rely on foreign discoveries and to have merely refined the ideas of others. What point was there in discussing natural philosophy with the Peripatetics <margin>The Peripatetics</margin> <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated the medieval universities.</note>, unless the Academy of the Platonists <margin>The Platonists</margin> was also summoned? And now, for the first time—as far as I know (and may these words be free from envy)—it is by me that their doctrine is brought out into the public for the test of a disputation after many centuries. <summary>Pico argues that true scholarship requires more than just repeating foreign or ancient wisdom; one must bring original, labored-over contributions to the "symposium" of philosophy. <margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Abu Ma’shar</margin>
<margin>Avenzoar</margin>
...is the science of numbering. Asking also why man is the wisest animal? He responds <note>original: "Respondet." This refers to a tradition often attributed to Pythagoras or Plato, asking about the nature of human wisdom.</note>: because he knows how to count. Aristotle also mentions this opinion in his *Problems* <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC). The *Problems* is a collection of questions on various subjects attributed to him; Pico refers to the section discussing why humans alone among animals can count.</note>. Abu Ma’shar <note>Abu Ma’shar (787–886 AD), known to the Latins as Albumasar, was a leading Persian astrologer whose works were central to medieval European astrology.</note> writes that it was a saying of Avenzoar the Babylonian <note>Avenzoar (c. 1094–1162) was a famous Arab physician from Spain. Pico’s attribution of "Babylonian" likely links him to the ancient "Chaldean" wisdom tradition he admires.</note> that he who knew how to count knew all things. These claims could not be true in any way if, by the "art of counting," they understood that art in which merchants are now primarily the most skilled. Plato also bears witness to this, warning us with a clear voice <note>Plato discusses this distinction in the *Republic*, arguing that the philosopher must study calculation for the sake of knowing "being" rather than for trade.</note> not to mistake this divine arithmetic for mercantile arithmetic. 

Therefore, since I seem to have thoroughly explored that highly praised arithmetic through many long nights of study, and intending to make a trial of this matter, I have promised to respond publicly through numbers to seventy-four questions which are considered principal among physical and divine matters.

<margin>Magical theorems</margin>

<summary>Pico distinguishes between "divine arithmetic" (the mystical study of numbers) and "mercantile arithmetic" (common counting), arguing that the former is the key to all wisdom. <meta>Continuity: Following his defense of the true "art of numbers" against mere mercantile calculation, Pico now transitions to his defense of Magic, distinguishing between its corrupt and divine forms before introducing his work on the Hebrew Kabbalah.</meta>

And that most wise man <note>original: "uir sapientissimus"; likely referring to Plotinus or Porphyry, Neoplatonic philosophers who distinguished between theurgy (divine magic) and goetia (black magic).</note> asserted: that he so abhorred the one form of magic that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more right that they should come to him than that he should go to them; and rightly so. For as that one renders man a subject and slave to wicked powers, so this other magic makes him their prince and lord. Finally, that corrupt magic cannot claim for itself the name of either art or science. This true magic, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the deepest contemplation of most secret things, and ultimately, the knowledge of all nature. 

This magic, calling forth into the light, as if from hiding places, the virtues scattered and sown throughout the world by the blessing of God, does not so much perform wonders as it diligently serves nature as she performs them. This magic, having more scrupulously examined from within that consensus of the universe—which the Greeks more expressively call *sympathy* <note>original: "συμπαθειαν" (sympatheia). In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the invisible "interconnectedness" or "binding force" that links all parts of the cosmos together.</note>—and having a clear understanding of the reciprocal knowledge of natures, applies to each thing its own native allurements—which the magi call *iynges* <note>original: "ιυγγεσ" (iynges). These were "magical wheels" or "charms" mentioned in the Chaldean Oracles, used to draw divine influences down to earth.</note> in the recesses of the world. It brings forth into public view, as if it were the artisan itself, the miracles lying hidden in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God. And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magus marries earth to heaven—that is, he joins lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. 

As a result, just as the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, this latter magic appears divine and salutary. For this reason especially, while the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God, the latter excites in him such admiration for the works of God that a ready charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. 

For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the persistent <margin>Note</margin> contemplation of the wonders of God; so that when we have well explored them through this natural magic of which we treat, being more ardently animated to the worship and love of the Creator, we shall be compelled to sing: *The heavens are full, the earth is full of the majesty of Your glory.* <note>original: "Pleni sunt cæli, plena est terra Maiestate gloriæ tuæ." A liturgical phrase from the "Sanctus" of the Mass, based on Isaiah 6:3.</note> 

And this is enough regarding magic, of which I have said these things; though I know there are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, so they themselves often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

I come now to those things which, unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, I have brought forward to confirm the sacrosanct and Catholic faith. Lest these things should perhaps be thought by those to whom they are unknown to be fabricated trifles or the fables of a charlatan, I want all to understand what and of what kind they are, from where they were sought, and from what and how illustrious authors they come.

<summary>Pico defines "natural magic" as a divine science that explores the hidden sympathies of nature to "marry" earth to heaven, contrasting it with demonic magic. He concludes by introducing his use of Hebrew Kabbalistic mysteries to support Christian doctrine.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico’s argument that true magic and wisdom are ancient, divine, and intentionally kept hidden from the uninitiated. ...preserved <note>original: "feruarunt." This concludes the sentence from the previous page regarding those who protected sacred knowledge.</note>. Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few short works which, as he lay dying, he entrusted to his daughter Dama. The sphinxes carved into the temples of the Egyptians served as a warning that mystic doctrines should be kept safe from the unlearned masses by the tangled knots of riddles. Plato, writing to Dion concerning the highest substances, said: "I must speak in riddles, so that if this letter should happen to fall into the hands of others, what we write to you may not be understood by them." Aristotle said that his books of *Metaphysics*—in which he treats of divine matters—were both "published and not published." <note>Pico refers to a famous tradition that Aristotle’s most difficult works were only truly "published" for those who had heard his oral lectures.</note>

What more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the teacher of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they, in turn, refused to write down, lest they become common property to the vulgar crowd. This is most strongly confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite, <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century who was then believed to be the direct disciple of St. Paul mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note> who says that the more secret mysteries were passed down by the authors of our religion

->from soul to soul<-
<note>original: "ex animo in animum."</note>

without the use of writing, through the medium of the spoken word. In exactly this same way, when the true interpretation of the Law, divinely handed down to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was called "Kabbalah" <note>The Hebrew word Qabbalah literally means "reception" or "that which is received."</note>—which is the same among the Hebrews as what we call "reception." This name was given because one man did not receive that teaching through written records, but through a successive order of revelations from another, as if by a hereditary right.

However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the Temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to the restoration of the Law. Esdras, then the head of the Church, <note>Pico uses the term "ecclesia" (Church) to describe the Jewish assembly, emphasizing continuity between the Old and New Testaments.</note> after revising the book of Moses, realized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and the captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by their ancestors of passing the doctrine from hand to hand <note>original: "per manus," meaning a physical or direct oral transmission.</note> could not be maintained. He saw that the secrets of the celestial doctrine granted to them by God would perish, as their memory could not endure for long without the aid of commentaries. 

He therefore decreed that the wise men then remaining should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he remembered concerning the mysteries of the Law. Scribes were employed to record these into seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the Sanhedrin). Regarding this matter, Fathers, you need not believe me alone; listen to Esdras himself speaking: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'The first things you wrote, put in public so that the worthy and unworthy alike may read; but the last seventy books you shall keep, to deliver them to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." These are the words of Esdras, verbatim. These are the books of the science of Kabbalah; in these books, Esdras rightly placed "the vein of understanding"...

<summary>Pico argues that all great spiritual traditions—Pythagorean, Platonic, Christian, and Jewish—intentionally hid their highest truths in "riddles" or oral traditions. He introduces the Kabbalah as the divinely revealed "reception" of Moses, which was later written down by Esdras in seventy secret books to prevent its loss during the Jewish exile.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page concludes Pico’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having just discussed the secret transmission of divine knowledge in the Christian and Hebrew traditions (Kabbalah), he now bridges these to the Greek tradition—specifically Pythagoras, Plato, and the "ancient theologians" like Orpheus and Zoroaster—before inviting his audience to the public debate of his 900 theses.</meta>

...the spoken word, as we read daily in the works of Jerome and Augustine. Indeed, regarding those matters which look toward philosophy, you would hear the very voice of Pythagoras and Plato, whose decrees are so closely aligned with the Christian faith that <margin>Augustine</margin> our Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). In his *Confessions*, he famously noted that the books of the Platonists contained the same truths about the Divine Word (Logos) found in the Gospel of John.</note> gave immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists had come into his hands. In short, there is almost no point of controversy between us and the Hebrews regarding which they cannot be so refuted and convicted by the books of the Kabbalists that not even a corner remains in which they might hide themselves. On this matter, I have a most serious witness: <margin>Antonio Cronico</margin> Antonio Cronico, <note>Antonio Vinciguerra, known as Cronico, was a Venetian diplomat and man of letters who moved in Pico's circle.</note> a most learned man, who heard with his own ears when I was at his table as <margin>Dactylus the Hebrew</margin> Dactylus the Hebrew, <note>Likely a reference to Yochanan Alemanno, Pico’s Hebrew teacher; "Dactylus" is a Latinized play on his name.</note> a man skilled in this science, descended "hand and foot" <note>An idiom meaning "entirely" or "with total agreement."</note> into the Christian opinion concerning the Trinity.

But to return to the specific chapters of my own disputation which must be reviewed: I have also brought my own opinion regarding the interpretation of the poems of Orpheus and <margin>Zoroaster</margin> Zoroaster. <note>Zoroaster and Orpheus were seen by Renaissance thinkers as "Prisca Theologi" (Ancient Theologians) who received divine revelations long before the Greek philosophers.</note> Orpheus is read among the Greeks in an almost complete state; Zoroaster is read among them in a mutilated form, though more fully among the <margin>Orpheus</margin> Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the fathers and authors of ancient wisdom. For I shall say nothing of Zoroaster, whose frequent mention among the Platonists is always accompanied by the highest veneration. <margin>Iamblichus of Chalcis</margin> Iamblichus of Chalcis <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who sought to revive pagan religion through "theurgy" or divine ritual.</note> writes that <margin>Pythagoras</margin> Pythagoras held Orphic theology as the very model upon which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. Indeed, they say that the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" for this reason alone: because they flowed from the teachings of Orpheus. From there, the secret doctrine of numbers and whatever great and sublime things Greek philosophy possessed flowed as if from a primary source.

But (as was the custom of the ancient theologians) Orpheus so wove the mysteries of his dogmas into the wrappers of fables and disguised them with a poetic veil, that if anyone should read his hymns, they would believe nothing lay beneath them except the most idle trifles and nursery tales. I have wished to say this so that it might be known what labor was mine, and what difficulty I faced: to draw out the hidden meanings of secret philosophy from the intentional thickets of riddles and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the aid of the work and diligence of other interpreters. 

And yet my "dogs" <note>Pico’s derogatory term for his scholastic critics, whom he portrays as barking at things they do not understand.</note> have barked that I have merely accumulated a few trivial and light things for a display of numbers—as if all these questions were not those which are most ambiguous and highly contested, in which the principal Academies clash; as if I had not brought many things to these very men who carp at me (and who believe themselves to be the leaders of philosophers) that are entirely unknown and unattempted. Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress the disputation into as few chapters as I could. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide it into its own members and tear it into pieces, it would surely have grown into an innumerable number. To say nothing of the rest, who is there who does not know that one dogma out of the nine hundred—namely, that concerning the reconciliation of the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—I could have drawn out into six hundred chapters (if not more) without any suspicion of "affected numbers," by enumerating one by one all the points in which others think they disagree, but I believe they agree? But certainly (for I will speak, though perhaps neither modestly nor according to my own character), I have wished to give proof through this gathering of mine, not so much that I know many things, but that I know things which many do not know.

So that this may now become openly clear to you in fact, most worshipful Fathers; and so that my speech may no longer delay your desire, most excellent Doctors—whom I see with great pleasure standing ready and girded for the battle—may it be happy and auspicious: let us now join hands as if the trumpet signal were sounding.

<meta>Continuity: Following the conclusion of his "Oration on the Dignity of Man," Pico turns here to a more personal and pastoral mode.
