->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco, greetings in Him who is true salvation.<-

That many opportunities for evil were immediately presented to you upon leaving me—opportunities which disturb you and oppose your newly-embraced purpose of living well—is nothing for you to wonder at, my son; nor should you grieve or be terrified. How much more of a miracle would it be if, to you alone among mortals, the path to heaven lay open without sweat—as if for the first time the deceitful world and the evil demon had ceased to be, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which <note>original: "concupiscit aduersus spiritum"</note> "lusts against the spirit." Unless we watch over our salvation with vigilance, the world, enticing us, transforms us—drunk on Circe's cups <note>A reference to the sorceress in Homer’s *Odyssey* who turned men into swine; Pico uses this to illustrate how physical lust degrades human dignity.</note>—into the monstrous shapes of beasts. But James also affirms that you should rejoice, <margin>James</margin> writing: <note>original: "gaudete fratres cum in tentationes varias incideritis"</note> "Rejoice, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations." And not without reason; for what hope of glory can there be if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is challenged to the fight—and especially to that fight in which no one can be conquered against his will, nor do we need any other strength to conquer than the will to conquer itself. <margin>The great happiness of the Christian.</margin> Great is the happiness of the Christian, since victory is placed in his own judgment, and the rewards will be greater than any victor’s prayer or expectation. Tell me, I ask you, my dearest son, is there anything in this life among those things for which the lust of earthly minds is driven, for the sake of attaining which many labors must not first be undergone, and many unworthy and wretched things endured? The merchant thinks he has done well if, after a ten-year voyage, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to his life, he has acquired a slightly more abundant fortune. Regarding the military service of this world <note>Pico uses the term <term>militia</term> (military service) to encompass the broader "struggle" of secular life, including the competitive and often sycophantic world of the Italian courts.</note>, there is no need for me to write to you; its miseries your own experience has taught and continues to teach you. In earning the favor of princes, in reconciling the friendships of equals, in seeking honors—what a mountain of troubles, how much anxiety, how much worry! I could sooner learn this from you than teach it to you—I, who am content with my books and my little leisure, have learned since childhood to live within my fortune, and, dwelling as much as possible within myself, I sigh for nothing and seek nothing outside of myself. Therefore, we sweat and pant and yet barely attain these earthly things—fragile, uncertain, cheap, and common to us and the beasts; yet toward the heavenly and divine things—which <note>original: "nec oculus vidit, neque auris audivit"</note> "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor heart conceived"—are we to be dragged like lazy, sleeping, and almost unwilling people by the gods? As if without us God could not reign, or those heavenly citizens could not be blessed. Truly, if earthly happiness were provided to us while we were idle, someone refusing labor might prefer to serve the world rather than God. But if we are exhausted no less—indeed far more—on the path of sinners than on the path of God, whence comes that cry of the damned: <note>original: "Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis"</note> "We are weary on the path of iniquity"? It cannot but be the height of madness to refuse to labor where one goes from labor to reward, rather than where one goes from labor to punishment. I pass over how great that peace is, and how great the happiness of a soul that is conscious of no wrong and turns pale at no fault—a peace which undoubtedly far outweighs all the pleasures that can be possessed or desired in this life. <margin>A memorable saying</margin> For what is desirable in the pleasures of the world? While they are sought, they exhaust; when they are acquired, they fail to satisfy; when they are lost, they torture. Do you doubt, my son, that the minds of the wicked are agitated by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, who can neither deceive nor be deceived: "Their heart is like a boiling sea that cannot rest." For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; everything threatens them with fear, everything with care, everything with death. Shall we then look to these people? Shall we envy them? And, forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our homeland and our heavenly Father, shall we make ourselves slaves of these things though we were born free? Living wretchedly with them and dying even more wretchedly, shall we at last be afflicted most wretchedly by eternal fires? O blind minds of men! O

Oh, blind hearts! <note>original: "pectora cœca"; a classical idiom for spiritual or intellectual ignorance, famously used by Lucretius.</note> Who does not see, even clearer than the light of day, that all these things are truer than truth itself? Yet we do not do those things which we know ought to be done; instead, we still stick fast, desiring in vain to pull our foot out of the mire. <note>The Latin "plantam" refers to the sole of the foot; Pico uses the imagery of a traveler whose feet are so deeply mired in the "mud" of worldly life that they cannot be extricated despite a desire to leave.</note>

Under the emperor the devil, under the banners of death, and under the wages of hell, this company wages war against heaven, against the Lord, and against his Christ.

->two most wholesome remedies<-

**Fasting and prayer.** <note>original: "f. atq; oŕo." The 'f' likely abbreviates *jejunium* (fasting), a standard ascetic pairing with *oratio* (prayer).</note> For what are we able to do without the help of God? Or how will He help one who has not called upon Him? But certainly, He will not hear you when you call if you previously despised a fellow man who called upon you. It is written: **In the same measure as you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.** <note>A reference to Matthew 7:2.</note> And elsewhere: **Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.** 

When I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of many words, but to that which is done in the secret retreat of the mind, in the inward parts of the soul. Speak to God with your very affection, which presents the mind to the Father not only in the **most bright darkness of contemplation**, <note>original: "lucidissima cōtēplatiōis tenebra"; a reference to the "Divine Darkness" of Pseudo-Dionysius, a mystical state where the soul is so blinded by God's light that it seems to be in darkness.</note> but unites it by certain ineffable ways known only to those who have experienced them. I do not care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning, and how much it is interrupted by sighs rather than by a continuous series of words or a diffusion of rhythmic speech. 

If your health is dear to you, if you wish to be safe from the snares of the devil, from the storms of the world, and from the ambushes of enemies; if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally happy: let no day pass in which you do not approach your God at least once in prayer. Prostrate before Him with a humble affection of mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from your innermost vitals—with the Prophet: <margin>Note</margin> **"Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances; but according to Thy mercy remember me for Thy goodness’ sake, O Lord."** <note>original: "Delicta iuuentutis meæ... "; Psalm 25:7.</note> 

Necessity itself will suggest to you every hour what you should ask from your God, as will the Spirit who intercedes for us. <margin>Prayer</margin> Sacred reading will also suggest it to you; I ask you again and again that, having set aside the fables and trifles of the poets, you always have this in your hands. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than if you never cease **to turn the sacred letters with a nightly hand and a daily hand.** <note>original: "litteras sacras nocturna uersare manu uersare diurna"; Pico is parodying Horace’s famous advice to poets to study Greek models "nocturna versate manu, versate diurna."</note> 

For there lies hidden in them a certain celestial power, living and effective, which, if one treats them purely and humbly, transforms the mind of the reader into divine love by a certain wonderful power. But this letter has already exceeded its limits, as the subject matter and a certain wonderful charity have drawn me along—a charity with which I have followed you in spirit, especially from that hour when I was made certain of your most holy purpose. 

Finally, I would wish you to be reminded of that which I often spoke of with you while you were here with me: never forget these two things: that the Son of God died for you, and that you too, even if you live long, will soon die. With these twin spurs—one of fear and the other of love—urge your horse through the brief course of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness. We neither ought to nor can set any other goal for ourselves than that we may enjoy the infinite Good without end, with perpetual peace for both parts of the man <note>Referring to the peace of both soul and body.</note>. Farewell. And fear God. May 15, 1492.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Filippo Beroaldo, Greetings.

I have received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter that was both amiable and erudite, along with many verses that truly challenge antiquity itself. That gift was most pleasing to me. Therefore, on your behalf, I have spent my leisure hours well, and I could not have spent them more pleasantly or more honorably in any other pursuit. 

I would act as a thoroughly ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent things with my own, which are the worst, or to exchange "the poisons of Suffenus" for Catullian wit. <note>Suffenus was a character in Catullus’s poems who thought he was a great poet but was actually terrible. <meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Lorenzo de’ Medici, in which he compares Lorenzo’s vernacular poetry to that of Petrarch and Dante Alighieri, ultimately arguing for the superiority of Lorenzo's work due to its integration of deep philosophy and refined style.</meta>

...so that whoever would take away from you would mutilate the work, while whoever would take away from him <note>Pico is comparing Lorenzo to Petrarch, whom he discussed in the preceding section.</note> would be trimming and cleansing it. Even if we granted—though I will never grant it—that the things he wrote are more pleasant and more elegant than yours, it was easy for a man to provide that for whom there was no struggle or battle with the meanings themselves. But those sharp and subtle thoughts of yours—and, to use a single word, those *Laurentian* sentiments—it can scarcely be told how they reject the **curling irons** <note>original: "calamistros"; a rhetorical term for artificial or excessive stylistic flourishes, likened to curling hair.</note> and do not willingly admit those **dyes** <note>original: "fucos"; refers to artificial rhetorical coloring or "makeup" used to mask a lack of substance.</note>. If he, whom we read as soft, polished, and pleasant, had been required to handle these subjects, we would surely read him as thorny, squalid, and unpleasant. For one can see that whenever he approaches anything sharp, intricate, or knotty, he falls in his style as much as he rises in his meaning.

But when he displays that famous furniture of his words—his ointments, his curls, and his flowers—Castricius <note>Titus Castricius, a 2nd-century teacher of rhetoric mentioned by Aulus Gellius.</note> would often warn him, as he warned regarding Gracchus, that we should not be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses; rather, we should inspect what lies beneath: what seat, what foundation, what depth is in the words. If you were to do that there, you would sometimes see an **Epicurean vacuum** <note>A reference to the physical theory of Epicurus and Lucretius regarding the "void"; Pico uses it here to mean a total lack of intellectual substance.</note>: so that either no meaning lies beneath, or it is cold and trivial. In this regard, which is the most important, even if you did not surpass him, I see no reason at all why he should surpass you for the sake of eloquence. For the words in your work could not be more illustrious, and their arrangement is so apt that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any possible way.

<margin>Note</margin> But now let us carefully weigh **Dante** with you, about whom perhaps more people will raise a controversy. For there are many who, in the comparison of writers, do not weigh merits so much as they count years; they order others to read the ancients with reverence, while they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. As for the first place, certainly concerning style, I think no one will deny it to you. Dante is sometimes so rough, harsh, and meager that he seems quite crude and unpolished; even his own admirers <note>original: "aurarii"; literally "gilders," referring here to those who try to put a golden shine on Dante's reputation despite his flaws.</note> confess this. But they throw the blame entirely upon that age and century. You are more cultivated in your speech, and he is not more grand.

But they will say he is grander and more sublime in his meanings. I ask you, what wonder is it that he speaks of physical matters <note>original: "physica re"; referring to natural philosophy or the workings of the universe.</note> when nature itself compels him to it and supplies the sentiments of its own accord? If it concerns God, the soul, or the blessed, <margin>Augustine. Thomas</margin> he brings forward what **Thomas Aquinas** and **Augustine** wrote about these things. And he was as frequent and assiduous in treating and meditating on these matters as you are in carrying out the greatest public and private business. It was not so much a distinguished thing for Dante to have done this, as it would have been shameful for him *not* to have done it. 

Yet it was, without a doubt, a work of the highest genius, which you yourself provide: to make philosophical matters out of things that are amatory, and to make things that are somewhat harsh in their inherent severity lovable by adding a touch of **Venus** <note>original: "superinducta uenere"; Pico means adding beauty, charm, or poetic grace to difficult subjects.</note>. Thus, in your verses, the serious matters of philosophers are mixed with the playful songs of lovers, so that the former gain dignity from the latter, and the latter gain joy and grace from the former; so that both by this bond, and each individually, they are greater than they were before. But this is not so much to be wondered at as that which moved me most: that these things were introduced by you as if they were not introduced from outside, but dug out from the bosom of the matter itself of which you treat. From that very soil—with you, so to speak, watering the ground—they seem to blossom, so that they appear native and not foreign, necessary and not merely brought in, entirely genuine and not artificial. This is what I cannot admire enough, and by which you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies high, he is raised up by the wings of his subject matter; you, though the matter resists and pulls downward, are raised on high by the wings of your genius; and thus you are raised...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that Lorenzo de’ Medici’s poetry surpasses both Petrarch and Dante because Lorenzo seamlessly integrates profound philosophical truths into elegant vernacular verse, whereas his predecessors either lacked substance or lacked style.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Lorenzo de’ Medici, in which he argues that Lorenzo’s vernacular poetry surpasses that of Petrarch and Dante. Pico is specifically praising Lorenzo's ability to weave profound Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy into his verse and his prose commentary (the "paraphrase").</meta>

...so that you do not depart from the matter: but rather you raise it up with you, as much as it was deservedly earned by Dante himself. Now one may see what the difference is between you, Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous humanist poet.</note>, and Dante; concerning them, I would add this: Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises, possessing that which charms at first glance but satisfies no further. Dante has that which sometimes offends upon meeting it, but yields more pleasure to one penetrating its depths. Your works possess no less in their retreat to hold the reader than they have in their first appearance to capture them. Add to this that they wrote their poems in seclusion, in the shade, and in the highest tranquility of their studies; you, however, sang yours amidst tumults, the noise of the court, the clamors of the forum, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while being most occupied.

For them, the muses were an ordinary and principal business; for you, they are a sport and a certain relaxation from cares. For them, they were the height of exhaustion; for you, when exhausted, they are leisure. Finally, by relaxing your spirit, you reached that point which they, straining all the nerves of their minds, perhaps did not attain. 

But what shall I say of "my" paraphrase? <note>Pico refers to Lorenzo’s *Comento*, a prose commentary Lorenzo wrote to explain the philosophical meaning of his own sonnets. Pico calls it "mine" as a sign of his deep affection for the work.</note> For why should I not call it mine? Or rather, why not call it mine by right of this name, since, though I venerate it as yours, I love it as my own? I truly admire it, and you within it, from which I gather how far I was from a true appreciation of your verses; in them, I had not peered into the greatest and most illustrious parts with my **night-owl eyes** <note>original: "noctuinis oculis"; a metaphor for being dim-sighted or unable to perceive the brilliance of the truth in the "daylight" of Lorenzo's genius.</note>. I saw them then revealed through you, who alone were both able and obligated to do so: obligated to yourself and to us, lest you cheat yourself of great glory and us of great pleasure. 

I read it (I call God to witness), O most great Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for instruction. For how many things are there from Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin>—from the *Physics*, the books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from the *Problems*—and how many from Plato <margin>Plato</margin>—from the *Protagoras*, the *Republic*, the *Laws*, and the *Symposium*? Although I have read all these things elsewhere in those authors, I read them in your work as if they were new and better, transformed by you into I-know-not-what appearance, so that they seem to be yours and not theirs; and while reading, I feel as though I am learning something. 

This is the greatest indication that you know these matters not so much from a commentary but from within yourself. For many are accustomed to exercise more <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: "σοφιστεια" (sophisteia); the use of clever but fallacious arguments, or a mere pretense of wisdom.</note> in literature than actual labor. When they are about to write something, they use philosophers as if they were **technical advisors** <note>original: "pragmaticos"; agents or advisors who provide specialized information for a fee.</note> suggesting certain dogmas to them, which they then thrust into their little books so that they might appear to be philosophers. <margin>Note</margin> But you may easily catch these men. For you can see that those ideas are neither properly arranged nor coherent; they are not explained by the authors, but rather entangled by them. And men who are otherwise eloquent appear like speechless infants when speaking of such things. 

But who would not see that you do not hold these ideas on loan, but as matters over which you have the right and power to turn, direct, and handle at your will? These things (O happy genius!) you have attained in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things which we, who are not even disciples but merely **lodgers** <note>original: "inquilini"; temporary residents or tenants, implying that scholars like Pico live in the "house" of philosophy without owning the knowledge as naturally as Lorenzo does.</note> of the philosophers, follow after in our life of shade and sedentary toil, rather than actually attaining them. 

But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? To me, it seems to be entirely like that of Caesar <margin>Caesar</margin> in the Latin tongue. For it is an oration not crafted by hand, not **gilded** <note>original: "bracteata"; covered in thin gold leaf, implying a superficial or deceptive beauty.</note>, not twisted, but by its own nature upright, shining, and robust; it does not run on recklessly but keeps its pace; it is neither excessive nor meager, neither playful nor unpleasing. It is sweetly serious and seriously lovely. The words are chosen but not strained for, illustrious but not counterfeit, necessary but not far-fetched; they do not merely explain the matter but place it right before one's eyes. I pass over the fact that you are always mindful of your own character, and that the seeds of your renowned prudence are scattered everywhere...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola praises Lorenzo de’ Medici’s poetry and philosophical commentary, arguing that Lorenzo possesses a natural mastery of Aristotle and Plato that exceeds professional scholars. He compares Lorenzo's prose style to the clarity and strength of Julius Caesar's Latin.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Lorenzo de’ Medici regarding his poetry and begins a famous exchange with the scholar Hermolao Barbaro. In the first part, Pico urges Lorenzo to finish his philosophical commentary on his own sonnets. In the second part, Pico addresses Barbaro’s criticisms of "barbarian" (medieval Scholastic) philosophers, setting the stage for a defense of philosophical substance over rhetorical style.</meta>

...I and many others see these traces, and each one sees much better ones. But beyond these, I saw two principal things, which perhaps not many see, even those with sharp eyes. The first is this: that she <note>Pico is personifying Lorenzo's muse or poetic style.</note> hides her riches to avoid envy; she keeps flowers in her lap and does not show them off; she does not grow tall into plants, but remains humble like a noble lady so that she appears smaller. The second thing I do not see clearly what it is, nor am I so skilled, but I see it is something—I know not what—that I would call most distinctly **Laurentian** <note>original: *laurentianum*; meaning uniquely characteristic of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>. For if one sees the gifts of Lorenzo, his genius, and his excellence, one would see the whole Lorenzo graphically portrayed. But perhaps I have said too much of these things; even against my will, the sentiment of my mind, as they say, has pulled me sideways into words. I will not omit to urge you with the greatest effort I can, that stealing some little bit of leisure from governing the republic, you might devote yourself to completing the paraphrase—both for the honor of your native tongue and your citizens, and for the use and pleasure of us all.

->At Florence, on the Ides of July, 1484.<-

<note>A faint circular mark or stamp is visible on the left side of the page, likely an archival mark.</note>

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his Hermolao Barbaro, greetings.**<- <note>original: "S." stands for *Salutem*, the standard Latin greeting.</note>

Indeed, my Hermolao, I can neither remain silent about what I feel concerning you, nor fail to feel those things which ought to be felt about a man in whom all things are found in the highest degree, as if individually. But if only my mind were capable of conceiving of you as your merits deserve; if only I had that power of speech to eventually express what I always feel. I know that what I have conceived of you falls infinitely below the heights of your learning. You also know that whatever we speak is far less than what we conceive; know that words are as lacking for the soul as the soul is for the matter. And yet, do you believe I dare so much as to hope I can imitate your works, whose magnitude I cannot even estimate? All can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And if only I had such good fortune that what I write might in some part reflect my Hermolao. 

For your style itself—to say nothing of the rest—to which you show so little favor: how much it affects me, how much it delights me! It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, refined, and ingenious. In it, nothing is exposed, nothing is trivial, whether you look at the words or the thoughts. Our friend Politiano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a leading humanist scholar and poet.</note> and I often read whatever letters of yours we have, whether addressed to others or to us. The subsequent parts always compete with the previous ones, and new graces bloom fruitfully during the reading, so that with a certain perpetual acclaim we have no room to catch our breath. But it is wonderful to say how you persuade and drive the reader's mind wherever you wish. 

I have experienced this, as always at other times, so especially in this most recent letter of yours to me. In it, while you attack these **barbarian philosophers** <note>This refers to the medieval Scholastic thinkers, whom the Renaissance Humanists often criticized for their "rough" or "un-Ciceronian" Latin.</note>—whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, rude, and uncultured; who did not live while they were alive, let alone live now that they are dead; and if they live now, they live in punishment and disgrace—I was so moved, and so ashamed and disgusted by my own studies. For I have already spent six years among them, so that I wish I had done less than to have struggled so laboriously in a matter of so little value. I have lost (I said) better years among <margin>Thomas</margin> Thomas, <margin>John Scotus</margin> John Scotus, <margin>Albert</margin> Albert, and <margin>Averroes</margin> Averroes <note>Pico lists the giants of medieval thought: Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Albert the Great, and the Islamic commentator Averroes.</note>; so many vigils in which I might perhaps have become something in good literature...

<meta>This page transitions from Pico della Mirandola's letter to Lorenzo de' Medici into his famous 1485 letter to the Venetian scholar Hermolao Barbaro. In the previous page, Pico praised Lorenzo's poetic genius. Now, he addresses Barbaro’s criticism of medieval "barbarian" philosophers. Pico adopts a clever rhetorical strategy: he writes a fictional defense from the perspective of one of those "barbarian" thinkers to argue that wisdom is more important than eloquent style.</meta>

I was thinking to myself, as a way of consoling myself, whether if any of those <note>Pico refers here to the medieval Scholastic philosophers, often mocked by Renaissance Humanists for their "uncultured" Latin.</note> were now to return to life, they—men who are otherwise full of arguments—would have anything by which they might defend their cause with some reason. Finally, it occurred to me that perhaps one of them, a bit more eloquent than the rest, would defend his "barbarism" <note>original: *barbariem*; here meaning a lack of classical rhetorical polish.</note> in as little a "barbaric" way as possible, perhaps in this manner: 

"We have lived as famous men, O Hermolao, and we shall live hereafter; not in the schools of grammarians and elementary teachers <note>original: *pedagogiis*; Pico distinguishes between those who merely teach the rules of language and those who seek the truth of things.</note>, but in the circles of philosophers, in the assemblies of the wise. In those places, the discussion and debate is not about the mother of Andromache <note>A reference to obscure mythological trivia often debated by grammarians.</note>, nor about the children of Niobe <note>A mythological figure whose children were killed by Apollo and Artemis; another example of 'light' literary topics.</note>, nor light trifles of that sort, but about the principles of human and divine things. In contemplating, inquiring into, and unravelling these matters, we were so subtle, sharp, and keen that we might perhaps seem to have been sometimes too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be too fastidious or excessively curious in the investigation of truth. And indeed, in these matters, if anyone should accuse us of dullness or sluggishness—come now, please, whoever he is, let him match his step with ours; he will find that we possessed..." <note>The text cuts off here, but Pico is setting up a challenge for the Humanists to match the intellectual rigor of the Scholastics.</note>

<meta>This page continues the fictional defense of the medieval "barbarian" philosophers against the criticisms of the humanist Ermolao Barbaro. Pico, writing as a Scholastic thinker, argues that ornate language is actually a distraction from the pursuit of truth.</meta>

[Marginal note: Synesius]
...pursue. We would condemn these things in a matron; therefore, it is not we, but those fools who celebrate the Bacchanalia at the feet of Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth and virginity; the Bacchanalia were wild, drunken festivals. The author argues that mixing flashy rhetoric with "chaste" philosophy is a sacrilege.</note>. They dishonor the gravity and chastity of philosophical matters with trifles and curling-irons, as it were. Truly, what Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neo-Platonist philosopher and bishop.</note> said of a youth can be aptly said of a speech: a well-coiffed speech is always an effeminate one <note>original: *cinedam*; refers to an effeminate man or a catamite, used here as a harsh critique of overly ornamental rhetoric.</note>. Therefore, we prefer our own style to be shaggy-haired, solid, and unrefined, rather than beautifully coiffed with the mark or suspicion of impurity.

And even if there were nothing else, this is most true: nothing is more contrary to the purpose of a 
[Marginal note: Socrates]
philosopher in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride in any part. Socrates <note>The famous Greek philosopher, known for his simple lifestyle and focus on ethical truth over style.</note> used to say that Sicyonian shoes were handy and fit the foot; but they did not suit Socrates at all. There is not the same rule for civic dress and philosophical dress, just as there is not for the table or for speech. The philosopher uses these things only 
[Marginal note: Pythagoras]
for necessity; the citizen uses them for elegance. If the citizen neglects elegance, he is not a citizen; and if the philosopher affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras <note>The pre-Socratic philosopher known for his asceticism and the doctrine of transmigration of souls.</note> could live without food, he would even spare the vegetables. If he could explain his thoughts by a look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not speak at all. So far is he from polishing and adorning his tongue; we must guard against this so that the reader, enticed by the "medicated skin" <note>original: *cute medicata*; a metaphor for artificial rhetorical beauty, like makeup.</note>, does not linger there and fail to reach the marrow and blood. We have often seen corruption underlying a face painted with white lead <note>original: *cerusato*; ceruse was a toxic white-lead cosmetic used in the Renaissance to achieve a pale complexion.</note>.

We have seen it, I say, in all those for whom it has come into use for this very reason:
[Marginal note: Musonius]
since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain, they hold the reader at the surface with various modulations and harmonies. If a philosopher does this, Musonius <note>Gaius Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD, known as the "Roman Socrates."</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player singing. Therefore, let it not be held against us as a vice that we failed to do what it would have been a vice to do. We seek *what* we should write, not *how*; or rather, we seek the "how" in this way: namely, without pomp or any floral display of speech. We do not want it to be delightful, charming, or witty, but useful, grave, and reverent—so that it may attain majesty from its ruggedness <note>original: *horrore*; in this context, it refers to a rough, unpolished, and serious aesthetic associated with ancient wisdom.</note> rather than grace from softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater, or a smooth or rhythmic closing cadence to soothe the ears, where one part is false and the other is charming.

Instead, we expect the silence of the few in their admiration, as they look deeply into something either unearthed from the inner sanctuaries <note>original: *adytis*; the most sacred, private parts of a temple.</note> of nature or brought down to men from the heavenly court. Let them find something so sharp in its reasoning that there is no room for defense, and so well-defended that there is no room for argument. Let them admire us, moreover, as keen in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, grave in judgment, binding the entangled, and easy in untying them. Let them admire in us a brevity of style pregnant with many great things: how well-instructed we are to remove ambiguities, to dissolve difficulties, to unroll what is folded, and to both weaken the false and confirm the true with persuasive syllogisms. 

By these titles, O Hermolao, we have defended our memory thus far, and we do not doubt we shall defend it from oblivion hereafter. For if we are held by the common crowd, as you say, to be dirty, rude, and uncultured, this is to our glory and not to our shame. We did not write for the common crowd, but for you and those like you. Just as the ancients kept the ignorant away from the mysteries with their enigmas and the veils of fables, so we have been accustomed to frighten them away from our feasts, which they cannot help but pollute...

He cites ancient authorities like Socrates and Pythagoras to argue that true wisdom should be unadorned and even "rugged" to discourage superficial readers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the "barbarian" style of the Scholastic philosophers is intentional and superior to the polished rhetoric of the humanists. Pico (speaking as a Scholastic) argues that true wisdom is hidden beneath a rough exterior, much like the Silenus statues of antiquity.</meta>

...since it is not fitting for philosophers to be merely approved of, nor even understood by the common people, it cannot but be unbecoming for anything they write to be theatrical, pleasing to the crowd, or popular—that which finally seems to accommodate itself to the judgment of the multitude. 

But you wish me to fashion an image of our speech. It is the very image of the Sileni of our Alcibiades <note>original: "alcibiadis"; referring to the famous comparison in Plato’s *Symposium* where Socrates is compared to a Silenus statue—ugly on the outside but containing golden images of the gods within.</note>. 
[Marginal note: Alcibiades]
For the images of these were of a shaggy, hideous, and contemptible appearance. But inside, they were full of gems, of rare and precious treasures. So, if you look from the outside, you might see a wild beast; if you look within, you would recognize a deity. 

But you will say: "My ears cannot bear it, now harsh, now gaping, always in an inconsistent texture. They cannot bear those barbarian names, almost terrifying in their sound." O delicate one, when you approach flute-players and lyre-players, leave your ears behind you <note>Meaning: surrender to the sensory pleasure of the music.</note>. But when you summon philosophers, return from the senses to yourself, into the inner sanctuary of the soul and the recesses of the mind. Assume those ears of Apollonius of Tyana 
[Marginal note: Thianeus]
<note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher credited with supernatural perception.</note>: with which, since he was not entirely in the body, he heard not the earthly Marsyas <note>A satyr in Greek mythology who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and was flayed for his hubris.</note>, but the celestial Apollo, tempering the melody of the universe with his divine lyre in ineffable modes. If you taste the words of philosophers with these ears, they will seem honeyed to you, enough to make Nestor <note>The eldest and wisest of the Greek heroes at Troy, known for speech "sweeter than honey."</note> envious. 

But let us leave these things aside, rising far too high. Truly, to loathe a less polished style in a philosopher who is disputing most subtly is the mark not so much of a delicate stomach as of an insolent one. It is no different than if someone, while Socrates was teaching about morals, were offended by a loose shoe or a gaping toga, or became angry over an unevenly cut fingernail. Tullius [Cicero] 
[Marginal note: Tullius]
does not demand eloquence in a philosopher, but rather that he satisfy the requirements of the subject matter and doctrine. He knew, being such a wise and learned man, that it is our task to compose the mind rather than our speech; to take care that reason does not go astray, rather than the oration. 

It pertains to us to have the "internal word" <note>original Greek: *en diathesei logon*; the internal thought or reason.</note>, not the "spoken word" <note>original Greek: *ton en prophora*; the external utterance or speech.</note>. It is praiseworthy in us to have the Muses in our soul and not on our lips, lest anything in the soul sound too harsh through anger, or too weak through lust; finally, lest there be any discord from that genuine harmony by which the soul is melodiously tempered. When Plato 
[Marginal note: Plato]
understood that these theatrical things and the poems of poets often corrupted the state, he banished all poets from his republic, but left the governance to philosophers. Surely, they would be condemned to exile if they ever imitated poets through the wantonness of their discourse. 

But Lucretius 
[Marginal note: Lucretius]
will insist that even if philosophical treatises do not need the pleasantness of speech in themselves, nevertheless, by its application, the austerity of the subjects themselves must be hidden. Just as wormwood drives out diseases by itself, yet the cups are smeared with honey so that the improvident age of children may be deceived <note>A reference to *De Rerum Natura* 1.936, where Lucretius explains he uses poetry to make his difficult philosophy more palatable.</note>. This, perhaps, was necessary for you to do, O Lucretius, if you were writing your works for children or for the common people; it was certainly necessary for you, who would serve not only wormwood but the purest poisons <note>Pico here attacks Lucretius's Epicurean philosophy as spiritually poisonous.</note>. 

But we must hold to a far different method: we who, as we said before, do not seek to allure the common crowd, but to frighten them away. We serve not foul wormwood, but nectar. But Lactantius 
[Marginal note: Lactantius]
<note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who used classical rhetoric to defend the faith.</note> will contend that it is well-established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners, even elders, when it is both equipped with force and adorned with the light of oratory. If you had been, O Firmianus [Lactantius], as frequent in the sacred scriptures as you were in fictitious lawsuits, you would not have said this; and perhaps you would have confirmed our views no less well than you destroyed those of others. 

Tell me, I pray, what moves more strongly and persuades more than the reading of the sacred scriptures? They do not merely move, they do not merely persuade; but they compel, they stir, they apply force. You read words that are rude and rustic, but living, animated, flaming, stinging, penetrating to the very depth of the spirit, transforming the whole man with a marvelous power. Alcibiades says 
[Marginal note: Pericles]
[Marginal note: Alcibiades]
that he was not moved at all by the elaborate and brilliant speeches of Pericles...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s famous 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro. Pico is defending the "barbarian" philosophers (the Scholastics of Paris) against the criticisms of the Italian Humanists, arguing that the substance of wisdom is far more important than the beauty of the language used to express it.</meta>

...Spanish, or what common people are accustomed to call Parisian. When they speak to you, it will happen that they are mostly laughed at and mostly not understood; the same will happen to you when speaking among them. **Anacharsis commits a solecism <note>original Greek: αναχαρσισ παραθηναιοισ σολοικιζει. αθηναιοι δε παρα σκυθαισ. A solecism is a grammatical error or "speaking incorrectly." Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher in Athens; Pico uses this to show that "correct" speech is relative to where you are.</note> among the Athenians, and the Athenians among the Scythians.** If the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we consult rhetoricians or philosophers—who alone have clearly seen and explored the nature of all things—concerning this correctness? Perhaps the things which the ears reject, as they are somewhat harsh, reason accepts, as they are more akin to the things themselves.

But why was it necessary for those philosophers to innovate their language, and if they were born among Latins, why not speak in Latin? They were not able, O Ermolao, while they were reading the laws of the fates and the order of the universe in the heavens, while they were reading the turns of being born and passing away in the elements, and the powers of simple things and the temperaments of mixtures—they were not able, I say, at the same time to annotate the properties, laws, and observances of the Roman tongue in Cicero, Pliny, or Apuleius. They were seeking what was repellent and what was accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care what the Romans did. 

Indeed, I now place you in a better position: I grant you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired in a mutual bond. <margin>Philostratus</margin> Philosophers have separated wisdom from eloquence; historians, rhetoricians, and poets have separated them; Philostratus lamented that eloquence was separated from wisdom. You do not doubt that these [the eloquent] will live with celebrated fame, while those [the philosophers] will live only in punishment and insult. <margin>Cicero</margin> See what you are doing! Cicero prefers an unpolished wisdom to a foolish loquacity. In money, we do not ask with what mint it was struck, but of what material it consists. Nor is there anyone who would not prefer to have pure gold under a German stamp than counterfeit under a Roman symbol. They sin who make a divorce between the heart and the tongue; but those who are entirely without a heart and are only a tongue, are they not mere <margin>Cato</margin> **funeral glossaries**, as Cato says? <note>original: "mortuaria gloſaria"; Cato the Elder used this term to describe people who are full of words but have no life or spirit.</note> 

We can live without a tongue, perhaps not comfortably; but without a heart, we cannot live at all. He who is unaccustomed to more polished literature is not inhuman; but he who is devoid of philosophy is not a man. The most unrefined <note>original: "iſantiſſima"; Pico often uses "insans" or "inept" to mean a style that lacks rhetorical polish.</note> wisdom can be beneficial; unwise eloquence, like a sword in a madman’s hand, cannot help but be extremely harmful. 

Therefore, you will say, are statues also commended not by their figure but by their material? <margin>Cherillus</margin> And if Choerilus had sung the same things as Homer, or if Bavius <margin>Homerus</margin> and Virgil had sung of the same things, would they have been equally received <margin>Meuius</margin> among the poets? Do you not see the disparity of the comparison? <margin>Vergilius</margin> 

We also assert that a thing is estimated by its form <term>species; in Scholastic philosophy, the "form" or "species" is the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</term>, not from its subject matter. For a thing is what it is because of its form. But someone is to be received among philosophers by one kind of form, and among poets by another. <margin>Lucretius</margin> Let Lucretius write about nature, about God, or about providence; <margin>Scotus</margin> let one of our own write about the same things; let John Duns Scotus write, and indeed in verse so that he might be more "inept" <note>inept: meaning lacking in poetic grace.</note>. 

Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the void; that God is corporeal and ignorant of our affairs; and that all things are carried along by the random collision of small bodies. But he will say these things in Latin and elegantly. John [Scotus] will say that things consist of nature, constituted by their matter and form; that God is a separate Mind, knowing all things and providing for all. Nor is He moved in the least from His peace because He sees and governs all things, even the lowest; but, as is usually said, **He descends without descending.** <note>original Greek: κατιοντα μη κατιεναι; a Neoplatonic concept of God’s providence reaching the world without God leaving His divine state.</note> 

But he [Scotus] will speak tastelessly, rudely, and not in Latin words. I ask you: who would doubt which is the better poet, or which is the better philosopher? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus philosophizes as much more correctly as the other speaks more ornately. But see how they differ: this one has an unsavory mouth, the other a foolish mind. This one is ignorant of the decrees of grammarians (not to mention poets); the other is ignorant of the decrees of God and nature. This one, most unrefined in speaking, feels those things which are to be praised...

SS iii

<meta>This page concludes Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Ermolao Barbaro and begins a new letter to the Carmelite poet Battista Mantovano. The previous page established Pico's rhetorical exercise of defending the "uncouth" style of scholastic philosophers by arguing that truth is more important than verbal elegance.</meta>

...they cannot be praised enough; that man, being most eloquent in speaking, utters unspeakable things. These men will perhaps assert these things, my dearest Ermolao, in defense of their own **barbarism**, or perhaps things that are far better in their subtlety. I do not entirely agree with their opinion, nor do I think any noble and free-born man should. But I have gladly exercised myself in this **infamous** subject, just as some write praises of the **Quartan fever** <note>The "Quartan fever" refers to a form of malaria. Pico is comparing his defense of "ugly" scholastic Latin to a common rhetorical exercise where a writer tries to praise something universally disliked to show off their skill.</note>: both so that my talent might be tested, and with this intention—much like that Glaucon in **Plato** who praises justice not out of personal judgment, but to stimulate **Socrates** to greater praises of justice. 

In the same way, I have been carried away, with my senses and nature rebelling a little, into attacking the cause of eloquence so that I might hear it defended by you. For if I thought eloquence should be neglected or held as inferior to the "barbarians," I would not have almost entirely defected from them to it—as I have recently done—to Greek literature, and to your never-sufficiently-praised **Themistius** <note>Themistius was a 4th-century statesman and philosopher known for his paraphrases of Aristotle, which Ermolao Barbaro had recently translated into Latin.</note>. 

However, I will say freely what I feel: certain **grammarians** turn my stomach. When they have mastered the origins of two small words, they show themselves off so much, they sell themselves so much, and they carry themselves about so boastfully that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want these philosophies of yours," they say—and what wonder? Neither do dogs want **Falernian wine** <note>A famous high-quality wine from antiquity; Pico implies the grammarians lack the refined "palate" to appreciate deep philosophy.</note>. 

But let us close this letter with this conclusion. If those "barbarians" earned any honor or name for themselves through the knowledge of things alone, it is not easy to say what place or what praises you should claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers and—to speak in Greek—**the most philosophical** <note>original: φιλοσοφωτατοσ (philosophōtatos)</note> among the eloquent.

Florence, the 3rd of the Nones of June, 1485.

***

Greetings, most beloved father. Concerning **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD. Pico and Battista are discussing his character, which was controversial among Christians.</note>, I feel nothing other than what you feel, about which matter I shall write more to you when there is leisure, and which will perhaps not be unwelcome to you. 

Regarding the difference of our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the **Book of Genesis**, where it deals with **Eve** and the **serpent**, this is indeed my opinion: It is in the Hebrew: "As you write, **he** shall crush your head," and it refers to the seed of Eve, about which it had been said, "I will put enmities between your seed and her seed." However, the **Septuagint** <note>The primary Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated it as "**she** shall crush your head." Yet the sense is the same in both cases: for what is said as "he shall crush" looks not so much to the person of Eve herself as to Eve’s **posterity**. Since that which is done in one's seed is said to be one's own doing. 

But as for why they preferred to translate it as "**she**" rather than "**he**," I believe the reason was to signify that since not only females but also males were to be propagated from Eve, that which was said of the "seed" should be referred to the female seed alone. These are the things that come to mind at present on this matter. 

I am constantly working on the **Harmony of Plato and Aristotle**. I give it its due time every morning; after the midday hours, I give time to friends, to my health, and occasionally to poets and orators, and whatever studies are of lighter labor. The night belongs to itself and to sleep. Your **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist scholar and close friend of Pico.</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me. 

Florence, the 20th day of March, 1485.

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Brother **Battista Mantovano** of the Order of Carmelites, distinguished poet, philosopher, and theologian, etc. 

From your son, Giovanni of Mirandola.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his famous defense of the "barbarian" philosophers to more personal letters. It features a letter to the famous printer Aldo Manuzio and several letters to his close friend and intellectual rival, Ermolao Barbaro, following Barbaro’s appointment as Patriarch of Aquileia.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Aldo Manuzio, greetings.**

I am sending the Homer which you desired, though later than you wished and I owed. I am so distracted by work, my dear Aldo <note>Aldo Manuzio (c. 1449–1515) was a famous humanist and printer, founder of the Aldine Press, known for his portable editions of Greek and Latin classics.</note>, that there is no room even to catch my breath. I have long since devoted myself to letters in servitude, as you well know. They, according to their own command, demand such a severe task of reading and dictating that I can scarcely redeem my health. As for what you write you will do: gird yourself for philosophy; but on this condition, that you remember no philosophy exists which should call us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks truth, theology finds it, religion possesses it. Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the 1490th year of grace.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, greetings.**

I hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people on receiving the best of pastors; the whole Church on a most strenuous soldier; and you on the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are nearly three kinds of living: the civil, the contemplative, and the religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; in the third—as if at the summit <note>original: "fastigio" - peak or rooftop</note> of the whole life—besides those two, we also require sanctity. Before this time, your city <note>Ermolao Barbaro was a Venetian nobleman; the "city" refers to the Republic of Venice.</note> found you to be most diligent and prudent in conducting the republic and in handling their great affairs; and all students love and admire you as a patron and defender of the liberal arts. As for what remained—this religious life—we know without doubt that you will fulfill it, and we rejoice so sincerely that the Church will surely owe no less to you in the future than your city and letters have owed you thus far.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his dear Ermolao, greetings.**

What shall I say this is, my Ermolao, that you daily burden me with new favors? It is as if you owed me something, to whom I have long since owed everything. My brother Antonio came here in recent days, returning to his homeland. I asked him what Ermolao is doing. "This is what he does," he replied: "He loves you, praises you, and carries you to the heavens—with me, with others, and even before the Pope himself; and he does this so constantly and so strongly as if he had nothing else to do." Friends I have there also write to me sometimes, especially one, Cosimo Pazzi <note>Cosimo Pazzi (1466–1513) was an associate of Pico and later became the Archbishop of Florence.</note>—a man worthy of your singular love, to sum up his praises at once. Truly, as often as he writes, he writes of your favors toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful inclination of mind, so that you always speak and feel of me most honorably. Oh, this unheard-of kindness of yours! You never think it enough for you to be among men of eloquence <note>original: "homines dictionis" - men of speech or orators</note>, and if you are such toward me so that you might make me more yours and bind me more closely, you are "doing what has already been done" <note>original: "actum... agis" - Pico uses a Latin idiom to suggest that Ermolao is working hard to win the friendship of someone who is already his most devoted friend.</note>, as they say. I cannot owe more, nor love more. But such a man you are: surpassing all others in prudence...

<meta>This page transitions from Pico's short note to Girolamo to a longer, more philosophical letter addressed to his dear friend, the renowned scholar Angelo Poliziano. Pico discusses the arrival of Poliziano's translation of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus and its transformative effect on his household.</meta>

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, greetings.**

My "loves" <note>original: "amores" — Pico is likely referring to his own writings or poetic works in a playful, personified way.</note> declare that they have never been received more courteously or more cheerfully than they were in these last <margin>18</margin> few days at your house. When they were most affectionately "stabbed" <note>A metaphor for Poliziano’s sharp editorial corrections or critiques.</note> they congratulated themselves most greatly and owed you very much. For who would not wish to die by that sword of yours? They grieve, however, that it was done more indulgently than was proper; and they are inclined to doubt whether love itself made you blind toward my "loves." And they doubt it so much that they do not quite trust your judgment—otherwise so grave—in their own case. They trust it nonetheless, and now they claim their chains; they do not know how to be at home, and they securely demand their freedom and the public. But what shall I say of the liveliness of your "Epictetus"? <note>Referring to Poliziano's Latin translation of the *Enchiridion* (Manual) of Epictetus, the Stoic philosopher.</note> Oh, what a humorous thing, worthy of a laugh from Cato himself! He was hardly across the threshold when, opening his robe, he said: "Behold the daggers! Behold the arrows!"—or, if you do not know Greek, "Behold the marks of criticism!" <note>original: "obelos" — the dagger-shaped marks used by ancient editors to flag errors or suspect passages.</note> "Behold me, ready to strike back if any of you should be bold enough." Who could have restrained their laughter when a man of the Stoa <note>The "Stoa" was the painted porch in Athens where Stoic philosophy was taught; Pico is personifying the book as a Stoic philosopher.</note> joked so charmingly? We certainly held back our weapons, both because he was determined to repay any injury and because his skin had grown so thick that it would not admit such light blows. Therefore, we received the old man with the veneration we owed him. Once he had finally settled among us, he began to philosophize about ethics. And he did so in Latin, not so much because he was among Latins (for there were those in that assembly who knew Greek), but so that he might taste more brilliantly through your own Latin benefit. But he did not waste his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he had made Stoics out of us Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle; Pico is saying they were converted from Aristotelianism to Stoicism by the book.</note>. And we all approved of that *apatheia* <note>original: "apathian" — the Stoic ideal of equanimity or freedom from emotional suffering.</note> of his, so that you might now see that those who were slightly delicate men a moment ago have now become the most tolerant of all. We can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves; we who would never struggle against fate, and who wish for things that are not our own to happen only as God wills. We would never blame nor accuse them; we would grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and not know how to be enslaved or conquered. Let us philosophize in deed, not just in speech, and we who are novices should observe ourselves as if we were adversaries. Let us neglect, rather than reject, the opinion of others about us and other external things of that kind. Let us care for the day as travelers care for an inn; finally, let us possess those things, rather than being possessed by them. Let us love silence, lest anything be vomited up undigested. And let us rarely cause laughter for others, and never for ourselves. To embrace the whole of Epictetus in a single word: we have abundantly learned both to endure adversity and to abstain from pleasures <note>original: "sustinere aduerſa / & abſtinere uoluptatibus" — a reference to the famous Stoic maxim, "Bear and Forbear."</note>. See how, point by point, we have shaped our life according to your Epictetus. See how quickly we have done so, lest in this part too we should not be Stoics, who want us to be warned that a man fails as long as he does not make progress. Though I have admired this in others, I have admired it most of all in myself. I, who have always spent time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The sites of Aristotle’s and Plato’s schools, respectively.</note> and never in the Stoa, have been so conquered by the old man’s speech that I have gone over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. I am sending you the index of the Greek books that are here with me, along with Manuel’s letter, as your correspondence requested. I likewise desire an index of yours. Give my greetings to the younger Lorenzo <note>Likely Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici (1463–1503), a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> in my name; I was going to write to him, but shame deterred me, lest I seem to compel the man with letters. **Farewell.**

<meta>The text transitions from a letter to Poliziano to a new piece of correspondence addressed to the Venetian scholar and playwright Thomas Medius (Tommaso Medin). This letter serves as a formal "thank you" for the dedication of Medius's comedic play, likely his work 'Epirota'.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Thomas Medius, greetings.

That you have dedicated your story—and a festive and elegant one at that—to my name was a proof to me of both your learning and your singular benevolence toward me. Each is a weighty cause that urges and impels me to love you; which of the two more so, I do not know. For as in love (as the proverb says), not to have returned love for love is a disgrace, so also not to have loved such a highly praised man, even if not provoked to it, is the mark of either a rustic or a truly wicked mind. See, therefore, how you do not merely call me but pull me toward friendship with "double ropes" <note>original: "geminis funibus" — An ancient idiom meaning to be doubly bound or pulled by twice the force.</note> (as they say), since there is nothing in that story that does not smell of learning and wit. Nor could you have deserved better of me than to consult my name so kindly and liberally in the dedication of such an excellent story. I am so far from neglecting or accusing its subject matter that I approve of it with the greatest effort.

For it has always been my opinion—and one I think no learned person will challenge—that it requires a sharper wit to write these jests and stories (provided it is done with erudition and elegance, as you have most abundantly achieved) than to have discoursed ornately on the gravest matters. Indeed, since we judge a beautiful statue to have been fashioned far more from the "file" <note>The "file" (original: "lima") was a common metaphor among Renaissance humanists for the painstaking process of editing and refining a piece of writing to perfection.</note> than from the bronze or gold, why should it not be the same regarding humble versus sublime material? To have spoken significantly on a humble subject is certainly a matter of more business and therefore more praiseworthy. For the dignity of the subject matter "seduces" <note>original: "lenocinatur" — suggests the subject matter acts as a sort of "lure," making the work look better than the writer's skill alone would allow.</note> the work of the former; whereas whatever the latter brings that is worthy is drawn entirely from the writer’s own storehouse. The material itself contributes nothing, as if providing no "contribution" <note>original: "symbola" — referring to a shared meal where everyone brings a dish; here, the subject matter brings nothing to the table, leaving the author to provide everything.</note> to the pot. Nature diligently helps the former; the latter certainly contend against nature.

And even if this is so, I would not deny that among these humbler subjects I have mentioned, some are wonderfully superior to others, and there are some of that genre so low and so tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. This can never be a fault in those things which are repaired by the charming urbanity of jests. But truly, I judge those works should be placed on the "highest benches" <note>original: "summis subsellis" — A reference to the seating in ancient theaters or Roman senates, where the most honorable people sat in the front rows.</note> which have wit mixed with a "vivid" <note>original: "graphicam" — lifelike or detailed portrayal.</note> portrayal of ages and characters. Your story has all those qualities found in the comic poets, and you have imitated them most beautifully in the story you sent to me. What cleverness is there! What a timely and ingenious mixture of wits! How it delights! How charming and perfect it is in every way! And if anything appeared somewhat sordid or weak due to the humility of the material, it raises itself up by the light and dignity of your oratory, assuming both brilliance and strength. It is indeed a work (to speak briefly) that clearly demonstrates it was perfected by a most lettered man. But among all other things, that exquisite and fitting notation of morals, ages, and characters is especially dear to my heart; in this alone your wisdom, and that...

<summary>Pico writes to Thomas Medius to thank him for dedicating a comedic story (fabella) to him, arguing that writing "light" literature with elegance is more difficult and praiseworthy than writing on "grave" topics.</summary>
<keywords>Thomas Medius, literary criticism, wit, comedy, the "file" of editing, humanism, dedication, Roman theater metaphors</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes a letter to the Venetian scholar Thomas Medius and begins a significant correspondence with the physician-humanist Niccolò Leoniceno, followed by the start of a letter to the famous poet and scholar Angelo Poliziano. The text highlights Pico's role as a patron and book collector, specifically his interest in the Dominican library in Bologna.</meta>

...was to be sought from me: there is a mutual friendship between us, which you yourself (as became a most excellent man) initiated with a perfect sense of proportion <note>original: "amussis" — A carpenter's rule or level, used here metaphorically to mean the friendship was started with perfect alignment or "by the book."</note>. It remains that as often as you need either my resources—however small they are—or my efforts, you should put my goodwill toward you to the test. Nor shall I (if any opportunity is given) omit any kind of service toward you, just as you yourself did first toward me at the very threshold of our friendship. Farewell.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his friend Niccolò Leoniceno, greetings. <margin>115.</margin>

I would have spoken with you much more often and more extensively through letters, my sweetest Niccolò, if your location had been known to me either by messenger, or letters, or rumor. Indeed, I anxiously inquired about this from many, and received a doubtful answer from everyone. At last, in recent days, a letter from Antonio of Faenza <note>Antonio Cittadini (Faventinus), a philosopher and physician who later famously engaged in a public dispute with Pico.</note>, a most serious philosopher, to Thomas Frignanus fell into my hands. From these I learned that you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I gave a letter for you to a courier bound for Florence. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there. I grieved exceedingly; today Thomas indicated that you had departed Florence and were in Bologna. I immediately ordered these letters to be brought to you.

In these letters, I shall not strive to open my benevolence or singular love for you at greater length; for you must not doubt even the slightest bit regarding my goodwill toward you, unless you thought me—which is not my way—forgetful of your excellent virtue and your services toward me. I could not, however, help but wonder greatly that when you rescued yourself from the tumults of the city to seek a seat where you could live both peacefully and pleasantly, you either forgot this little town of ours or certainly looked down upon it. You seemed, Niccolò, to distrust either my will or my capacity; though the latter is indeed less than your merits deserve, the former is greater than you might think. It will be pleasing to me if you inform me of your plan, and most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my hearth with me, to live at leisure with me while others are occupied with Mars <note>Mars was the Roman god of war; Pico is referring to the political and military conflicts troubling the Italian states at the time.</note>.

For the rest, I am sending you *John the Grammarian* <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle whose works were essential to the Renaissance recovery of ancient Greek philosophy.</note> to you, which after not being found for many days has now been recovered. I am yours and I wait for you. Farewell. At Mirandola, July 20th, 1482. If you love me, take care with all diligence to get me an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic <note>The library of the Basilica of San Domenico in Bologna was one of the most prestigious scholarly collections in Italy.</note>; send it or bring it with you. Farewell again.

I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough considering the condition of the place and region; I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you, and the poem will not be unpleasant. Again, farewell.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Angelo Poliziano, greetings.

Because you praised me so much in your last letter, I owe you as much as I fall short of being worthily praised. For that is owed to each which is given freely, not what is paid out as a debt. Therefore, I myself owe you everything you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely the result of your kindness and singular benevolence toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are novices and little recruits <note>original: "tirunculi" — A term for beginner soldiers or young apprentices.</note>, who have only just moved a foot out of the shadows of ignorance; we have advanced almost nothing. It is kindly dealt with us if...

among the ranks of the studious. The learned possess a name—something else entirely—which is peculiar to you and those like you; such great honors do not suit me. Since of those things that are preeminent in literary studies, I have not only nothing fully explored, but have not yet even seen them except **through a lattice** <note>original: "pertransennam" — A classical idiom meaning to see something only partially or in passing, like looking through a screen or window.</note>. I too will use a similar refuge, so that I may find approval among poets and rhetoricians because I am said to philosophize; and among philosophers because I speak like a rhetorician and cultivate the Muses—though my situation is quite different from yours. For while I wish to **sit on two stools** (as they say) <note>original: "geminis... sellis sedere" — A proverb for trying to occupy two positions at once; Pico self-deprecatingly suggests he fails at both poetry and philosophy, whereas Poliziano masters both.</note>, I am excluded from both, and it finally happens (to put it briefly) that I am neither a poet, nor a rhetorician, nor a philosopher. You, however, so fully satisfy both that it is not sufficiently clear which you excel in more; you who embrace both Greek and our own **learning** <note>original: "minervam" — referring to Minerva, the goddess of wisdom; used here to denote literary and intellectual mastery.</note> so beautifully, like a swan of both languages, that it cannot easily be discerned what is unlearned and what is genuine. For, to say nothing of the Latins (for to whom would you yield first place among them?), who would believe (as was said of the Emperor Hadrian) that a Roman man could speak so much like a Greek? Our friend **Emanuel** <note>Probably Manuel Adramyttenus, a Greek scholar who worked closely with Poliziano and Pico in Florence.</note> swore while he read your works that Athens itself was not so Attic. You are that man, my Angelo—**away with flattery**—to whom only one or two of our men, if any at all, may be compared. If there were more such men, these centuries would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I beg you, and rescue literature as much as you can from its decay, lest that brilliance of the Roman language completely wither away through the injustice of time. Always forge something new that may help and illustrate the Latin cause. And those things you have at home, let them finally come forth for the common benefit of students. I indeed love and desire all your works just as I love yourself—all the more because I have set you before me as a model to be shaped by, even if you are one whom all ought to follow, but few can attain. Farewell.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Paolo Cortesi, Greetings.

<margin>b</margin>

You think well, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by the distance of places, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It is customary to relieve the longing for those absent if you perhaps have a statue or an image of them at home. To me, however, there seems to be this difference between an image and a letter: the latter portrays the **mind**, while the former portrays the body; the former sketches only the outer parts, while the latter clearly expresses and fashions even the innermost depths. The former represents, as it were, the tunic and garment of a friend; the latter represents the true friend to us. The former emulates the colors and shape of the flesh as best it can; the latter represents thoughts, counsels, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all emotions. And those secrets of the soul which almost no one speaks to himself when present, he transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. In short, the latter is a living and effective thing; the former is a dead and mute likeness. Let us, therefore, send these images of our souls to one another: you indeed the **golden and silver** ones you are capable of; I, perhaps, those of **bronze or clay** <note>Pico is using a common humanist trope of humility, comparing his own prose to base metals or common pottery, while praising Cortesi's style as precious metal.</note>. Thus we shall be beyond all injury of places and times. Just as the power of the mind itself knows neither the distances of space nor the delays of time. But truly, how much do I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, for...

you called me to this duty first, especially with such a letter—one that has held and delighted me so much that I cannot remember being more charmed by any reading for many days now. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and benevolence. Perhaps you were expecting me to say it was full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say that as well; for I am not so "iron-hearted" <note>original: "ferreus" — a classical metaphor for being unfeeling or stoic.</note>, or if you prefer the term, so much of a "philosopher," that I am not delighted by the praises of my friends. If those praises are true, they commend me to myself; if they are false, they commend to me the love and goodwill of the writer. Therefore, I shall easily persuade my philosophy to let me read your letters both often and with pleasure, even the parts where they praise me. But it is not so easy for me to appear sufficiently polite, or at least not ungrateful, in repaying this literary duty. For an **imperious mistress** <note>original: "imperiosa domina" — Pico refers here to Philosophy or his intense program of study, which he personifies as a demanding lady.</note> so distracts me, so exacts her daily task, and finally so occupies me entirely, that there is scarcely anything of "me" left even for myself. But such is your kindness that you will take even bad letters in good part when I write, and take my silence in good part when I am still. Poliziano, our common delight, sends you his greetings. Farewell.


->**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to Troilo Malvezzi.**<-

<note>The letter 'l' in brackets refers to a "guide letter," a small character printed as a cue for an illuminator to later paint a large decorative initial.</note> [l] Your **little book on lots** <note>original: "Libellus de sortibus" — Likely a treatise on divination or the theological implications of "lots" (casting dice or drawing names) to determine fate.</note> affected me with as much pleasure as usually affects one who has drawn the best lot of all. ->**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to Taddeo Ugolino.**<-

<note>The letter 'g' in brackets is a guide letter for the rubricator.</note> [g] I received your most welcome letters, full of love, faith, and charity; not only because you remembered me, but because in them you kindly remind me of myself—that is, of my virtuous studies and of the need to uphold the expectations I have raised. I hasten to Rome, where I shall make a trial of our studies—even a trial involving peril. If we achieve anything, it is God’s gift; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own frailty; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours; such is the integrity of your life and character that I would scarcely yield the first place in loving you even to **our Girolamo** <note>original: "Hieronymo nostro" — Likely a reference to the friar Girolamo Savonarola, who was a close spiritual friend to Pico during his final years.</note>. Farewell, from Fratta.

Thus, if you look at the words, nothing is more conflicting; if you look at the matter itself, nothing is more in concord. And if ever the opportunity is given—which is the summit of my prayers—to practice philosophy with you for several days, we shall discuss these matters more extensively in person, and we shall make some trial of this opinion of mine. Farewell, the glory of our age.

->Florence, December 6, 1484.<-
