->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Baldassare Migliavacca, Greetings.<-

You will be angry, and indeed not without cause, that my response to your letters comes much later than you perhaps desired and than your letters themselves deservedly required. Let me briefly explain why this happened. At almost the same time I received your letters, an honest man, though previously unknown to me, was about to travel to you. He said he was a merchant from Milan <margin>m</margin>. I thought this an opportune departure for me, through which it would happen that my letters would be delivered to you by a faithful messenger and—what I wished for most—without delay. But I struck the south wind <note>original: "austrum perculi" — a Latin idiom meaning to meet with bad luck or to have one's plans frustrated.</note>: for when he had postponed his departure for a month by delaying day after day, he finally left, but with me entirely unaware. Since I had become more negligent in the hope of a certain messenger, forgetfulness of the letters had almost crept upon me. Now at last, when your letter happened into my hands, it immediately woke me as if I were sleeping and reminded me of the time passed without performing my duty. I grieved (God is my witness) no small amount, and I grieve even now; nor would I wish these things said to excuse myself, but rather to accuse myself. I will easily allow myself to be condemned for negligence, and if you prefer, you may call it a punishment from you.

Now to your letters. I received no small pleasure both from the letters themselves and from the Greek books, of which you so generously and so kindly gave me the use. This was not so much because their use would do much for my studies, but because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual bond between us. This one friendship I value more than the entire library of either Sunandius <note>A likely reference to an ancient or legendary collector, contrasted here with the famous Library of Alexandria.</note> or Ptolemy <note>The Royal Library of Alexandria, founded by the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt.</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of concern or closer to my heart. Moreover, I know what place you claim for yourself among learned men; for indeed your letter was to me the clearest evidence of your teaching, erudition, and humanity. Therefore, if I did not love you very much, I would surely have forgotten myself and would be acting far differently than I am accustomed. I love you singularly, although I have never seen you; I love you so from my heart that I love few others more, so that, in short, something might be added to our intimacy, but to our love, nothing can. And if there is anything that could be added, it will all come from your arrival here. This you promised of your own accord in your letters, and we seek it so ardently as we impatiently desire it. If you obtain for me John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), an Alexandrian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly prized by Renaissance humanists.</note> on [Aristotle's] *Physics* and *Metaphysics*, you will have bound me to you in perpetual obligation. For I do not have them, and I am in great expectation of them. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Jacopo of Feltre, Greetings.**

Your letters have delighted me now more than ever before; in them, I have learned of the high regard you hold for me—an opinion so favorable that a better one could not even be imagined in one's prayers. One thing alone troubled me: since you noted nothing to criticize in what I wrote to you, you have caused me to suspect that you deemed nothing at all worthy of note. For I would have believed that most things pleased you only if you had indicated that at least some things displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony in my own case, however highly esteemed it may otherwise be. 

For you love everything of ours just as much as we do; and since, from the innate kindness of your nature <note>original: "ingenii tui facilitate" — refers to a gracious and approachable character common in Renaissance humanist ideals.</note>, you lift everyone up, this happens to you especially regarding my affairs—for you are the one from whose fountain everything that is in me has flowed. Indeed, I neither stop nor shall I cease to emulate you and to follow in your footsteps. If only I might one day catch up to you! 

But I grieve that the distance between our locations prevents me from hearing you in person as you treat the most profound topics of philosophy with your customary gravity. <meta>This page transitions from the correspondence with Jacopo of Feltre to a series of letters addressed to the famous humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano. <margin>c</margin>
# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

Since I have arranged those slender muses of mine—with which I toyed regarding my loves while my age permitted—into five small books, I am sending you the first of them. I shall send the rest if, in this one instance, I find you to be a friend and not a flatterer. Indeed, they come to you under the law that they be corrected and "beaten," so that they may pay the penalty for their errors with both the nail and the obelisk <note>original: "ungue et obeliscis" — technical terms for editorial marks; the "nail" (ungue) refers to scraping away mistakes, while the "obelisk" (†) was a mark used in ancient manuscripts to denote suspect or spurious text.</note>. Therefore, show yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unfair one; that is, be severe, rather than indulgent. For what greater injustice is there than to deceive a friend who expects everything of you? I am not of so delicate a nature as to be offended by another’s deletions, nor do I seem so handsome to myself that I would either neglect or accuse my censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me; even in those parts that please me more, I fear lest I be like that "Suffenus" <note>A reference to a character in the poems of Catullus who wrote prolifically but poorly, yet was utterly charmed by his own bad work.</note>. Truly, we are all deceived, and we do not see the knapsack that is on our own back <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable: humans carry two bags, one in front for their neighbors' faults and one behind for their own, which they never see.</note>. Therefore, do not deny your labor in this honest and noble matter to a man who is most friendly to you—especially one who requests it with such great zeal and from the bottom of his heart. If I were someone who could return the favor to you in such a matter, I would not remain silent about that Greek saying: that Lysippus was accustomed to use the work of Apelles, and Apelles the work of Lysippus, in turn <note>Pico refers to the legendary collaboration and mutual critique between Lysippus the sculptor and Apelles the painter, the greatest artists of antiquity.</note>. Farewell.

<margin>c</margin>
# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

When I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you which, as often happens, I had composed almost as a boy for the sake of exercising my mind. They were indeed insipid, unlearned, and trivial, easily betraying the author’s age and ignorance. You, however, approved of them—not because they deserved it, but out of your own kindness and indulgence. And for that very reason, to prove that you approved of them, you asked for copies; surely you were not unaware that such things are the sharpest incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue, so that, enticed by the desire for praise, they might soon strive to taste more deeply the small measure of glory they have sipped. For just as strength lies flat and cold in the face of despair, there is no one who doubts that it is raised up and set on fire by hope. 

But now the protection of my age is being taken away, and the errors which were previously excused will now be turned into a fault against me, because I, now more mature in years, have neither cleansed them better nor deleted them. Therefore, if you love me, either return to me those poems of mine which are in your possession, or tear them up, or commit them to the flames. All those works, more carefully elaborated, and many others which have fallen from my pen during my leisure since I departed from there, will soon be entrusted to your "file" <note>original: "limae" — a common humanist metaphor for the process of polishing and refining a literary text.</note>. In the meantime, let those things which cannot live without harming a friend be condemned by a fatal vote <note>original: "capitali damnentur calculo" — literally "the capital pebble," referring to the ancient practice of using black stones to cast a vote for a death sentence or total condemnation.</note>. 

Furthermore, I would very much like for you to send me your *Epictetus*, and whatever you have translated from Homer up to this day; likewise, what you composed regarding Giuliano de' Medici in our native tongue <note>referring to Poliziano's famous poem "Stanze per la giostra," written in Italian (the "native tongue") rather than Latin.</note>, and whatever else you have composed in the Latin language. I ask this of you as urgently as possible; for I desire them as one who is most impatient. There is no reason for you to refuse on the grounds that they have not yet been "brought to the navel" <note>original: "ad umbilicum... deducta" — an ancient idiom meaning "finished" or "completed," referring to the stick (umbilicus) around which a finished scroll was rolled.</note>. Since, if this is your wish, I already announce and promise you that all these things shall remain secret with me. Farewell.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.

It has always been my judgment, O most learned Marsilio, that there is no matter upon which one should labor more than ensuring that we do not, through sloth and laziness, in any way fall away from that nobility of soul by which—on the testimony of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a mythical figure thought by Renaissance scholars to be an ancient Egyptian contemporary of Moses and a primary source of divine wisdom.</note>—we are considered next after Jupiter <note>original: "Iovem" — In the context of the Platonic Academy in Florence, this refers to the supreme Divine Intellect.</note>. This has always been my chief concern: to acquire for myself, from wherever I could, the cultivation of the mind and the disciplines of the liberal arts. 

Although this purpose of mine has been most constant since my childhood, your exhortations, when I was with you in previous years, so greatly stirred and inflamed me; and never more ardently than from that time until this very day have I devoted myself entirely to letters. For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle. Pico spent several years studying Aristotelian philosophy and Scholasticism at the University of Paris and elsewhere before returning to the Platonic circles of Florence.</note>, and I have omitted nothing, as far as was in my power...

...think it necessary to write so that this might be paid as a debt to friendship. For this whole business of writing and sending letters belongs to a friendship that is weak and somewhat cold—one that does not stand firm enough supported by its own strength and seeks from elsewhere a foundation on which to rest. But for that friendship which has already taken deep root in the very retreats of the mind, why, I ask you, does it need the support of letters? 

I will give these letters of mine to Ermolao Barbaro <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a brilliant Venetian scholar and diplomat, known for his work in "cleaning up" corrupt ancient texts, particularly Aristotle and Pliny the Elder.</note> to bring to you, so that I may entice yours from you, which I most greatly desire. You, in turn, will return yours most abundantly so they are not desired by me in vain. For just as it belongs to a weak mind to use letters as if they were props <note>original: "tibicines" — literally 'flute-players' or 'supports/buttresses' used in architecture to keep a wall from falling.</note> for friendship so that it does not totter, so too it is a mark of exceptional liberality and benevolence to show oneself easy and beneficial to friends. 

Farewell. And please send to me Ptolemy’s *Music* <note>Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*, a foundational Greek text on the mathematical and philosophical ratios of music theory.</note>—if it is not an inconvenience to you—to remain here for a few days. For what should I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated all my own things?

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings.

I have never either pleased myself more or owed more abundantly than at this time, when I have summoned such sweet, such learned, and such letters so like yourself to me with a single letter of my own. If your absence from Padua while I was there, and my longing for your company for these two years, was the reason why you wrote these things to me, it cannot be anything but pleasant to me now. One single letter of yours has not only fulfilled but even surpassed my every wish. For I shall say nothing of the elegance, charm, learning, and sweetness of the letter, the reading of which demands a return of the favor in full. 

How much do you think it means to me that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so much from the heart? And, though I would not dare to wish for anything greater, you so liberally promise your effort on every side in honoring me. Indeed, I would not blush to confess openly that this kind of service is not only to be received but even to be sought after by me. For as you know, even the Stoics themselves do not approve of *apatheia* <note>original Greek: "απάθειαν" — freedom from passion or suffering, a state of emotional indifference.</note>, nor among these which the Greeks call *pathe* <note>original Greek: "πάθη" — passions or affections of the mind.</note> can any be more praiseworthy or more honorable than this: if only it is among those called the desire for name and glory. 

Truly, this can be provided to me by no one more fruitfully than by yourself, in whom all virtues, as if individually, strive to claim the palm of victory for themselves; and I certainly have no one to whom I would more willingly be indebted. Therefore, this promise of yours is as pleasing and desirable to me as it is honorable, and I rejoice in it most of all because it gives proof of a certain extraordinary love and a most loving goodwill toward me. At last I have what I have long desired before now; thus I now seriously triumph. I have, I say, Ermolao Barbaro, the delight of the Latin language and the distinguished storehouse of all the good arts, not only well-disposed toward me but as a most intimate friend. You likewise have Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, so devoted to you and so zealous for you that one could not be more devoted or more zealous. In mutual services toward you, since I can provide nothing either grand or worthy of Ermolao, I shall indeed be unequal; but if you look at my spirit, it will certainly be either equal or superior. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, etc.**

Nothing was sweeter to me while you were here among us than your company; likewise, nothing was more useful, such is the sweetness of your character and the depth of your learning. But see how sweet and how pleasing you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now, while you are absent, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But surely, if the seat of friendship is the soul—and we are, most of all, our souls, as Plato and Aristotle write <note>Pico references the classical philosophical idea that the true "self" is the intellect or soul, not the physical body; therefore, friends who are "of one soul" are never truly apart.</note>—there is no reason why any distance of place or long intervals of time should be able to create a separation between us. I was thinking just now how I might achieve being with you by some other means, and nothing else came to mind except that my late-night labor on the seven-fold narration of the six days of Genesis <note>This refers to Pico’s *Heptaplus* (1489), a complex mystical and philosophical commentary on the creation story in the Book of Genesis.</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were children—and the greatest part of a father is in his son—I too shall come to you in that which I have begotten. Receive, therefore, my little son as he comes to you, as cheerfully and willingly as you are accustomed to receive me. It will please you, I know, because you love me. I know also it will displease you, for the same reason: because you love me. For it is the nature of such devotion to look deeply into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and, having looked into them, to indulge them lightly so that we do not cause distress.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to F.B.C.Th.** <note>These initials likely refer to a specific theologian or cleric, possibly Fra Bernardino Cataneo or a similar figure whom Pico addressed as a spiritual father.</note>

<margin>f</margin> Hail, most beloved father. Here is Apollonius <note>Likely referring to the life of Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher, or a manuscript related to him.</note> for you; if I did not owe him to your virtue and your kindness toward me, I would certainly owe him because of this letter in which you demand him with such great love and humanity. For it is a mark of the highest love to call me to that place where you have already arrived—namely, to the purgation of the soul <note>original: "ad animi purgationem" — a Neoplatonic concept where the soul is cleansed of material distractions to prepare for divine contemplation.</note>, which is to say, toward true happiness. And it is a mark of the highest humanity to exhort me as if I were an equal, though you could give laws to me as if to a son. But would that it might happen one day in some retreat that we could, at last, philosophize piously together. You will see that for me, nothing comes before the joining of piety with wisdom. You will see that I am most firmly persuaded that there is no wisdom that should blot out the image of eternal wisdom within us <note>Pico argues that human philosophy is useless if it obscures the divine "image of God" within the human mind.</note>, for that makes us like the witless beasts. I have my guardian angel as a witness that I count as gain in my daily studies only as much as I emerge from them better instructed and stronger for the struggle of purifying the soul. This multifaceted handling of disciplines, and whatever literature can offer us, merely colors the skin and, as if with a painted face, makes us more beautiful. But we cannot hope for a sound, firm, and robust mind from anywhere else than from integrity of life, from morals, and finally, from divine religion. Therefore, you compel one who is already willing (if I may put it this way) to be even more willing. But help me also with your sacred prayers, so that I may be able to achieve what I myself desired and what you so greatly wish me to desire. Farewell, most loving father, whom I love uniquely and hold before my eyes. Florence, January 13, 1490. I await all your news. My dear Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous Renaissance poet and scholar who was Pico's closest friend.</note>, the delight of all literature, bids me send you his greetings.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings.**

I remember when I was deliberating which of the universities <note>original: "gymnasiis" — referring to the great Italian centers of learning.</note> of Italy I should most preferably choose as my seat for the study of philosophy, and although many things called me to Padua, I sought that place more willingly so that my love for you, which I had long nourished in my soul, might be confirmed through mutual company...

<meta>This page continues the letter from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the Venetian scholar and diplomat Ermolao Barbaro. It was clear: I was in Padua for two years. Yet, who would believe that I neither saw Ermolao nor knew him, except by the reputation I had heard long before? Thus it often happens that while we despise an offered opportunity through a certain idle procrastination, it slips from our hands like something slippery.

I have repented of this matter vehemently and continue to do so—and all the more so because that learning of yours in all matters, which I had previously known only by rumor, I have now recognized with these very eyes and these very ears, while I heard that "Roman Themistius" <note>original: "Romanum themiftium" — This refers to Ermolao Barbaro’s celebrated Latin translations and paraphrases of the works of Themistius, a 4th-century Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle. --- Page 312 ---
<meta>This page continues the letter from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro. In the preceding text, Pico was praising Barbaro's scholarship. Here, he shifts to a defense of his own choice to remain a private scholar dedicated to the "contemplative life" rather than entering political or "civil" service.</meta>

I do not oppose it, nor do I condemn or accuse those who do so. But it is far from the truth that it is not an error to have moved from the contemplative life to the civil life, or that it should be judged a disgrace—or marked as a fault or crime—not to have moved. Should it then be turned into a vice for someone if he perpetually strives for and pursues virtue itself for the sake of virtue, seeking nothing outside of it? While such a man searches out divine mysteries and the secrets of nature, let him enjoy this leisure <note>original: "otio" — In the Renaissance, *otium* (leisure) was not laziness, but the productive, dignified time a scholar spent away from public business to focus on study.</note>, despising and neglecting other things—since those pursuits are enough to satisfy the desires of those who follow them. 

Therefore, is it ignoble <note>original: "illiberale" — literally 'unworthy of a free man.' Pico is playing on the distinction between "liberal" studies (pursued for their own sake) and "servile" or "mercenary" work done for pay.</note>, or altogether unbefitting a prince, not to make the study of wisdom a mercenary pursuit? Who could endure or even listen to such things with a calm mind? Truly, he has never practiced philosophy who has done so only so that he might one day be able to—or want to—stop being a philosopher. That man was engaged in commerce, not philosophy. 

You write to me that the time is approaching for me to devote myself to one of the great princes of Italy. Until now, that opinion which philosophers hold concerning themselves...

<summary>Pico defends the contemplative life of a scholar, arguing that philosophy must be pursued for its own sake rather than as a tool for political advancement. He rejects the suggestion that he should leave his studies to serve a prince, equating "mercenary" philosophy with mere trade.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Ermolao Barbaro. Pico has just finished defending his commitment to a private life of study. ...is lacking in literary matters. In Rome or wherever on earth I may be, those princes will have someone whom they can command, whom they can turn at their whim like a treadmill-grinding slave <note>original: "trusatilem... molam" — an allusion to the Roman playwright Plautus, referring to a manual mill pushed by slaves as a form of punishment. Pico is saying he refuses to be a "tool" for princes.</note>, as Plautus says.

Regarding what you write about marriage <note>original: "re uxoria" — literally "the matter of a wife."</note>, I do not think it was said lightly or without reason. But I am Davus, not Oedipus <note>A classic proverb from the playwright Terence: "Davus sum, non Oedipus." Davus is a simple slave in the play; Oedipus famously solved the riddle of the Sphinx. Pico means he is a simple man who cannot solve the "riddles" of complex social or romantic schemes.</note>, nor would I wish to be if I could. Whatever it is, if it seems right, explain it more broadly; if not, remain Harpocrates <note>The Greek and Egyptian god of silence, often depicted with a finger to his lips.</note>. And as things unfold, I adapt my plan to the situation. 

There is no reason for you to desire my Tuscan verses <note>original: "Rhythmos meos ethruſcos" — Pico's early vernacular Italian poetry. As he grew more devoted to philosophy and theology, he became embarrassed by his youthful, secular love poems and reportedly burned many of them.</note>. For a long time now I have sent a dismissal to those amorous trifles, as I am meditating on other things. But I want you to be warned of this as well: regarding your "Laura" <note>This likely refers to a literary work or a specific lady Barbaro was writing about, perhaps echoing Petrarch's famous muse, Laura.</note>, if you were intending to publish it, hold it back for a few more days. For perhaps very soon our people will read things concerning love (mark what I say!) which they have not yet read. And you will be able to note many things that will be very useful for your project.

Regarding Alibrana <note>Likely a servant or assistant who had recently left Pico's service under poor circumstances.</note>, although he is not worthy of me speaking about him, I will say this: he has returned poor thanks to a master who deserved better. Nor is there any reason for him to cast or divert the blame for his flight onto anyone other than himself, since he owes my household—which he cannot deny—hardly less than he owes me. But this is not the first time, as you know, that he has either broken his word or mocked his master. I know what he has been saying against me and about me since he fled, but the elephant does not care about the gnat <note>original: "non curat culicem elephas" — a proverb expressing that a person of great status or mind is not bothered by petty insults from those beneath them.</note>. And I am willing to forgive you whatever this fickle man has done wrong until now. But let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced eventually to show myself to him in the same way he (undeservedly) showed himself to me. 

As for the fact that you excused that friend of yours—whose love affair turned out badly—to our friend Florian, you acted out of duty. Indeed, he has examples from history, from the poets, and even from philosophy itself with which to defend himself from the mark of a crime. He has means to protect himself by the precedents of great men: King David, and especially Solomon, not to mention Aristotle. Aristotle, while he often fell desperately in love with certain courtesans, remembered none of his own moral precepts when he performed sacrifices to his beloved woman as if to Eleusinian Ceres <note>Ancient sources claimed that Aristotle offered divine honors to his mistress or wife, Pythias, mirroring the sacred rites of the goddess Ceres (Demeter) at Eleusis.</note>. 

But he [your friend] does not merely embrace or love these defenses and bulwarks for his deed; rather, he hates, rejects, and refuses them. He laments his loss; he does not beg off his fault. He grieves because he sinned; he does not defend it. And for this very reason, it seems to me he should be excused by others, because he does not excuse himself at all. Nothing is weaker than man; nothing is more powerful than love. Even the invincible and unshaken mind of Saint Jerome, while it clung entirely to heaven, found itself among troupes of dancing girls <note>A famous reference to Saint Jerome's letter to Eustochium, where he describes how, even while fasting in the desert, his mind was tormented by visions of Roman dancing girls.</note>. 

What plague could infest a man that love would not tame? If love could do this in the wilderness, on the ground with limbs bruised, amidst weeks of fasting, what could it not do in a feather bed, in the shade, and in every abundance of delights? Add to this that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. He who has suffered shipwreck only once can complain to Neptune <note>A Latin proverb: "Improbe Neptunum accusat, qui iterum naufragium facit." It suggests that a first-time mistake is pitiable, but a second time is the victim's own fault.</note>. If he should strike the same stone again, let no one stretch out a hand; let no one take pity. Now, he cannot rightly *not* be excused, since he repents of the deed so much that he does not even judge himself worthy of the favor of an excuse. But this is already too much, since your friend desires that the memory of such a deed not only be kept out of writing but be entirely obliterated by his subsequent life.

Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received your letter. Commend me in no ordinary way to your lord and to the entire Borromeo family, whom I have always loved and now love very much. 

At Perugia, October 15, in the year of grace 1491.

<meta>The previous page concluded Pico’s correspondence with Ermolao Barbaro, where he defended his rejection of secular poetry and political service in favor of a life of study. # Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Giovanni Francesco, sends warmest greetings.

Your letters were most welcome to me. Not only because I had heard nothing from you for a long time, but also because they indicated things in which I took wonderful delight; since those same things are pleasing to you, I do not doubt they are also most pleasing to God. You too should have no doubt: if you continue on the path you have begun, your reward will be plentiful in heaven.

I have not yet sufficiently determined whether I must go to Rome or not. And as far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it more likely that I will have to go there; you know the reason <note>Pico was likely referring to his ongoing legal and theological negotiations with the Papal court following the condemnation of his 900 Theses.</note>. As soon as I have certainty on this, I will inform you immediately, so that if you happen to come here (which I would otherwise very much desire), you do not find me gone, or find that you must return to your homeland just as I am leaving.

In the meantime, you can remain at home, unless you feel otherwise. But remember also that you have a wife, to whom you owe your body just as you owe your soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some measure; you must consider what she either desires or could desire based on her physical condition and age, and what she might not ask for out of modesty or virtue. For why should I be ashamed to write these things which the Apostle Paul also wrote? <note>Referring to the First Epistle to the Corinthians (7:3-4), where Paul discusses the "marital debt" and mutual authority spouses have over one another's bodies.</note> There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could be more prone to error. Indeed, our men are greatly mistaken, thinking their wives are bound and devoted to them, but that they owe nothing to their wives—thinking they can decide whatever they please regarding themselves as they wish. Ultimately, you cannot belong entirely to yourself once you have submitted to the laws of marriage and willed to belong to a wife. Nevertheless, you can belong entirely to God, whose favor you earn when, in order to obey His law, you obey your own will less, even in those matters that concern God.

But I have spoken of these things with you in person elsewhere. As for me, as soon as the air turns to spring—that is, during the first days of Lent—when I have extricated myself from these thickets <note>original: "fasibus" — likely a variant of *fascibus* (bundles or stacks), referring here to his heavy workload of Greek manuscripts.</note> of Greek books, I will come immediately to Ferrara. Meanwhile, devote yourself to sacred scripture, and especially to the reading of the Gospels, which repeatedly brings the soul back to God; for the world with its lures and the devil with his deceits never cease, day and night, to lead it away from Him.

Farewell, half of my soul <note>original: "animae dimidium meae" — a classical expression of deep friendship used by Horace and Augustine.</note>, and pray to God for me. As soon as I have decided anything regarding my journey toward Rome, I will inform you. Florence, November 27, 1492.

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his dear Jacopo Antiquario, sends greetings.

Among the pleasures I used to take most from the company of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist scholar and poet who was a close friend of Pico and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> while I was in Florence—a man who is, in my opinion, the most learned of all in our age—it was no small delight that as soon as he received your letters, which were always so weighty and elegant, he would immediately give them to me to read. In them, I was greatly delighted by a certain singular prudence for which you are commended by the wisest of men, even in the handling of great matters and business; and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Moreover, because you made honorable mention of me in several of them, not only did your letters please me, but I even pleased myself in them—certainly yielding to the testimony of such a great man...

...while you call forth into the public eye my foolishness and those trifles that flowed from me in my more tender years. For all these things are quite inept and unlearned—or, if one were to judge them most kindly, they certainly are not of such a quality that they could sustain the opinion that those men have perhaps already conceived of me through your speech. I would wish you, however, to be asked to consider all these as lighter matters. For if you eventually desire my real works, I have more serious matters in hand which have not yet been brought to the final polish <note>original: *ad umbilicum nundum ducta sunt*, literally "not yet led to the navel." Giovanni Pico of Mirandola. <note>The initials R.C.C.S. following his name are likely abbreviated formal titles or a signature style specific to his rank as a Count of Concordia.</note>

<margin>Matthew</margin> Our friend Matthew <note>Probably Matteo Bosso (1427–1502), a regular correspondent and intermediary for Pico.</note>, a most dutiful man, both gave me much greeting in your words and most clearly declared with what love and benevolence you regard me. He promised, moreover, in your name, your zeal and your labor, if it should ever happen that I might use them. To which duty would that I were equal, most humane father. For I have always both desired and hoped to be taken into your trust and to be counted among your own. But to have you come to meet me of your own accord so kindly, approaching with such friendly and liberal promises, and calling me, as it were, to your friendship—if I may say so, yet you permit it—has surpassed my every hope and my entire vow. For what or how great a thing is it to be invited by one from whom it would have been enough simply not to be excluded? And you have done a thing which, even if it is not worthy of me, is nonetheless worthy of you. For according to my own merits, I might not have been admitted; yet, according to your humanity, I could not have gone uninvited. Therefore, how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe to you, I cannot explain, for I cannot even conceive of it. Certainly, I owe you all the more because you owe me nothing in return. For those things are neither too grand nor too numerous which Matthew and my other friends have reported, estimating me out of goodwill rather than judgment. But whatever or however great I am, allow me also to be among all those who honor and admire your virtues (to say nothing of the rest), through which one may see in you that which surpasses antiquity and that which cannot be surpassed by posterity. I would say this deservedly, since in you nothing is lacking that is placed in honor, prudence, or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you, one day, according to the wish of Plato <note>Refers to the famous "Philosopher King" ideal from Plato's *Republic*, where the state only finds peace when power and wisdom are united in one person.</note>, supreme power might be joined with supreme wisdom. But these things are from God. Meanwhile, I ask and pray this of you: that you provide me an opportunity not for returning thanks—for there is no room for that either because of your greatness or because of my insignificance—but for testifying to my spirit toward you, and for testifying to my faith and respect. You will find Giovanni Pico a man dedicated and devoted to you beyond all expectation. You cannot promise yourself more from him, but you can use all those things, whatever they may be, that are in him; when you use them, you will bring something of your own splendor to them, and they will become great when they begin to be yours, which, while they are mine, cannot be great. Farewell.

->### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Alessandro Cortesi, Greetings.<-

**Y**our letters were most welcome to me, which you recently sent—not, as you suppose, as one stranger to another, but as a friend and indeed an old friend to a friend, rather than a stranger to a known man; for you know me. You also knew me before, as you write, and you deemed me worthy of your love. I, likewise, have heard quite often of your learning and virtue, both from many others and especially from our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), one of the greatest scholars of the Italian Renaissance and a close associate of the Medici family.</note>, in whose judgment who would not trust? He created in me a faith in your integrity, just as he can create in you a faith in the benevolence I have long felt toward you. Indeed, even if that benevolence was already very great, know that through your letter it has received such additions as few could even conceive in their minds. For what is more pleasant than that letter? What is more learned? How scholarly it is, how amiable! You subscribe most generously to our friend **Poliziano**, who speaks of me more as a friend than with strict truth. Certainly, nothing more pleasing could have come to me from you, nor anything more honorable than your opinion of me. For all these things, I give you the greatest possible thanks, and I confess that whatever I have, or whatever is in me, I owe to my dear Alessandro. The letter of ours to **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and the most famous patron of the Italian Renaissance.</note> which you requested, I am sending to you.

->### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Domenico Benivieni, Greetings.<-

**G**reetings, my Domenico, chosen for the Lord's portion. <note>original: *in domini fortem*, a play on words regarding Domenico's name and his clerical or spiritual status.</note> Your letters were welcome to me, but it was even more pleasing to learn—both in person from your brother while he was here, and through letters from our friend Pietro Antonio—that you are of a stronger physical constitution and have a better stomach. If you care for all of us, and if you care for literature, then take care of your health. I have always been, and am now, solicitous for your health not only because I love you (for I love you vehemently), but because I love learning, which I believe—and indeed certainly know—is endangered along with you. If your brother reported to you any of my goodwill toward you, have the fullest faith in him; but if he said anything regarding my praises, believe him as little as he loves me much. There is no reason for you to wonder at our little commentary <note>original: *Commentariolum*. This likely refers to Pico's "Commentary on a Poem of Love" (*Commento*), a Neoplatonic exploration of beauty and desire based on a poem by Girolamo Benivieni.</note>; we intended to be at leisure and to do nothing at all, so we did this while relaxing our mind rather than exerting it. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries we are meditating upon regarding **Plato’s Symposium**. In those, there will be something that you, at least, will love and praise, you who love and praise all our things. Concerning the council and the questions <note>This refers to the "900 Theses" Pico intended to debate in Rome in 1487, a grand project to reconcile all philosophies.</note>, I think your brother has already told you why I wrote that I am working for you. This I shall do most gladly when I understand that you have been restored to your primary and desired health from that physical weakness with which you have labored until now. I pray for and wish this for you with the same spirit with which you pray for and wish for the salvation of my soul. Farewell. From **Fratta** <note>A location where Pico frequently stayed, possibly Fratta Polesine or a similar estate.</note>, the 10th of November, 1486.

->### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, Greetings.<-

**E**ven if I have sent letters to you either rarely or never, I have thought about you and your affairs either often or always. But I do not wish to "sell you hope" <note>An idiom meaning to make empty promises or give false expectations.</note>, nor will I write to you about what I might do for your benefit until I am able to write what I have actually accomplished. If it should never happen, due to either your misfortune or mine, I would prefer you believe that I have done nothing rather than that I have worked in your affairs in vain.

->### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Battista Guarino, his teacher, Greetings.<-

**W**hy do you furrow your brow? Is it because I have addressed you as "teacher" against your instructions, and thus have done you an injury? If you are not my teacher, then by right I am not bound by your instructions; if you are my teacher, then by right I call you teacher. But why do you reject the student whom you praise so much? These things conflict with each other, unless perhaps one is born of love and the other of judgment; and while you proclaim his praises out of benevolence, you fear his errors out of conscience, lest they bring shame upon you. For you might be able to praise things as a supporter that you cannot acknowledge as a teacher. But receive me, I pray, into this partnership of learning on the condition that I admit you into the partnership of our little glory, if any shall be; I alone would bear the blows. 

But why do I delay the heat of my joy with cold jests—the joy I conceived from your letter and from your so grave and honorable praise? Now at last it brings me a smile. Now my **Heptaplus** <note>Pico’s work *Heptaplus* (1489), an esoteric sevenfold commentary on the first chapters of Genesis.</note> is welcome to me, now that under your proclamation, as if under the shield of Pallas <note>The Aegis of Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, which offered divine protection.</note>, it shows itself invulnerable to rivals. You urge me toward other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain, were it not that by signing your name to my work so fully, you have planted sparks of good hope and made me far stronger for writing than I was before. Indeed, I trust so much in your judgment that I have taken up the burden of explaining the entire Old Testament <note>original: "totius instrumenti veteris," using the term "instrumentum" as a synonym for "testamentum."</note>. Though I am entirely unequal to it, I shall now bear it much more strongly than usual. 

As for books, perhaps I would satisfy you better if I had an index of those books which are in your possession, since many might serve your purpose which you nonetheless do not need. Your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly recommended to **Lorenzo de' Medici**. Never does a mention of the learned men of this age pass between us without the name of **Guarino** being much on our lips, especially when our friend **Poliziano** intervenes (and he always intervenes), who grants you as much respect as...

## **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Antonio Pizzamano, greetings.**

<margin>n</margin> Nothing in my whole life has been more pleasant to me than those letters I recently received from you, full of love, duty, and kindness. May I be so happy—and I do not deceive you—if perhaps that day was not even more pleasant on which you and Grimani <note>Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), a Venetian nobleman and later Cardinal, who was a lifelong friend of Pico and a great collector of books.</note> (I know not whether he is more yours or mine) met with me as friends and greeted me honorifically. For although, as if borrowing a mask, you presented yourselves to me not as who you were, but with a witty fiction of names <note>Pizzamano and Grimani had visited Pico in Florence incognito to see if his intellect matched his fame; Pico recognized them through their sophisticated conversation.</note>, nevertheless your sweetest wit, singular learning, amiable gravity, noble modesty, honest countenance, and most charming conversation represented the true and open Grimani and Pizzamano to me.

Therefore, even if I was deceived by the nomenclature itself, I could not be cheated of the pleasure that was due to me from your company. You were able to disguise your names, but you were not able to hide your virtue, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and knows not how to remain concealed. That so serious a treatment of physical matters, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they announce to me but yourselves?

I was congratulating myself silently while I listened to you, thinking that our age had more fruitfully brought forth not just one Grimani and one Pizzamano, as I thought, but two Grimanis and two Pizzamanos. But as soon as our friend Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous humanist poet and Pico’s closest intellectual companion, who eventually revealed the visitors' true identities.</note> indicated who you actually were, I began to congratulate not so much my age as my own judgment; for I seemed to have recognized in you every quality that I had learned existed in you by the constant testimony of everyone.

But see how your praises lead me astray and draw me away from your letter. Although your letter also calls me to the same topic even against my will, I will restrain myself, lest I seem to want to repay with mutual effort the many praises with which you have heaped upon me. Whether those praises come from a natural inclination of your heart or from your considered judgment, I do not know whether they brought me greater honor or pleasure. I owe very much, my dear Pizzamano, to that spirit of yours toward me. But I ask that you also make a trial of me if ever an opportunity arises—that is, regarding my goodwill toward you. You will find a man so loving and studious of your virtue that I will not yield the first place in loving you even to your own Grimani. Farewell. July 9, 1489.

<meta>The previous page concluded a letter to Antonio Pizzamano regarding the authenticity of Hebrew historical texts. **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Giovanni Francesco Pico, sends greetings.**

You are happy, my son, when God grants you not only that you live well, but also that while living well, you are spoken ill of <note>original: "male audias," a Latin idiom meaning to have a bad reputation or be slandered</note> by the wicked, and precisely because you live well. For it is equal praise to be praised by the praiseworthy and to be disapproved of by the wicked. But I do not call you happy for that reason—that this slander is glorious for you—but because the Lord Jesus, who is truthful, or rather Truth itself, affirms that our reward will be plentiful in heaven when men speak ill of us and speak every kind of evil against us, lying for his sake. 

If you do not know it, this is an apostolic dignity: to be considered worthy to be defamed by the ungodly for the sake of the Gospel. Thus we read in Luke <note>A reference to the Acts of the Apostles 5:41, authored by Luke the Evangelist</note> that the apostles rejoiced when leaving the presence of the council because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus. Let us therefore also rejoice, if we are worthy of such glory before God: that his glory may be revealed through our shame. And if...

<keywords>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, slander, virtue, apostolic dignity, persecution, Christian ethics</keywords>

--- Page 322 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with an encouragement for Gianfrancesco to embrace the "apostolic dignity" of being slandered for his faith. This page continues that exhortation, urging him to ignore his critics and focus on the brevity of life and the deceptive nature of worldly success.</meta>

Let them gape, let them bark, let them bay at you; you, however, continue the journey you have begun, intrepid. Consider how much you owe to God regarding their wickedness and misery. He has enlightened you while you were sitting in the shadow of death; He has moved you from the assembly of those who wander to and fro like madmen <note>original: "bacchātur," referring to the frenzied, drunken behavior of the followers of Bacchus</note> without a guide in the densest darkness, and He has joined you to the children of light. Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound in your ears always: "Let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me" <note>Matthew 8:22</note>. For they are truly dead who do not live for God; in this brief span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves.

If you were to ask these people where they are heading, or to what purpose they direct their studies, works, and cares—or finally, what end they have set for themselves in the pursuit of which they hope to be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that are contradictory and inconsistent with themselves, like the ravings of the fanatical. For they do not even know what they are doing, but like those swimming in rivers, they are carried along by the force of poorly adopted custom as if by the rush of a torrent. Blinded by their own wickedness, they rush headlong into every crime at the urging of Satan toward evil—blind leaders of the blind—until an unforeseen death seizes them and it is said to them: "Friend, this night they will demand your soul from you; but these things you have prepared, whose will they be?" <note>Luke 12:20</note>. Then they will envy those they once despised; they will praise those they once mocked. They will wish to imitate those whom they cannot, though they preferred to persecute them when they were able to follow them.

Therefore, my dearest son, block your ears with wax <note>An allusion to the Odyssey, where Odysseus (Ulysses) uses wax to protect his crew from the deadly song of the Sirens</note>. Whatever men may say or feel about you, hold it as nothing; look only to the judgment of God. He will render to each according to his works at His revelation from heaven with the angels of His power, in a flame of fire taking vengeance on those who did not know God nor obey His gospel. As the apostle says, they will pay the penalty of eternal destruction away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of His power when He comes to be glorified in His saints and to be admired by all who have believed. It is written: "Do not fear those who can kill the body, but Him who can cast the soul into Gehenna" <note>Matthew 10:28</note>. 

How much less should you fear those who can harm neither your body nor your soul! If they disparage you now for living according to reason, they will disparage you no less if you abandon virtue and are overwhelmed by vice—not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparagement always pleases them. Flee, if your salvation is dear to your heart; flee their company as much as you can. Returning to yourself, pray often in secret to the most merciful Father, crying out with the prophet: "To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust, I shall not be ashamed" <note>Psalm 25:1-2</note>, even if my enemies mock me. For indeed, all who hope in you shall not be confounded. Let those who act wickedly for no purpose be confounded. "Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths; direct me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and in you I will hope all the day long" <note>Psalm 25:4-5</note>.

Likewise, ensure that you always meditate on imminent death, and that the life we live is but a point <note>A mathematical metaphor common in Stoic and Neoplatonic thought, suggesting that a single moment in time is an infinitesimal "point" compared to the line of eternity</note>—indeed, less than a point. Consider how evil the ancient enemy is who promises us the kingdoms of the world so that he may snatch from us the kingdoms of heaven; how false are the pleasures that embrace us only to strangle us; how deceitful are the honors that lift us up only to cast us down; how lethal are the riches which poison us the more they feed us; how brief, uncertain, shadowy, false, and imaginary is everything that contains all these things together.

<keywords>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, spiritual guidance, vanity, memento mori, Satan, Psalm 25, Gianfrancesco Pico, salvation, virtue</keywords>

...even if they flow to us according to our wishes. How great are the things promised and prepared for those who, despising present things, sigh for that homeland whose king is Divinity, whose law is Charity, whose measure is Eternity. Occupy your mind with these and similar thoughts, which may awaken the sleeper, kindle the lukewarm, confirm the wavering, and offer the wings of divine love to one striving toward heaven: so that when you come to us—which we all expect with great desire—we may see you not only as the person we want, but in the state we want you to be. Farewell. And love God, whom you once began to fear. Bigus <note>Lodovico Bigi Pittorio (c. 1452–1525), a Latin poet from Ferrara and a friend of Pico.</note> greets you. Ferrara, July 2, 1482.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s Prayer of Entreaty to God.**

Nourishing God, to be revered with the highest majesty,
You truly possess one divinity in a threefold power <note>A reference to the Christian Trinity: one God in three persons.</note>.
For whom, above the flaming walls of the high world,
The blessed crowd of the angelic choir serves.
Whose almighty right hand once created this immense work,
Visible to our eyes:
You who turn the heavens, who direct the world with a nod,
From whose command the sent lightning-bolts fall:
Spare, I pray, the wretched; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of your fury drive us.
But if our debts were weighed on an equal scale,
And if the norm of your judgment were severe,
Who could bear the horrendous whip of the living 
Avenger, and endure heavy blows?
The Fabric of the world itself <note>original: "Machina," a common Renaissance term for the "world-machine" or the complex structure of the universe.</note> would not withstand your angry right hand—
The Fabric that is not destined to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned from the origin of the first fault <note>original: "primæ... culpe," referring to the doctrine of Original Sin.</note>?
Or what mind has not been made guilty by its own crime?
But surely You are that very one whose nature it is always to spare,
And who holds justice with equal mercy:
You who repay rewards far greater than merits,
And likewise punishments lighter than the evils committed.
For your mercy is greater than our faults,
And to give to those who are unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
Although they are worthy enough, if He deigns to love them—
He who makes those worthy whom He found unworthy.
Therefore, pitying, I pray: look upon your own with a peaceful countenance,
Whether you prefer to call them servants, or rather, the accused:
Accused indeed, if you look upon the crimes of our life...

<meta>This page concludes the "Prayer of Entreaty to God" by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, which began on the previous page. The poem transitions from acknowledging human frailty to a final plea for salvation and intimacy with the Divine.</meta>

...would be the work of an excessively ungrateful mind.
But if you would rather see your gifts within us—
Gifts ennobled by your most excellent blessings—
We are those whom nature once made your servants,
But whom holy grace soon made your own children.
Yet, alas, the indulgence of such a great destiny weighs upon the wretched:
Grace made us children, but guilt made us defendants.
Guilt made us defendants; but let grace conquer guilt,
So that your honor may increase through our crime.
For whether your wisdom or your power might
Otherwise be known to display its riches to the world,
A greater glory of goodness shines in our errors,
And that love, to be loved above all things, shines forth:
Which could lead the Lord down from the high heaven,
And lift the limbs of the highest God onto the cross,
So that the blood and water from your side might wash away
The filth badly contracted from our father’s seed <note>original: "patrio de ſemine," referring to Original Sin inherited from Adam.</note>.
Thus your love and piety, O most mild King,
Allows our evils to provide the material for such great goods <note>This echoes the theological concept of *O felix culpa* (O happy fault), the idea that the fall of man led to the greater good of the Incarnation and Redemption.</note>.
O love, O piety, so well-provided for our affairs!
O goodness, made a servant to your own servant!
O love, O piety, so poorly understood in our age!
O goodness, now almost conquered by our evils!
Grant, I pray, that for this so great love which always burns,
There may be an equal ardor within our own hearts.
Grant that I may cast off the dominion of Satan—whom I repent
Serving for so many years—and throw off his yoke.
Grant, I pray, that the fires of a mad mind be extinguished,
And let your love live within our breast:
So that when the spirit, having performed its duty of mortal life,
Shall be led before its Lord,
Having obtained the happy lot of the promised kingdom,
It may feel you to be not a Master, but a Father.

THE END

# Various testimonies of the life, doctrine, and writings of Giovanni Pico of Mirandola.
Collected from various places: though many from these most celebrated men, as well as others, have been omitted.

### Two letters from Brother Battista Mantuanus, a most learned and eloquent Carmelite theologian, to Giovanni Francesco Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, etc., concerning the death of Giovanni Pico, his uncle.

<margin>Illustrious Lord.</margin> Having recently heard of the death of Giovanni Pico, your most renowned and learned uncle, I was so dismayed in spirit that neither my feet nor my mind could sufficiently perform their duty. I was almost driven to complain both against God and against Nature: that they have taken such a great light from the world so quickly—such an ornament of Italy, such a glory of our age. It is as if they begrudged the earthly commonwealth of such goods and, having no regard for us, they cut him down. They cut him down, I say, while he was still growing, while he was flourishing, and while he was nourishing everyone with the most abundant fertility of his genius.

But remembering the sentiment of Paul, where he says that the judgments of God are a "great abyss" <note>original: "iudicia dei abissus multa," a reference to the Latin Vulgate's rendering of Psalm 36:6 and the themes of Romans 11:33, emphasizing that God's reasons are beyond human understanding.</note>, I restrained myself, lest through impious rashness I speak ill of God and his works...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence from Brother Battista Mantuanus to Gianfrancesco Pico. It transitions from mourning Giovanni Pico's death to a remarkable account of a dream visitation and an exhortation for Gianfrancesco to write his uncle's biography.</meta>

Illustrious Count Gianfrancesco, the very honorable delay of your response had led me to believe that my letters had perished on the road. While I was therefore determining to send you new ones—and had already begun to write them—your most longed-for, most elegant, and most delightful letters arrived. On the following night, I believe because of what I had been thinking about during the day, as I slept near dawn (the time when true dreams are usually seen), an image of your uncle, who has already departed this life, appeared to come over me. With the greatest pleasure for both of us, he discussed many things with me concerning the nature of angels, and the types, names, and duties of aerial, earthly, and even aquatic spirits. 

And when I asked him why he was stammering <note>original: "balbus," meaning a stammerer or one with a lisp. In this context, it serves as a metaphor for the inadequacy of human language to express divine truths.</note>—for he seemed to be a stammerer—he replied that it was a sign of the imperfect and incomplete speech which he had long ago begun concerning the nature of things and philosophy. I seemed to be inflamed with a desire to inquire about many occult matters which are marvelous and unknown to us mortals. Somehow, the first thing that occurred to me was whether amulets were of any use to infants, as well as coral and other things of that kind which are tied around the necks of little children. He replied that sometimes there is some power <note>original: "uirtutis"</note> in these things, and that this pertains to **natural magic** <term>Natural Magic: A branch of science in the Renaissance that sought to understand and use the hidden, inherent powers of the natural world (like the medicinal or magnetic properties of stones and plants) without involving spirits or demons.</term>. However, he said that for the most part, they are condemned customs and superstitions. Having said these things, he vanished. 

Having woken up, I thought long and hard about what we had discussed in the dream, because the words did not seem empty but appeared to carry some weight. I write this, however, not because I place any faith in dreams—for that is foreign both to my profession and my nature—but because I cannot marvel enough at how it happens that those who sleep may dispute, teach, learn, and do many things that are impossible or certainly difficult for those who are awake. Our soul certainly possesses something of the divine. If we were to live holily and piously, and if our minds were not driven around by so many winding paths of business, we would have great commerce with the departed spirits. 

But enough about these things. As for your wish, as you write, to compose a life of your uncle: I both praise this and I urge and beseech you to do it more maturely. For this duty is most fitting for you, and must be undertaken by you for many reasons. You are very strong in both style and eloquence, which is a singular gift of nature, diligence, and God. Likewise, you are his kinsman, and related by the closest blood to such a wonderful man; thus it happens that you cannot help but share in his glory. Nor should you in any way allow your most famous family to lose any of such great ornament and splendor. Added to this is the fact that his life ought to be known to no one more than to you, whom you had long ago proposed to yourself as a model to imitate—and most wisely so, for he was an outstanding exemplar of sanctity and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom appeared. 

I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the apostles: "Gather the fragments, lest they perish." <note>original: "colligite fragmenta ne pereant," a reference to John 6:12. Mantuanus uses this biblical quote to urge Gianfrancesco to collect the remaining notes, writings, and memories of Pico before they are lost to time.</note> This must be done all the more studiously because it will be of greater profit to those of us who survive and to future posterity. Undoubtedly, although I see he is more to be congratulated because, after such a short voyage, he gathered so many spiritual riches and reached port so happily, I cannot help but grieve with you over the loss of such a great man. 

The death of Giorgio Merula <note>An Italian humanist and historian (c. 1430–1494) who had a public rivalry with Poliziano.</note>—who was first a fellow student and later my teacher (for we served together under Gregorio Tiphernas)—affected me with sadness; but he was already elderly and, with old age weighing him down, was already failing and had completed his duty. But the deaths of Hermolao and Poliziano <note>Refers to Hermolao Barbaro (d. 1493) and Angelo Poliziano (d. 1494), two of the most brilliant scholars of the age, both of whom died very young, shortly before or after Pico.</note>, two...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence from Brother Battista Mantuanus to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola. After describing a mystical dream involving the deceased Giovanni Pico, the author shifts to a formal eulogy and an urgent request for Gianfrancesco to preserve his uncle's intellectual legacy by writing his biography.</meta>

The lamentable passing of such illustrious men has brought a heavy sorrow <note>original: "cordolium," a late Latin term for heart-grief or deep affliction</note> both to me and to all men of letters. But this wound has settled deeper within me: for the world of scholarship <note>original: "res litteraria," literally "the literary thing," often translated as the Republic of Letters</note> has suffered a far greater loss in our Pico. The fields of eloquence are in mourning; the studies of the mathematical arts have collapsed. All philosophy, and the highest speculations of metaphysics and theology—which he had already begun to expand and illuminate—will henceforth fall silent.

But I shall stop now, lest I indulge more than is right in my justified grief. We must instead take care to become like him, both in the study and practice of the sciences and in integrity of character and religion. Thus, enriched by the same spiritual labor <note>original: "negotiatione," referring here to the "business" of intellectual and holy work</note> as he was, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have reached. I will come to you as soon as I am able, so that I may see and venerate the immortal remains of his divine genius <note>original: "divini eius ingenii reliquas," referring specifically to Pico's unpublished manuscripts and papers</note> which are in your possession. In the meantime, devote your effort to writing his biography <note>original: "scribendæ eius uitæ," literally "the writing of his life"</note>, and continue to hold me in your affection. Farewell. I commend myself to Your Lordship. At Mantua, the 3rd day of January, 1495.

->Frater Baptista Mantuanus, Carmelite.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the end of a letter written from Milan in January 1487 to a new letter from the Venetian scholar Ermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviato. The tone remains focused on the intellectual circle surrounding Pico della Mirandola and the Florentine humanists.</meta>

...the more one admires someone and wishes to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they desire. Even when they conceive something great in their mind, words fail them, and they seem to have been able to struggle rather than to speak. Therefore, do not listen to these words of mine which I write about you and put forth publicly; rather, understand those things which I speak of you within myself, alone and in silence—which are, by Hercules, as much greater as thought is than speech. 

Greet Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> and your friend Salviati. There is no need to trouble yourself over Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist poet and scholar.</note>, because shortly (as I hear) he will be with me, and nothing more pleasant could happen to me in this entire legation <note>Barbaro was serving as the Venetian ambassador to the Sforza court in Milan.</note>. I am so happy that the library there is being built up to be larger and more ornate every day that I can hardly express it; literature owes much to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent" (1449–1492).</note>, who fosters this ancestral honor of his family with no less care than he does the republic, which he has the right of administering and establishing. Farewell. From Milan, on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>, 1487.

### Ermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviato, greetings.

You are mistaken, Salviati, if you suspect anything other than my preoccupations to be the reason why I have answered you so briefly; this is a common and much-flaunted excuse for silence. But by Hercules, it is so true that unless you accept it, you would seem to have poorly deserved my love, faith, and zeal toward you. All your letters are always most welcome to me, but especially those in which the name and mention of my Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note> appear. There is nothing in literature more wonderful than that man; there is no one whom I would rather see praised, honored, and raised to the heavens. There is no one from whose praise I can depart less easily. In this, perhaps, I am intemperate, yet I seem so to no one; there is so much praise in him and so little limit to it that there is no longer any room for ambition or flattery. 

I have read his *Apologia* <note>Pico's "Defense" of his 900 theses, which had been challenged by a papal commission.</note>; and in it, why does he attribute so much to me who deserves so little? Why does he announce me with such an honorable preface, as if I were a primary witness—not to say a Gregory? <note>Likely a reference to St. Gregory the Great, implying a level of authority Barbaro feels he does not possess.</note> Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more powerful, or more acute. However, my judgment of it is broader; I will delay it for a while until I have clearly read the whole thing through. 

As for what you wish to know regarding what I am doing, what else can I say but that I am studying? Public duty <note>original: "publica curatio," referring to his diplomatic work.</note> indeed takes something away from my application—or rather from my studies, but not from my drive. For I press on more sharply and demand a harsher task of myself; the more my public business has increased, the more greed and eagerness for study it has struck into me. Thus, all those breaks that a private man would give to his health, I distribute into my public work; what I lose for one reason, I gather back through another. 

I believe I wrote to you at another time, or told those who heard it from me, that the *Instrument* of Aristotle <note>term: <term>Instrument</term> (Latin: Organon), the collective name for Aristotle's works on logic.</note>—for that is what the Peripatetics usually call Logic—as well as the eight books of *Physics* and his three books on *Rhetoric* have long since been translated into Latin by me. My *Dioscorides* <note>Barbaro's massive commentary and translation of the ancient Greek botanist Dioscorides.</note> is now finished; the final hand is being laid to it by me now. The "daughter's dowry" is ready; it will soon be settled <note>A metaphor meaning the work is ready for the "marriage" of publication.</note>. Then, relieved of that burden, I shall devote my whole self to Aristotle. Unless God calls me elsewhere, it will come forth finished within about two years after the edition of Dioscorides, certainly the works on Logic, and with them the commentaries which I have already finished on the *Posterior Analytics*...

<meta>This page continues Ermolao Barbaro’s correspondence. It concludes a letter written from Milan regarding his editorial work on Aristotle and begins a new, highly complimentary letter to the young prodigy Giovanni Pico della Mirandola regarding his recent work, the Heptaplus.</meta>

...once these are released, I will enter into those matters both natural and divine. Likewise, I shall prepare all the volumes of that philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> with both commentaries and annotations as far as I am able. There are, indeed, in the *Problems* and in the *History of Animals*, several passages that lack clarity and light; I will pass over these quickly, providing the light of a brief annotation. Furthermore, I have decided to attempt nothing new for the rest of my life; for I must restrain my greed, or rather this lack of restraint in my mind, which wishes to be considered not only correctable and fertile, but also laborious and ambitious. I experience daily that it is more true than is usually said that "to embrace everything is to embrace nothing" <note>original: "paria esse amplecti omnia & nihil"</note>. Farewell. From Milan, October 21st, 1488.

### Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico, Greetings.

Your *Heptaplus* <note>original: "e Xameron" (Hexameron), referring to Pico's "Heptaplus," a mystical seven-fold explanation of the six days of creation</note> was brought to us three days ago by the effort of Salviati. I read it so greedily that on the very first day, and not without inspiration, I drank it all in. Three things in it wonderfully delight me: first, that your speech both teaches and moves. This is something the ancient theologians in sacred scripture, and even the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy, are known to have observed, while more recent writers sweat only at teaching. Second, that in such a great abundance of material and such freedom to "plunder" <note>meaning to borrow from earlier sources</note>, you have such chaste and innocent hands; or rather, in this kind of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no one else. This is something not shared with the ancients or the moderns, but is peculiar to you and yours alone. In this matter (I will open my mind to you), I am so affected that, because those earlier men did not say what you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. Third, I see you are initiated into the sacred rites not only of Aristotle but also of Plato and his school; you have brought full drafts from those sources into this nocturnal study. I omit how many excellent things from Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> you have touched upon briefly and elegantly, so that whatever is contained in his fifty-four volumes (divided into six "Enneads" <note>A collection of nine-book sets</note> by Porphyry <note>Plotinus' student and editor</note>), you seem not just to have read but to have mastered. Nor can I pass over how you bear yourself in the middle between the new and ancient theologians, so that you neither hate the simple majesty of the former nor are carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate one group, you are able to; you have picked the best of both kinds, which we hope you will also do in your explanation of the Davidic poem <note>The Book of Psalms</note>. Farewell. From Venice, September 4th, 1489.

### Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Greetings.

Greetings, most kind Mirandola. I indeed speak of you so willingly everywhere that I do nothing with greater pleasure; not only because nothing (as Plato says) is more pleasant to hear than the truth, but also because, as Polemo <note>An Athenian Platonic philosopher</note> says, it is much more pleasant to speak truths than to hear them. It happens with no labor, as it is written in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides <note>Three of the most famous Greek dramatists</note>, that often the unsought truth comes forth; it is often expressed even by a most unwilling man, forced by no questions but by its own power alone.
