<meta>This page continues Ermolao Barbaro’s correspondence with Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page discussed Barbaro's editorial work on Aristotle and his initial enthusiastic reaction to Pico’s "Heptaplus."</meta>

...it is that tyranny: which you, following your own purity, interpret as humanity and goodness; and by Hercules, you are already so great that he who does not praise you detracts from his own judgment and reputation. They look out for their own interest; they consult their own reasons; they redeem their own fame: those who favor and desire yours. There are many names in your journal that you do not know; they are your debtors, yet you think they are your creditors <note>Barbaro is playing with the idea of social and intellectual debt; he suggests people "praise" Pico only to increase their own standing.</note>. Many follow the advice of Prodicus <note>A Greek philosopher who taught that one should act for the sake of utility.</note>: they give so that they may receive; **hand washes hand** <note>original: "manus manū scabit"</note>, as Epicharmus sings. Certainly, the less you owe your creditors—that is, your praisers—the more they owe you: you who make them your creditors, whether they like it or not. O unheard-of kind of debt, where the creditors exist but the debtor does not!

But I am too busy to play with you any longer. But how free you are, good gods, that you allow anyone to be idle. Thus far, I pray you have borne with me in this long joke. I do not ask you to admit me [to your company]; I ask only for a **brief little yawn** <note>original: "oscitaciunculam breuem." Barbaro uses a humorous diminutive to ask for just a moment of Pico's attention.</note>. Farewell, with my Politiano <note>referring to Angelo Poliziano, the renowned scholar and friend to both men.</note>.

Rome, August 13th, 1490.

### Ermolao Barbaro, Venetian Orator and Patriarch of Aquileia, sends greetings to Giovanni Pico.

It is well; it is fitting. You who love much, congratulate me much on my appointment as Patriarch of Aquileia; you even grant me much greater things and prophesy more for me than I could either hope for, were I most greedy, or deserve, were I most modest. I know your piety toward me; I see how much you value me. I recognize the force of your love; I have found nothing more certain. If only it might happen someday that I may live with you, to philosophize about nature, about God, and about holy morals. How much I desire this, and how much I judge it would add to my prosperity if this should happen, I can neither express, nor if I could, would I wish to in this place. 

I pray, if you ever judged me worthy of your benevolence, let me be counted in the same number, and in an even better place if possible, in your esteem. Let Ermolao as a priest be more closely cherished and held dearer, just as you loved him when he was a layman of the world and now that he has been made a soldier of Christ <note>Barbaro refers to his recent elevation to the Patriarchate of Aquileia, moving from a secular political role to a high ecclesiastical one.</note>. As for me, I am as unable to stop proclaiming, admiring, and exalting you and your most brilliant virtues, as you are unable to stop increasing them. If I flatter you or lie to you, let me be an object of contempt to all learned men; a wonder and ecstasy of knowledge took hold of me long ago regarding you and your affairs. 

Now you will read these things patiently, and your heart will not be puffed up, nor will you have haughty eyes. For why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these good things you possess are not yours, nor from your own **private savings** <note><term>peculio</term>: A Roman legal term for property that a person under another's authority (like a son or slave) was allowed to manage as their own, though it technically belonged to the head of the household.</note>, but are granted and belong to the Lord. Forgive me. The **North Wind** <note>original: "aquilo"</note> of truth and the **West Wind** <note>original: "fauonius"</note> of charity have seized me and carried me away. Farewell. 

Rome, March 31, 1491.

...I have always pursued its author with reverence. But in reading it, while I desire to quench my thirst, another longing has grown: namely, the desire to see the rest. When I have obtained this through the gift of your excellence, I will consider myself to have attained a great part of happiness. 

In my judgment, your uncle Giovanni Pico has surpassed the philosophers of our entire age, especially for these reasons: that while others waste their lives only on the dogmas of Aristotle and the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (peripatos) of the Lyceum in Athens where they walked and talked.</note>, he himself, with Herculean boldness <note>original: "herculea audatia"</note>, has scrutinized the sects and schools of all philosophers, ancient and modern, with a marvelous vigor of mind. And whereas the moderns <note>original: "neotericis." This refers to the "modern" Scholastic philosophers of the universities, whom the Humanists often criticized for having a dry, unpolished writing style.</note> pursue no beauty of speech, he so joined philosophy with eloquence that he can be said to have restored the ancient and true Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the school of Plato; the author is praising Pico for making philosophy elegant and literary again, as it was in ancient Greece.</note>. 

These things are worthy of even greater admiration because he ascended to such a height of virtue and glory with swifter study and in fewer years than most. Nor does he seem to have sought knowledge, as others do, through labor, study, and many midnight vigils <note>original: "lucubrationibus," meaning work or study performed by lamplight late into the night.</note>, but to have found it all at once by chance—as happens to those who, while doing something else entirely, unexpectedly stumble upon a treasure.

Happy, therefore, is your family with such a foster-son; happy is our age, illuminated by the great splendor of this man. Farewell, most worthy prince, and remember how much you must strive to be held as a worthy imitator of your uncle. I hate these distances between us, for I desire to be with you, so that we might share in each other's studies—you in mine, and I in yours. Again, fare well, and fear God. 

At Mantua, the 29th day of October, 1494.

### From the letter of Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico.

Your genius is noble and clearly divine, Pico. While your own writings are of the highest quality, you express and shape the ideas of others—even the poorest ones—in such a way that they seem to be your own, which are the best. For I consider it a greater thing to stoop and descend than to strive for the heights. For although the latter may be more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and of greater effort. 

Therefore, whether you believe my works are such that you should spend effort imitating them, or whether you do this for the sake of earning my favor, I am deeply indebted to you in both ways. I shall return the favor someday; I will not say "when I can" (for I shall never be able), but when you yourself or your family think I can. For the kindness and humanity of your whole family is such that you are accustomed to count as a benefit that which is not. Therefore, I will have acted for my own benefit if I leave both the manner and the time of repaying the favor to you, so that in the settling of accounts, any miscalculation or deception proceeds not from me but entirely from you. 

What you wrote about the method of your studies and wished to communicate with me has brought me the greatest pleasure. I have congratulated this age on a man of such great learning that he knows almost everything, yet with such great care that he seems to know nothing at all <note>This is a classic Humanist compliment: "Socratic irony," where the most learned man acts as if he knows nothing.</note>. I see that you are an excellent poet and a most eminent orator. I perceive that you were first an Aristotelian philosopher, and now you have become a Platonic one as well. 

I see that you have not only learned, but fully mastered Greek literature—the only thing that could have been found lacking in you, and without which you would have been nothing. You did this with such ease and speed that neither you yourself remember, nor could you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek letters. This is something I say of my friend Girolamo Donato <note>Girolamo Donato (c. 1457–1511) was a Venetian diplomat and humanist, noted for his Greek scholarship.</note> with as much pleasure as truth. I would exhort you to these letters so that you might hold them as clearly and familiarly as Latin, but you do not need spurs <note>original: "non indiges calcaribus," a common idiom meaning someone is already highly motivated and does not need to be pushed.</note>, and so forth.

**F**or when I myself, in a certain corner of a letter to you, as if occupied with something else and only in passing, had attacked the "barbarian" philosophers <note>The "barbarians" refer to the medieval Scholastic philosophers, such as Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus, whose technical Latin was considered crude and "un-classical" by Renaissance Humanists.</note> of our age, and wrote that you also had become hostile toward them and had sent them a formal notice of your departure. It was finished with such great speed that, if I did not already have the most thorough knowledge of the riches of your genius, I would have believed this argument had been prepared by you long ago, so that you might bring it forth at the very first opportunity.

<meta>This page continues the letter regarding the works of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from general praise of his intellect to a specific discussion of his cosmological theories and his work, the Heptaplus. The speaker reflects on the "three worlds" described by Pico and uses the metaphor of "rumination" to describe his deep study of the text.</meta>

...observed that they rotate not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and triform motion. <note>original: "triplici triformique motu." In Renaissance cosmology, this refers to the complex nested movements of the celestial spheres.</note> Yet, who is unaware that all these things fall within our senses? The third world, however, he gave to me to be traveled in such a way that, with all senses lulled to sleep (for these hinder such inspection rather than help), it is traversed by the mind alone; for only by the mind are these great spaces wandered. I would have surely seen and perceived it clearly, but its sight—like an owl blinking at the sun's rays—could not endure such splendor. Therefore, whatever in this kind of pilgrimage—or to speak more truly, this return to the fatherland—either remained hidden from me or escaped my eyes, the indicator himself is not to blame, if he to whom it was indicated is easily found at fault. For the divine genius of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola both promises and provides that he will demonstrate everything. 

What is there then, my Robert, <note>Robert is likely a mutual friend or patron, possibly Robert Salviati, who facilitated the exchange of Pico's writings.</note> that I should not confess I owe you, having been enriched by you with such a gift? As soon as I began to taste it, such a greed was stirred in me, and such a love of feasting arose from the sweetness of the food, that, impatient of all delay, I committed nothing to be chewed by the jaws, but like a most greedy young bull, I devoured everything whole. But when I had gone through the whole matter in a continuous reading, in the manner of that same beast, calling back to the mouth what was gathered in the stomach, I chewed the cud <note>original: "ruminaffem." The author uses the "ruminant" metaphor—common in medieval and Renaissance scholarship—to describe the process of slow, meditative rereading and internalizing a text.</note> more diligently. Then indeed, a marvelous sweetness appeared; then a stupor such as never before came upon me. 

But you will say: "Were you not already an admirer of the man's learning?" I did admire how he was so practiced in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one. No place in physics, no place in mathematics escaped him in dispute; and in metaphysics indeed, and in every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred by Mercury <note>original: "a mercurio excitata." A reference to Hermes Trismegistus and the Hermetic tradition of ancient wisdom.</note> and brought to perfection by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and truest of all—these our ages, and even several previous ones, have seen nothing more learned than him. But lest you think (a vice with which many of us have struggled) that he separated eloquence from wisdom: does he not describe everything most weightily, most copiously, and moreover, most ornately? Thus, he can now be rightly joined with those ancient orators. 

Up until now, I admired these things about him so much that I thought nothing could be added to such an invention. But I began to admire his completed *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's *Heptaplus* (1489) is a mystical, seven-layered commentary on the first chapters of Genesis, attempting to reconcile creation with Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> even more than those previous things. Therefore, I would believe that it happened neither rashly nor by some chance, but by God’s command, that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For **Giovanni** <note>original: "Ioannes."</note> is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord," or "in whom is grace," or "one to whom a gift is made by God." Who would not see that he could not have attained the learning he reached without the special and greatest grace of God? In the name **Pico**, <note>A play on the Latin *picus*, meaning woodpecker.</note> however, we know there is such hardness of the beak and such strength of the head that you will find no wood, no matter how bony (so to speak) or stony, that this bird does not pierce; and it skillfully carves out a hiding place therein, where it may retreat and build its nest. In the same way, nothing from all the disciplines is so difficult for human genius to know that he himself, by hammering at its hardest parts, has not penetrated it, nested there, hatched his young, and brought them forth. And since all things in that man are to be wondered at, <note>original: "miranda."</note> who would not judge that he should be called **Mirandola**? 

For this reason, just as I congratulate you, who enjoy his constant familiarity, so I grieve for myself—for myself, I say, who consider myself unhappy in this, for whom, because of many necessary...

my occupations do not permit me to cling to him day and night, though I most ardently desire it. If indeed it were permitted, I would never depart from his side—I do not say the side of an old man, but of a youth; a youth, I say, in whom all wisdom and all senile and hoary doctrine resides. 

But you, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure, and to whom nature has granted an excellent intellect—which your long and frequent exercise in all the liberal arts has successively increased and polished—enjoy this good that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather, this immense ocean; and drink so much that it may be enough to quench not only your present thirst but all future thirst as well. 

Consider, therefore, calculate, and debate with yourself how few mortals have ever received such a great good. Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexander ille magnus." The Macedonian king was famously a pupil of Aristotle.</note> boasted that he happened upon the times of so great a philosopher as Aristotle. But to you, by your most happy lot, it has been given to live familiarly with Aristotle and Plato at the same time—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the Academics and Peripatetics <note>terms: "Academics and Peripatetics" refers to the followers of Plato and Aristotle, respectively.</note>, we see our Pauls, Johns, Dionysii, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other such lights reflecting. <note>The author lists the "lights" of the Church: St. Paul, St. John the Evangelist, Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, St. Augustine, St. Jerome, and St. Thomas Aquinas, suggesting Pico’s work harmonizes their theology with pagan philosophy.</note> 

Therefore, gather from these things how much you ought to love either yourself or him for this, best Robert: you whom fortune has favored and you who by your own prudence have succeeded in making yourself most familiar with this man. 

Farewell. November 22nd. <note>original: "x. Kalen. Decembris." In the Roman calendar, this date is ten days before the Kalends of December.</note>

## Alessandro Cortesi to his friend Pico, greetings.

In my whole life, I have received no greater pleasure than recently from your letters; and although I had believed everything highest of you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion. And you have conquered it in such a way that, even though your glory is spread far and wide, I now consider its boundaries narrow. Let us speak more openly and far from flattery, from which illustrious minds have always recoiled. 

What in you is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities that could honor anyone are gathered equally in you alone. From all men (so to speak), you alone have stolen away all the Graces. <note>original: "ueneres." Literally "the Venuses," referring to the Graces (Charites), the Greek goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity.</note> And although your ancestors reached such heights that only those born of them could easily attain, you have nevertheless emerged so great that you seem to return more grace to them than you received. 

Old age brings authority to others, but youth exalts your dignity; and what others surpass by time, you have overcome by invincible virtue. In my judgment, you are placed beyond every gamble of intellect, and I would search for Greek praises for you—which you deserve—but they cannot be seen at this time. Let all the ingenious forgive me: they are all surpassed by Pico alone. The kindness of nature has so cherished him that it must seem a wonder even to her that such a great abundance of all praises has been bestowed upon one man. 

Why do you blush? Do you think I am lying? Indeed, I will yield if you attribute it to love, which is famously painted as blind. But I have witnesses in my friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a leading humanist scholar and close associate of both Pico and the Medici family.</note>, who is deceived only regarding me. He is a most reliable witness, even if he, as I hear, daily increases his riches of gold no less than those of speech. For that reason, I congratulate him as much as I thank him; may he possess the horn of plenty <note>original: "copiæ cornu," the Cornucopia.</note>, since he is not unmindful of hospitality...

### Filippo Beroaldo to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

While staying with Mino Rossi <note>Mino Rossi was a refined Bolognese nobleman and patron of the arts</note>, who is most polished in the study of letters and the greatest ornament of our local senate, I was reading through the plays of Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC) was a Roman playwright known for his comedies</note>, which bubble over with the most sophisticated wit. It was then that your letters were brought to me—exceedingly literate, polished, and discerning. Immediately, setting aside that comic charm, I began to read your most delightful writings in haste. Good gods, how much grace, how much learning, and how much majesty we recognized in them! A great reputation had preceded Giovanni Pico, but he was found to be even greater: your writings resonate with nothing worn out, nothing trivial.

The matter fits the words, and the words fit the matter perfectly <note>original: "ad amussim," literally "by a builder's level," a technical term for perfect precision</note>; you speak in Latin and with purity. You use an eloquence that is splendid and magnificent. Your style is full of pleasantry and brilliance; you have a most abundant store of the best words. Your thoughts are frequent and well-rounded; you express the feelings of your mind so clearly and elegantly that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have given to very few: namely, to think the best things and to say the best things. And you encompass this no less in verse than in prose.

Livy and Homer write, almost by divine inspiration, that the gods have not granted all things to one man. For this reason, we often read that some have flourished by being outstanding in eloquence, while others were gifted with learning; yet very few have emerged who were both eloquent and learned at the same time. Hence the two summits of the Latin language, Terentius Varro and Marcus Cicero, are mentioned: from one, knowledge of things was sought; from the other, knowledge of words. One is called "most learned in every respect" by Terentianus; the other is called "most eloquent" by everyone. 

Virgil—as Seneca so well says—was abandoned by that happiness of talent when it came to prose; Cicero wrote poems with no beauty and no charm, for the Muses (it seems) were unwilling and resistant. But you are both most learned and most eloquent. You are powerful in prose and in verse. You write things worth reading; you are skilled in the art of writing. You can rightly be called a foster child of the Muses, for you have not, like many, drunk only one or two cups of the Muses' wine, but like a second Apuleius <note>Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 AD) was a North African scholar and prose writer, most famous for "The Golden Ass."</note> you have drained every cup—and especially that clear and nectar-like cup of philosophy, which very few touch even with the tips of their lips, and which they hardly greet from the threshold. 

Oh, great fecundity of mind! Oh, most blessed abundance of immortal talent, which has forged such great virtues in Pico della Mirandola while he is still a boy, still a youth; which has poured in so many various disciplines; which has implanted such great gifts of the soul. He who is a mere recruit <note>original: "tirũculus," a diminutive of tiro, meaning a beginner or young soldier</note> in age is a veteran in learning. Proceed, most learned man, in the direction you have begun; ensure that as the years increase, your knowledge grows, your talent matures, and your memory becomes more vigorous and supportive. You, who in your youth are the glory of our age and an example of virtue—what will you be in old age? Papinian <note>term: "Papinian" (Aemilius Papinianus) was a celebrated Roman jurist, often cited as the pinnacle of legal scholarship.</note> is called by Spartianus <note>Aelius Spartianus, one of the historians of the "Augustan History."</note> a "sanctuary of the law" and a "treasury of legal learning." You shall be called by us a "sanctuary of the liberal disciplines." To us, whenever something hidden in literature...

...you will find a treasure in your innermost parts; or rather, to speak more truly, you are already a treasure yourself.
Everything, even the most profound depths of literature, is at your fingertips; all things appear ready and waiting for you.
That circle of learning <term>orbis doctrinae: the "circle of learning," from which we derive the word "encyclopedia"</term> which is so highly praised by the learned, seems to be in your service. Both Greek
and Latin letters act as your handmaidens. It is permitted to you to invigorate your genius now with this meditation, now with that;
for the one is a seasoning <note>original: "condimentum," suggesting that different subjects "flavor" or complement one another</note> for the other. And just as various and rotated seeds restore
and refresh the soil, so too does a change of studies revive and delight the mind. You are able to gladden your genius
with the sweeter studies of poetry, whenever it grows weary from the harsher dogmas of philosophy. You, finally, stand in the citadel and at the very summit of the good disciplines, while we
toil and sweat on barely the first slope. You have climbed the narrow path of virtue with a giant's stride <note>original: "gradatoris gradu," referring to a steady, rhythmic, or great pace</note>;
we attempt to climb with the pace of a tortoise or an ant, and we labor on rugged paths,
repeatedly slipping, repeatedly nodding, and stumbling. I write what I
feel.
F. <note>likely "Filippus," the author's signature or initial</note>

<meta>This page continues the correspondence addressed to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page featured Filippo Beroaldo praising Pico's "encyclopedic" mastery; here, Battista Guarini continues this theme with a playful debate over who is truly the teacher and who is the student, followed by an excerpt from Ermolao Barbaro praising Pico’s natural and unforced literary style.</meta>

### Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.

<margin>n</margin> I do not yet concede that the case should be decided in your favor. For I can easily turn those arguments of yours back against you <note>original: "αντιστρεφοντα" (antistrephonta), a rhetorical term for an argument that can be inverted to affect the speaker</note>. If I am a teacher to you, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this title because I look down on you as a student—you, whom I assert is my own teacher. But it is because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In this learning, I am aware that you have progressed not because of my genius, nor by the mark of my pen <note>original: "transuersi calami," referring to a teacher's corrections across a page</note>, nor by little wax marks, nor finally by an obelisk <term>obeliscus: a critical mark used in manuscripts to indicate a passage is doubtful or superfluous</term> or an asterisk. Rather, we seem to have stumbled into a new kind of legal dispute while you strive to grant me that title of "possessor" which I am trying to grant to you. What orator ever had a plaintiff or a defendant in a case of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never hold out the grass to you <note>original: "herbam porrigere," an ancient Roman idiom meaning to admit defeat</note> in this fight unless we first settle it with good grace: since you will not yield otherwise, let each of us be judged as both teacher and student to the other.

But let us leave jokes aside and act seriously. Both your *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s famous work, a seven-fold mystical commentary on the first chapters of Genesis</note> and you yourself can rightly be pleased. For you have won every vote <note>original: "omnia puncta," a Roman metaphor for universal approval</note> of learned men, so that not even a hidden speck of envy appears on the voting tablet. It is to be hoped that the same success will be granted to you more easily in your remaining writings, especially when the benefit of experience is added, which is usually considered the best teacher in writing. 

As for what pertains to me, I rejoice greatly that I am spoken of by that man who is praised by everyone, everywhere: Lorenzo <note>referring to Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note>. I am especially glad to have the endorsement of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a renowned humanist scholar and close associate of Pico</note>, whose extensive and secret reading of many-sided disciplines I so embrace and admire that I never stop commending him. Because of this, I feel as though I have been granted a triumph, being placed by him beyond the reach of criticism. 

As for your request for a list of my books, that is a laborious task for me and quite useless; it will be enough if you assist my needs as time allows. For now, I desire the works of Martianus Capella <note>a late antique author of an influential encyclopedia of the liberal arts</note> and Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, provided the volumes are free of errors. For the works of the Sibyl which are here among us are in poor condition. If I can buy them in printed form, I will be more pleased; otherwise, they will return to you after a short "homecoming" <note>original: "postliminio," a legal term for the recovery of rights by a person returning from exile or captivity</note>. Farewell, my hope and the hope of the good disciplines, and continue to love me.

Ferrara, the Nones of December [December 5th], 1489.

#### From a letter of Ermolao to Giovanni Pico.

<margin>q</margin> Although I love these letters of yours because they flow and are not affected; they do not know—I will not say care—but they reject artificiality. That is, they do not accept it by design, and they shut out anyone who wishes to force it in. Thus, there are traces of diligence deep within them, but they are somehow suppressed and rejected. I am not so skillful that I can look into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fruitfulness. But I think I see—and perhaps I am not mistaken—where you are heading and where you will arrive shortly. Nothing is more noble than that natural talent of yours; nothing is more pleasing; and to put it simply, it produces nothing that is over-strained, if indeed it should be called "talent," which has already produced fruits that should not be looked down upon even by those of mature age and practiced learning. Come now, how great is your poetic spirit, as I hear! What happiness! What strength! Finally, what nobility and splendor in every act of literature!

### From a letter of Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico.

I have congratulated this age on a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing <note>The author uses a paradox here: Pico's knowledge is so vast it encompasses everything, yet he remains humble or "unaware" of his own brilliance</note>; and of such great care that he seems to know nothing at all. <margin>g</margin> I see that you are already an excellent poet and a most eminent orator, or will be very soon. I notice that you have become a philosopher—formerly an Aristotelian, and now also a Platonic one. I see that you have not only learned Greek letters—which alone could have been found wanting in you, and without which you would have achieved nothing—but you have truly "drunk them in." This you have done with such ease and speed that you yourself cannot remember, nor could you persuade others, that there was ever a time when you were ignorant of Greek. This is a claim I make about my friend Girolamo Donato no less willingly than truly. I would exhort you, and the rest.

### From a letter of Jacopo Antiquari to Angelo Poliziano.

Cease, therefore, to let the offspring of your long "incubation" <note>Antiquari refers to Poliziano’s long-developing literary works</note> waste us away in expectation. For you have now accepted Pico as a guarantor for the security of your name—Pico, whose whole life is full of glories. I hope with all my prayers to be received by him into the flock of your friends on your behalf. I always adore his footsteps. Whatever is born at home from your "flock of fattened birds" <note>original: "altilium cohorte," a metaphor for refined, well-developed literary works</note> meant for looking, reading, or learning by heart, send it out! You will hold all those captive by your strings <note>likely referring to the strings of a lyre, symbolizing poetry</note> who are said to possess some image of virtue or harmony. Farewell.

### Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.

I have burned almost always (perhaps too shamelessly) with a desire for perpetual fame, such that I considered any glory that did not survive me to be worth nothing. <margin>a</margin> But since the things I was writing scarcely promised even the longevity of my own name, you appeared, Pico, and provided what I could not. You did this by dedicating your commentary *On the One and the Being* <note>original: "de uno & ente"</note> to me (for that is the title you give it). In that work, you call back the streams running through the Lyceum <note>The school of Aristotle</note> and the Academy <note>The school of Plato</note> to a single source. And since philosophy is more a single entity than a twin, you also couple it with our theology. Why then should I now seek the grass of Glaucus <term>Glaucus's grass: in Greek mythology, the fisherman Glaucus became an immortal sea-god after eating a magical herb</term> to live forever, when I shall live eternally through you? Indeed, I shall live with you, and posterity will one day tell that there was once a Poliziano...

<meta>This page transitions from the general praise of Pico della Mirandola’s intellect to a somber report of his death and the state of his unfinished works. Marsilio Ficino, the leading figure of the Platonic Academy in Florence, writes to the French official Germain de Ganay to confirm the tragic news of Pico’s passing and that of their mutual friend, the poet Angelo Poliziano.</meta>

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to Germain de Ganay, President at Paris.

You wish to be more certain regarding the death of Pico della Mirandola, which, it seems, remains uncertain to you; surely, Germain, you wish to grieve more deeply. For while you have until now grieved heavily over this ambiguous loss, once you are made certain, I believe you will soon grieve most profoundly. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tormented by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my dearest Germain? I myself would prefer to still be in doubt. Nor can I, at this present moment, make you certain without tears.

Last November, on the very day that Charles, the great King of the Franks <note>original: "Carolus rex francorum magnus." Referring to Charles VIII, whose invasion of Italy in 1494 began a long period of conflict.</note>, entered our city of Florence, our Mirandola abandoned us. He affected the learned with almost as much grief as the King meanwhile brought joy to the city. Thus did the providential genius of the place <note>original: "genius loci." A tutelary spirit or "atmosphere" of a location.</note> balance the groans of the scholars with the joy of the people; and in place of an extinguished philosophical divinity, it lit a royal light. Lest Florence appear too dark on that day, the light of Mirandola was extinguished on earth only to be returned to heaven. For Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed, without doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his heavenly fatherland.

Furthermore, you desire to know what things Pico once composed, or what he was composing just now. He wrote the *Heptaplus* <note>original: "Exameron." A commentary on the seven days of the creation in Genesis.</note>, the *Apology*, and the treatise *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de uno & ente." Pico's attempt to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle regarding the nature of existence.</note>, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed regarding love during the heat of his youth, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be utterly destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injustice. I, for my part, knew the final will of this pious man. For in age, Pico was like a son to me; in familiarity, a brother; and in love, truly another self. 

Every day he labored toward three goals: the harmony of Aristotle with Plato; commentaries on the Sacred Scriptures; and the *Refutations of the Astrologers* <note>original: "Confutationes astrologorum." One of Pico’s most famous works, arguing against the deterministic influence of stars on human will.</note>. All these were disputed with as much eloquence as subtlety. But as much as they were brilliant in style, they were sketched out in such new and obscure characters <note>This refers to Pico's notoriously difficult handwriting and his use of idiosyncratic shorthand or "ciphers."</note> that they could scarcely be read even by him. Therefore, they have not yet been completed or revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless perhaps they possess the gift of prophecy. For if by chance they could be, we would not so much long for our Pico as if he were absent, nor would we ever suspect him to be extinct. 

But his pious nephew, Gianfrancesco <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, who became a significant philosopher and biographer in his own right.</note>, a man powerful in letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue these works from the shadows into light, and he is writing the life and deeds of his uncle. Receive, finally, this epigram of ours regarding him:

-> High priests rarely allow the more secret mysteries to be seen by eyes, but immediately hide them away; so did God show to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year. <-

Furthermore, so that the rest of the loss to literature that occurred this autumn in Florence might be known to you: our Angelo Poliziano <note>A renowned poet and classical scholar who died only two months before Pico.</note>, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, left behind seven books of *Miscellanea*, his *Sylvae*, and certain declamations and letters—all of them composed with keenness and elegance. Every day he also noted down many things necessary for elegance in the same uncertain characters as Pico, so that a heavy loss to letters has occurred in the case of both men. 

The 23rd day of March, 1494. <note>In the Florentine calendar, the year 1495 did not begin until March 25th; therefore, by modern reckoning, this letter was written in 1495.</note>

->### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to Giovanni Francesco, Count of Mirandola and Concordia.<-

I sent a short letter regarding the death and praises of Pico to France after your departure. However, one may gather his long and singular praises from many of my writings here and there over a long period: from my books of letters, especially the later ones (for twelve are now in print); from the preface to Plotinus <note>Ficino's 1492 translation and commentary on the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, which was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici and Pico.</note>; from the book *On the Sun*; and from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and the *Parmenides*. Accept this epitaph for him: 

"The high priests very rarely grant the more secret mysteries to be seen by the eyes, and they hide them away immediately. Thus did God [show] to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year." 

Let the epitaph end here. God seems to have given Giovanni Pico all the most abundant goods of mind, body, and fortune, if only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to blame Providence in this. For if God, in a very short time, had already led him above the powers of nature to the peak, perhaps he could not have progressed to anything better. For the restlessness of nature does not allow one to remain in the same state, and perfected virtue does not permit one to slip back into something worse. But you yourself have written these and other things of that kind better and more extensively in your *Life of Pico* <note>Gianfrancesco Pico wrote the standard biography of his uncle, "Vita Ioannis Pici Mirandulae," which often accompanied editions of Pico's works.</note>—not so much to illuminate him (for who would add light to the sun? <note>original: "Quis enim addiderit soli lumen?" A classical proverb used to describe a redundant action.</note>) but so that you might clear away the clouds and bring into the serene light his works, which were indeed hidden but most worthy of light. Therefore, mortals will wonderfully commend your great devotion to your uncle, and God will judge it worthy of no small rewards.

November 1, 1495.

### Twelve rules of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, partly for awakening and partly for directing men in the spiritual struggle.

**First Rule:** If the way of virtue seems hard to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world: let him remember that whatever life he chooses, even according to the world, he must suffer many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and hardships.

**Second Rule:** Let him remember that in worldly matters, the struggle is longer, more laborious, and more fruitless; in these, labor is the end of labor, and finally, eternal punishment.

**Third Rule:** Let him remember that it is foolish to believe one can reach heaven except through a struggle of this kind, just as our head, Christ, did not ascend into heaven except through the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of the master <note>A reference to Matthew 10:24, reinforcing the idea of "Imitatio Christi" (the Imitation of Christ).</note>.

**Fourth Rule:** Let him remember that this struggle should not only be borne with difficulty, but even desired, even if no reward should come to us from it, solely so that we may be conformed to Christ, our God and Lord. And as often as you resist some temptation or do violence to any of your senses <note>term: "do violence to your senses" (vim facis). In ascetical theology, this refers to mortification or self-discipline against physical desires.</note>, consider which part of the cross of Christ you are being made to conform to. For instance, when resisting gluttony you afflict your sense of taste, remember that He was given gall and vinegar to drink. When your hands—

### Twelve weapons of spiritual battle which ought to be kept ready at hand when the lust for sinning subdues the mind.

Short and small pleasure.
Companions are loathing and anxiety.
Loss of a greater good.
Life is a dream and a shadow.
Death is imminent and unforeseen.
The suspicion of impenitence <note>The terrifying possibility of dying suddenly without the opportunity to repent for one's sins.</note>.
Eternal reward: eternal punishment.
The dignity and nature of man.
The peace of a good mind.
The benefits of God.
The cross of Christ.
The testimony of martyrs and the examples of saints.

### Twelve conditions of a lover.

To love one only and to despise all things for him.
To think him unhappy who is not with the beloved.
To suffer all things to be with him, even death.
To adorn oneself to please him.
To be with him however one can: and if not in fact, at least in thought.
To love all things that belong to him: all friends: houses: clothes: images.
To desire his praises, and to be unable to suffer any of his shame.
To believe all the highest things of him, and to desire that all others believe the same.
To choose even to suffer some discomfort for him, and for that discomfort to be sweet.
To weep with him often, either from sorrow if he is absent: or from joy if he is present.
Always to languish, always to burn with desire for him.
To serve him thinking nothing of reward or payment. However, we are usually led to this especially by three causes. The first is when the service itself is desirable for its own sake: The second when he whom we serve is in himself truly good and lovable: as we are accustomed to say, we serve him for his virtues. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's spiritual guidance, moving from the general "Twelve Conditions of a Lover" into a specific meditation on the Psalms. It focuses on the psychological state of the believer—specifically how to maintain humility when one begins to grow in virtue, using Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Vulgate) as a primary guide.</meta>

...He has bestowed many benefits upon you: and these three things are in God: because for His service nothing is received anew that is not good for us, both in regard to the soul and in regard to the body; for to serve Him is nothing else than to tend toward Him—that is, toward the highest good. Likewise, He Himself is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; He possesses all the qualities that usually move us to love someone and to serve them freely. He has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, since He created us out of nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of His Son.

### PRESERVE me, O Lord.
<note>original: "CONSERVA me domine," the opening of Psalm 16:1.</note>

If any person striving for perfection wishes to examine their spiritual state, they face one particular danger: that they may become proud of their own virtue. Therefore David, speaking in the person of a righteous man about his state, begins with this word: *preserve me*. This word, when rightly considered, removes every occasion for pride; for whoever is able to acquire something by their own effort is also able to preserve it for themselves by their own power. Therefore, he who asks God to be preserved in a state of virtue shows by this request that he did not acquire that virtue by himself in the beginning. He who remembers that he obtained virtue not by his own strength, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it, but is instead humbled before God, according to that saying of the Apostle: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" <note>original: "Quid habes quod non accepisti?," quoting Saint Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> There are, therefore, two phrases that we ought always to have on our lips: one is "Have mercy on me, O God" <note>original: "miserere mei deus," from Psalm 51.</note>, used when we remember our sins; the other is "Preserve me, O God," used when we remember our virtues.

### BECAUSE I have hoped in Thee.
<note>original: "QVONIAM speraui in te," continuing Psalm 16:1.</note>

This is the one thing that allows us to obtain from God what we ask: namely, when we hope that we shall truly receive it. If we observe these two conditions—that we never ask God for anything except what is beneficial for our salvation, and that we seek what we ask for ardently with a firm hope that God may hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. When we do not obtain what we ask for, it is either because the thing is harmful to us—for we "do not know what we should pray for" <note>original: "nescimus enim quid petamus," from Romans 8:26.</note> as Christ says—and Jesus said, "Whatever you ask in my name shall be given to you." <note>original: "quicquid petieritis in nomine meo," from John 14:13.</note> This name "Jesus" signifies "Savior," and therefore nothing is truly asked in the name of Jesus unless it leads to the salvation of the person asking. Or, He does not hear us because, though we ask for good things, we do not ask *well*—that is, we ask with very little hope. For he who hopes timidly asks coldly; as James said: "But let him ask in faith, with no doubting." <note>original: "postulet autem in fide nihil haesitans," from James 1:6.</note>

### I HAVE SAID to the Lord: Thou art my God.
<note>original: "DIXI domino deus meus es tu," from Psalm 16:2.</note>

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his inner state. The entire state of a righteous person consists in this phrase: "I have said to the Lord: Thou art my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can say it truly. For a person holds as their "god" whatever they hold as their supreme good. We consider something our supreme good if, when we possess it alone, we think ourselves happy even if everything else is missing; and if it alone is missing, we think ourselves miserable even if we possess all other good things. Thus, the greedy man says to his money: "Thou art my god." For even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, so long as he has money, he is content. But if he has all those other good things we mentioned and lacks money, he considers himself unhappy.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola discusses the necessity of humility in the spiritual life, interpreting Psalm 16 to show that all virtue comes from God and must be preserved by Him. He concludes by defining a person's "god" as whatever they value as their supreme source of happiness, contrasting the righteous man's devotion to God with the greedy man's devotion to money.</summary>

<keywords>humility, pride, Psalm 16, prayer, salvation, supreme good, greed, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, spiritual warfare</keywords>

--- Page 348 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Vulgate). Having established the need for humility in the previous section, the author now explores the exclusivity of devotion to God and the nature of the "heavenly fatherland" compared to the distractions of the material world.</meta>

The glutton is a slave to his excess, the lustful to his desire, and the ambitious to power or glory; each says: "You are my god." Observe, then, how few can truly say: *I have said to the Lord, you are my God* <note>original: "Dixi domino deus meus es tu," from Psalm 16:2.</note>. For only he who finds God alone to be sufficient can say this—the man who, even if all the kingdoms of the world and all heavenly and earthly goods were offered to him, would not offend God even once to obtain them. In this saying, therefore, consists the entire state of the righteous man.

### BECAUSE you have no need of my goods.
<note>original: "QVONIAM bonorum meorum non eges," the second half of Psalm 16:2. In older translations, this emphasizes that God's happiness is not dependent on human service.</note>

He provides the reason for his proposal: namely, why he says only to the Lord, "You are my God." The reason is that God alone does not need our goods. There is no creature that does not need other creatures that are more imperfect than itself, as philosophers and theologians prove. For if those did not exist, these would not exist; since if one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed. When the whole is destroyed, all the parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one single universe; but God himself is not a part of this universe, but its principle <note>The "principle" (principium) refers to the source or starting point of all existence, which remains independent of its creation.</note>, depending on nothing. 

For God acquired nothing from the fact that He created the world, and He would lose nothing if the entire world were annihilated. Therefore, God alone has no need of our goods. We should be ashamed to hold anything as God that needs our goods, which is true of every creature. Furthermore, we ought not to hold anything as God—that is, as the highest good—except that in which the highest good resides. But in no creature is every good found. Therefore, only to the Lord should we say: "You are my God."

### TO THE SAINTS who are in his land.
<note>original: "SANCTIS qui sunt in terra eius," Psalm 16:3.</note>

After God, we ought most to love those who are most closely joined to God, such as the angels and the blessed in the fatherland <note>The "fatherland" (patria) is a common theological term for Heaven, our true home.</note>. Therefore, after he said to the Lord, "You are my God," he adds that God...

### HAS MADE HIS WILLS wonderful.
<note>original: "MIRIFICAVIT uoluntates suas," Psalm 16:3.</note>

This means He has made His loves and His desires wonderful toward the saints who are in His land—that is, in the heavenly fatherland, which is called the land of God and the land of the living. Truly, if we consider how great the happiness of that fatherland is, how great the misery of this world is, and how great the goodness and charity of those citizens are, we will always desire to depart from here so that we may dwell there. 

However, when we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not unfruitful. Instead, we should always acquire some virtue from every meditation. From this meditation on the goodness of that higher fatherland, we ought to acquire the virtue of not only bearing death bravely and patiently when our hour comes (or if it must be undergone for the faith of Christ), but even desiring it of our own accord—longing, that is, to depart from this valley of miseries <note>original: "ualle miseriarum," similar to the "valley of tears" in the Salve Regina.</note> so that we may reign with God and His saints in that happy fatherland. Therefore, when the righteous man has described his state—that his whole affection is toward God and that he looks down upon earthly things—he then looks from on high at the state of evil men and says:

### THEIR INFIRMITITIES are multiplied.
<note>original: "MVLTIPLICATAE sunt infirmitates eorum," Psalm 16:4.</note>

By "infirmities," he understands idols; and the Hebrew text <note>The author refers to the Hebrew word *atzbotam*, which can be translated as "sorrows" or "idols." Humanist scholars often checked the original Hebrew to clarify the Latin Vulgate.</note> holds this as well. For just as the good man has one God whom he worships, so the wicked have many gods and idols; for they have many pleasures, many vain desires, and various passions which they serve. Therefore, they seek many pleasures...

<summary>This page explains that God is the only true "good" because He is entirely self-sufficient, whereas all other beings are interdependent. It encourages the reader to focus on the "heavenly fatherland" and identifies worldly passions and idols as the "infirmities" that distract the wicked.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 16, self-sufficiency of God, heavenly fatherland, idols, meditation, virtue, death, Hebrew text, philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Psalm 16 (Vulgate 15). The previous section concluded by emphasizing that God is independent of human goods. This page explores the contrast between the restless wandering of those who follow vice and the firm resolution of the righteous to find their entire inheritance in God alone.</meta>

...because they find nothing to bring them peace, and therefore "they wander in the circle of the wicked" <note>original: "in circuitu impii ambulant," a reference to Psalm 12:8 (Vulgate 11:9). The OCR "imperii" is likely a transcription of "impii."</note>. He adds afterwards that they cried out, because they rush headlong and thoughtlessly after their own desires. From this we are taught that we should run toward virtue no less swiftly than they run toward vice, nor should we serve our Lord less diligently than they serve their lord, the devil. The righteous man, however, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves—as we always ought to do—that he in no way wishes to follow them; and he says:

**I WILL NOT gather their assemblies of blood, nor will I be mindful of their names.**
<note>Psalm 16:4 (Vulgate 15:4).</note>

He speaks of "blood" [in the plural] partly because idolaters used to perform their ceremonies around the gathered blood of victims, and partly because the entire life of the wicked, having abandoned reason, follows the sensuality that is situated in the blood <note>In medieval thought, "blood" often represented the physical passions and animal nature of man as opposed to his rational soul.</note>. Moreover, he says that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols, but will not even name them. This is said and done to show that a perfect man must abstain not only from illicit pleasures, but even from lawful ones, so that he may be more fully carried toward heaven and devote himself more purely to the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it to be folly to deprive oneself of all pleasure, he adds:

**THE LORD is the portion of my inheritance.**
<note>Psalm 16:5 (Vulgate 15:5).</note>

As if to say: "Do not wonder if I leave all other things behind to possess God, in whom all other good things are ultimately possessed." This ought to be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." For we Christians, to whom God Himself is promised as an inheritance, ought to be ashamed to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem like presumption to some to dare to promise such things to themselves, he adds:

**YOU ARE He who restores my inheritance to me.**

As if to say: "Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to You, I cannot by my own strength ascend to possess You. But You are the one who draws me to You through Your grace, and You are the one who will give Your very self to me to be possessed." Let the righteous man then consider how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance; he adds:

**THE MEASURING LINES have fallen for me in excellent places.**
<note>original: "FVNES," literally "ropes" or "cords" used in ancient times to measure out and divide plots of land.</note>

For in ancient times, portions and lots were divided by measuring lines. And because there are many who, although they are called to this happiness—as all Christians are—nevertheless make nothing of it, often exchanging it for some trivial pleasure, he therefore adds:

**MY INHERITANCE is excellent to me.**

As if to say: "Just as it is excellent in itself, so I consider it excellent; and all other things in respect to it—as Paul used to say—I consider as dung" <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in Philippians 3:8.</note>. Furthermore, because having this light of understanding—so that a man may recognize the happiness given to him—is a gift of God, he therefore adds:

**I WILL BLESS the Lord, who has given me understanding.**

Since, however, a man often judges according to reason that he should serve God, but sensuality and the flesh rebel, a man is only perfect when not just his soul, but also his flesh is directed toward God, according to that saying: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God" <note>Psalm 84:2 (Vulgate 83:3).</note>; therefore he adds:

<summary>This page provides a moral and mystical commentary on Psalm 16, explaining that the righteous soul rejects the sensory "blood" of the wicked to find a complete and superior inheritance in God. It emphasizes that such devotion is not a human achievement but a gift of divine grace and spiritual understanding.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 16, inheritance, grace, sensuality vs reason, measuring lines, idolatry, Saint Paul, spiritual understanding</keywords>

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Psalm 16 (Vulgate 15), moving from the righteous man’s rejection of worldly passions to his inner transformation and the ultimate hope of resurrection. The previous section established that the speaker finds his entire inheritance in God; this section explores the internal "rebuking" of the conscience and the promise of eternal life.</meta>

**AND EVEN until night my <term>reins</term> <note>original: "renes." In medieval physiology and biblical language, the "reins" or kidneys were considered the seat of the emotions, desires, and the most secret parts of a person's character.</note> have rebuked me.**

That is, the reins themselves—in which there is usually the greatest inclination toward lust—not only do not incline me toward evil, but rather they rebuke me: that is, they draw me back even until night. This means to such an extent that they even spontaneously afflict their own body. For affliction is often signified by "night." He shows then what is the root of such privation <note>The "privation" or removal of sinful desires mentioned in the previous paragraph.</note>, and says:

**I HAVE SET God always in my sight.**

For if someone were to always have God before their eyes as a rule for all their actions, and in all their actions sought neither their own advantage, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God, they would shortly become perfect. And because one who acts in this way always prospers in all things, therefore he says:

**HE IS at my right hand, that I be not moved.**

He shows then how great the happiness of the righteous man is: namely, that he will be happy forever in both soul and body; therefore he adds because of these things:

**MY HEART is glad.**

That is, my soul is glad, knowing that after death heaven is prepared for it.

**AND MY FLESH shall rest in hope.**

That is, although the flesh itself does not rejoice as if it were to receive its state immediately after death, it nevertheless rests in the grave with this hope: that it will rise on the day of judgment with its soul, immortal and most glorious. And he declares all of this in the following verse; for because he had said the soul rejoiced, he adds the reason:

**FOR YOU will not leave my soul in <term>hell</term> <note>original: "inferno." In this context, it refers to the Hebrew "Sheol," the abode of the dead, rather than the place of punishment.</note>.**

And because he had said that the flesh rested in hope, he adds the reason, saying:

**NOR WILL YOU give your holy one to see corruption.**

Because that which was corruptible shall rise incorruptible; and because Christ was the first who entered paradise and opened life to us, and was the first who rose, and his resurrection is the cause of our resurrection; therefore, these things we have said about the resurrection are understood principally of Christ—as Peter the Apostle declared <note>A reference to Peter's sermon in Acts 2:25-31, where he cites this Psalm to prove Christ’s resurrection.</note>—and secondarily they can be understood of us insofar as we are members of Christ. He alone did not see corruption, because his body was not decayed in the tomb. Since, therefore, the way of living well leads us to the perpetual life of soul and body, he adds:

**YOU HAVE made known to me the ways of life.**

And because the entire happiness of this life consists in the clear vision and enjoyment of God, he adds:

**YOU WILL fill me with joy with your countenance.**

And because happiness will endure for eternity, he adds:

**DELIGHTS at your right hand even unto the end.**

He says, moreover, "at your right hand," because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, according to that saying of John: "This is the whole reward, that we may see God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ" <note>original: "Hæc ē tota merces ut uideamus deū & quē miſiſti ieſum xp̄m." A paraphrased reference to John 17:3.</note>.

The End

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on Psalm 16, interpreting it as a prophecy of the resurrection of Christ and, through him, the resurrection and eternal joy of all the faithful. It emphasizes that a life focused on God transforms even the internal passions into a source of discipline and hope.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of humanist correspondences. The previous page introduced Angelo Poliziano’s defense of his work to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. This page features a letter likely from the Neapolitan humanist Juniano Maio to a colleague named Robert, praising the intellectual synthesis of a young prodigy—undoubtedly Pico della Mirandola—and expressing a desire for scholarly friendship.</meta>

For as soon as that most profound work—so hidden and removed from the knowledge of many—reached my hands, I began to read it with great diligence. It brought me not only pleasure and admiration, but it even raised my contemplating mind to such a height of sublimity that I have never seen or heard anything more wonderful or more clearly explained. Indeed, his genius stands above the sharpest minds of others; he is skilled in an incredible investigation of the sciences, and already possesses a knowledge of all things beyond what is believable. Especially at this age, having just barely passed through the threshold of youth, he has attained such a knowledge of things as has not been permitted even to the most learned and those advanced in years to reach. 

Wherefore, I shall never fear to name him the sacred dwelling-place of all good arts and sciences, and the <term>miracle of our age</term> <note>original: "nostri saeculi miraculum." This was a frequent epithet for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who famously attempted to defend 900 theses in Rome at the age of 23.</note>. This is especially true when I read more accurately the hidden meanings of the work—conceived by only a few men—the progressions of nature, the revealed hiding places of God, and finally the secret riches of the Highest Creator now brought into the open. I do not know if I have ever heard anything more admirable, nor do I know if I have read anything more profound. 

A peace has now been entered into between the philosophers and Moses <note>The "Peace between the Philosophers and Moses" refers to the Renaissance project of *syncretism*, attempting to prove that ancient Greek philosophy (like Plato and Aristotle) was fundamentally in harmony with Biblical revelation.</note>, who previously wove the creation of the world by different paths; certain joined covenants of nature and God are now understood without controversy. But I reserve repeating this more deeply and explaining it more wordily for another time. 

I come now to you, my dear Robert <note>Likely Roberto Salviati, a Florentine patron and friend to the circle of Poliziano and Pico.</note>, a truly excellent man, whom I love uniquely because of your writings. Though they be few, they nevertheless show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise no less a harvest of genius to come than the pleasant hope of blossoms they now offer. So therefore, know your Junianus <note>Juniano Maio (c. 1430–1493), a humanist scholar from Naples known for his work on grammar and his proximity to the Aragonese court.</note>—and if you give me any of your writings hereafter—know him to be no less a herald of your affairs than a lover of you for that very reason. 

Victorius <note>A mutual acquaintance, possibly an earlier scholar of the same name or a member of the Salviati/Medici circle.</note> thus proclaims the excellence of your genius and your learned humanity in these letters, so that I am provoked to desire and proclaim the same things. One thing, however, I ask: that you do not cease to pursue with your kindness—which you have shown and will embrace—the one whom Victorius invited to love with flattering encouragements. Whereby you will rouse my laziness, so that I may write to you more often, provided you do not despise our efforts. And if, based on the words of our Victorius, you do not reject my friendship, you will summon me by a bond of necessity to pursue you with every duty. For there is nothing I would prefer more than to contend with noble and learned men in mutual love and the exchange of letters.

### Also from chapter 94 of the same work.
At one time, I and this Pico della Mirandola—a man who can never be praised enough—ran through the ancient commentators of the <term>old sacred instrument</term> <note>original: "instrumenti sacri veteris." This was a humanist term for the Old Testament, viewing the Bible as a legal or musical instrument of divine will.</note> in our leisure hours, especially the Greeks: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severianus, and many others of that kind. He, just as he does with all the opinions of the Latin writers, most diligently compared them with the opinions of the Jewish and <term>Chaldean</term> <note>original: "chaldeorum." In this context, it refers to Aramaic or Syriac translators and the mystical traditions of the Near East.</note> interpreters, sifting and weighing everything. From this, truth might be drawn out, or obscurity removed, or faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

### From the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* by Johannes, Abbot of Sponheim.
Giovanni Pico, Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola, and Lord of Concordia: a man most studious of all good literature, and just as he is most noble by his illustrious blood, so too is he most noble by his truly divine genius. Surrounded by a great crowd of all kinds of arts, worthy and most deserving, whose perfection the Muses follow: he is the most learned philosopher of our age and a most sharp debater. He wrote several things in a most elegant style, which our age will have cause both to approve and especially to admire. By these works, he has rendered an eternal and worthy memory to his name and glory.

### From the *Compendium of Revelations* of the most learned and holy man, Brother Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers.
Count Giovanni of Mirandola, a man singular in our times for his genius and manifold learning.

### From the second commentary on Propertius by the most learned and eloquent man, Filippo Beroaldo of Bologna: on that verse, *not so many Achaemenians* and so forth.
I read the word *Susa* written instead of *Etruscan* in the manuscript of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He is a man worthy of the memory of ages, gifted in manifold disciplines, who adorns the glory of our age. To him can be applied what Terentianus wrote of Varro: "Pico, a most learned man from every side." He not only esteems you, Memmius—as one most learned would a learned man, and one most noble a noble man—but loves you vehemently. He speaks honorably of you and thinks most highly of you. After his more serious studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of <term>Propertius</term> <note>Sextus Propertius was a Roman elegiac poet. The humanists often turned to classical poetry as a form of intellectual relaxation.</note> as if in a most pleasant inn. He agreed with me in reading the passage this way and showed me that in his own manuscript, *Susa* was written, not *Etruscan,* and so forth.

<note>The front cover of this historical volume showcases a traditional "half-binding" technique. The outer portion is constructed from plain wooden boards, revealing a natural grain and the surface wear expected of an aged manuscript. The inner portion, which wraps around the spine, is made of dark reddish-brown leather. A decorative embossed border has been pressed into the leather where it meets the wood, providing an ornamental transition. No titles or text are visible on the exterior, a common feature for manuscripts of this era which were often identified by their placement on a shelf or by internal titles.</note>
